Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Engineering A comprehensive review: surface modification strategies to enhance corrosion resistance of zirconia-based biomaterials in implant applications Gopi Srinivasan1, Anushiya Manickam1, Sivasakthi Sivakumar1, Jeevadharani Murugan1, Shinyjoy Elangomannan2 and Surendiran Mohan1* Abstract In contemporary dental practice, there is a significant demand for materials that not only exhibit superior mechanical strength and durability but also offer excellent biocompatibility and aesthetic appeal. Zirconia (ZrO2) has emerged as a leading biomaterial addressing these needs, owing to its exceptional properties such as high fracture toughness, resistance to corrosion and wear, and tooth-like translucency. These characteristics make zirconia ideal for various dental prosthetics, including crowns, bridges, and abutments. Advancements in zirconia composites, particularly yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) and zirconia-toughened alumina, have further enhanced its mechanical properties and stability. YSZ, for instance, is widely utilized in dental ceramics due to its increased strength and fracture tough- ness. To optimize zirconia’s performance, especially in terms of corrosion resistance and osseointegration, various surface modification techniques have been developed. These techniques encompass acid etching, coating, polishing, biofunctionalization, sandblasting, ultraviolet light exposure, and laser treatments. These modifications significantly improve bone integration by altering surface texture, structure, wettability, chemical resilience, and antibacterial characteristics. In summary, zirconia’s combination of mechanical strength, biocompatibility, and aesthetic appeal, along with ongoing advancements in composite formulations and surface treatments, solidify its role as a leading biomaterial in implant applications. Keywords Zirconia (ZrO2), Surface functionalization, Bio-ceramic materials, Osseointegration, Aesthetic properties, Bioactive properties, Clinical performance, Bio-medical implants Introduction Ceramics, originating from the Greek term “keramos,” which means pottery or fired material, include sub - stances such as glass, advanced ceramics, and cement- based materials. These inorganic, non-metallic solids are produced through heat treatment and cooling, forming covalent, ionic, or occasionally metallic bonds. Among these, zirconium dioxide (ZrO2), or zirconia, is particu - larly significant in medical devices due to its superior properties (Bauer et al. 2013). Zirconium (Zr), a transi - tion metal with the atomic number 40, is renowned for its exceptional mechanical, thermal, and corrosion-resistant *Correspondence: Surendiran Mohan sschemsurender@gmail.com 1 Department of Chemistry, School of Arts and Science, Vinayaka Mission’s Chennai Campus, Vinayaka, Mission’s Research Foundation, Paiyanoor, Chennai 603 104, India 2 Department of Chemistry, Vinayaka Mission’s Kirupananda Variyar Arts and Science, Vinayaka Mission’s Research Foundation, Salem, Tamil Nadu, India Page 2 of 25Srinivasan et al. J Mater. Sci: Mater Eng. (2025) 20:76 properties, making it highly suitable for various indus - trial and biomedical applications. Its most abundant iso - tope, 90Zr, constitutes over half of naturally occurring zirconium. Zr is typically found in nature in the form of zirconia (ZrO₂), primarily in the mineral baddeleyite. However, natural zirconia contains impurities, includ - ing radioactive and elemental elements, which must be removed through complex processes to obtain pure zirconia powder for biomedical use (Piconi et al. 1999; Deville et al. 2006; Kuboki et al. 1999). In dentistry, tita - nium and its alloys have traditionally been the materi - als of choice for implants due to their biocompatibility, mechanical strength, and clinical success (Depprich et al. 2008b, a; Steinemann et al. 1998; Heydecke et al. 1999). However, titanium’s drawbacks, including its unaesthetic grayish color (Tschernitschek et al. 2005) susceptibil - ity to galvanic reactions with saliva and fluoride (Sterner et al. 2004) and potential inflammatory effects caused by titanium particles (Akagawa et al. 1993), have driven the search for alternatives. Zirconia has emerged as a promising alternative, offering excellent osseointegration (Scarano et al. 2003; Kohal et al. 2004), superior biocom - patibility (Steinemann et al. 1998), and aesthetic advan - tages due to its tooth-like color (Jackson et al. 1999). Additionally, zirconia is radiopaque and resists bacterial colonization more effectively than titanium (Ahmad et al. 1998; Pekkan et al. 2011; Rimodini et al. 2002; Gahlert et al. 2018). Unlike titanium, zirconia does not produce corrosion byproducts at the implant site (Sterner et al. 2004). These exceptional properties underscore zirconia’s potential as an outstanding material for dental implants. Its dense oxide layer provides long-term corrosion resist - ance, even in highly acidic environments (Qi et al. 2022). In addition, zirconia’s excellent wear resistance and mini- mal metal ion release help to mitigate the risks of inflam - mation and toxicity. This review emphasizes that while zirconia offers superior corrosion resistance—especially against pitting and crevice corrosion (Muller-Heupt et al. 2022)—its clinical limitations lie in brittleness, lower elastic modulus, and suboptimal osseointegration. To overcome these drawbacks, recent advances focus on material reinforcement (e.g., YSZ composites), surface modification (e.g., coatings, laser treatments, bioac - tive functionalization), and implant design innovations. These strategies aim to address zirconia’s mechanical and biological limitations, ensuring improved performance and broader applicability in dental implantology. Zirconia exists in three distinct crystalline forms Zirconia exists in three distinct phases: monoclinic (sta - ble at room temperature), tetragonal (stable above 1170 °C), and cubic (stable above 2370 °C) (Fig. 1). These phases vary in their coordination numbers, with the monoclinic phase being thermodynamically stable at lower temperatures due to the strong covalent Zr–O bonds. However, doping with oxides such as MgO, Y2O3, CaO, and Ce2O3 can stabilize the tetragonal or cubic phases even at room temperature, improving both the mechanical properties and phase stability of the mate - rial. The tetragonal phase, in particular, is prized for its Fig. 1 A schematic illustration of the space groups for three distinct polymorphs of ZrO2, along with their respective mechanical properties, adapted from reference Hannink et al. (2000) with permission Page 3 of 25 Srinivasan et al. J Mater. Sci: Mater Eng. (2025) 20:76 enhanced stability and defect-induced activity. Moreover, it exhibits superior performance in catalytic applications (Kelly et al. 2008). Categorization of biomedical zirconia Magnesium partially stabilized zirconia (Mg-PSZ), yttrium-stabilized tetragonal zirconia polycrystals (3Y- TZP), and other materials like hydroxyapatite (HAP) and silicon carbide (SiC) are notable in biomedical applica - tions. Mg-PSZ, a bi-phasic material comprising cubic grains and tetragonal precipitates with approximately 8 mol% MgO, has limited application in biomedicine due to its inadequate phase stability, high porosity, and subopti - mal mechanical properties (Hannink et al. 2000; Pezzotti et al. 2014). On the other hand, 3Y-TZP , a monophasic zirconia variant stabilized with 2–3 mol% Y2O3, demon- strates excellent strength and fracture toughness, making it highly suitable for therapeutic and dental uses (Han - nink et al. 2000). Zirconia-toughened alumina (ZTA), a composite containing 5–30% zirconia within an alumina matrix, combines improved mechanical strength, wear resistance, fracture toughness, and resistance to aging degradation by optimizing the size and distribution of particles, without requiring additional dopants (Dongxu Tang et al. 2012) (Table 1). Ceramic implants Zirconia in dental implant applications The introduction of the first ceramic dental implant dates back to 1974 with the development of the Tübin - gen implant, which was crafted from alumina (Al2O3) to overcome the limitations of metal implants Umar DM et al. (2024). Despite its biocompatibility and resistance to plaque, alumina implants were discontinued due to frequent fractures and low survival rates (Han J et al. 2017). Zirconia, with superior mechanical properties compared to alumina, marked a significant advancement in ceramic implants (Andreiotelli et al. 2009a, b) with the development of the Z-system® by Volz (Han J et al. 2017; Carinci et al. 2004). This innovation led to the applica - tion of zirconia ceramics in dental implantology (Fig. 2). Zirconia implants, introduced as a metal-free alternative, excel in aesthetics due to their white color, making them ideal for patients with thin gingiva or hypersensitivity to titanium. They show excellent biocompatibility, minimal immune reaction, and strong integration with both bone and soft tissues. Surface treatments such as acid etch - ing, UV irradiation, and plasma treatments enhance their bioactivity and promote osteoblast attachment and osse - ointegration. One-piece zirconia implants reduce risks of bacterial colonization and peri-implantitis compared to two-piece designs, though their fabrication poses techni - cal challenges due to ceramic brittleness. While survival rates for zirconia implants (74–98% after 12–56 months) are promising, they remain slightly lower than titanium implants (97–100% over 3–10.4 years), with issues like early failure, fractures, and bone loss requiring further improvements (Oliva et al. 2010; Depprich et al. 2008b, a; Akagawa et al. 1998). The corrosion resistance of zirconia in medical implants is a critical factor influencing their performance and longevity. Zirconia, particularly in its stabilized forms, exhibits excellent corrosion resistance due to the formation of a protective oxide layer, which enhances its biocompatibility and suitability for various biomedical applications (Carinci et al. 2004). This over - view will delve into the corrosion behavior, advantages, and implications of zirconia in medical implants. Zirconia bio-ceramics have been utilized in various biomedical applications, including orthopedic implants, thin films and coatings for metallic implants, porous bone scaffolds, substitute materials, and bone cements (Stadlinger et al. 2010). Despite extensive research, the impact of surface modi - fications on the biological response and mechanical sta - bility of zirconia implants remained underexplored until recent advancements. Current efforts focus on optimiz - ing zirconia surfaces to enhance their integration with bone tissue while improving mechanical and biologi - cal performance. Stadlinger et al. (2010) compared the bone-implant contact (BIC) and peri-implant bone vol - ume density (rBVD) of one-piece zirconia and titanium implants in minipigs’ mandibles. Zirconia implants were tested in submerged and non-submerged conditions, while titanium implants were all submerged. The results showed the following: BIC, submerged zirconia = 53%, submerged titanium = 53%, non-submerged zirconia = 48%; rBVD, submerged zirconia = 80%, submerged titanium = 74%, non-submerged zirconia = 63%. Zirco - nia implants exhibited comparable or superior results, particularly in rBVD (Gomes et al. 2011). Att et al. (2009) investigated the effect of UV treatment on zirconia (Y-PSZ) implants, finding enhanced osteoblast attach - ment, proliferation, and mineralization. UV treatment made the zirconia surface hydrophilic and reduced sur - face carbon, improving bioactivity. Han et al. (2011) later studied alumina-sandblasted yttrium-stabilized tetrago - nal zirconia polycrystals (Y-TZP) and found increased osteoblast differentiation and proliferation when com - bined with bone morphogenetic protein-2 (BMP-2). Lee et al. (2013) also observed improved osseointegration and early bone formation around alumina-sandblasted Y-TZP implants with recombinant human BMP (rhBMP- 2) gel. However, a recent study by Kohal et al. (2013) showed that sandblasted and acid-etched zirconia (TZP) implants exhibited slower cell proliferation and osseoin - tegration compared to titanium implants, though they were still accepted by osteoblastic cells and supported osseointegration in rat bone tissue after 28 days. Zirconia ceramic coatings and thin films for enhanced performance in orthopedic implants Liu et al. (2006) utilized a filtered cathodic arc system with oxygen plasma to deposit zirconia thin films, pro - ducing stoichiometric zirconia nanoparticles that pro - moted bone-like apatite formation in simulated body fluid (SBF) due to their nanoscale surface features. These films demonstrated remarkable bioactivity and cytocom - patibility, as evidenced by the growth and proliferation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem (BMMS) cells. Sol - lazzo et al. (2008b, a) highlighted the potential of these zirconia coatings for enhancing the biocompatibility and osseointegration of metallic implants. Subsequent research confirmed that zirconia coatings improve the osseointegration properties of implants. Han et al. (2009) synthesized monoclinic zirconia thin films via micro-arc oxidation and exposed them to UV light, leading to the formation of hydrophilic groups on the surface, which enhanced bioactivity, as shown by increased apatite for - mation following UV treatment. G. Wang et al. (2010a , b) explored osteoblast behavior on nanostructured mon - oclinic zirconia coatings produced by plasma spraying. Their study demonstrated excellent in vitro bioactivity, with bone-like apatite formation on the coating surface Fig. 2 Structural distinctions between one-piece and two-piece zirconia implants. a The first two components on the left represent zirconia abutments and implant bodies, which can be bonded to form a two-piece zirconia implant system. b The two components on the right showcase different configurations of one-piece zirconia implants, adapted from reference Yuriy May et al. (2025) with permission Page 5 of 25 Srinivasan et al. J Mater. Sci: Mater Eng. (2025) 20:76 after 6 days in SBF. Cellular differentiation tests showed successful attachment, adhesion, and proliferation of MG63 osteoblast-like cells. Furthermore, zirconia was combined with bioactive hydroxyapatite (HAp) to create ZrO₂/HAp composite coatings for orthopedic implants, offering enhanced mechanical properties and biocom - patibility compared to pure ZrO2 or Hap. J. Wang et al. (2010a, b) further developed nanocomposite coatings on titanium through electrodeposition, incorporating fluori- nated HAp and zirconia. These coatings exhibited strong bonding, low dissolution rates, and improved in vitro bioactivity. Zirconia ceramic scaffolds and bone regeneration solutions: advancements in bone grafts and cements Porous bone scaffolds play a critical role in bone tissue engineering, serving to fill defects and promote regen - eration. Extensive research has been conducted on bio - degradable polymers, ceramics, and polymer-ceramic nanocomposites with porous structures for these appli - cations (Hutmacher et al. 2000; S. Yang et al. 2021). Zir - conia, with its exceptional biomechanical properties, has emerged as a promising material for bone substi - tutes (S. Yang et al. 2002). Chen et al. (2006) developed zirconia-based porous scaffolds using replication and electrospray techniques, yielding scaffolds with supe - rior mechanical strength and greater stiffness than those made using traditional slurry dip coating methods. This improvement was attributed to the reduction in micro - cracks and micropores, which enhanced the mechani - cal reliability of the zirconia scaffolds. When reinforced with nanocrystalline calcium phosphate (CaP) powders such as hydroxyapatite (HAp) and tricalcium phosphate (TCP), zirconia displays outstanding mechanical proper - ties, including high bending and compressive strengths, stiffness, microhardness, and fracture toughness. HAp coatings and reinforcements also improve the biologi - cal activity and osseointegration of zirconia ceramics. As a result, significant attention has been given to the syn - thesis, characterization, sintering, and phase stability of zirconia-HAp composite scaffolds for bone regeneration. It has been noted that bone ingrowth is more prominent in microporous HAp scaffolds than in zirconia scaffolds with similar porosity. However, the mechanical tough - ness of zirconia complements HAp and TCP ceramics, providing additional strength. For example, Matsumoto et al. (2011) achieved impressive results with micropo - rous zirconia/HAp composite scaffolds in a 70/30 ratio, demonstrating strength comparable to cortical bone, high protein adsorption, and tissue affinity shown in Fig. 3. Further studies by the same team revealed that the compressive strength of zirconia/HAp scaffolds, with porosity ranging from 72 to 91%, increased from 2.5 to 13.8 MPa by adjusting the zirconia content from 50% to 100 wt.%. Later developed porous scaffolds made from tetragonal zirconia, biphasic calcium phosphate, and poly(caprolactone) multilayers via extrusion. These scaf - folds exhibited excellent cell viability, attachment, high porosity (78%), and compressive strength (12.7 MPa) (Mondal et al. 2013). Kotha et al. (2009) investigated the reinforcement of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) bone cement by incorporating high-strength zirconia fibers, both with and without an acrylic coating. The zirconia fibers, approximately 200 µm in length and with diam - eters of either 15 or 30 µm, were encapsulated in PMMA through a novel emulsion polymerization process. The study found that adding zirconia fibers enhanced the tensile and compressive properties, as well as the frac - ture toughness, of the bone cement. Specifically, frac - ture toughness increased by 23% with 15-µm fibers and by 41% with 30-µm fibers, while acrylic coating did not significantly improve the material properties. Based on these results, the study recommends using uncoated or acrylic-coated 30-µm zirconia fibers to significantly enhance the strength and fracture toughness of bone cements. Additionally, Pattnaik et al. (2011) developed a mul - ticomponent porous scaffold made from chitosan, nanoscale silica, and zirconia. These scaffolds demon - strated improved protein adsorption, biomineralization, and controlled biodegradation properties, and were non- toxic to rat osteoprogenitor cells, indicating their poten - tial for bone tissue engineering applications. In another study, Gillani, Qiao, and Webster investigated the effect of incorporating zirconium dioxide (ZrO2) nanoparti - cles into PMMA bone cement. The study showed that osteoblast adhesion was significantly higher on bone cements containing unfunctionalized nano-ZrO 2 com - pared to unmodified cements after 4 h. Furthermore, osteoblast proliferation was also significantly greater on ZrO2-containing bone cements after 24 h, suggest - ing that the addition of ZrO2 nanoparticles improves the bioactivity of bone cement, promoting better osteoblast adhesion and proliferation (Gillani et al. 2009). Lee et al. (2009) assessed the osseointegration of nano-technology- modified, micro-structured zirconia implant surfaces in rabbit femoral condyles. The study compared calcium phosphate (CaP)-nano- coated zirconia implants (types A and C) with uncoated zirconia (ZiUnite) and titanium porous oxide (TiU - nite) implants. After 3 weeks, TiUnite implants exhib - ited significantly greater bone-implant contact (BIC) (77.6%) compared to the CaP-coated zirconia implants A (64.6%) and C (62.2%). However, after 6 weeks, no sig - nificant differences in BIC were observed between the Page 6 of 25Srinivasan et al. J Mater. Sci: Mater Eng. (2025) 20:76 groups, concluding that while TiUnite and ZiUnite sur - faces demonstrate high osseointegration, the addition of CaP nano-coating did not enhance the osteoconductivity of zirconia implant surfaces. Finally, Koller et al. (2011) studied the survival rates of teeth, implants, and double crown-retained removable dental prostheses (RDPs). The study revealed that the survival rates of teeth ranged from 60.6 to 95.3% over periods of 4 to 10 years. RDPs supported by teeth had survival rates between 90.0 and 95.1% after 4 to 5.3 years. Implants supporting prosthe - ses in the mandible showed survival rates between 97 and 100% over 3 to 10.4 years, and implant-retained RDPs in the mandible had survival rates between 95 and 100% after 9 to 10.4 years. The study concluded that the long- term outcomes of double crown-retained RDPs remain under-researched, recommending further studies with higher levels of evidence to confirm these treatment modalities. A comparative analysis of zirconia and titanium implants This section presents a concise comparison between zirconia and titanium implants, highlighting their key differences and similarities. The analysis focuses on criti - cal factors such as material properties, cost, aesthetics, strength, biocompatibility, and clinical performance. By organizing the data into a structured table, it enhances clarity and supports informed decision-making for clini - cal applications. The comparison also identifies current limitations and ongoing research directions for zirconia implants (Table 2). The choice between zirconia and titanium implants depends on their distinct benefits and limitations. Tita - nium offers proven long-term reliability, while zirconia appeals to patients seeking superior aesthetics. A den - tist’s consultation is crucial to select the most appropriate option based on individual needs and clinical conditions GS Kaliaraj et al. (2016). Corrosion resistance of zirconia implants A study (Subramanian et al. 2015) assessed zirconia and zirconia-silica coatings on titanium dental implants to enhance corrosion resistance. Single-layer coat - ings, unlike double or triple layers with structural flaws, showed reduced surface roughness and improved corro - sion resistance (Fig. 6). Zirconia-silica layers provided superior protection and demonstrated stability in artificial saliva over 3 weeks. Biocompatibility tests confirmed osteoblast compatibil - ity, highlighting single zirconia-silica coatings as promis - ing for titanium implants (Table 3). (2025) 20:76 Potentiodynamic polarization studies revealed that coatings on titanium greatly enhanced corrosion resist - ance in Ringer’s solution after 1 h of immersion. The cor- rosion potential shifted positively, and the current density decreased by approximately two orders of magnitude. Among the coatings, 1Si-Zr-Ti demonstrated notable changes in Tafel slopes, with anodic reactions being pre - dominant. This was attributed to the minimized contact between titanium and the electrolyte, which increased charge-transfer resistance and slowed down the corro - sion process (Fig. 7). New titanium alloys, such as Ti-Zr-Pd and Ti-Sn-Pd, exhibit superior cytocompatibility compared to Ti-6 Al-4 V ELI, with Ti-15Zr4 Nb2 Ta-0.2Pd and Ti-15Sn4 Nb2 Ta-0.2Pd showing the best performance in L929 and MC3 T3-E1 cell tests. These alloys also demonstrate enhanced tensile strength, with Ti-15Sn4 Nb2 Ta-0.2Pd achieving a strength of 989 MPa and elongation of 14.4%, and Ti-15Zr4 Nb2 Ta-0.2Pd showing 725 MPa strength and 23.6% elongation. While the Titanic, a metal vessel, deteriorated rapidly after sinking in 1912 and was nearly completely corroded by the 1980 s, many of these ancient ceramic containers have been recovered from the ocean floor after thou - sands of years and remain largely intact. Some even still contain liquid. Unlike metals, ceramics like terracotta do not corrode or rust over time, even in harsh, underwa - ter environments. This durability contrasts sharply with materials like titanium alloys used in dental implants, which, though resistant to corrosion in many settings, may not provide the same level of longevity in the long term. While amphorae are durable in passive marine environments, dental implants are subject to additional stresses such as mechanical loading, chemical interactions with saliva and food, and microbial activity, which may affect their lon - gevity differently. (2016) observed a reduction in zirconia strength after 4 h of HF etching, suggesting that 1 h of etching yields optimal results, although it did not significantly enhance the morphological characteristics. Despite HF etching’s potential to improve osseointegration, further studies are needed to refine the etching conditions that preserve zirconia’s mechanical properties. Roehling et al. (2017) discovered less biofilm growth on grit-blasted and acid- etched zirconia surfaces (ZrO2-ZLA) compared to grit- blasted titanium surfaces (Ti-SLA). In another study by Flamant et al. (2016), zirconia disks were treated with 5%, 20%, and 40% HF at varying times. The most uniform and rapid roughening occurred with 40% HF for 60 min, Page 18 of 25Srinivasan et al. J Mater. Sci: Mater Eng. (2025) 20:76 though no strength or fatigue tests were conducted. The etching process dissolved zirconium and yttrium oxide, creating fluoride and hydroxide complexes, with yttrium trifluoride crystals precipitating on the surface. Oh et al. (2017) and Flamant et al. (2016) examined different con - centrations and durations of HF etching on pure zirconia, porcelain, and bioactive glass-infiltrated zirconia. They found that neither etching time nor acid concentration had a significant effect on zirconia roughness, while bio - active glass-infiltrated zirconia exhibited a surface com - parable to grit-blasted and acid-etched titanium. Sandblasting Sandblasting is a technique used to create a rough sur - face on implants, enhancing osseointegration by improv - ing bone-implant contact (BIC) and removal torque (RTQ), which are indicators of bone growth quality and the strength of the bond between the implant and bone. In a study by Gahlert et al. (2007), zirconia implants with machined and sandblasted surfaces were placed in the maxillary incisor area of thirteen miniature pigs. The results demonstrated that the sandblasted zirconia implants had a rougher surface than the machined ones. Similarly, Yang et al. (2003) explored zirconia coatings, containing 4% CeO2 and 3% Y2O3, applied to titanium and CoCrMo implants via plasma spraying. The surface roughness of these coatings was influenced by the ini - tial powder size and substrate type. The 3% Y2O3 zirco- nia had a powder size of 40–100 μm, while the 4% CeO2 zirconia had a much finer powder size of 10–20 nm. While no significant differences in hardness were found, the adhesive strength of the 4% CeO2 zirconia coat - ing on both titanium and CoCrMo substrates exceeded 68 MPa, significantly outperforming the 3% Y2O3 coat- ing, which had adhesive strengths of 32.3 MPa on tita - nium and 24.7 MPa on CoCrMo. In a different study, the effects of machined, sandblasted, and SLA zirconia sur - faces were assessed. Both airborne particle abrasion and acid etching increased the surface roughness, with cell proliferation showing notably higher values for surface- treated zirconia at 3 days compared to machined zirco - nia. However, no significant differences in cell behavior were observed between surface-treated zirconia and SLA titanium after 6 and 12 days (Depprich et al. 2008b, a). Stübinger et al. (2008) studied the effect of various laser irradiations (Er:YAG, CO2, and diode lasers) on the sur - face characteristics of polished zirconia implants. SEM analysis revealed no noticeable surface changes with the diode and Er:YAG lasers, while the CO2 laser caused vis - ible alterations to the zirconia surface. Manzano et al. (2014) conducted a clinical study comparing the perfor - mance of zirconia and titanium implants in animal mod - els, focusing on BIC and removal torque. Their analysis of 16 selected studies revealed no significant differences in BIC and RT between the two materials. The varia - tions observed were attributed to differences in surface treatments and microporosity rather than the materi - als themselves. The authors concluded that surface- modified zirconia implants could be a viable alternative to titanium implants, though additional clinical studies are needed for further confirmation. Buser et al. (1998) compared the removal torque values (RTVs) of titanium screw-type implants with different surface treatments in miniature pigs’ maxillae. Implants with a sandblasted and acid-etched surface (SLA) exhibited significantly higher RTVs than those with a machined and acid-etched sur - face (Osseotite), indicating stronger bonding at the bone- implant interface for the SLA surface. In a study, Taniguchi et al. (2016) explored how fiber laser-induced grooves on zirconia implants influenced osteoblast behavior and bone formation. Their findings showed enhanced osteoblast proliferation and differen - tiation on roughened zirconia surfaces, with increased alkaline phosphatase activity and osteocalcin expres - sion. In vivo tests on rat tibiae demonstrated improved bone-to-implant contact and removal torque for laser- treated zirconia implants, indicating better osseointegra - tion. Aivazi et al. (2018) examined the effects of surface treatments on the viability of L929 fibroblast cells cul - tured on zirconia nanocomposites. Various treatments, such as sandblasting, acid etching, and laser irradiation, were applied to enhance the surface properties of the nanocomposites. The results, measured via MTT assays, showed that all surface modifications promoted cell pro - liferation, with laser irradiation leading to the highest cell viability. This suggests that laser treatment optimizes zirconia nanocomposites for better cellular attachment and growth. Lastly, Liu D. et al. (2013b) evaluated three surface treatments—sandblasting, sandblasting followed by regeneration firing, and laser irradiation—on the bond strength between porcelain and zirconia. Both sandblast - ing and laser irradiation improved shear bond strength (SBS) significantly, with no notable difference between the two methods. X-ray diffraction analysis revealed that sandblasting caused a tetragonal-to-monoclinic phase transformation in zirconia, which was reversed by regeneration firing, while laser irradiation did not alter the crystalline structure of the zirconia. These findings suggest that laser irradiation could be a suitable alter - native to sandblasting for improving porcelain-zirconia bonding without affecting the material’s crystallographic structure. Ultraviolet light T Tuna et al. (2015) explored the impact of UV irra - diation on zirconia disks and found that a 15-min UV Page 19 of 25 Srinivasan et al. J Mater. Sci: Mater Eng. (2025) 20:76 exposure significantly lowered the contact angles, reduc - ing them from 56.4°–69° to 2.5°–14.1°. Their findings revealed notable alterations in the surface composition, including a 43–81% reduction in carbon content and a 19–45% increase in oxygen levels, indicating a transition from hydrophobic to hydrophilic characteristics (Hen - nigesen et al. 2018; Al Qahtani et al. 2015). Addition - ally, an increase in the monoclinic phase of zirconia was observed. However, other studies did not report a phase transition from tetragonal to monoclinic, suggesting that UV treatment can mitigate zirconia aging without induc - ing significant crystalline transformations. Further inves - tigation is required to fully comprehend the potential of this approach (Roy M. et al. 2017). Plant-based coatings Leveraging plant-based bioactive coatings offers a dual advantage—enhancing microbial resistance and pro - moting biointegration without compromising biocom - patibility. Studies, including those by Wan Mohamad Ikhmal et al. (2020), have shown that such coatings sig - nificantly improve the performance of metallic substrates like SS 316, indicating their adaptability to ceramic sur - faces. Additionally, plant-derived inhibitors such as Uncaria cordata, Leucas aspera, and Salicornia begolovi have demonstrated high corrosion resistance in acidic environments through adsorption and protective film formation (Selma Lamghafri et al. 2024). Although zir - conia inherently resists corrosion, it lacks these organic interaction mechanisms; thus, integrating plant-based bioactives can introduce antimicrobial functionality and improved bioactivity, aligning with green chemistry and enhancing the clinical longevity of zirconia implants. Among the various surface treatments explored (Fig. 16), biofunctional coatings—notably hydroxyapatite, polydopamine-mediated mineralization, and phytochem- ical-based layers—demonstrate superior performance for zirconia dental implants. These modifications pro - mote osteointegration and antimicrobial efficacy while preserving the material’s phase and mechanical stability. Advanced nanostructured coatings like graphene further contribute to enhanced cellular responses and durabil - ity. In contrast, conventional methods such as sandblast - ing and acid etching, though effective in roughening, risk tetragonal-to-monoclinic phase transformation. Ultra - violet and machined surfaces, while structurally safe, exhibit limited biological stimulation. Thus, bioactive and multifunctional coating strategies represent the most clinically viable pathway for optimizing zirconia implant integration. Mechanical strength Minamizato et al. (1990) investigated the compressive strength of zirconia dental implants with laser-drilled tunnels and found that the implants with tunnels exhib - ited a reduced compressive strength of 237 kg/mm 2, compared to 371.5 kg/mm 2 for those without tunnels. They concluded that zirconia implants, despite the lower Fig. 16 Schematics and SEM images of various zirconia surface treatments, including machined surfaces (Gahlert et al. 2007), acid-etched surfaces (Flamant et al. 2016), multi-layered coatings (M.S. Laranjeira et al. 2014; G Feng et al. 2021; M. Liu et al. 2015), ZLA-treated surfaces (M. Liu et al. 2015), and grit-blasted surfaces (Liu YT et al. 2013a) Page 20 of 25Srinivasan et al. J Mater. Sci: Mater Eng. (2025) 20:76 strength, retained sufficient mechanical properties for occlusal use. Silva et al. (2009) explored the effect of full crown preparation on the fracture strength of one-piece zirconia implants, reporting fracture strengths of 1023.3 N without preparation and 1111.7 N with preparation. However, other studies indicated that head preparation adversely affected fracture strength. After simulating 5 years of clinical use, zirconia implants fractured at forces between 725 and 850 N without preparation and 539 and 607 N with preparation, indicating that zirconia implants maintain adequate fracture strength within clinical lim - its. The mechanical characteristics of Y-TZP , CP Ti, and Ti-6 Al-4 V alloys for dental implants vary significantly as shown in Table 4. Zirconia (Y-TZP) has a bending strength of 1000 MPa, which is appropriate for dental applications, though it is less robust than titanium alloys. Its fracture toughness, ranging from 6 to 8 MPa m1/2, is higher than alumina but considerably lower than tita - nium (66 MPa m1/2). Zirconia also has lower notch sta - bility, which diminishes its fracture resistance compared to titanium. Due to its high Young’s modulus of 210 GPa, zirconia is less efficient at absorbing occlusal forces than titanium alloys, which have a modulus between 100 and 110 GPa. This stiffness may also lead to prob - lems with screw fixation, resulting in loosening (Apratim et al. 2015). Qeblawi et al. (2010) examined the effect of various mechanical surface treatments on the flexural strength of yttria-partially stabilized zirconia (4 × 5 × 40 mm), including (1) control (no treatment); (2) airborne- particle abrasion (APA); (3) silicon coating; and (4) wet hand grinding. The results showed the following flex - ural strengths in MPa: control (571.7 ± 79.2), APA (798.8 ± 138.2), silicoated (594.3 ± 100.5), and hand ground (1727.7 ± 112.7), with hand grinding yielding the highest strength. Abrasion resistance and material durability An ideal dental restoration should exhibit excellent wear resistance without causing excessive wear to the opposing natural teeth. Zirconia, a rigid ceramic material, stands out for its superior wear resistance when compared to both human enamel and porcelain. Research has inves - tigated whether zirconia, especially non-veneered zirco - nia, leads to significant wear on opposing teeth. Oh et al. (2002) explored the factors influencing enamel abrasion caused by dental ceramics and concluded that there is no direct correlation between ceramic hardness and enamel wear. Instead, the microstructure, surface roughness, and individual patient risk factors have a more substan - tial impact. For full-contour zirconia crowns, appropri - ate surface treatment is essential. Beuer et al. (2012) demonstrated that glazing helps maintain zirconia’s wear resistance, preventing excessive wear on opposing teeth. However, the 30–50-μm glazed layer tends to wear off after approximately 6 months, revealing a rougher sur - face that could increase abrasion. Polishing zirconia to a smooth finish, similar to glazing, further enhances wear resistance. Despite this, full-contour zirconia polished with 3-μm diamond paste still does not fully protect enamel from excessive abrasion. Long-term reliability Flinn et al. (2012) examined the aging resistance of three commercial 3Y-TZP zirconia grades: Lava, Zirkonzahn, and Zirprime. After exposing the materials to 200 h of autoclaving at 134 °C and 0.2 MPa, they found that the monoclinic phase content varied between 25 and 80%, with the depth of the transformed zone ranging from 2 to 60 μm. The biaxial flexural strength was measured between 100 and 700 MPa. The study highlighted that the zirconia’s resistance to aging is influenced by factors such as the material’s initial properties, processing methods, and microstructure. It was also observed that reducing the grain size of zirconia could lower the driving force for phase transformation, thus stabilizing the tetrago - nal phase and enhancing the material’s aging resist - ance. In a critical review, Lughi et al. (2010) examined low-temperature degradation (LTD), a key factor in the aging of zirconia ceramics for dental use. They empha - sized that LTD is primarily governed by factors such as stabilizer type, concentration, grain size, and residual stresses. The authors warned against using accelerated aging tests to predict the long-term performance of zir - conia, as these tests may not accurately simulate real-life conditions. They suggested optimizing stabilizer content and controlling grain size to improve the durability and longevity of zirconia dental restorations. Hallmann et al. (2012) found that zirconia ceramics sintered at temper - atures between 1350 and 1450 °C exhibited improved Table 4 Mechanical properties of zirconium and titanium alloy (Apratim et al. 2015) Mechanical property Y-TZP Cp-Ti (grade 2) Ti-6 Al-4 V alloy Tensile strength (MPa) - 345 869 (Annealed) Bending strength (MPa) 1100 (without HAp) 1800 (with HAp) 100 950 Young modulus (GPa) 210 100 110 Vickers hardness (HV) 1200 150–170 270–320 Fracture toughness (MPa M1/2) 6–8 66 50 Page 21 of 25 Srinivasan et al. As the sintering temperature increased, both the tensile/compressive stress ratio and monoclinic phase content also increased. Research on doping with elements like Al, Ce, and Si showed that these dopants could help mitigate LTD by enhancing the material’s stability. Ardlin et al. (2002) noted that the aging behavior of colored zirconia has been less studied, but their findings indicated that although the monoclinic phase content increased slightly after aging, the bend - ing strength of the material remained largely unchanged, suggesting that aging does not significantly compromise the material’s strength in dental applications (Samudu - rova et al. 2015). Nakamura et al. (2015) examined the impact of LTD and cyclic loading on the fracture resist - ance of monolithic zirconia molar crowns. After auto - claving zirconia samples at 134 °C for various durations, they observed an increase in the monoclinic phase frac - tion with longer autoclaving times, which plateaued after 50 h. The depth of the monoclinic phase continued to increase, but the fracture resistance decreased from 5683 to 3975 N after 100 h. Despite this reduction in strength, the crowns still maintained adequate fracture resistance for typical chewing forces in the molar region. Zirconia, being an inert ceramic, does not naturally bond well with other materials, so surface modifications are essential to enhance adhesion. Y-TZP surfaces are typically treated through mechanical methods such as sandblasting with Al2O3 or tribochemical silica coating, followed by chemi - cal treatment with primers like MDP . The phosphate groups in MDP promote bonding with the zirconia sur - face, improving adhesion. However, these treatments may sometimes induce micro-cracks or phase transfor - mations, potentially affecting the long-term performance of the zirconia material (Cheung GC. et al. (2014). Progression of zirconia ceramic implants Dental implantology in Europe saw pioneering advance - ments (Fig. 17) in both titanium and ceramic implants. Swedish inventor Per-Ingvar Branemark created the first titanium implant in the 1960 s, while ceramic implants emerged as an alternative due to concerns about metal’s potential immunological, aesthetic, and allergic issues. Ceramic implants, particularly made from zirconia, have been in clinical use since the late 1960 s. Zirconia implants were first developed in 1967 by Swiss dentist Sami Sandhaus, who believed zirconia’s tooth-like color, biocompatibility, and mechanical properties made it an ideal implant material. By the 1970 s, alumina ceramic implants were also being tested, with research showing their high bio-inertness, aesthetic appeal, and ability to integrate with bone. In the 1980 s, zirconia-toughened alumina (ZTA) implants replaced alumina, leading to the development of today’s zirconia implants made from yttria-stabilized zirconia (Y-TZP), which offers superior strength and resilience compared to earlier materials. Despite early setbacks in acceptance, ceramic implants gained recognition by the 1980 s, especially after Sami Sandhaus reported positive clinical outcomes in 1997. Today, zirconia implants remain a strong alternative to titanium, offering advantages in aesthetic appearance, biocompatibility, and reduced plaque buildup (Yuriy May et al. 2025). Sci: Mater Eng. (2025) 20:76 Summary and conclusion Zirconia (ZrO2) stands out in orthopedic applications for its superior mechanical strength, fracture toughness, and wear resistance. Its excellent biocompatibility and corro - sion resistance make it ideal for load-bearing implants, coatings, and bone scaffolds. Advances in composites like yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) and zirconia-tough - ened alumina have further enhanced its performance. To improve osseointegration, surface treatments such as laser texturing, biofunctionalization, and acid etching are employed, optimizing surface chemistry and topogra- phy. Overall, zirconia’s robust properties and adaptability through surface engineering make it a premier choice for next-generation orthopedic implants. Acknowledgements The corresponding author, Dr. M. title: Hydroxyapatite in Oral Care Products A Review

Roosevelt, 50—CP 165/61, 1050 Brussels, Belgium; Amin.Shavandi@ulb.be * Correspondence: jithendra.ratnayake@otago.ac.nz; Tel.: +64-3479-7355 Abstract: Calcium phosphate compounds form the inorganic phases of our mineralised tissues such as bone and teeth, playing an important role in hard tissue engineering and regenerative medicine. In dentistry and oral care products, hydroxyapatite (HA) is a stable and biocompatible calcium phosphate with low solubility being used for various applications such as tooth remineralisation, reduction of tooth sensitivity, oral bioﬁlm control, and tooth whitening. Clinical data on these prod- ucts is limited with varied results; additionally, the effectiveness of these apatite compounds versus ﬂuoride, which has conventionally been used in toothpaste, has not been established. Therefore, this review critically evaluates current research on HA oral care, and discusses the role and mecha- nism of HA in remineralisation of both enamel and dentine and for suppressing dentine sensitivity. Furthermore, we position HA’s role in bioﬁlm management and highlight the role of HA in dental applications by summarising the recent achievement and providing an overview of commercialised HA dental products. The review also indicates the existing limitations and provides direction for future research and commercialisation of apatite-based oral care products. Keywords: hydroxyapatite; hydroxyapatite toothpaste; remineralisation; teeth whitening; bioﬁlm; dentine hypersensitivity 1. Introduction Dental caries is a global disease affecting all ages and sectors of the population. Dental caries remains the most common chronic bacterial driven disease despite advancements in early detection and treatment [1]. According to a study by The Global Burden of Disease in 2017, it is estimated that 2.3 billion people suffer from caries of permanent teeth and more than 530 million children suffer from caries of primary teeth [2]. Untreated caries can progress into the tooth pulp, lead to dental abscesses, cause signiﬁcant pain and suffering, and ultimately tooth loss [1]. Dental caries is caused by the action of acids on the enamel surface. The acids are produced as a byproduct from bacteria in the dental bioﬁlm (plaque) metabolising the sugars in foods or drinks [1]. The produced acid leads to a loss of calcium and phosphate from the enamel; this process is called demineralization [1]. The gingiva can also become inﬂamed in response to plaque irritation, diagnosed as gingivitis [ 3]. The Global Burden of Disease Study 2017 also reported that the prevalence of severe periodontal (gum) diseases affect almost 10% of the global population [2]. Consequently, controlling oral microbial bioﬁlms on the tooth surface is essential to prevent the progression of caries and periodontal disease. Hydroxyapatite (HA) is a bioactive and non-toxic ceramic that has a close analogy to the inorganic portion of human teeth and bone. It is arranged in a typical lattice structure with the chemical formulation of (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) [4]. Depending on the manufacturing Materials 2021, 14, 4865. https://doi.org/10.3390/ma14174865 https://www.mdpi.com/journal/materials Materials 2021, 14, 4865 2 of 20 technique employed, various synthetic apatites are produced today [ 5]. HA used for biomedical applications is chemically prepared to achieve tailored properties such as chemical purity, crystal morphology, and crystal size [5]. HA’s bioactive, non-toxic, and osteoconductive properties mean it can form direct chemical bonds with living tissues. Thus, HA is a bioceramic that is widely used as an implantable material in dentistry, maxillofacial and orthopaedic surgery to repair bone defects and as a coating material for metallic implants [6]. Studies of the osteogenesis effectiveness of HA-based coatings have shown favourable results, however, their validity has been critically considered [7]. Most of these favourable results were observed in in vitro studies rather than clinical and in vivo studies, and there is a demand for more standardised comparison criteria of the published research to draw sound clinical conclusions [ 7]. It has also been noted that the clinical effectiveness is dependent on the speciﬁc geometry, pore size, and degradation rate of the HA, whereby a smaller particle size is desirable [8]. The biocompatibility of nano-HA has also made it attractive as a potential novel reinforcing ﬁller in composite restorations [9]. However, so far, nano-HA has been shown to be clinically unsuitable due to high water uptake, high refractive index and hence light scattering [9]. Therefore, no signiﬁcantly improved properties compared to conventional composites with regard to tooth mechanical properties and bioﬁlm protection [9]. However, there is suggestive more promise with smaller HA particles and increasing total ﬁller amount [9]. The external layer of human teeth, the enamel, is composed of 97% inorganic compo- nent, and the dentine is composed of 70% inorganic component; these inorganic phases are mainly made up of HA [ 10,11]. In the past 50 years, calcium phosphate for daily oral care has been thoroughly researched, especially in preventative dentistry. HA can be extracted from various natural resources such as bovine, ovine, porcine bone and marine structures [12–16]. Trace elements such as zinc, sodium, magnesium and carbonate present in some natural sources of HA have been found to mimic the apatite produced from human bone and inﬂuence the physical properties of HA such as crystal structure, morphology and solubility, and also the thermal stability [4]. Naturally sourced HA can also be a more environmentally friendly, sustainable, and economical substitute than synthetic HA [12]. However, using naturally sourced HA in oral care products has not been investigated. HA dentifrice with synthetic HA for teeth brushing was ﬁrst produced by NASA (U.S. National Aeronautics and Space Authority) as a repairing material for the astronauts who lost minerals in their teeth and bones due to the absence of gravity in 1970. In 1978, the Japanese company Sangi Co. Ltd. (Tokyo, Japan) developed the world’s ﬁrst enamel restorative dentifrice. In 1993, nano-HA was approved as an anti-caries agent. Since then, in 2003, nano-HA particle size has been reduced from 100 to 50 nanometers, making it more effective at penetrating below the surface of the enamel [11,17]. Moreover, HA has also been incorporated into oral rinses and gels for oral home care to aid remineralisation and bioﬁlm control [18–20]. The ideal properties of a dentifrice include minimal abrasive effect, non-irritating, non-toxic, non-staining, protects against caries and bioﬁlm formation, while being cost- effective and readily available [21]. Many studies have been conducted to test the efﬁcacy of HA, especially in enamel and dentine remineralisation, bioﬁlm control, reducing dentine sensitivity, and tooth whitening [5,10,11,22–30]. Currently, only a few reviews report on nanomaterial in oral care products or HA in dentistry which includes restorative, preventa- tive, and regenerative applications [5,10,11,31,32]. Therefore, this review aims to summarise current knowledge and provide an update on the claims of HA oral care products and recognise the limitations and future directions to guide clinical decision-making. 2. Hydroxyapatite in Oral Care Products As HA is naturally found in enamel and dentine, synthetic HA is incorporated into dental products in various examples such as dental cement, ﬁllings, and oral care products, including dentifrice, mouthwash, and gels [8]. HA can be synthesised in different crystallite Materials 2021, 14, 4865 3 of 20 morphologies such as spherical or needle-like and particle sizes (micro to nano) [ 5,33]. Currently, there are two types of HA; the nanocrystalline and the microcluster form, both nano and micro-HA are available in oral care products [10,30]. The inorganic component of enamel is made of HA crystallites in the range of ~50 nm in diameter [34]. HA crystallites are tightly packed and strictly organised as enamel prisms [5]. Micro-HA particles are about 5–10 microns in size, and this is signiﬁcantly larger than enamel HA and dentinal tubules. Therefore these are not as effective in remineralisation and in reducing sensitivity [5]. Nano-HA particle size ranges from 20–100 nm, with a rod-shaped morphology resem- bling those in natural enamel (Figure 1) [11,22,35]. Nano-HA have a high afﬁnity to bind to substances due to an increased surface area which may improve remineralisation and reduce sensitivity as HA with a 20–50 nm size matches the nano-sized defects due to acidic erosion at the enamel surface [32,36]. Nano-HA are also thought to be more effective than micro-HA in bioﬁlm management. The interaction with microorganisms is only possible if the particles involved are smaller than the microorganisms. Nano-size particles are small enough to directly interact with the bacterial membrane [19,32]. Materials 2021, 14, x FOR PEER REVIEW 3 of 23 products, including dentifrice, mouthwash, and gels [8]. HA can be synthesised in differ- ent crystallite morphologies such as spherical or needle-like and particle sizes (micro to nano) [5,33]. Currently, there are two types of HA; the nanocrystalline and the microclus- ter form, both nano and micro-HA are available in oral care products [10,30]. The inor- ganic component of enamel is made of HA crystallites in the range of ~50 nm in diameter [34]. HA crystallites are tightly packed and strictly organised as enamel prisms [5]. Micro- HA particles are about 5–10 microns in size, and this is significantly larger than enamel HA and dentinal tubules. Therefore these are not as effective in remineralisation and in reducing sensitivity [5]. Nano-HA particle size ranges from 20–100 nm, with a rod-shaped morphology re- sembling those in natural enamel (Figure 1) [11,22,35]. Nano-HA have a high affinity to bind to substances due to an increased surface area which may improve remineralisation and reduce sensitivity as HA with a 20–50 nm size matches the nano-sized defects due to acidic erosion at the enamel surface [32,36]. Nano-HA are also thought to be more effective than micro-HA in biofilm management. The interaction with microorganisms is only pos- sible if the particles involved are smaller than the microorganisms. Nano-size particles are small enough to directly interact with the bacterial membrane [19,32]. Figure 1. Particle size of nano-hydroxyapatite. UK 3. Beneﬁts of Hydroxyapatite Dentifrice/Oral Care Products 3.1. Tooth Remineralisation Modern dentistry has taken a more preventative approach through the understanding of enamel remineralisation in early carious activity [17]. Demineralised enamel and dentine have mineral ions removed from the HA crystals [40]. If the HA is partially demineralised, then this process is reversible if exposed to favourable oral environments [40]. This process is called remineralisation, where lost mineral ions in the HA crystals are restored [40]. There are many methods of remineralisation, saliva can aid in remineralisation by providing a constant source of calcium and phosphate required for the process to occur [ 40,41]. Fluoride also promotes remineralisation by forming ﬂuorapatite with the calcium and phosphate released from demineralisation, this is more resistant to acid attack [ 40,41]. Casein phosphopeptide–amorphous calcium phosphate (CPP-ACP) is another system that promotes the precipitation of minerals to hard tooth tissue [ 41]. At present, there has been an increasing trend for biomimetic nano-HA to be used as a preventative agent for oral care products [ 17]. Research has shown nano-HA acts by providing a calcium and phosphate reservoir to remineralise enamel and dentine [ 8]. In dentine, nano-HA penetrates the demineralised collagen matrix, acting as a scaffold for remineralisation and providing a calcium and phosphate source locally [ 8]. In incipient enamel lesions, nano-HA penetrates into porosities to replace dissolved phosphate and calcium ions and forms a synthetic enamel layer on the tooth surface which can acts as a “sacriﬁcial layer” during future acid attacks (Figures 2 and 3) [ 8,10,11,31,42]. As when demineralisation Materials 2021, 14, 4865 6 of 20 occurs once the HA layer is deposited on the tooth surface, the dissolution of HA will produce calcium and phosphate ions which may act as a buffering solution to neutralise acids [31]. Released calcium and phosphate ions in excess can also bring the pH balance back to favour remineralisation [31]. Table 2 provides a summary of the studies conducted on HA and its effects on remineralisation. Several in vitro studies have proved the superior remineralisation properties of HA and ﬂuoride; however, most studies could not prove a statistically signiﬁcant difference between HA and ﬂuoride’s remineralisation properties [ 18,38,43–45]. An in vitro study comparing the remineralisation effect between nano-HA paste and ﬂuoride varnish on young permanent teeth concluded no signiﬁcant difference in remineralisation between nano-HA and the ﬂuoride group [ 44]. However, high ﬂuoride exposure was not recom- mended due to the risk of ingestion in children and pregnant females [ 44]. Therefore, nano-HA may still be recommended as an alternative remineralising agent [44]. Likewise, similar ﬁndings were obtained in an in-vitro study that compared the remineralisation abil- ities between HA and ﬂuoride gel on bovine teeth, with artiﬁcial saliva as the control [ 18]. Both studies used various pH-cyclical conditions to mimic acidic challenges in the oral cavity [18,44]. Alternatively, another study assessed the remineralisation effects through Vickers Hardness Number values and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and did not ﬁnd signiﬁcant differences between nano-HA and ﬂuoride [45]. Additionally, no signiﬁcant changes were observed when the synergistic remineralisation effects of ﬂuoride and nano- HA were studied [45]. Huang et al., investigated the remineralisation effects of different concentrations of nano-HA on bovine teeth. The results showed a self-limiting response where following a statistically positive correlation, the plateau was seen after nine days of cycling [43]. Thus, proving that the remineralisation abilities of HA may be effective up to a certain point [43]. Other research supports this claim and suggests that a concentration of 10% nano-HA may be optimal for remineralisation of early carious lesions [ 42]. The plateau is explained as an unavoidable aggregation of the particles at higher concentrations, blocking surface pores and restricting further penetration of HA into the lesion to allow Materials 2021, 14, 4865 7 of 20 for a further remineralisation effect [43]. Only one in vitro study concluded that nano-HA toothpaste had a higher remineralising effect than the amine ﬂuoride toothpaste control on both bovine enamel and dentine [38]. However, this study did not take all oral factors into account, especially the complexity of the tooth-pellicle–plaque-saliva interface which may have impacted the results obtained [38]. Substitutions in the HA lattice can change the physical properties of HA, including crystal structure, morphology, solubility, thermal stability, and bioactivity [36]. The remineralisation abilities of HA can be improved by substituting ions such as zinc, ﬂuoride, magnesium, and strontium to the HA lattice [ 47]. The addition of these ions improves the stability, solubility, and strength of the HA, aiding in the remineralisation potential of enamel surface lesions and in preventing bioﬁlm formation [47]. Beta-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP) is another attractive calcium phosphate system as it can emerge as a transitional phase in the conversion of HA. Furthermore, it is compatible with biological systems and is bioactive [ 4,36]. In a study where the β-TCP structure was altered by combining with carboxylic acids and surfactants to generate functionalised β-TCP (fTCP), the toothpaste containing fTCP and ﬂuoride increased remineralisation of the artiﬁcial enamel subsurface lesions during pH-cycling [ 48]. In another study, fTCP containing toothpaste effectively reduced white spot lesions (WSL) compared to 1000-ppm ﬂuoride- containing toothpaste [49]. However, an in situ study showed that the remineralisation efﬁcacy of fTCP toothpaste was similar to that of ﬂuoride toothpaste [ 50]. Although β-TCP has shown the potential for tooth remineralisation, further investigations are required to establish its clinical efﬁcacy. Currently, novel research has also been interested in investigating the synergistic effects of ﬂuoride and nano-HA. A study investigating sodium ﬂuoride (NaF) combined with HA demonstrated a synergistic effect between NaF and nano-HA for remineralisa- tion [51]. However, more studies are needed to determine the optimal nano-HA and NaF mouth rinse conditions for human use [51]. This is supported by a study that investigated the synergistic effects of ﬂuoride and nano-HA on preventing enamel demineralisation around orthodontic brackets [ 29]. Results revealed signiﬁcantly less demineralisation depth in the combined nano-HA and ﬂuoride group [ 29]. Additionally, the combination of nano-HA with ﬂuoride has shown better enamel resistance to erosion in bovine teeth [ 52]. Meyer et al., concluded that the addition of ﬂuorides to calcium phosphate may reduce the bioavailability of ﬂuoride intraorally by forming insoluble compounds, including cal- cium ﬂuoride or ﬂuorapatite [ 10]. As data in this area are scarce, future investigations are required to gauge whether there are any beneﬁts in incorporating both ﬂuoride and HA in oral care products. The synergistic effect of HA with other substances or therapy is also of interest. A RCT investigated the remineralisation between nano-HA gel, in-ofﬁce ozone therapy, and a combination of both compounds [28]. Results showed that a higher rate of remineralisation was seen when nano HA and ozone therapy were used in conjunction [28]. Furthermore, when the combined effects of Galla Chinensis (GCE: a traditional Chinese medicine) with nano-HA was investigated, results proved a signiﬁcant synergistic effect of combined GCE and nano-HA on the depth reduction of initial enamel lesions [53]. More research is required on the mechanism of this synergistic effect. However, these studies give promising insight and research possibilities of investigating other substances and therapy when used together with HA oral care products. 3.2. Dentine Hypersensitivity Dentine hypersensitivity is one of the most prevalent dental conditions, affecting 8–57% of the adult population [54]. Its occurrence has been explained by a few theories, Materials 2021, 14, 4865 9 of 20 with the most favoured being the hydrodynamic theory [55]. The hydrodynamic theory explains that open dentinal tubules allow ﬂuid movement, which stimulates the pulp nerves to induce pain [55]. Various kinds of toothpaste have been developed to reduce tooth hypersensitivity, where their components occlude dentinal tubules to reduce hydraulic conductance and minimise sensitivity [55]. The effect is enhanced by their remineralisation abilities, where a mineralised layer creates a barrier [55]. Dentifrices containing potassium ions can also depolarise pulpal sensory nerves and interrupt the transmission of pain stimuli [55]. Nano-HA has been proposed to combat tooth sensitivity more effectively compared to conventional toothpaste by bio-chemically binding to both collagen and HA from dentine, and due to their nano-sized diameters, they are able to reliably occlude the tubules (Figure 4) [31]. Studies that investigate the effect of HA on teeth sensitivity are shown in Table 2. Materials 2021, 14, x FOR PEER REVIEW 10 of 23 Figure 4. The majority of studies investigating the effectiveness of nano-HA on tooth sensitiv- ity are based on clinical studies due to the subjective nature of tooth sensitivity. In various comparative clinical investigations, nano-HA ha s proven superior over controls such as fluoride and potassium nitrate in reducing tooth hypersensitivity [55–57]. In a RCT, a commercial nano-HA toothpaste (PrevDent ®) showed reduced tooth sensitivity compared to fluoride toothpaste [55]. A similar effect was seen when HA was compared against a placebo toothpaste, suggesting that HA is more effective in occluding dentinal tubules compared to the controls [56,57]. These two studies minimised bias through the placebo effect by having a placebo control group [56,57]. When the effectiveness of zinc-carbonate hydroxyapatite (Zn-CHA) nanocrystals dent ifrice was compared with potassium ni- trate/fluoride dentifrice, Zn-CHA proved superior once again [56]. In this study, Zn-CHA dentifrice is suggested to work through a dentinal tubule plugging action, and potassium nitrate through depolarising pulpal nerve action [56]. An explanation for the reduced den- tine hypersensitivity in the test dentifrice was its lower abrasiveness when compared to that of the control dentifrice [56]. Various non-comparative, quasi-experimental clinical studies have also been carried out on the topic. A study was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of a desensitising toothpaste containing potassium nitrate, sodium monoflurophosphate, and nano-HA, as well as antioxidants phloretin, ferulic acid, and silymarin [58]. The dentifrice showed sig- nificant improvement in sensitivity after 48 hours and two weeks, highlighting its effec- tive speed in relieving dentine hypersensitivity [58]. A similar study that used a tooth- paste containing Zn-CHA nanocr ystals over a more extended period of four to eight weeks, found statistically significant reductions in tooth sensitivity, highlighting Zn-CHA toothpaste’s long-term clinical effects [59]. However, a major limitation of these studies is that they do not have placebo controls, with each subject being their control [58,60]. In a RCT, a commercial nano-HA toothpaste (PrevDent®) showed reduced tooth sensitivity compared to ﬂuoride toothpaste [ 55]. A similar effect was seen when HA was compared against a placebo toothpaste, suggesting that HA is more effective in occluding dentinal tubules com- pared to the controls [56,57]. These two studies minimised bias through the placebo effect by having a placebo control group [56,57]. When the effectiveness of zinc-carbonate hydrox- yapatite (Zn-CHA) nanocrystals dentifrice was compared with potassium nitrate/ﬂuoride dentifrice, Zn-CHA proved superior once again [ 56]. In this study, Zn-CHA dentifrice is suggested to work through a dentinal tubule plugging action, and potassium nitrate through depolarising pulpal nerve action [ 56]. An explanation for the reduced dentine hypersensitivity in the test dentifrice was its lower abrasiveness when compared to that of the control dentifrice [56]. Various non-comparative, quasi-experimental clinical studies have also been carried out on the topic. A study was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of a desensitising toothpaste containing potassium nitrate, sodium monoﬂurophosphate, and nano-HA, as well as antioxidants phloretin, ferulic acid, and silymarin [ 58]. The dentifrice showed signiﬁcant improvement in sensitivity after 48 h and two weeks, highlighting its effective speed in relieving dentine hypersensitivity [58]. A similar study that used a toothpaste con- taining Zn-CHA nanocrystals over a more extended period of four to eight weeks, found statistically signiﬁcant reductions in tooth sensitivity, highlighting Zn-CHA toothpaste’s long-term clinical effects [59]. However, a major limitation of these studies is that they do Materials 2021, 14, 4865 10 of 20 not have placebo controls, with each subject being their control [58,60]. In vitro studies on the effects of HA on tooth sensitivity have also been conducted. These provide quantiﬁca- tion of tubule occlusion and statistical data through the assessment of SEM images [ 54]. An in vitro study was conducted to evaluate and compare the effects of three different desensitising denitriﬁes; a nano-HA containing dentifrice, Novamin (commercially avail- able bioactive glass-based toothpaste that consists of calcium sodium phosphosilicate), and Proargin (a system that contains both calcium carbonate and arginine) on dentinal permeability and tubule occlusion [54]. Results showed a higher percentage of dentinal occlusion with nano-HA when compared to Proargin and Novamin [54]. However, these ﬁndings are inconsistent with those of Dhillon et al., which showed the superiority of calcium sodium phosphosilicate over Proargin and HA [61]. The differences may be due to processing differences in the dentin specimens and different regimes of desensitising dentifrice application [54]. A combined in vitro and in vivo study highlighted the impor- tance of considering the in vivo effects in comparison to the in vitro effects as they can produce contradictory results [62]. As when their study investigated the in vitro effects in the absence of saliva, HA containing toothpaste was most effective in reducing dentine permeability, and arginine and calcium carbonate was the least [ 62]. In contrast, in the presence of saliva and ageing, HA dentifrice was the least effective, and arginine and calcium carbonate were the most effective at reducing dentine permeability [62]. From the reviewed literature, it can be concluded that HA dentifrices have shown deﬁnite clinical efﬁcacy in reducing dentine hypersensitivity both in the immediate and long term [58,59]. However, the placebo effect remains a major limitation in investigating tooth sensitivity [58,60]. Many comparative in vitro studies exist between desensitising toothpaste, but further investigations of their in-vivo implications are required [62]. Ad- ditionally, many quasi-experimental but not enough comparative clinical studies were conducted between existing desensitising toothpaste [58]. Continued research is required in this area to highlight the beneﬁcial plausibility of nano-HA dentifrice over already existing desensitising toothpastes. 3.3. Oral Bioﬁlm Management: Effect on Periodontal Conditions In patients with periodontal and gingival disease, as well as mechanical removal of plaque, the addition of pharmacological agents to bioﬁlm control has also been an area of focus in recent years, which may support favourable treatment outcomes [ 63]. The development of bioﬁlm control using ﬂuoride has effectively reduced plaque formation and improved periodontal health, leading to ﬂuoride being the gold standard in oral care products [63]. Likewise, chlorhexidine (CHX) as an antimicrobial agent is the gold standard in a mouth rinse. However, current issues include long-term use of CHX, resulting in side effects such as tooth discolouration and dysbiosis of oral ecology [64]. HA‘s role in bioﬁlm control has been an area of interest recently due to its biomimetic properties in keeping the microbiome in balance [64]. HA is effective in bioﬁlm control through mainly an anti-adhesive property by pre- venting bacteria from binding to the tooth surface [ 11,63–65]. The mechanism of action (Figure 5) is explained by the binding of microorganisms to free HA particles incorporated into dentifrice or mouth rinse [ 10,31]. HA also binds to proteins and plaque; therefore, it inhibits the development and aggregation of bioﬁlm on the enamel surface [ 11,63,64]. HA particle size is important as nano-size HA exhibits greater active surface area, which inﬂuences the stability of incorporation into the bioﬁlm and interaction with the bacteria cell membrane [19,65]. An in vivo study was conducted to analyse the quantitative parameters of micro-HA in improving periodontal disease in patients [63]. The study concluded that HA tooth- paste had comparable effects to amine and stannous fluoride toothpaste in reducing plaque index, bleeding on probing, and the gingival index, thus improving periodontal health [63]. Another in vivo study drew a similar conclusion where HA mouth rinse was proven to be as effective as CHX in plaque reduction and gingival index [66]. In another study that used questionnaires to evaluate the effect of HA toothpaste on various param- eters, results showed that a subjective feeling of “tooth smoothness” was reported by par- ticipants [25]. Such results can be explained by the reduction of bacterial colonisation and biofilm formation due to binding to HA particles [25]. Substituting ions into HA not only allows synthetic HA to be more biomimetic, but it also improves properties such as the antimicrobial ability of HA. Zinc and silver have been extensively researched in this area, with results showing that exposure to zinc sub- stituted HA reduced the bactericidal viability of Streptococcus mutans [19,63]. It has been proven that zinc ions can inhibit bacterial metabolism and prevent halitosis by inhibiting volatile sulphur compounds [10]. Research on the antimicrobial properties of silver has also been long established [36]. Studies have shown that silver ions leached out of the HA structure can inhibit the growth of Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and Pneumococcus [36]. The substitution of other cations and anio ns has been extensively researched; how- ever, the focus has been more on implants an d bone regeneration [36]. More evidence is needed for their benefits in oral care before these ion-substituted HA can be added to oral care products promisingly. In summary, in situ and in vivo studies have found that the effect of HA on biofilm formation on the tooth surface is comparable to CHX and amine/stannous fluoride [19,63,65,66]. Therefore, it is a sensible supplement in oral care. HA particles have been found to do so without any antibacterial effect due to their anti-adherent properties [65,67]. Therefore, acting as a biomimetic biofilm control without disrupting the biofilm ecological balance in the oral cavity [19]. Currently, evidence suggests toothpaste and mouth rinse with nano and micro-HA can contribute to oral biofilm management [19,63,65,66]. More in-situ and in-vivo studie s with an increased number of participants and a longer time frame need to be conducted to provide optimal insight into the mecha- nism of the anti-adhesive proper ty of HA in oral care products to stimulate natural oral conditions. Teeth Whitening Age-related changes and lifestyle habits result in darker teeth colour [68]. An increas- ing number of oral care products has shifted the focus towards teeth whitening mainly due to cosmetic reasons. White teeth and a bright smile are preferred by many and can lead to an improved quality of life [68]. Although HA-incorporated oral care products have been proven to be effective in preventative dentistry through remineralisation, it is only in the past 20 years that research has been directed to investigate the whitening properties of HA [68]. In vivo and in vitro studies have been carried out to understand HA’s teeth whitening mechanism compared to the whitening property of conventional whitening products such as hydrogen peroxide and other commercial dentifrice and rinses [26,27,69–73]. Studies have also investigated the effect and efﬁcacy of teeth whitening by HA [5]. Table 2 shows a summary of studies that investigated the whitening effects of HA oral care products. HA’s effect on whitening is physiological rather than mechanical or chemical [71]. HA increases the brightness and whiteness of the tooth surface by remineralisation which adds to the smoother and glossier appearance [31,71]. A combined experimental and clinical study investigated both the polishing prop- erties and the brightening and whitening properties of dentifrice with three different concentrations of HA [71]. It concluded that the addition of HA to dentifrice resulted in a dose-response relationship between the concentration of HA and the brightness and whitening of the tooth surface [71]. Results also showed that the addition of HA did not alter its polishing properties; therefore, the whitening effect is not due to abrasiveness [71]. Results also show that after four months of use of HA dentifrice, the brightening and whiteness became stable due to the remineralisation effect, which turns the tooth surface smoother and glossier up to a particular state [71]. The whitening effect is explained by the adherence of HA to the tooth surface, forming a layer of synthetic enamel. As HA is white, it will reﬂect more light resulting in an increase in brightness for a long-lasting whitening effect [73]. In two randomised, double-blind clinical trials with 150 and 85 participants respec- tively, one showed that dentifrice containing HA or calcium peroxide did not produce any reduction in tooth staining compared with a placebo ﬂuoride dentifrice [ 70]. The other showed that the hydrogen peroxide-containing dentifrice caused signiﬁcant lightening of tooth colouration than the HA and placebo dentifrice [69]. An observational pilot study showed that the subjective whitening perception of HA dentifrice of 25 participants was increased to varying degrees over four weeks of use [26]. However, no long-term clinical data are available on the whitening properties of HA, which is a limitation [69–71,74]. Multiple studies have concluded that the addition of HA in dentifrice has a whitening effect on the tooth surface that is not as damaging as other methods that use abrasion or oxidation, is easier to apply as it can be self-administered, and provides a good alterna- tive [26,27,71,73]. In addition, a whiter tooth colour was observed after one-time application when HA dentifrice was used, which could be enhanced after regular use [27,75].
