Introduction The domain of biomaterials holds great significance in the biomedical field because of its potential to revolutionise healthcare and enhance the quality of life for individuals all over the world. Biomaterials are artificial or natural compounds that interact with biological systems ranging from cells and tissues to whole organs (Basu 2020). They are employed in a wide range of medical applications, such as implantable devices, tissue engineering scaffolds, and drug delivery systems. Biomaterials have a long history, dating back many decades when researchers saw the need for materials that could merge smoothly with the human body, aiding healing and restoring functionality. The discovery of biocompatible and bioactive materials has opened the path for medical breakthroughs, such as joint replacements, artificial organs, and regenerative treatments (Mubarak et al. 2023). The value of biomaterials is found in their capacity to replicate the characteristics and operations of natural biological tissues, thereby providing compatibility, toughness, and biointegration. They are essential in dealing 1 1 Michigan Technological University, Houghton, MI, USA. 2 Department of Translational Medicine, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, India. 3 Industrial Waste Utilization, Nano and Biomaterials, CSIR-Advanced Materials and Processes Research Institute (AMPRI), Hoshangabad Road, Bhopal - 462026, MP, India; Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR), Ghaziabad - 201002, India. 4 Center for Disease Biology and Integrative Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo 113-8655, Japan. * Corresponding author: arpana_parihar@yahoo.com 2 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization with medical issues, such as chronic illnesses, tissue damage, and organ failure (Freedman and Mooney 2019). With the use of biomaterials, personalised medicine is made possible, allowing for customised approaches to interventions and therapies that are distinct for each patient. Additionally, biomaterials promote the development of targeted medicines, drug discovery, and diagnostic methods. They offer platforms for controlled medication release, enabling the administration of exact dosages and localised therapy. Biomaterials encourage innovation and improve healthcare technology by promoting the development of innovative medical devices (Mohd Isa et al. 2022). Additionally, materials science, engineering, biology, and medicine are all involved in the research and development of biomaterials. In order to advance this profession, it is crucial for scientists, engineers, and physicians to work together. Emerging health issues, including tissue regeneration, personalised medicine, and the incorporation of technology into medical devices, may be addressed with the research of biomaterials (Zhang et al. 2022a). The objective of this chapter is to give a general overview of biomaterials used in biomedical applications, including their history, characteristics, existing and new biomaterials, and their uses in diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. The purpose of this chapter is to emphasise the importance of biomaterials in transforming healthcare and enhancing patient outcomes. It paves the way for more developments and discoveries in the field of biomaterials research by discussing the difficulties and potential directions for the future. 2. Biomaterials: History The history of biomaterials dates back centuries, with early examples of their use in medical practises. Ancient civilisations, such as the Egyptians and Romans, utilised various natural materials, including wood, ivory, and metals, for prosthetic limbs and dental restorations. These early applications laid the foundation for developing biomaterials as a distinct field of research and innovation. In the mid-20th century, significant advancements in materials science and engineering led to the emergence of biomaterials as a specialised discipline (Hildebrand 2013). The discovery and understanding of biocompatible materials, such as stainless steel and titanium alloys, opened new possibilities for medical implants and devices. These materials exhibited improved mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and biocompatibility, setting the stage for transformative developments in healthcare (Sidambe 2014). In the 1950s, the field of polymer science began to contribute significantly to biomaterials research. Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), for instance, gained prominence as a bone cement for joint replacements. This marked a shift toward using synthetic polymers in biomedical applications, driven by their versatility, tuneable properties, and processability (Bauer et al. 2013). The 1970s witnessed a surge in biomaterials research with the advent of tissue engineering and regenerative medicine. The pioneering work of researchers such as Robert Langer and Joseph Vacanti paved the way for the concept of using biomaterial scaffolds to support tissue regeneration (Sohn et al. 2020). Synthetic and natural polymers, such as poly (lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) and collagen, became vital components in tissue engineering strategies, enabling the development of three-dimensional constructs to promote cellular growth and tissue formation (Rahmati et al. 2021). Biomaterials: An Overview for Future Utility in the Biomedical Domain 3 Over the years, biomaterials research has continued to evolve and diversify. Advances in nanotechnology have enabled the fabrication of nanostructured materials with unique properties and functionalities, leading to innovations in drug delivery systems and diagnostic devices (Suwardi et al. 2022). Integrating biomaterials with biotechnology and bioengineering has further expanded the possibilities for creating biologically inspired materials and devices (Huang et al. 2018). Figure 2 depicts the evolution of biomaterials in the biomedical domain. Today, biomaterials play an indispensable role in various fields of medicine, including orthopaedics, cardiovascular interventions, dentistry, and ophthalmology, among others. They are instrumental in developing artificial organs, biosensors, and advanced wound healing technologies (Pazhouhnia et al. 2022). Ongoing research focuses on enhancing the biocompatibility, bioactivity, and functionalisation of biomaterials, as well as exploring emerging technologies like 3D printing and bio-fabrication (Sonatkar et al. 2022). 3. Properties of Biomaterials Biomaterials for biological applications have various desired characteristics that are now the subject of intensive study and development. These characteristics are intended to improve the efficiency of biomaterials in various biological fields and solve certain problems. One key property of biomaterials is biocompatibility, ensuring that they interact harmoniously with biological systems without causing adverse reactions or toxicity. To increase the biocompatibility of materials and their integration with surrounding tissues, researchers are investigating innovative surface modifications, such as biomimetic coatings or bioactive compounds (Ostroff et al. 2022). Mechanical characteristics continue to be an important factor in the study of biomaterials. Researchers work to develop materials that are strong, stiff, and elastic enough to meet the biomechanical needs of particular tissues or organs. For instance, Figure 1: Classification of biomaterials. 4 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization Figure 2: Timeline for biomaterials in the biomedical domain. Biomaterials: An Overview for Future Utility in the Biomedical Domain 5 scaffolds used in tissue engineering must have mechanical characteristics that are similar to those of the original tissue in order to encourage correct cell migration, proliferation, and differentiation (Wang et al. 2020). Biodegradable or bioresorbable materials have drawn a lot of interest recently. These biomaterials do not require surgical removal since they gradually break down and resorb within the body over time. They are thoroughly investigated for uses including temporary implants, medication delivery mechanisms, and scaffolds for tissue engineering (Mukherjee et al. 2023). In order to maximise the pace of resorption and guarantee proper tissue repair, researchers are looking into innovative biomaterial compositions, processing methods, and degradation kinetics. The current research also focuses on the surface characteristics of biomaterials (Zhang and King 2020). To improve cell adhesion, manage protein interactions, stop bacterial adherence, or enable targeted medication delivery, researchers are looking at surface changes. The performance of biomaterials in biomedical applications will be enhanced by exploring surface patterning, functionalisation, and coating approaches to customise the interactions between biological entities and biomaterials (Khan and Alamry 2021; Yang et al. 2021). Furthermore, a rising field of research is the integration of biomaterials with cutting- Figure 3: Characteristics of an effective biomaterial to be utilised in the biomedical field (Vaiani et al. 2023). 6 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization edge technology. To generate biomaterials with exact structures, controlled release qualities, and adaptable designs, researchers are experimenting with the inclusion of nanomaterials, 3D printing technologies, and bio-fabrication approaches (Khalilov 2023). This connection creates opportunities for patient-specific tissue engineering techniques, on-demand medication administration, and personalised treatment. In a nutshell, the ongoing search for biocompatible, bioactive, mechanically appropriate, resorbable, and surface-engineered materials is the driving force behind contemporary research in biomaterials for biomedical applications (Vasanthan et al. 2022). In order to revolutionise healthcare in areas like tissue engineering, regenerative medicine, drug delivery, and medical device technologies, researchers are constantly improving these qualities. Their goal is to create biomaterials that can smoothly integrate with the human body and promote healing. 4. Traditional Biomaterials Conventional biomaterials have been employed extensively in the biomedical field for many years. These materials have a demonstrated track record of reliability, effectiveness, and body compatibility. Traditional biomaterials most frequently come in the form of metals and alloys, ceramics, and polymers (Egbo 2021), as shown in Figure 4. Orthopaedic implants, cardiovascular devices, and dental applications have all made substantial use of metals and alloys like titanium, stainless steel, and cobalt-chromium alloys. Excellent mechanical strength, longevity, and corrosion resistance are all features of these materials (Thanigaivel et al. 2022). Metals are appropriate for load-bearing applications because they can endure physiological stresses and offer structural support. It is common practise to use surface coatings and alterations to increase biocompatibility and tissue integration (Bandyopadhyay et al. 2022). Dental implants, bone graft alternatives, and coatings for metal implants all use ceramic materials, such as alumina, zirconia, and hydroxyapatite. High biocompatibility, exceptional wear resistance, and chemical stability are all characteristics of ceramics (Choi et al. 2023). In order to encourage osseointegration and establish solid contact between the implant and the surrounding tissue, they can closely match the characteristics of natural bone. Biomedical uses for polymers, both natural and artificial, are many. Natural polymers with strong biocompatibility and biodegradability include collagen, chitosan, and alginate, which are produced from biological sources (Arif et al. 2023). They are often utilised in medication delivery systems, wound dressings, and tissue engineering scaffolds. Synthetic polymers with a variety of mechanical and degrading qualities include polyethylene, polyurethane, and poly (lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) (Mukherjee et al. 2023). The development, testing, and optimisation of conventional biomaterials have been substantial. They are easily accessible for clinical usage because of the regulatory framework that has existed for a long time (Basu et al. 2022). They have a lengthy history of usage, yielding useful clinical information on their effectiveness, safety, and long-term consequences. Traditional biomaterials, however, also have drawbacks. Despite being robust and long-lasting, metals and ceramics are relatively stiff and can result in implant-related issues such as stress shielding (Losic 2021). Polymers may have constraints regarding mechanical strength and degradation control while being more Biomaterials: An Overview for Future Utility in the Biomedical Domain 7 Figure 4: Traditional biomaterials along with biomedical application (Nguyen et al. 2019; Troy et al. 2021; Vaiani et al. 2023). 8 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization flexible and versatile. Additionally, conventional biomaterials might not be bioactive enough to stimulate a particular biological response, necessitating additional alterations or coatings (Mondschein et al. 2017). 5. Emerging Biomaterials Due to their distinct qualities and potential to completely change how healthcare is provided, emerging biomaterials have attracted much attention in the biomedical community. These materials, which are frequently at the cutting edge of research and development, provide cutting-edge capabilities and functions that can solve present problems and open up new applications (Wang et al. 2021). Natural polymers, synthetic polymers, biomimetic materials, nanomaterials, and smart materials are some important subcategories of developing biomaterials. In applications for tissue engineering, wound healing, and drug administration, natural polymers generated from biological sources, such as collagen, silk, and hyaluronic acid, are becoming increasingly popular (Liu et al. 2023). These biomaterials display excellent biocompatibility, biodegradability, and bioactivity. Natural polymers can enhance cell proliferation, provide a bioactive environment, and encourage tissue regeneration (Zhang et al. 2022). When it comes to adjusting their characteristics for particular biomedical applications, synthetic polymers provide great adaptability. Examples include poly(caprolactone), poly(ethylene glycol), and poly(ethyleneimine) (Radu et al. 2023). Mechanical characteristics, degradation rates, and surface functions of synthetic polymers may all be precisely controlled through engineering. They are used in medical equipment, tissue engineering scaffolds, and drug delivery systems (Zielińska et al. 2023). The goal of biomimetic materials is to replicate the composition and operation of biological tissues or organs. Decellularized extracellular matrices (ECMs) made of tissues, for instance, offer a scaffold that closely replicates the milieu of the genuine tissue (Brown et al. 2022). These materials can all aid the adhesion, migration, and tissue regeneration of cells. Using biomimetic materials in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine is extremely promising (Anjum et al. 2022). At the nanoscale level, nanomaterials such as nanoparticles, nanofibers, and nanocomposites provide distinctive features. They are useful in biological applications because of their high surface-to-volume ratio, adjustable characteristics, and adaptable surface changes (Hassan et al. 2021). Targeted medication delivery, biosensing, bioimaging, and tissue engineering may all be accomplished with nanomaterials. Gold nanoparticles, quantum dots, and carbon nanotubes are a few examples (Harish et al. 2022). Smart materials, often referred to as stimulus-responsive materials, have dynamic characteristics that may react to outside stimuli like temperature, pH, light, or magnetic fields. Hydrogels, shape memory polymers, and drug-releasing systems are a few examples of intelligent materials (Malekmohammadi et al. 2021). When certain triggers operate on these materials, reversible alterations can occur, allowing regulated medication release, tissue actuation, or on-demand therapeutic treatments. Innovative drug delivery methods, personalised treatment, tissue regeneration, and diagnostic technologies can all benefit from emerging biomaterials, as shown Biomaterials: An Overview for Future Utility in the Biomedical Domain 9 in Figure 5. They make it possible to manipulate the characteristics of materials precisely, how they interact with biological systems, and how treatments work (Han et al. 2022). However, to completely comprehend their long-term biocompatibility, regulatory issues, and scalability for widespread clinical usage, more study is required. Researchers want to overcome current constraints, create novel solutions, and influence the future of biomedical applications by continually investigating and optimising developing biomaterials (Øvrebø et al. 2022). These resources have a huge potential to boost treatment plans, enhance patient outcomes, and progress healthcare. 6. Biomaterials in Biomedical Diagnostic Applications Biomaterials are essential for breakthroughs in disease diagnosis, monitoring, and personalised treatment in diagnostic biomedical applications. In order to improve sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy, these materials are included in a variety of diagnostic instruments and processes. Applications for biomaterial-based diagnostics are numerous and include microfluidic devices, imaging agents, and biosensors. In order to identify and measure certain biomolecules or analytes, analytical tools called biosensors combine a biomaterial with a transducer. Antibodies, enzymes, nucleic acids, and synthetic receptors that specifically bind to target molecules can all be utilised as biomaterials in biosensors (Khan et al. 2021, 2022; Parihar et al. 2022a, 2022c, 2023b, 2023a). To identify and measure certain antigens or antibodies in biological samples, immunosensors, for instance, use antibodies immobilised on a biomaterial surface (Huang et al. 2021). This makes detecting illnesses, including autoimmune disorders, quickly and accurately, cancer biomarkers, and infectious microorganisms possible. A “turn-on” magnetic fluorescence biosensor based on graphene quantum dots (GQDs), iron oxide (Fe 3O4), and molybdenum disulfide Figure 5: An overview of recent and current biomaterials research trends in the biomedical area (Sánchez- Cid et al. 2022). 10 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization (MoS2) nanosheets is an illustration of a natural biomaterial utilised in a biosensing application. This biosensor is made to separate and identify circulating tumour cells (CTCs) quickly, effectively, and sensitively. The biosensor uses photoluminescent GQDs functionalised with an aptamer that specifically targets receptors for the adhesion molecule for epithelial cells (EpCAM). A potential biosensing nanocomposite for fluorescence-guided tumour cell enrichment and bioimaging, the biosensing system exhibits minimal cytotoxicity, high capture efficiency, quick detection, and the capacity to identify as little as ten tumour cells in whole blood (Cui et al. 2019). Likewise, an example of a biopolymer used in an immunosensor is a label-free electrochemical strategy employing a glassy carbon electrode (GCE) modified with a biocompatible and conducting biopolymer functionalised molybdenum disulfide-reduced graphene oxide (CS–MoS 2/rGO) nanohybrid. This immunosensor detects specific antibodies against the SARS-CoV-2 virus through the interaction of recombinant SARS-CoV-2 Spike RBD protein (rSP) with the antibodies, resulting in decreased current responses measured by differential pulse voltammetry (DPV) (Yadav et al. 2023a). Medical imaging techniques include magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), positron emission tomography (PET), and ultrasound, all employ imaging agents based on biomaterials. These substances, which are frequently nanoparticles or contrast agents, are made to make certain tissues, organs, or disease signs more visible. Lignocellulosic- based nanoparticles made from rose biomass waste illustrate a biomaterial utilised as an imaging agent. When stimulated, these nanoparticles’ inherent luminescence causes them to produce light in the near-infrared (NIR) spectrum. They provide a strong photoluminescence signal without the necessity for encapsulation or imaging agent functionalisation. With an average size of 156 nm, they exhibit little in vitro toxicity (IC50 approximately 3 mg/mL), and at dosages as high as 57 mg/kg, they exhibit no in vivo toxicity (Arcentales et al. 2023). Due to their favourable properties, including simple manufacturing, biodegradability, and biocompatibility, biopolymers have drawn much interest. In addition, early transition metal nanoclusters known as inorganic polyoxometalates (POMs), a type of metal-oxygen anionic compounds, have a variety of useful applications in both the biomedical and industrial sectors (Mousavi et al. 2022). Similarly, Shaheen et al. (2023) produced composite hydrogel beads using biopolymers and ammonium metavanadate (AMV) to develop a biomaterial-based imaging agent. Through electrostatic interactions, cationic chitosan, chitosan/gelatine, or chitosan/methylcellulose were crosslinked with AMV to create the hydrogel beads. These hydrogel beads were yellow in colour and showed strong mechanical properties. The biomaterial-based hydrogel mixture demonstrated outstanding luminescence and adsorption abilities, good swelling behaviour (up to 432% maximum swelling), and adjustable physicochemical characteristics. The hydrogel beads demonstrated specific ascorbic acid sensing behaviour, making them appropriate for imaging applications. Furthermore, the hydrogels’ antibacterial efficacy and cytotoxicity against embryonic kidney cells were evaluated, which revealed the dose-dependent cytotoxicity of the embedded imaging agents (Shaheen et al. 2023). Biomaterials: An Overview for Future Utility in the Biomedical Domain 11 Biomaterials are used in microfluidic devices as microchannels, surfaces, or coatings to manipulate, analyse, and categorise biological samples precisely. These gadgets provide portable, high-throughput, and miniature diagnostic platforms (Parihar et al. 2020, 2021b, 2021a, 2023e; Yadav et al. 2023; Parihar and Dube 2023; Parihar et al. 2023d; Parihar and Khan 2023). Wearable contact lenses for non-invasive diagnostics are being developed, thanks to biomaterials revolutionising microfluidic devices. Yang et al. (2020) have developed flexible contact lenses with biocompatibility, hydrophilicity, and elasticity using a UV-curable biomaterial. Tears may now travel via capillary networks and reservoirs thanks to tear inlets built into the lenses. Biomarkers, such as glucose, chloride, and urea, elicited colorimetric changes by interacting with chemical substrates embedded into the lenses. In order to calculate the concentrations of biomarkers, external equipment was used to take pictures and analyse RGB data. In vitro investigations employing a synthetic microfluidic hydrogel eyeball showed reliable lens functioning. The tear storage and diagnostic capabilities of these biomaterial-based microfluidic contact lenses represent an interesting development for point-of-care diagnostics (Yang et al. 2020). In addition to this, Wang et al. (2023) created a point-of-care (POC) detection tool for salmon rotting utilising biomaterials. They combined bromothymol blue (BTB) and silk fibroin methacryloyl (SilMA) to generate a pH-responsive colorimetric microneedle (MN) patch (BTB/SilMA@MN patch). The MN patch included needle points that could cut through cling film on food and draw fluids from the fish tissue. The MN patch’s colour changed as a result of the extracted fluids being transferred to the backing layer. The salmon’s freshness could be seen in the colour transition from yellow to yellowish green to green. With the use of this POC equipment, salmon spoilage may be quickly and non-destructively determined, giving customers a simple and reliable way to gauge the quality of their food (Wang et al. 2023). Biomaterials, including hydrogels, quantum dots, gold nanoparticles, DNA/RNA probes, and fluorescent dyes, are a few examples that are employed in diagnostic applications. With the help of certain biological ligands, hydrogels may be functionalised to collect and concentrate desired biomarkers from difficult samples (Liu et al. 2022). Improved sensitivity, quick analysis, smaller sample quantities, and the possibility for point-of-care testing are some benefits of biomaterial-based diagnostics. They make it possible to diagnose diseases early, track treatment outcomes, and use personalised medical techniques (Gačanin et al. 2020). Current research focuses on creating new biomaterials, enhanced sensing methods, and digital technology integration for more accurate, effective, and easily accessible diagnostic instruments. By enabling early detection, precise diagnosis, and focused treatments for different diseases, these developments have the potential to revolutionise healthcare, as briefly described in Table 1. 7. Biomaterials in Biomedical Therapeutic Applications By providing a wide range of therapy and recovery options, biomaterials have transformed biomedical therapeutic applications. These materials are widely employed in many therapeutic methods, such as implanted medical devices, drug delivery systems, tissue engineering, and regenerative medicine. Biomaterials 12 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization serve as a scaffold or matrix in tissue engineering to facilitate the development and regeneration of sick or damaged tissues. They support the development of functional tissues by fostering an environment that is favourable for cellular adhesion, migration, and differentiation (Abdollahiyan et al. 2021). Natural polymers, synthetic polymers, or hybrid materials can be used to create biomaterial scaffolds that replicate the characteristics of the target tissue. They act as a support structure for cells to proliferate and regenerate, allowing for the replacement or repair of damaged organs or tissues (Elhadad et al. 2022). Biomaterials with electroconductive qualities are gaining popularity in tissue engineering applications for regenerating tissues, including myocardial, neurological, musculoskeletal, and bone tissue—tissues that require electrical activity. 2D MXene (Ti 3C2Tx) was covalently crosslinked with collagen type I to develop a biohybrid platform by Asaro et al. (2023). Together with the increased rigidity and improved electrical conductivity offered by the two-dimensional titanium carbide material, the resultant platform demonstrated the bio functionality of collagen. Additionally, biomaterials are essential in drug delivery systems because they improve the effectiveness, security, and targeted administration of medicinal substances. Controlled release profiles can be obtained by encapsulating medications inside biocompatible and biodegradable carriers, such as nanoparticles, liposomes, or hydrogels. Biomaterial-based drug delivery methods enable localised or targeted distribution to certain tissues or cells, reducing adverse effects, and improving therapeutic results (Fenton et al. 2018). They can also increase medication stability, solubility, and bioavailability. For illustration, Kamaci and Kaya (2023) produced biodegradable hybrid hydrogels for drug delivery applications employing polyurethane with azomethine as a synthetic polymer and chitosan as a natural polymer. The hydrogels’ thermal, mechanical, wettability, water uptake, biodegradation, protein absorption, drug loading, and release characteristics were examined, and FT-IR and SEM analyses were used to characterise them. The outcomes showed that the hybrid hydrogels had good mechanical strength, hydrophilicity, ability to absorb water, and biodegradation behaviour. The hybrid hydrogels also had a 50% drug release, which along with their favourable characteristics for drug delivery applications, made them a good choice for the controlled administration of the medication 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) (Kamaci and Kaya 2023). Biomaterials serve as the basis for the creation and operation of implantable medical devices. Implants, prosthetics, orthopaedic devices, and cardiovascular devices are all made using biomaterials with the right mechanical characteristics, biocompatibility, and corrosion resistance. For instance, bioceramics or titanium alloys are frequently utilised in orthopaedic implants, whereas biocompatible polymers are used in tissue scaffolds or cardiovascular stents. The quality of life for patients is enhanced by the support, durability, and integration with the surrounding tissues that biomaterials in implanted devices offer (Nasr Azadani et al. 2022). Biomaterial advancements have resulted in the creation of mechanically compliant craniofacial implants that prioritise the preservation of the cerebrum after trauma or neurosurgery treatments. Rahmani et al. (2022) used powder bed fusion technology and powder metallurgy to embed three different types of bioactive ceramic powders into metallic scaffolds. The study also looked at using TiNi and Ti 22Al25Nb alloys 14 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization for their dynamic impact resistance (Rahmani et al. 2022). The results demonstrated reduced porosity and limited cracking in the impact region, indicating the promise of these advancements in creating more effective and durable craniofacial implants. Biomaterial-based implant technological advancements have addressed the critical concern of peri-implant infection in dental implants. However, a recent development by Wu et al. (2021) involves an N-halamine polymeric coating on the titanium surface that exhibits long-lasting, renewable antibacterial properties while maintaining stability and biocompatibility. Importantly, the coating’s antibacterial activity lasts long in vitro, in animal models, and even in the human oral cavity during the osseointegration process. Furthermore, the coating is easily reusable using chlorine, allowing for a renewable antibacterial coating idea for dental implants (Wu et al. 2021). Challenges and Future Directions Although the field of biomaterials has made significant strides, there are still a number of obstacles to overcome and possibilities to seize for future development and use. The demand for increased biocompatibility and long-term stability of biomaterials within the physiological milieu is a significant problem. While many biomaterials initially appear compatible, extended interactions with host tissues may result in Biomaterials: An Overview for Future Utility in the Biomedical Domain 15 unfavourable reactions or degradation, limiting their usefulness (Winter et al. 2007; Raza et al. 2022). It is still important to create biomaterials that can operate properly and maintain their structural integrity throughout time. The ability to precisely regulate how cells and tissues interact with biomaterials is another difficulty. In order to encourage tissue regeneration and integration, biomaterials should be made to direct cellular behaviour, such as adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation (Yu et al. 2015). A greater comprehension of cell-material interactions, including surface changes, bioactive chemicals, and tissue-specific signals, is necessary to accomplish this (Joyce et al. 2021). Additionally, the creation of biomaterials with many functions is a developing field. Highly desired biomaterials can administer therapeutic agents, offer prolonged drug release, react to outside stimuli, or actively engage with cells and tissues (Fenton et al. 2018). In order to create such multifunctional biomaterials, the integration of cutting-edge technologies such as nanotechnology, 3D printing, and bio-fabrication offers promise. Another crucial factor is dealing with the biomaterials’ scalability and cost-effectiveness. The production of many biomaterials in large numbers or at reasonable prices is frequently difficult, especially for those with complicated structures or advanced characteristics (Ventola 2014). The transition of biomaterials from the lab to clinical applications can be facilitated by streamlining production procedures and investigating novel fabrication techniques. Future potential for biomaterials includes personalised and regenerative medicine, which are developing fields. Intense research is being done on producing tissue-engineered constructions for organ replacement and regeneration, as well as customising biomaterials to the demands of individual patients (Bomkamp et al. 2022). In a nutshell, even though the field of biomaterials has made great progress, issues including biocompatibility, cellular interactions, multifunctionality, scalability, and personalised medicine still need to be resolved (Wang et al. 2023). The future of biomaterials will be enabled by creative solutions for a variety of biomedical applications, eventually improving patient outcomes, as shown in Figure 6, by addressing these issues and using developing technology. Conclusion With their enormous potential to revolutionise healthcare and raise people’s quality of life worldwide, biomaterials have become an essential part of the biomedical sector. They have a long, illustrious history, and conventional and novel biomaterials have developed significantly in recent years. The effectiveness of the use of biomaterials in diverse biological areas is greatly influenced by their features, including biocompatibility, mechanical capabilities, biodegradability, and surface changes. Both diagnostic and therapeutic applications benefit greatly from the use of biomaterials. Biomaterials are used in diagnostics to create microfluidic devices, medical imaging agents, and biosensors that enable early illness detection, accurate diagnosis, and individualised care. Biomaterials are used as scaffolds in therapeutics for tissue engineering, drug delivery systems, and implanted medical devices, promoting controlled drug release, controlled tissue regeneration, and better patient outcomes. However, biomaterials face a number of difficulties and chances in the future. The development of multifunctional biomaterials, scalability, cost-effectiveness, and precise control of cell-material interactions are continuing problems. Personalised medicine, regenerative medicine, and the incorporation of cutting-edge technologies like nanotechnology and 3D printing are the future directions. The future of biomaterials will be paved with solutions to these problems and the effective use of cutting-edge technology. It will result in novel treatments for a variety of biological issues, revolutionising medical care and eventually enhancing patient outcomes. Biomaterials will continue to influence medicine’s future and help progress healthcare technology as long as scientists, engineers, and doctors collaborate on their research. Introduction The term “biomaterial” refers to any material that can be employed for biomedical and therapeutic applications. Biomaterials are not a new field of study; they have been exercised in medical science over the last many decades. Non-biological elements were first introduced into the human body many ages ago, in pre-history. They are non-viable materials that are utilized in medical devices to interface with the biological system. They are employed in cardiovascular materials, neural prostheses, bone substitutes, dental implants, orthopedics prostheses, plasma and cytapheresis, and dialysis (Hanker and Giammara 1988). Different branches of sciences, viz . medicine, biology, tissue engineering, chemistry, and material science, are all incorporated under biomaterial science. In some cases, surgical repairs to the body are frequently required because of trauma, degeneration, and illness. Some organs, viz. knees, elbows, hips, finger joints, teeth, vertebrae, and other bodily vital organs such as kidney, heart, and skin are generally replaced in these procedures. All of these materials, each performing a certain function when live materials are substituted, are referred to as biomaterials. There are many definitions given to biomaterials; according to Helmus et al. (2008), biomaterials are materials employed in medical applications in medical devices, especially in situations where the device contacts are temporarily inserted and have specific design requirements. A biomaterial is a material used in the form of specialized structures to construct prostheses and biomedical devices that are designed to replace or restore impaired body functions in order to save or make life better (Gobbi et al. 2020; Miljana et al. 2020). A biomaterial is a substance that has been designed to take a form that can be utilized to direct the course of any therapeutic or diagnostic operation in human beings and veterinary medicine by controlling interactions with living system components (Heimann 2020). Some commonly used biomaterials for medical implants are described as bioactive materials, synthetic and biodegradable polymers, natural macromolecules, metal, carbon, and ceramics that may include cellulose, silicon rubber, dacron, poly (methyl methacrylate), polyurithanes, hydrogels, stainless steel, alumina, titanium, hydroxyapatite and collagen (Boretos and Eden 1984; Helmus 2003; Markhoff et al. 2017). Different biomaterials are used to design different types of medical devices depending on their properties (Table 1). The major goal is to extend the lifespan of the biomaterial implanted or to ensure that it lasts to the end of life without defects or the need for reoperation, thereby improving the patient’s quality of life. In nature, a variety of materials and alloys are accessible, but only a few of them are biocompatible (Jenkoa et al. 2018). As a result, the biomaterial must meet a number of basic properties particular to the application, including acceptable mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, biocompatibility, high wear resistance, low friction, and mechanical compatibility (Gobbi et al. 2020). The objective of this chapter is to introduce the reader to some basic properties of biomaterials. 2. Properties of Biomaterial Three fundamental properties must be met for any material to be used for biomedical applications. The first requirement is that the material be compatible, meaning the organism should not perceive it as a foreign thing. Second, the material must be biodegradable; it must disintegrate harmlessly in the organism’s body, allowing it to resume normal function. Third, the material must be mechanically sound; for load-bearing structural replacements, the material must have similar or superior mechanical stability to assure the graft’s high reliability. The factors that should be taken into account while selecting a biological material include a clear specification of the material’s intended function, a precise description of the environment in which it must operate, as well as the influence that environment will have on the material’s qualities; a clear knowledge of what it means to be safe for human usage. Some of the important properties (Figure 1) that a biomaterial should possess in order to perform well as an implant in a biological system are given below: 2.1 Biocompatible One of the most important properties that differentiate a biomaterial from other materials is its biocompatibility. The proper host response to biomaterials is a concept used to describe this phenomenon. Biomaterials success is inextricably linked to their acceptance by the human body. A biomaterial must not cause any adverse effect to the beneficiary, viz. any injury, cytotoxicity, mutagenicity, or carcinogenicity (Freire et al. 2015). A biomaterial implant should be compatible in order to work properly in the body of the patient (Todros et al. 2021). Biocompatibility generally refers to biomaterial’s ability to perform in a given application while exhibiting a sufficient host reaction without causing an inflammatory or allergic reaction (Davis et al. 2022). Biomaterials are required to undergo a variety of tests to determine their biocompatibility, which are carried out by following the recommendations of several regulatory organizations (Williams et al. 2008). Biocompatibility testing determines a 24 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization biomaterial’s technical suitability for human use by scrutinizing possibly detrimental physiological effects (Davis et al. 2022). Some of the common problems associated with biomaterials mainly include premature wear and dislocation of hip and knee prostheses, infection and rejection of dental implants, restenosis and obstruction of coronary stents, etc. Furthermore, it is estimated that bacterial biofilms formed on surfaces of biomaterials, implants, or surgical devices cause 80% of infections in hospitals. These biofilms are up to thousands of times more resistant to antimicrobial agents than planktonic bacteria (Costerton et al. 1999). Henceforth, the implant’s own physical, mechanical, degradation properties, sterilization (implant’s surface free from all types of microorganisms), toxicological aspect (intoxicating substances), implantation site, surgical procedure, material-cell interfacial interactions, and load- bearing capacity all play a significant role in the biocompatibility of a biomedical implant’s clinical performance (Figure 2) (Davis et al. 2022). Biomaterial must be non-thrombogenic in blood-contacting applications to avoid thrombi and emboli-related problems. Biomaterials and tissue-engineered constructions that imitate the vasculature are being established in response to this challenge. Various biomaterials-based blood-contacting medical devices are frequently utilized to treat a variety of cardiovascular disorders. Cardiovascular device failure is frequently caused by thrombus development (Braune et al. 2019). There are presently no clinically viable biomaterials that can completely prevent thrombosis in more difficult situations (i.e., low flow in the venous system). Although some biomaterials diminish protein adsorption or cell adhesion, thrombosis and inflammation are still a concern. Elastin is an extracellular matrix macromolecule that contributes to arterial elasticity, accounting for up to 50% of the vessel’s non-hydrated mass. Elastin is a widely used biomaterial because of its non- thrombogenic properties (Waterhouse et al. 2021). 2.3 Biodegradable Biodegradable biomaterials are of considerable interest because of their potential to be absorbed gradually by the body. A biodegradable product must have a harmless breakdown product that the body’s metabolic pathways can eliminate. Biopolymers are now widely recognized and employed in biomedical applications for a variety of functions. Tissue engineering, drug delivery systems, and therapeutics have all benefited from these biodegradable polymers. (1) Large implants including bone Figure 2: Important factors affecting biocompatibility of biomedical implant. 26 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization plates, bone screws, and contraceptive reservoir; (2) small implants viz . sutures, staples, and micro-sized drug delivery vehicles; (3) multifilament meshes or porous structures for tissue engineering; and (4) plain membranes for guided tissue regeneration are some of the present biomedical applications of biodegradable polymeric materials (Vert 2005). The most widely utilized biodegradable compounds are homopolymers or copolymers of alpha hydroxyl acids, such as lactic and glycolic acid. The most important significance of biodegradable implants over metal implants is that they do not need a second surgical procedure to remove the devices. Drug delivery systems or other implants made of natural polymers reduce the risk of persistent inflammation, immunological responses, and toxicity, which are common with synthetic polymers (Bostman and Pihlajamaki 2000). Polymeric materials are quickly displacing other material types in biomaterials, such as metals, alloys, and ceramics, due to their versatility. The sales of biomaterials are continuously increasing every year, and it was predicted that there will be a huge market for biodegradable biomaterials in the coming decades (Naira et al. 2007). Biodegradable biomaterials should have some important properties, as shown below (Lloyd 2002).  The substance must have a long shelf life.  The breakdown product must not be hazardous, digestible and excreted from the body.  The material should have permeability and processibility suitable for the intended use.  The deterioration time of the material should correlate to the healing or regeneration process.  Mechanical properties of the material must really be appropriate for the application, and changes in mechanical properties with deterioration must be compatible with the healing and regeneration process.  The material’s mechanical characteristics should be appropriate for the application, and the change in mechanical properties with deterioration should be compatible with the healing or regeneration process. Polymeric biomaterials can be divided into two types based on how they degrade: (1) hydrolyticӓlly degrӓdӓble polymers and (2) enzymӓticӓlly degradable polymers. 1. Hydrolyticӓlly Degrӓdӓble Polymers Polymers with hydrolytically labile chemical linkages in their backbone are hydrolytically degradable. Esters, orthoesters, anhydrides, carbonates, amides, urethanes, ureas, and other functional groups are sensitive to hydrolysis (Li et al. 1999). Natural polymers were the first biodegradable biomaterials to be employed in clinical trials. When compared to enzymatically degradable polymers, hydrolytically degradable polymers are chosen as implants because there is less variation from location to location and patient to patient (Katti et al. 2002). Properties of Biomaterial 27 2. Enzymaticӓlly Degrӓdӓble Polymers The majority of polymers found in nature are degraded by enzymes. However, depending on the availability and quantity of enzymes, the rate of enzymatically degradable polymer degradation in vivo varies substantially depending on the implantation site. The rate of degradation of these polymers can also be influenced by chemical modifications. 2.4 Non-Toxic Non-toxicity applies to biomaterials that are non-carcinogenic, non-pyrogenic, non-allergic, non-inflammatory, and blood-compatible. The term “toxicology of biomaterials” refers to the components that emerge from biomaterials. In the live body environment, a well-designed biomaterial should do its purpose while causing no harm to other cells. A well-designed biomaterial should fulfill its function in the living body environment while causing no harm to other cells, organs, and entire organisms. It is plausible to believe that unless it is designed to do so, a biomaterial should not release or create anything from its mass (Ratner et al. 2003; Raghavendra et al. 2015). 2.5 Mechanical Properties and Performance The physical parameters of a biomaterial must be coordinated with the target tissue or organ in the live system where it will be transplanted. Biomaterial utilized for medical devices must meet mechanical and performance parameters comparable to those of the organ or tissue being replaced (Hans et al. 2021). Metal biomaterials are said to make up 70–80% of implant biomaterials, and they are significant in the remodeling of tissues that have been damaged, particularly hard tissues (Niinomi 2012). The mechanical and physical characteristics of the designed biomaterials can be placed into three categories. 2.5.1 Mechanical Performance The mechanical performance of biomaterials, as medical devices, reveals their mechanical qualities in order to function properly in the living bodily environment. The biomaterial’s mechanical properties differ depending on the application spot. Some of the most important properties of biomaterial to evaluate prior to implantation include elastic modulus, tensile strength, yield strength, corrosion, creep, and hardness (Prasad et al. 2017). Mechanical characteristics are extremely important in hard tissue applications. The production of acceptable biomaterials that can assist human tissue repair and regeneration is ongoing, and biomaterial mechanical qualities are important to their effectiveness in the therapeutic context. 28 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 2.5.2 Mechanical Durability The amount of time it takes a biomaterial to perform its principal function efficiently is referred to as durability. Properties of Biomaterial 29 2.6 Non-Carcinogenic A designed biomaterial must fulfill its purpose in the living body tissues without affecting the other parts of the body. For that, biomaterial should be non-carcinogenic. Any carcinogenic or mutagenic action, physical irritation, inflammation, and toxicity should be avoided by patient body parts or tissues that come into contact with implants (Fathi et al. 2003; Freire et al. 2015). Under certain circumstances, the implantation of biomaterial-related products into body tissues is linked with the growth of tumors. There are many factors that can be responsible for carcinogenicity, viz., the nature of the material themselves, the nature of the host, and the relationship between the host and biomaterial. Some of the properties of biomaterial that are known to have an influence on the carcinogenicity process mainly include surface chemistry, intrinsic chemistry, chemical nature of released components, if any, physical and crystallographic nature of any released particulate components, size, shape, hardness of the surface, electrical and magnetic properties and radioactivity of the biomaterial. With respect to interactions within the host-material system, some factors that should be taken into account also include the extent and method of surgery, subsequent complications, and the duration of contact between the host and biomaterial (Thevenot et al. 2009). When assessing the potential of implanted materials to cause cancer in humans, host characteristics such as sex, age, occupation, lifestyle, genetic factors as well as pharmacological status must be considered. 2.7 Corrosion, Wear, and Fatigue Properties Biomaterial should be highly corrosion-resistant. This is particularly problematic in the case of metal implants. Corrosion is one of the most important factors impacting the life and performance of metal and alloy orthopedic implants. Metal implants can produce metallic ions that can collect in adjacent tissues or be transferred to other parts of the body when bodily fluids are present. Released ions have been discovered to trigger allergic and harmful reactions (Geetha et al. 2019). The corrosion resistance of an implant material influences its usefulness and endurance, as well as being a key factor in biocompatibility. The body’s environment is hostile, posing a number of issues in terms of corrosion control. Some of the major issues associated with medical device implant failure have been identified as fatigue, fracture, and wear. Though fatigue fracture and wear are common in orthopedic applications such as hip joint prostheses, they can also be lethal in mechanical heart valves (Teoh 2000). The prevention of biomaterial corrosion has become essential, especially in order to avoid the inflammation and allergic reactions generated by biomaterial implants in the human body (Asri 2017). Low wear resistance leads the implant to discharge wear debris into the surrounding tissue, resulting in the development of harmful enzymes, inflammation, infection, osteolysis, pain, and bone resorption (Li et al. 2004). The material’s wear resistance is important for the biomaterial’s correct functioning, preventing it from unraveling and causing reactions in the tissue where it is deposited, therefore increasing the patient’s quality of life (Gobbi and Gobbi 2018). Therefore, the implants should be designed with wear-resistant materials. 30 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 2.8 Design and Manufacturability A biomaterial is a non-viable substance designed to interact with living processes. One of the most important considerations for biomaterials is proper material design. The biomaterials’ reliable and efficient qualities allow them to be used in a physiological medium (Yoruc and Sener 2012). In order to create well-known biomaterials, these distinctive features are equipped with an appropriate combination of chemical, biological, mechanical, and physical capabilities (Williams 1987). These biomaterials were created by combining polymers, viz. metals, ceramics, and composite materials. Manufacturability refers to an item’s ability to be manufactured with relative ease and at a low cost while maintaining high reliability. In the case of biomaterials, manufacturability refers to the material’s ability to be sterilized using a verified sterilization process that is considered adequate for biomedical purposes. Standard sterilization treatments, such as autoclaving, dry heat, ethylene oxide, radiations, etc., are expected not to harm the material. Advances in material technology have helped to broaden the ingredients used to design various types of orthopedic implants. As a result, nanoparticles may mimic the surface characteristics of natural tissues, such as wettability, topography, chemistry, and energy (Chen et al. 2022). 2.9 Absence of Foreign Body Reaction Foreign body response (FBR) is an inherent reaction that occurs when any foreign material is introduced into the body (Franz et al. 2011). Immune responses to foreign bodies defend the organism from bacteria, fungi, viruses, and traumas, but they also isolate the implant, rendering it non-functional. FBR generally consists of foreign body giant cells and macrophages that may remain at the interface of tissue and implant for the rest of the implant’s life (Anderson 2001). In severe cases, the implants must be removed or replaced. The implantation procedure damages the tissue surrounding the foreign object, resulting in an inflammatory response. This inflammatory response transforms into a fibrotic response that surrounds and isolates the implanted material (Carnicer-Lombarte 2021). When a foreign material is implanted with the intention of delivering a therapy, both the acute and chronic stages of FBR pose significant challenges to its integrity and therapeutic function. The body’s system activates the rejection mechanism, which causes the foreign body to be eliminated if the chemical signal from implanted material is detected as a threat and cannot be terminated (Bharadwaj 2021). There are some ways by which foreign body reactions can be prevented or decreased. The surface of the artificial implant can be changed with condensed aromatic structures containing free radicals, allowing for covalent attachment of host proteins in their native shape. Immune cells are not stimulated because the entire protein coating precludes direct contact with the implant surface. As a result, the organism’s immune response is not elicited, and the artificial implant is not isolated from the surrounding tissue. There is no collagen capsule, macrophage activity is low, cell proliferation is low, and inflammatory activity is minimal. The best implants are ones that are reactive yet do not induce immunological reactions (Sohling et al. 2022). According to the literature review, Properties of Biomaterial 31 all artificial implants generate an immunological reaction and 35% of them require a secondary operation. Immunosuppressive drugs can control the immune response to artificial implants (Kastellorizios 2015). However, such a depressed immune system cannot protect the living body from diseases. 3. Conclusion The increasing demand in the medical field for bio-alternatives that may perform the live activities of biological organs in their absence has perked researchers’ interest in developing biomaterials with unique properties. Currently, numerous biomaterials with different properties are accessible for designing medical devices. However, there are several obstacles to overcoming different reactions of the body tissues against them. Henceforth, there is a strong need for novel research to generate biomaterials that are more compatible with living bodily tissues. Because of its properties, such as strong corrosion and wear resistance, high strength, and stiffness compared to other types of biomaterials, composite or biocomposite biomaterials may be able to meet these needs in the future. In order to get the best clinical results, future trends must combine mechanically superior metals with ceramics and polymers’ biocompatibility and biofunctionality. Further, biomaterial properties covered here provide the necessary basis for stakeholders, tissue engineers, material scientists, and emerging researchers to design befitting biomaterial devices and implants. The major problem that arises here is the overlapping understanding of bio- erosion and biodegradation. Some ecologists define biodegradable polymers as solely related to biological environments, while others compare them to processes such as thermal oxidation, photolysis, radiolysis, hydrolytic breakdown, etc. However, Gliding proposed that biodegradable polymers actually undergo in vivo degradation, while Graham and Wood define them as systems that automatically degrade into simple and soluble products that can easily escape from the site of degradation (Christopherson et al. 2009). According to Griffin, only such substances can be called biodegradable polymers, which require bio-substances like enzymes or microorganisms for degradation. However, polylactides cannot fall under this category because they require only a high temperature and neutral pH, which are physical factors for the degradation of substances. A polymer can be further categorized as absorbable, resorbable or bioabsorbable with respect to the time it requires for degradation, regardless of both enzymatic and non-enzymatic hydrolysis. 1.3 Bio-Erosion Heller described “bio-erosion” as a conversion of water-insoluble to water-soluble material, where the involvement of major chemicals is not mentioned, whereas Langer and Peppas discussed erodibility in context with the ability of a polymer to degrade and, as a result, control rate of drug release (Repanas 2016). Kumar coined the term “biodegradable polymer”, referring to polymers that secrete degrading enzymes linked to physiological cleavage in the molecular structure of the polymer. However, bio-erodible or bio-assimilable processes involve hydrolytic cleavage without enzyme participation (Corey 2007) (Figure 3). Vert et al . have elaborated this process as a breakdown of polymer without any proof of exclusion of substances Designing of Materials for Biodegradation and Bio-Erosion 39 from the body, whereas they defined bioresorbable as substances which, after degradation, further resort and elimination of materials is done through natural pathways respectively as by-products of metabolism (Frohbergh 2012). 1.4 Nanomaterials The biosynthesis of materials has gained increasing attention for the use of novel products, leading to the development of new products and devices with great impacts across different fields, from sensoristics to biomedicine. Such nanomaterials have become an important field of research and development. In spite of varied applications, they also look toward environmental and sustainability concerns, which also include a wide range of domains that influence our society and our way of life (Lin and Kang 2021). Investigations for improvements in properties and new functionalities are important goals for the discovery and better understanding, characterization, and manufacturing of new nanomaterials for adequate systems (Kim et al. 2019). Investigation of nanocellulose/nanocarbons hybrid materials have demonstrated both academic and technological importance and offered great research opportunities within cross-disciplinary areas. Nanocellulose, which refers to cellulose with a nanoscale dimension, encompasses cellulose nanocrystals, cellulose nanofibrils, and bacterial cellulose (Hutmacher et al. 2015). It displays outstanding features such as biocompatibility, eco-friendliness, renewability, interesting reinforcing potential, hydrogen-bonding capacity, low thermal expansion coefficient, dimensional stability, high elastic modulus, high specific surface area and low density (Parihar et al. 2024; Schuman et al. 1995; Phull et al. 2016; Wakitani et al. 1989; Wiesmann et al. 2003). Various nanocellulose-based composites, which found application in different fields, have been developed during the last two decades. However, numerous challenges need to be addressed to achieve the full requirement of advanced materials (Yang et al. 2018; Khan et al. 2018; Marks et al. 1991; Lepistö et al. 1994; Wachol-Drewek et al. 1996). Accordingly, several research activities continue to be performed by different research groups worldwide to develop the next generation of nanomaterials and fully explore the potential of nanocellulose. Nanocarbons are another exciting type of potential nanomaterials, which has received tremendous attention since the discovery of fullerenes over 30 years ago (Vaneerdeweg et al. 2003; Mitra et al. 2013; Liu et al. 2020; Bello et al. 2020; Young et al. 2005). They include carbon nanotubes, graphene and carbon dots. They exhibit outstanding thermal, electrical, optical and mechanical features, and they can be employed in a wide range of applications such as composites, microelectronics, biomedical, conductive films, sensors, adsorbents, catalysis, energy storage, and coating, among others. Actual and possible applications of biodegradable polymers in medicine are shown, and most of the applications are for surgery. The largest and longest use of biodegradable polymers is for suturing. Suture materials are required to keep wounds together until they hold sufficiently well by themselves. They provide artificial fiber support until the natural fiber (collagen) is synthesized and woven into a strong scar. Collagen fibers obtained from animal intestines have long been used as absorbable sutures following chromium treatment (Meftahi et al. 2009). Throughout the history of surgery, absorbable sutures have been derived almost exclusively from various forms of collagen, such as catgut. Catgut, however, produces an allergic reaction in a number of patients, along with other problems such as fast loss of mechanical strength, problems with knot holding, etc. (Figure 7). Baptist presented the idea of synthetic biodegradable sutures based on PHB, and in 1966, Soppimath et al. reported the manufacture of biodegradable poly (L-lactic acid) sutures (Garg et al. 2004) Huggins (Yang et al. 2018) reported the spinning of poly (glycolic acid in 1954). In 1967, Schmitt and Polistina obtained a patent on PGA sutures, which led to the first commercial synthetic biodegradable suture (Dexon®) manufactured by American Cynamid Co in 1970 (Yang et al. 2018). DuPont considered the polymer of homologous poly (lactide) (PLLA) for the same purpose (Ma et al. 2020). A copolymer of 92 mol% glycolide and 8 mol% lactide led to the development of the second commercial synthetic biodegradable suture (Vicryl®) (Sun et al. 2020; Gomes et al. 2019). The sutures made from these glycolide polymers are of braid type processed from multi -filaments, but synthetic absorbable sutures of mono-filament type also at present are commercially available. Biodegradable sutures have wide applications not only in closing wounds in soft tissues but also in repair of tendons, ligaments, and dislocation of joints (Ahmed and Ikram 2016; Lubben et al. 2003). Also, by constructing gauzes, felt or velour dressings from biodegradable fibers one can manufacture surgical dressing to protect a wound surface, such as burn, traumatic injury or surgical incision and adhesion to tissues (Zhao et al. 2017). Liquid-type products are mostly used for these purposes. Immediately after application of a liquid to a defective tissue where homeostasis, sealing or adhesion is needed, the liquid sets to a gel and covers the defect to stop bleeding, seal a hole, or adhere two separated tissues. As the gelled material is no longer necessary after healing of the treated tissue, it should be biodegradable and finally absorbed into the body. The biomaterials used to prepare such liquid products include fibrinogen (a serum protein), 2-cyanoacrylates, and a gelatin/resorcinol/formaldehyde mixture. 2-cyanoacrylates solidify upon contact with tissues as a result of polymerization to polymers that are hydrolyzable at room temperature and neutral pH but yield formaldehyde as a hydrolysis by-product (Chenouard et al. 2014). Regenerated collagen is also used as a hemostatic agent in forms of fiber, powder, and assemblies. Another possible application of biodegradable polymers is the fixation of fractured bones. Currently, metals are widely used for this purpose in orthopedic and oral surgeries in the form of plates, pins, screws, and wires, but they need removal after re-union of fractured bones by further surgery. It would be beneficial to patients if these fixation devices could be fabricated using biodegradable polymers because there would be no need for a re-operation. 1.10 Pharmaceutical Use In order to deliver drugs to diseased sites in the body in a more effective and less invasive way, a new dosage form technology, called drug delivery systems (DDS), was started using polymers. The objectives of DDS include the sustained release of drugs for a desired duration at an optimal dose, targeting drugs to diseased sites without affecting healthy sites, controlled release of drugs by external stimuli and simple delivery of drugs mostly through skin and mucous membranes. Polymers are powerful for this new pharmaceutical technology. If a drug is administered through a parenteral route like injection, the polymer used as a drug carrier should be preferably absorbable because the polymer is no longer required when the drug delivery has been accomplished. Therefore, biodegradable polymers are widely used, especially for the sustained release of drugs through administration by injection or implantation into the body. For this purpose, absorbable nanospheres, microspheres, beads, cylinders and disks are prepared using biodegradable polymers (Lee and Mooney 2012). The shape of the most widely used drug carriers is a microsphere, 46 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization which incorporates drugs and releases them through physical diffusion, followed by resorption of the microsphere material (Figure 9). If the drug carrier is soluble in water, the polymer need not to be biodegradable because this polymer will be excreted from the body, associated with urine or feces, although excretion will take a long time if the molecular weight of the polymer is extremely high. 1.11 Use for Tissue Engineering Tissue engineering is an emerging technology that creates biological tissues to replace defective or lost tissues using cells and cell growth factors. Also, scaffolds are required for tissue construction if the lost part of the tissue is so large that it cannot be cured by conventional drug administration. At present, such largely diseased tissues and organs are replaced either with artificial organs or transplanted organs, but both therapeutic methods involve some problems. As mentioned earlier, the biocompatibility of clinically used artificial organs is mostly not satisfactory enough to prevent severe foreign-body reactions and fully perform the objective of the artificial organs aimed at patients. The biofunctionality of current artificial organs is still poor. On the contrary, the biofunctionality of transplanted organs is as excellent as that of healthy human organs, but the patients with transplanted organs are suffering from side effects induced by the immunosuppressive drugs administered. Another major problem of organ transplantation is the shortage of organ donors. The final objective of tissue engineering is to solve these problems by providing Figure 9: Immunomodulatory biomaterials and their application in therapies for chronic inflammation- related diseases (Nakkala et al. 2021). Designing of Materials for Biodegradation and Bio-Erosion 47 biological tissues and organs that are more excellent in both biofunctionality and biocompatibility than conventional artificial organs. Biodegradable polymers are required to fabricate scaffolds for cell proliferation and differentiation, which result in tissue regeneration or construction (Queen et al. 2004). Biodegradable polymers are also necessary for a sustained release of growth factors at the location of tissue regeneration. Generally, scaffolds used in tissue engineering are porous and three- dimensional to encourage the infiltration of a large number of cells into the scaffolds. Currently, the polymers used for scaffolding include collagen, glycolide-lactide copolymers, other copolymers of lactide, and cross-linked polysaccharides. 1.12 Ecological Applications (Processing of Plastic Wastes) The other major application of biodegradable polymers is in plastic industries to replace biostable plastics for keeping our earth’s environment clean. The first choice for processing plastic waste is reuse. However, only some plastic products can be reused after adequate processing, and many of them are difficult to recycle. In these cases, wastes are processed by landfill or incineration, but these processes often pollute the environment. If biodegradation by-products do not exert adverse effects on animals and plants on the earth, biodegradable plastics can be regarded as environment-friendly or ecological materials. Therefore, much attention has been focused on manufacturing biodegradable plastics, which, however, should address several requirements. They are to be low in product cost, satisfactory in mechanical properties, and not harmful to animals and plants when biodegraded. Biodegradation kinetics is also an important issue of biodegradable plastics. Applications of biodegradable polymers in plastic industries can be seen in a wide range of industries, including agriculture, fishery, civil engineering, construction, outdoor leisure, food, toiletry, cosmetics and other consumer products. It is possible that the waste left as a result of outdoor activity and sports will stay for a long time in natural environments, possibly damaging them (Figure 10). On the other hand, when plastics are used indoors as food containers that are difficult to separate from the food remaining after use, the waste can be utilized as compost if it is biodegradable (Balakrishnan et al. 2006). 1.13 Modes of Biodegradation Polymer degradation occurs mostly through the scission of the main chains or side chains of polymer molecules, induced by their thermal activation, oxidation, photolysis, radiolysis, or hydrolysis. Some polymers undergo degradation in biological environments when living cells or microorganisms are present around the polymers (Rabbany et al. 2010) (Figure 11). Type A: In these systems, water-soluble polymers are insolubilized using hydrolytically or enzymatically unstable cross-links. As a result, the polymeric matrix is highly hydrophilic and completely permeated by water. Since the active agent is located in an aqueous environment, compounds with high water solubility will be rapidly leached out independent of the matrix erosion rate. A useful application of these systems is for the slow release of water-soluble macromolecules that can be 48 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization entangled in these systems and consequently cannot escape until a sufficient number of cross-links have cleaved and the matrix cross-link density has been reduced. Type B: These systems include polymers that are initially water insoluble and are solubilized by hydrolysis, ionization or protonation of a pedant group. Since no backbone cleavage takes place, the solubilization does not result in any significant changes in MW. Polymers in this category are only useful in topical applications where the elimination of high molecular weight, water-soluble macromolecules proceeds with no difficulty, e.g., partial esters of methyl vinyl ether and maleic anhydride copolymers. Zaikov has reported the in vivo breakdown of a polymer in terms of three degradative components, these being water (diffusivity), salt content/ pH of the physiological environment, and lastly, enzymatic attack (Boontheekul et al. 2005). 1.15 Designing of Biodegradable Polymers The synthesis and development of biodegradable polymers are among the leading frontiers of research in polymer science at present. More recently, with the emphasis on reducing environmental pollution, attention has been directed toward biodegradable polymers (Boontheekul et al. 2005). In addition, there is now a wide variety of medical applications of synthetic and natural polymers that are biodegradable. Rodriq has discussed a number of possible approaches to biodegradable systems (Lee et al. 2011). He suggested a search for new organisms for conventional polymers, the introduction of vulnerable units in the polymer chain, or adding nutrients, e.g., cellulose or amylose, on reinforcement in polymer composites. Gilbert have reviewed two approaches to the designing of biodegradable systems (Madan et al. 2013). The first is concerned with the synthesis and in vivo caprolactone) and its copolymers. The second approach was based on synthesizing block and graft copolymers containing naturally occurring segments, such as cellulose and amylose, which are known to be biodegradable. Sudesh Kumar has classified the possible approaches to developing new biodegradable polymers in the following four areas: studies of a series of polyesters, such as PLA, PGA, and poly (Lee et al. 2013). ● Modification of natural polymer ● Biodegradable polymer composites ● Synthesis of new biodegradable polymers ● Modification of synthetic polymers 1.16 Modification of Natural Polymers Chemical modification of the natural polymers serves the two-fold purpose of utilizing renewable, naturally derived products such as polysaccharides and proteins as replacements for synthetic, petroleum-based products and as biodegradable compositions, which can be tailored for a slower or faster rate of degradation. Several new polymeric materials have been prepared through the chemical modification of natural polymers. 50 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization Among the polysaccharides, the commonly employed polymers include cellulose, starch, dextran and amylose. Various cellulose ethers have been reported to be biodegradable by various microorganisms (Zulkifli et al. 2021). 1,4 linkage between the glucose units in the cellulose could be made susceptible to hydrolysis by introducing chemical modifications. One such product is periodate-oxidized cellulose, which is formed by oxidizing cellulose with sodium periodate, leading to the conversion of anhydro-D-glucose units to dialdehyde units. Also (Wu et al. 2019), Singh et al. have reported that this product is degradable in the physiological environment, and the degradation products are glycolic acid and 2,4-dihydroxy butyric acid (Nam et al. 2019; Ravichandran et al. 2015). Another approach reported by Gilbert et al. was the biodegradable graft and copolymers of cellulose and amylose (Parihar et al. 2023). Grafting reaction leaves the main chain of a polymer intact, and it can be expected to add new properties associated with the side chains without drastically changing the main chain properties. Regenerated cellulose, cellulose acetate, and ethyl cellulose are commercially available and find application in packaging. Ferruti et al. reported succinic esters of starch and dextran as biodegradable drug-release matrixes. Dextran, as such, is used clinically as a plasma expander (Salehi et al. 2020). Schacht has many questions concerning the immunological properties of polysaccharide derivatives (Hennecke et al. 2013). Also, the strength of polysaccharides is not outstanding when compared to other classes of materials. Bishop reported that fibers useful in surgery could be prepared by extruding the ethyl ether of dextran (Huemmerich et al. 2004). Among the proteins, collagen and gelatin-based polymers are commonly employed. Collagen was used for a long time as a bioabsorbable suture. Gelatin has found many applications in the biomedical field as a bioabsorbable agent. For surgical use, gelatin is prepared as a foam or film and cross-linked with formaldehyde to decrease solubility. It is used to fill voids after tissue resection. A new surgical procedure was developed using a cross-linked gelatin cup prosthesis, which participated in the temporary substitution of tissues. Kumar et al. investigated the biodegradation of gelatin graft copolymers with poly (methylacrylate) using pure cultures and mixed bacterial inoculums (Huemmerich et al. 2004). As they are proteinaceous in nature, both collagen and gelatin also have the potential to incite an immune response. 1.17 Polymer Composites Several polysaccharide plastic blends have been developed as degradable plastics, with the majority of them containing starch, cellulose or their derivatives as polysaccharides (Barbosa et al. 2016). The primary goal of that work was to replace plastic with inexpensive renewable resource materials derived from plants. These blends have been suggested as desirable alternatives to non-degradable plastics for which a number of solid waste disposal and environmental problems exist (Table 4). The principal degradable materials are mixtures of starch and polyethylene or starch, polyethylene and ethylene-co-acrylic acid.
