Conclusion and Future Prospects The development of natural and synthetic biodegradable polymers is apparent and has progressed in response to a clearer definition of the need for materials with special characteristics. For instance, fibers that are strong and required for sutures, bulky, and perhaps porous masses are indicated for tissue void filling or scaffolding, and flexible but rapidly absorbing forms are suitable for drug release vehicles. The 54 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization wide variety of polymer systems expected with varied and special characteristics will allow an increase in successful applications to many problems in medicine and surgery requiring such materials. Future challenges include meeting the rising demand for improved sensitivity and selectivity, enabling real-time, low-cost monitoring of molecules in analyzing challenging clinical and environmental samples. The impact of nanotechnology on biosensors is also extensively covered in this study, along with the past, present, and future of these rapidly developing and burgeoning research endeavors. It is supported by the quick advancements in nanotechnology; these works of multidisciplinary research are progressing and starting to find their way to the market. The study emphasizes the main milestones accomplished and clarifies the emerging trends further by concentrating on the key advances from the views of novel smart materials, device topologies, and functionalities. Shah,2 Sudarshan Singh,3,* Ozioma F . Nwabor,4 Devesh Kapoor5 and Sankha Bhattacharya6 1. Introduction Polymers are extensive molecules consisting of repeating structural units. They are compounds formed by covalently linking monomeric units into substantial molecular chains. Natural polymers are vast resources with extensive applications in diverse processing and production sectors. A wide range of natural polymers find application in pharmaceuticals for drug delivery, serve as biocompatible composite scaffolds in bone tissue regeneration, and contribute to the preparation of wound healing composites. These versatile materials offer biocompatibility and unique properties that enhance their role in improving healthcare and regenerative medicine. Compared with synthetic polymers, natural polymers are non-toxic and biocompatible with human cells and tissues and hence are preferred in biomedical applications. Several natural polymers are employed in food science as food hydrocolloids, used as stabilisers, gelling agents, and for fabricating packaging composites. Natural polymers are categorised into three groups: polysaccharides, including cellulose and chitin; polypeptides, such as collagen and keratin; and polynucleotides, exemplified by DNA and RNA. Natural polymers are highly reactive, biodegradable, biocompatible, and renewable. Natural polymers are sourced from diverse sources, including plants, animals, bacteria, fungi, and algae. The demand surge for natural polymers is expected to translate into increased market value. The current projection suggests that the worldwide natural polymer market is expected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 5.6% between 2018 and 2027. This growth reflects the increasing demand for sustainable, bio-based materials across various industries. The economical, non-toxic, and biodegradable nature of natural polymers is anticipated to drive the global natural polymer market growth during this period. Several natural polymers have demonstrated the desired qualities for various industrial, medical, agricultural, and environmental applications. Deploying natural polymers as a replacement for synthetic counterparts is considered a sustainable option. In addition, due to the biodegradability of natural polymers, they pose no hazard to the environment, as do synthetic polymers like nylon, polyethylene, polyester, Teflon, and epoxy. The valorisation of waste from natural resources is a rich source of natural polymer. Chitin and its deacetylated form, chitosan, are extensively obtained from waste materials, including bones, pens, scales, and shells of sea animals and other terrestrial Mollusca (Mohite et al. 2023a). Microorganisms find extensive applications across diverse sectors, including food, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, agriculture, textiles, biotechnology, and environmental chemistry, playing pivotal roles in product development, sustainability, and scientific advancement (Morin-Crini et al. 2019; Kumar et al. 2023b). Several studies have investigated the biomedical applications of chitosan for a variety of uses, including in wound dressings, antimicrobial agents, anti-cancer, drug delivery systems, gene therapy, tissue engineering, dental repair/replacement, bone regeneration, etc. (Patel et al. 2007; Mohite et al. 2023a; Prajapati and Sawant 2009; Mohite et al. 2023a). 2. Natural Polymer in Biomaterial Fabrication Natural polymers are increasingly being used in biomaterial fabrication, with various studies showcasing their versatile applications. These bio-friendly materials hold promise in fields like tissue engineering, drug delivery, and wound healing, contributing to innovative and sustainable solutions. The fabrication of hydrogels using natural polymers has been experimentally demonstrated as biomaterials for human use. Research is ongoing, and efforts are being made to improve the medical applications of natural polymers for more efficient and effective processing of biomaterials. Naturally derived polymers such as cellulose, chitosan, alginate, agarose, and composites have undergone extensive research to determine their potential as tissue engineering scaffolds. These materials offer biocompatibility and structural support, making them valuable candidates in the field of regenerative medicine (Ko et al. 2010). Hydrogels are also seen as carrier matrix for drug and bioactive compound delivery. A cellulose-based dual stimuli-responsive hydrogel with an intelligent switch for controlled drug delivery exhibited precise control of the release process, with considerable biocompatibility and antioxidant properties (Song et al. 2021). Natural polysaccharide-based transdermal drug delivery is a promising Natural Biopolymer 65 device with prospective future uses (Li et al. 2022). A novel dual-responsive hydrogel, utilising tamarind gum in conjunction with poly(N-isopropyl acrylamide- co-ethylene glycol vinyl ether), demonstrates significant potential as an innovative platform for precise colon-specific anti-cancer drug delivery (Nagaraja et al. 2022). 3. Source With Derivatives, Characterisation, and Application in the Fabrication of Biomaterials Natural biomaterials are found in abundance in nature or derived from plants, animals, or fungi sources like cellulose, chitosan, gelatine, chitosan, alginate, etc. In most instances, these biomaterials are biodegradable; however, not all biomaterials are biodegradable, which may limit their application. Natural biopolymers have recently received increased attention from the market, as well as the scientific and industrial communities. 3.1 Source/Extraction/Isolation and Chemical Modification In the current scenario for natural polymers, there has been a gradual transition in recent years. The increased attention is primarily owing to recent environmental concerns, as well as the inexpensive cost of obtaining natural polymers, which are an excellent option for synthetic polymers that may be harmful. Natural polymers derived from natural sources had their own set of benefits, including no seasonal restrictions on raw material availability, low inorganic salt content, and no regional restrictions on industrial manufacturing. Most of these natural polymers are used in the pharmaceutical industry as well as a possible food additive. Polymers can be found in abundance in nature. Proteins, cellulose, gelatine, starch, chitin, and chitosan are among the natural polymers found in the human body, plants, and animals (Singh 2022). For increased functionality in diverse applications, these polymers can be isolated, purified, and changed. Polysaccharides, like other naturally generated biopolymers, are harmless and biodegradable, which expands their potential application in a variety of sectors. Polysaccharides are intensively studied, with cellulose being the most important representation due to its abundance and availability. Although the most used biopolysaccharides come obtained from natural resources (e.g., cellulose), they are also obtained from animals (e.g., chitin/ chitosan) and microbial sources (e.g., bacterial cellulose). Using microorganisms to produce bio-based polymers has received significant interest in the recent decade as a sustainable production method. DNA, RNA, proteins, cellulose, chitin, starch, and other biopolymers are produced by all living creatures (Subramanian et al. 2020). These biopolymers are essential in the body for energy storage, genetic information preservation and transmission, and cellular construction. DNA and RNA are genetic materials that allow all living organisms to store and transmit genetic information. Proteins aid in chemical reactions (enzymes), as well as provide structural support (haemoglobin) (e.g., collagen) (Hennet 2019). Cellulose is Natural Biopolymer 67 the most important structural component of plant cell walls. Using biopolymers as a key component of biopolymeric products can be a cost-effective strategy in the field of pharmaceuticals as well as food and nutrition. Polysaccharides are a natural choice as they are composed of monosaccharides (sugars) allied together by Oglycosidic links (Sun et al. 2018). Polysaccharides, such as cellulose and chitin, make up the majority of natural polysaccharides. Natural or synthetic polymers are obtained from various sources, and before utilisation in pharmaceuticals or food, industries were extensively characterised based on their qualities. The characterisation techniques involved in the evaluation of natural bio-based polymers in accordance with the American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) standards to ensure the product meets the required quality standards are presented in (Figure 2). 3.2.1 Instrumentation and Characterisation for Biopolymers 3.2.1.1 Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) NMR is an excellent analytical tool for gaining detailed and especially impartial information on the structural and dynamic properties of various polymer systems. The 2D and 3D NMR spectral analysis reveals information on isotropic chemical shifts (primarily of 1H and 13C). Numerous NMR techniques employ diverse solvent systems for characterising polymer composition, structure, and dynamics, addressing specific material attributes with precision. These methods offer unique insights into polymer behaviour and are vital for comprehensive material analysis and research. Figure 1: Methods for preparation and isolation of biopolymers. 68 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization Characterising polymer systems using NMR is challenging due to the coexistence of processes at various timescales, including the intermediate timescale of the NMR experiment, structural disorder, and dynamic heterogeneity. This complexity makes precise characterisation a formidable task in NMR analysis. 3.2.1.2 Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) Spectroscopy Analytical tools such as FTIR are used to identify the functional and structural properties of biopolymers and evaluate the quality of materials. The FTIR uses interferometry to encode material information and to identify or quantify material, and the Fourier transform decodes the signal into spectra. Moreover, the FTIR is a non-destructive method for determining biomass components in the mid-IR region. FTIR spectroscopy reveals molecular fragments, functional groups, and even the fibre structure (Bhattacharya et al. 2023). 3.2.1.3 X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) Analysis The size and shape of polymer domains within a sample can be determined using XRD techniques such as low-angle or small-angle scattering. For more advanced structural investigations, the diffractometer is configured to analyse polymer fibres and films (Kotadiya et al. 2016). Figure 2: Characterisation techniques involved in the assessment polymers Natural Biopolymer 69 3.2.1.4 Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA) TGA is a valuable tool for assessing the thermal stability of various materials, including biopolymers and product fabricated using it. This approach measures changes in the weight of a specimen as its incremental temperature rises per unique time (Moin et al. 2002). The moisture and volatile content of biopolymers can be determined using TGA. In a series of research investigations, thermogravimetric (TG) analyses were conducted on natural polymers, including cellulose, chitin, and chitosan, using a PerkinElmer Pyris1TGA instrument equipped with a 20-sample auto-sampler manufactured by PerkinElmer in Waltham, MA. To record the temperature profiles, individuals used a high-resolution mode to record them from 37 to 900°C in a nitrogen atmosphere (20 ml/min) with a constant temperature rise rate of 10°C/min. 3.2.1.5 Scanning Electron Microscopy Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) is a valuable tool for morphological/ topographical characterisation of biopolymers, bridging the gap between high- resolution methods such as AFM, TEM, and light microscopy, which measures large dimensions at low resolution. In addition, SEM used to capture the image of fracture and failure mechanics, the size and shape of particles, the orientation, and dispersion of fillers in polymer matrices, as well as how fillers are oriented and spread out in the matrix. 3.2.1.6 Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM) FESEM is an advanced version of SEM that captures images with resolution and a wider energy range than traditional SEM. The latter employs a field emission gun as an electron-generating device, which is one of the key distinctions between SEM and FESEM. This produces highly concentrated electron beams, which increase spatial resolution and allow sample examination at low potentials. Several studies indicate that FESEM has been previously successfully employed to get high-resolution pictures of biopolymer systems instead of SEM. 3.2.1.7 Physicochemical Characterisation Rheological techniques and procedures have been used in the characterisation of polymers for decades. Rheology estimation is used to evaluate the viscosity and flow behaviour of synthetic polymers (Kumar et al. 2023a). Biopolymer solutions and gels are characterised using a variety of rheological methods. The major classes of biopolymers is proteins and polysaccharides. Depending upon the behaviours of the material under stress conditions, the materials are characterised as a Newtonian or non-Newtonian system. The fundamental sequence structure of biopolymers governs just a small portion of their functional capabilities. The space-filling conformations used are far more significant. The tertiary structure, or the overall form of the macromolecule, follows the secondary structure. Some marine polysaccharides, including carrageenan and agarose, have large double-helical structures (Picout and Ross-Murphy 2003). Biomaterials are materials that are designed to interact with living biological tissue and are utilised for therapeutic and diagnostic purposes as well in diverse fields of the food industry. Biomaterials can be categorised into two origins: naturally occurring and synthetically produced. In a broader classification, they fall into four main groups: metals, ceramics, polymers, and composites, each serving vital roles in various medical and engineering applications (Bagheri et al. 2022). The properties of biomaterials, whether natural or synthetic, are intricately linked to the chemicals used in their preparation and modification. Polymers, with their diverse applications, play a pivotal role in therapeutic methods, from drug delivery to reconstructive techniques, and they even find utility in the food industry (Lastra Ripoll et al. 2021). Biomaterials and their derivatives may aid in developing innovative food packaging materials with an improved barrier, mechanical strength, antibacterial and antioxidant capabilities (Rukmanikrishnan et al. 2020). The present book chapter will review some of the biomaterials, namely chitosan, carrageenan, alginate, cellulose, gelatin, guar gum, xanthan gum, agarose, hyaluronic acid, Tamarindus indica L. seed gum, Hibiscus sabdariffa fibres, and starch with its fabrication, chemical, and physical properties, and application in the pharmaceutical and food industry. Moreover, the short regulatory status of the US FDA and European Union is also discussed. 3.3.1 Chitosan The inherent biological compatibility, versatile chemical composition, and tuneable physical characteristics of natural polymers render them ideal for a wide array of applications within the food and pharmaceutical sectors. The outer skeleton of shellfish such as crabs, lobster, and shrimp are the prominent sources of chitosan (Mukherjee Swarupananda et al. 2024; Mohite et al. 2023b; Pawar et al. 2024; Singh et al. 2021). Chitosan (deacetylated chitin) comprises a major portion of the natural polymer used in the food and pharmaceutical industry, and compared to cellulose, chitin as a biopolymer is present in abundance (Aranaz and Acosta 2021). Chitosan, illustrated in Figure 3, is a linear polysaccharide comprising randomly arranged β-(1→4)-linked D-glucosamine (deacetylated) and N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (acetylated) units. It is produced by subjecting chitin to alkaline treatments under rigorous conditions or through enzymatic hydrolysis, often employing chitin deacetylase (Wang et al. 2022). The diverse chemical properties of chitosan, including its aqueous solubility, reactivity, and pH characteristics, are intricately linked to its physical attributes, notably its crystalline structure, molecular weight, degree of deacetylation (Wang et al. 2021), etc. 74 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 3.3.1.1 Crystalline Structure Partially re-acetylated chitosan exhibits lower crystallinity compared to pure chitosan. In order to achieve less crystalline chitosan, reacetylation of fully deactivated chitosan is favoured over direct solid-state deacetylation of chitin. Moreover, various other process parameters, such as re-precipitation, drying, and lyophilisation, also play a pertinent role in establishing the crystalline state of chitosan (Qiao et al. 2019). 3.3.1.2 Molecular Weight Chitosan molecular weight is widely varied, and hence they are polydisperse in terms of molecular weight. Depending upon the source of chitin, the molecular weight of chitosan varies considerably. The molecular weight characterisation can be done by a variety of solvents depending upon the concentration of protonation for chitosan. The molecular weight of chitosan can vary significantly due to source and deacetylation conditions, with chitosan from crustacean chitin often exceeding 100,000 daltons. This variability underscores the importance of precise control in chitosan production processes (El Knidri et al. 2019a). Moreover, the aqueous solubility of chitosan is related to the molecular weight of chitosan; the lower the molecular weight, the higher the aqueous solubility (Ru et al. 2019). 3.3.1.3 Degree of Deacetylation Chitosan, derived from chitin, consists of β-1,4-D-glucosamine units. The degree of deacetylation quantifies the proportion of these units with acetyl groups removed, a critical factor in its properties and applications (Kurita et al. 2000). The degree of deacetylation is a pivotal parameter for chitosan, profoundly influencing its chemical and biological attributes. A higher degree of deacetylation would result in a higher concentration of amino acids, and higher protonation of amino groups would lead to Figure 3: Synthesis of chitosan via deacetylation of chitosan. Natural Biopolymer 75 higher aqueous solubility and subsequent higher biological activity (Cheung et al. 2015). 3.3.1.4 Derivatives of Chitosan Chitosan, a versatile biopolymer, is extensively used in drug delivery and the food industry. In order to tailor its properties for diverse applications, chitosan derivatives are created via modifications with hydrophobic groups, notably acyl, and alkyl groups, a well-researched approach for enhancing its functionality. 3.3.1.4.1 Acylation of Chitosan The amphiphilic polymer can be made using entirely natural, biodegradable, and renewable ingredients by grafting fatty acid onto chitosan. Acylation reaction can occur in amino groups, hydroxyl groups, or both groups, depending on the reaction circumstances (Zhang et al. 2017). Because of their high hydrophobicity, derivatives with a short chain length and low-to-moderate degree of substitution are soluble in water, whereas derivatives with a long-chain length are practically insoluble in water (Ma et al. 2009). 3.3.1.4.2 Alkylation of Chitosan Reductive amination of chitosan yields alkyl chitosan derivatives in most cases. The stiffness and interaction properties of modified chitosan are almost unaffected by short alkyl chains (C5), but longer chains promote more efficient hydrophobic contacts and intra-aggregation of the polymer. Furthermore, in forming hydrophobic domains through alkyl-alkyl interactions, the degree of substitution is an important parameter (Sahariah et al. 2015). 3.3.1.4.3 Thiolated Chitosan The variety of thiolated chitosan with its significant applications has risen dramatically since this chitosan was demonstrated to have considerably improved characteristics than the unmodified polymer (Dalvin 2022). The thiolated chitosan shows appreciable change in various properties of chitosan, such as adhesion to biological surfaces (Wibel et al. 2021), in situ gelling properties (Li et al. 2020), swelling behaviours solubility, controlled release of a drug, enhancement of permeation, and cellular uptake (Bastaki et al. 2021). Thiolated chitosan has varied applications, such as therapeutic agents, drug delivery systems, theranostic, tissue engineering, wound material, cosmetics, etc. 3.3.1.5 Regulatory Status The first topical hemostatic chitosan dressing (HemConTM Bandage) was cleared by the FDA in 2008 (US FDA 2008). Recently, Axiostat, a chitosan hemostatic dressing, has been found to be substantially equivalent (SESE) by the US FDA and approved for marketing in the US (US FDA 2018). However, the inactive ingredient database does not list or approve any maximum daily exposure for chitosan through any delivery route (US FDA 2022), and hence the use of chitosan for drug delivery must 76 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization be reviewed on a case-to-case basis. European Food Safety Authority believes that the consumer dietary risk assessment can be waived, and chitosan hydrochloride can be used as a plant elicitor (EFSA 2020). 3.3.2 Carrageenan Carrageenans are a type of sulfated polysaccharide, also known as carrageenins, derived from red edible seaweeds. Carrageenans are mostly employed in pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and the food sector because of their unique qualities (thickening and gelling agents) and biological activity (antiviral and anticoagulant). As shown in Figure 4, Carrageenans are sulfated linear polysaccharides made up of repeated disaccharide units with alternating 3-linked -d-galactopyranose and 4-linked -galactopyranose or 3, 6-α anhydrogalactopyranose (Yermak et al. 2020). Figure 4: Carrageenan structure. 3.3.2.1 Types and Sources of Carrageenan There are three kinds of carrageenan depending upon the degree of sulfation: Kappa (қ) carrageenan (Rudhziaha et al. 2015), iota carrageenan (Chitra et al. 2018), and lambda carrageenan (Yermak et al. 2020). Қ-carrageenan consists of repeating units composed of 3-linked -d-galactose 4-sulfate, and 4-linked 6-anhydro- galactopyranose, with each unit carrying a negative charge. The tropical seaweed Kappaphycus alvarezii, sometimes known as Eucheuma cottonii in trade, is used to extract қ-carrageenan. The chief species to manufacture iota carrageenan is Eucheuma spinosum (or simply spinosum). At the same time, lambda carrageenan is a type of seaweed derived from a variety of species in the Genera Gigartina and Chondrus. 3.3.2.2 Synthesis of Carrageenan The first step of synthesis is to harvest the carrageenan-containing seaweeds, which is an expensive process because the seaweed is collected by raking or hand- gathering. Mechanical harvesters have been used, but yields have shown little to no improvement. After that, the seaweed is washed to eliminate any sand, stones, or other contaminants. Then, seaweeds are transported to a production facility, where they are extracted under alkaline conditions to generate high-quality carrageenans at temperatures near the boiling point of the alkaline solution, which lasts for several Natural Biopolymer 77 hours. After that, the extract is filtered and concentrated and then dried and pulverised to the required particle size after being precipitated with a suitable solvent (Yermak et al. 2020). 3.3.2.3 Properties of Carrageenan The unique property of carrageenan makes them suitable for the pharmaceutical and food industry. All the grades of carrageenan are soluble in hot water. The swelling of carrageenan depends upon the particle density and is varied. Iota carrageenan is sensitive to calcium ions, and it will swell to generate thixotropy, which is caused by creating bivalent calcium bridges between the swelled particles, resulting in a loose 3-D network (Valetti et al. 2013). Protein reactivity is known to exist in all carrageenans. The isoelectric point of a protein, pH of the solution, weight ratio of protein to carrageenan, type of protein, and molecular weight all influence its reactivity (Cui et al. 2018). The interaction of proteins and carrageenan is mediated by a mixture of processes. Divalent bridging and ionic bonding are the mechanisms. Because the carboxylic acid groups of the protein are ionised above the protein’s isoelectric point, the carrageenan does not interact with it due to negative-negative repulsions (Cui et al. 2018). 3.3.2.4 Regulatory Status Carrageenan obtained from Chondrus crispus, Chondrus ocellatus, Eucheuma cottonii., Eucheuma spinosum, Gigartina pistillata to Gigartina stellata; may be safely used in food as per the given guidelines in the US FDA. Carrageenan may be used orally, nasally, topically, and transdermally, with the maximum daily exposure limits have been mentioned in the database for Inactive Ingredient for Approved Drug Products (US FDA 2022). Moreover, carrageenan is also authorised as a food additive in the European Union with a daily acceptable limit of 75 mg/kg of body weight (Younes et al. 2018). 3.3.3 Xanthan Gum Polysaccharides are versatile biomolecules sourced from bacteria, plants, and animals, finding applications across diverse industries like food, agriculture, and biomedicine. Their natural abundance, accessibility, biocompatibility, cost-efficiency, and processing ease make them invaluable in fields like tissue engineering and drug delivery, paving the way for innovative solutions (Souza et al. 2022). Xanthan gum, a polysaccharide, is synthesised through the fermentation process involving gram-negative bacteria Xanthomonas campestris, as reported by Elella et al. This natural production occurs in carbon-rich environments under aerobic conditions, yielding a versatile and widely used thickening agent (Elella et al. 2021). Due to its exceptional matrix-forming qualities and outstanding biocompatibility, xanthan gum ranks as the second most widely utilised bacterial polysaccharide, following dextran. Its versatile applications span various industries, with a prominent role in the field of biomedicine (Pooja et al. 2014). 78 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 3.3.3.1 Chemistry and Physical Properties of Xanthan Gum Xanthan gum primarily consists of pentasaccharide structures comprising glucose, mannose, and glucuronic acid in a balanced mole ratio of 2:2:1. These core units may also incorporate pyruvyl and o-acetyl residues in varying quantities, providing unique functional properties (Petri 2015). In Figure 5, the backbone consists of a sequence of glucose residues interconnected through (1–4 linkage) while being further connected to a trisaccharide chain through a -mannopyranose unit via (1–3 linkage). Xanthan gum exhibits distinctive properties, including non-Newtonian fluid behaviour, remarkable thermal resilience at elevated temperatures reaching 90°C, and exceptional stability in acidic (pH 2) and alkaline (pH 12) environments (Lastra Ripoll et al. 2021). An increased presence of pyruvyl groups and reduced acetyl groups promotes the formation of highly viscous solutions, while the opposite composition results in lower viscosity. However, xanthan gum has several drawbacks, such as an uncontrollable degree of thickness, microbial attack, hydration, and delayed dissolution frequency. Various derivatives of xanthan gum have been prepared to address these issues (Riaz et al. 2021). Physical, enzymatic, and chemical approaches are the major broad categories of xanthan gum alterations (Battistel et al. 2011). Chemical modification and degradation have been extensively investigated; however, such modification also influences other uncontrolled aspects of xanthan gum. The physical modifications are done by sonication, radiation, annealing, using surfactants, etc., and can help to achieve the desired physical and chemical properties of xanthan gum. Xanthan lyase, xanthanase, cellulases, and acetyl esterases can be used for enzymatic modification to achieve the desired properties of xanthan gum. Chemical modification by grafting and crosslinking, etherification and esterification, Figure 5: Xanthan gum structure. Natural Biopolymer 79 acetylation, and pyruvate have been studied extensively to modify xanthan gum chemically (Said et al. 2021) due to its unique physical qualities; xanthan gum has a wide range of applications in the pharmaceutical and food industries. Mixability, pumpability, and pourability of industrially manufactured dressings and sauces are further aided by the shear-thinning flow behaviour. Xanthan gum is frequently used in conjunction with other hydrocolloids to get the required flow behaviour for various semi-prepared food conveniences (Saha and Bhattacharya 2010). In the cosmetics industry, the most common use of xanthan gum is in the manufacturing of toothpaste. Xanthan gum’s shear-thinning flow characteristic enables easy extrusion from the tube or the pump dispenser. It also guarantees that the toothpaste remains stable on the toothbrush (Hublik 2012). 3.3.3.2 Regulatory Status The US FDA has granted authorisation for xanthan gum due to its non-toxic nature and its ability to enhance the texture and mouthfeel of food products. It must contain no more than 750 parts per million of residual isopropyl alcohol and should yield positive results in both the locust bean gum gel test and pyruvic acid test, as per US FDA regulations. The Inactive Ingredient for Approved Drug Products database suggests that xanthan gum can be administered via various routes, including oral, ophthalmic, rectal, and topical routes, in a variety of dosage forms within the maximum tolerable limit (US FDA). Considering a previous study reported that a 214 mg/kg of xanthan gum repeated oral dose for ten days, the European Food Safety Authority approved it as a food additive (Mortensen et al. 2017). 3.3.4 Alginate Alginates represent a non-toxic, naturally derived polymer with exceptional versatility. Their unique properties allow for the creation of chelates and pH-responsive gels. With biocompatibility, biodegradability, and a non-antigenic, non-toxic nature, alginates offer a safe and adaptable choice (Singh et al. 2023; Patel et al. 2023). As a result, alginate has gained widespread acceptance as a viable gel carrier choice. Alginate is a structural substance found in the extracellular matrix of brown algae. Laminaria hyperborea, Macrocystis pyrifera, and Ascophyllum nodosum are three of the most common algae sources (Grøndahl et al. 2020). 3.3.4.1 Chemistry and Physical Properties Alginate polymers consist of alternating blocks of β-D mannuronic acid (M) and α-L-guluronic acid (G), linked by glycosidic bonds. These homopolymeric M and G blocks, along with heteropolymeric MG or GM blocks, define the complex structure of alginates, which is crucial in various applications (Jain and Bar-Shalom 2014). However, high molecular mass polymers are exceedingly viscous, posing difficulty in processing conditions. For instance, high shear rates cause damage when protein and cells are mixed in highly viscous alginate solutions (Kim et al. 2019). Figure 6 represents the structure of alginic acid. 80 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization Guluronic acid containing sodium alginates is water-soluble in a positive manner, whereas mannuronic acid containing sodium alginates is water-soluble in a negative manner. To render alginates water-soluble, three essential conditions must be fulfilled: (a) maintaining an appropriate ionic strength in the alginate medium, (b) introducing gelling ions into the solvent, and (c) ensuring a high pH level in the solvent while deprotonating the carboxyl groups. This combination of factors facilitates the dissolution of alginates in water (Rosiak et al. 2021). Heavy metals, proteins, and endotoxins, among other contaminants found in alginates, cause an immunological reaction at the implantation or injection site (Lee and Mooney 2012). 3.3.4.2 Chemically Modified Alginate Chemical modification of alginate biopolymers plays a pivotal role in enhancing their bio-integration and affinity in various applications. This is achieved by introducing highly reactive functional groups, such as aldehyde groups, or incorporating chemical moieties like phosphate or sulfate. These modifications not only improve the biocompatibility of alginate-based products but also expand their versatility in biomedical and industrial contexts (Szabo et al. 2020). Alginates play a pivotal role in diverse applications, serving as rate-controlling agents in drug delivery systems, providing a versatile matrix for biomolecules and pharmaceutical excipients in localised administration, contributing to advancements in biomedical engineering, and facilitating freeze-drying processes (Gheorghita Puscaselu et al. 2020). Innovative packaging featuring alginate-based films infused with antifungal agents offers a promising solution for safeguarding cheese and fruits from mould contamination. This approach not only enhances food safety and quality but also extends shelf life while preventing product deterioration. Additionally, alginate’s versatile applications extend to the biomedical field, encompassing protein and cell delivery, wound care, bone regeneration, and neovascularisation (Sun and Tan 2013). 3.3.4.3 Regulatory Status Sodium alginate is generally recognised as safe by the US FDA and can be used as a food additive (US FDA). Sodium alginate and other salts of alginate, such as calcium alginate, propylene glycol alginate, ammonium calcium alginate, etc., have been approved in the Inactive Ingredient for Approved Drug Products and can be used within the maximum daily exposure limit (Younes et al. 2017). This marked the first formal identification of cellulose as a fundamental element within plants (Chidrawar et al. 2023; Singh et al. 2023a; Singh et al. 2023b; Kendre et al. 2023). Cellulose stands as the world’s most abundant biomass resource, a timeless and nearly limitless natural polymer deployed for millennia in various forms and applications. This renewable, cost-effective, and biodegradable marvel, produced not only by plants but also by microbes, offers a multitude of advantages. Moreover, the transformation of cellulose into water-soluble derivatives has significantly broadened its scope across diverse fields, making it an invaluable resource for sustainable innovation (Seddiqi et al. 2021). 3.3.5.1 Plant and Bacterial Cellulose Cellulose can also be derived from species other than plants, such as algae, fungi, and bacteria. This biopolymer is produced by each creature and has specific supramolecular structures, which are extensively researched in studies focusing on the structure, crystallinity, and reactivity of the biomolecule, as well as the potential to build new biomaterials (Freeman et al. 2015). Apart from having a sturdy chain and several distinct functionalities, what distinguishes cellulose from other synthetic polymers is its sensitivity to acetal hydrolysis and oxidation; these features govern its chemistry and manipulation (Reddy et al. 2021). As shown in Figure 7, cellulose is a linear polysaccharide of long-chain joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds. The functional groups in a cellulose monomer are hydroxyls and a methanol group. The absence of side chains or branches indicates that the polymer’s structure is organised. The development of crystalline areas results from these interactions between glucose units. It also serves as the foundation for cellulose’s enormous hydrogen bond networks, which provide the material with a variety of partly crystalline fibre topologies and morphologies (Reis et al. 2019). 3.3.5.2 Derivatives of Cellulose Cellulose compounds have been investigated and used extensively in a variety of industries, including wastewater treatment, papermaking, food additives, pharmaceuticals, and textile applications. The functions of many cellulose derivatives are determined by the substituent group. Various derivatives such as hydroxypropyl Figure 7: Cellulose structure. 82 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization methylcellulose (HPMC) and its various grades, such as cellulose xanthate, cellulose nitrate, cellulose phthalate esters, microcrystalline cellulose, etc., have been prepared to modify the properties of cellulose as per the requirements. 3.3.5.3 Regulatory Status Methylcellulose and sodium carboxymethylcellulose are generally regarded as safe by the US FDA (US FDA). Ethylcellulose, hydroxypropyl cellulose, and hydroxypropyl methylcellulose have been approved by the US FDA for human consumption (US FDA). Cellulose and its specific derivatives have been approved by the European Food Safety Authority as food additives (Younes et al. 2017). 3.3.6 Gelatin Gelatin, a natural polymer derived from collagen protein through hydrolysis, boasts unique amino acids that offer numerous health benefits. This water-soluble substance, produced by partially hydrolysing collagen from animal sources, involves the loss of collagen’s primary, secondary, and tertiary structures (Singh et al. 2024). Unlike most hydrocolloids, which are polysaccharides, gelatin is a protein containing all essential amino acids except tryptophan, making it a unique and versatile ingredient (Pang et al. 2014). Gelatin, a diverse ingredient, can be derived from collagen sources like cattle bones, hides, pig skins, and fish, offering both agricultural and non-agricultural origins. Notably, gelatin lacks plant sources, and so-called ‘vegetable gelatins’, like seaweed extracts, are chemically distinct. Various sources, such as a mammalian, fish, and insect origins, yield gelatin with varying properties (Mariod and Adam 2013). 3.3.6.1 Synthesis and Structure of Gelatin Collagen pre-treatment yields two distinct gelatin types: Type A (pH 6-9) from pigskin with less crosslinking and Type B (pH 5) from bovine hides with complex collagen structures. These gelatins find diverse applications due to their unique properties and origins (Aramwit et al. 2015). Gelatin’s primary structure and makeup are like that of parent collagen. This similarity has been established for various tissues and species. The molecular weight of gelatin has been used to explain several characteristics of its behaviour in solutions and gels. Although gelatin is not polydispersed, it does have a distinct molecular weight distribution pattern that correlates to the α-chain and its oligomers. Gelatin is made up of a variety of polypeptide chains, including α-chains, (dimers of α-chain) and γ (trimers of -α chain) (Hanani et al. 2014; Zhang et al. 2020). 3.3.6.2 Functional and Physical Properties of Gelatin The functional properties of gelatin, such as gel strength and viscosity, are intricately tied to its chemical composition, particularly its molecular weight distribution and amino acid content. Proline and hydroxyproline play pivotal roles in gelatin’s renaturation process. The conversion of collagen to gelatin involves the disruption of inter and intramolecular bonds, along with specific peptide bonds. The extent Natural Biopolymer 83 and type of crosslinking found in bones and skins are different. The distribution of molecular weights, shapes, and compositions of gelatine’s subunits affect its functional properties (Zhang et al. 2020). 3.3.6.3 Applications of Gelatin Gelatin’s unique gelling properties make it a key ingredient in modern cuisine, and it is used to craft gourmet sweets with texture and stability. In addition to confectionery delights like fruit salads and ice cream, gelatin finds applications in cosmetics and health products, from bath salts to facial creams, offering versatility in various industries (Alipal et al. 2021). In the realm of skincare, collagen and gelatin products play a vital role, serving as key ingredients in functional and nutritional foods. Gelatin finds versatile applications in hydrogels, nanospheres, nanofibers, pharmaceutical additives, and cell transplantation carriers, fostering innovation in skincare formulations (Kamatchi and Leela 2016). 3.3.6.4 Regulatory Status The Inactive Ingredient for Approved Drug Products lists that gelatin can be used in a variety of dosage forms for drug delivery through different routes within the maximum daily exposure limit (US FDA). However, Subpart B of Part 189 of the Code of Federal Regulations prohibits using cattle materials (gelatin) in manufacturing or processing human food (US FDA). 3.3.7 Guar Gum Guar gum, derived from the seeds of Cyamopsis tetragonolobus, serves as a white to yellowish-white, high molecular weight seed gum. Its versatile applications span multiple sectors, including food, textiles, paper, cosmetics, and pharmaceuticals (Singh et al. 2022). Its unique qualities, such as biocompatibility and sustainability, make it an excellent candidate in the realm of pharmaceutical research and development (Phadke et al. 2014). The remarkable swelling properties of guar gum in water can be effectively modified through functional group derivatisation, crosslinking, and grafting. These alterations open up diverse possibilities for its utilisation in various biomedical applications, overcoming its inherent limitations. 3.3.7.1 Structure and Properties of Guar Ggum Guar gums, characterised by their hydrophilic nature, exhibit a distinctive rod-like polymer structure. Within this structure, D-galactose side chains are intricately connected to the D-mannose backbone, maintaining an approximate molecular ratio of 1:2. These polysaccharides feature straight chains of D-mannose units linked together through β (1-4) glycoside linkages, with D-galactose units linked in the opposite orientation (Dionísio and Grenha 2012). As depicted in Figure 8, including hydroxyl groups within the polymer’s composition plays a pivotal role in generating diverse derivatives essential for numerous industrial purposes. Guar gum exhibits extraordinary and captivating physical attributes. It remains impervious to hydrocarbons, lipids, alcohols, esters, and ketones, with its exceptional solubility 84 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization reserved exclusively for water (Kocira et al. 2021). The solution of guar gum exhibits non-Newtonian pseudoplastic flow; increasing the shearing stress decreases the viscosity of the solution. Because guar gum is anionic, it maintains stability and provides consistent viscosity across a wide pH range. The pH range of 6–9 yields the most viscosity, whereas pH 3.5 yields the lowest (Wang et al. 2000). 3.3.7.2 Guar Gum Processing Commercial extraction of guar gum from seeds employs various mechanical methods such as sieving, polishing, attrition, and roasting. These techniques capitalise on the disparities in hardness among the seed constituents, facilitating the separation of the endosperm from its components. The result is the formation of guar splits once the hull and germ have been successfully isolated. Following heat treatment, the hull can be efficiently separated through attrition milling or impact mills. Sieving facilitates the retrieval of finer germ and hull fractions from the endosperm. Guar gum powder is subsequently acquired via milling. Further refinement involves dissolving it in water, precipitating, and recovery using ethanol or isopropanol (George et al. 2019). Sugars are usually added to clarified guar gum, which is readily available in markets. The viscosity of resultant dispersion is high since a large amount of water is imbibed by guar. The basic characteristics of guar gum are influenced by temperature. The loss of water of hydration around the polymer molecules was caused by a rise in temperature. 3.3.7.3 Chemical Modifications on Guar Gum Guar gum is frequently combined with other polymers to generate interpenetrating polymer networks (IPN), which provide the otherwise fragile hydrogel with durable mechanical and thermal properties. Guar gum has also been produced in conjunction with pH-sensitive polymers and tested for its efficacy in delivering targeted drugs (Chandrika et al. 2016; Kaur et al. 2013). 3.3.7.4 Regulatory Status The regulation of guar gum as a food additive is generally documented by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) (US FDA). It is GRAS-listed and can be Figure 8: Guar gum structure. The Inactive Ingredient for Approved Drug Products states that guar gum can be used in oral, buccal, sublingual, topical, and vaginal dosage forms within the maximum daily exposure limit (US FDA). Guar gum (E 412) is authorised as a food additive in the European Union (EU) (Mortensen et al. 2017). 3.3.7.5 Future Perspectives Several attempts have been made to introduce functional biomaterials for a variety of applications, spanning from diagnostics to treatment. Recent findings suggest that a thorough understanding of the chemical components and chemistry of biomaterials can be crucial to success in either the food or pharmaceutical industry. Polymers, manufactured specifically to solve the challenges, have been used to circumvent the limitations of traditional dosage forms. Using new polymers has advantages, but they can also be hazardous due to their toxicity and incompatibility. When choosing polymers for a delivery system, extreme caution should be exercised. The most important goal is to develop biocompatible, multifunctional, less toxic polymers that can be used in cost-effective delivery methods. 3.3.8 Agarose Agarose is a prominent marine polysaccharide representing reversible thermogell behaviour and switchable chemical reactivity for functionalisation. Agarose is isolated and purified from red seaweed, known as agar/agar-bearing algae, or isolated from an agar-peptide with a particular structure and spontaneous gelation. Agarose is an inactive ingredient used in various research fields, including drug delivery, food, DNA electrophoresis, and tissue engineering. 3.3.8.1 Structure and Properties Structurally, agarose is a natural polymer, consisting of alternative β-D-galactose and 3,6-anhydro-L-galactose units of agarobiose (Figure 9). Agarose, a non-toxic substance, possesses versatile properties ideal for various applications like nucleic acid electrophoresis, chromatography, and cell culture overlays. With a reported molecular weight of approximately 120,000 g/mol and a white appearance, it readily forms a gel in hot water near its upper critical solution temperature (Zarrintaj et al. 2018). Agarose exhibits solubility in various organic solvents, including dimethyl sulfoxide and 1-Butyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride. This diverse solubility profile extends its utility in various scientific and industrial applications, offering versatility in research and biotechnology (Buskila et al. 1997). Agarose gelation involves three distinct stages: induction, gelation, and pseudo-equilibrium, driven by hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions that lead to the formation of a helical agarose molecular structure and subsequent gel formation. The melting and gelation temperatures of agarose are influenced by factors like molecular weight, concentration, and lateral groups (Buskila et al. 1997). 86 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization Agar is the originating source for agarose, classified by the US FDA as a direct food substance affirmed as GRAS. The FDA has established specific acceptable limits for agar’s use in various food categories, such as 0.8% in baked goods, 2.0% in confections and frostings, 1.2% in soft candy, and 0.25% in all other food products. Additionally, agar serves as a stabiliser in animal drugs, feeds, and related products, provided it adheres to good manufacturing and feeding practices, ensuring safety and compliance in these applications (Potter and Hotchkiss 2012). The properties of agarose are tunable by concentration, functionalisation, and blending to mimic the desire tissue performance. Several reports indicated the biomedical application of agarose due to its excellent pharmaceutical additive properties, including controlled self-gelation, water-solubility, adjustable tensile strength, and non-immunogenicity. Moreover, agarose demonstrates skin regeneration efficacy due to the presence of functional groups and water absorption capacity that support cellular adhesion, proliferation, and other cellular activity (Zarrintaj et al. 2017). In addition, the agarose-based hydrogel has been considerably utilised in the investigation of mechanical load reactions for chondrocytes and mesenchymal stem cells (Park et al. 2009). Further, agarose has acquired a wide range of pharmaceutical applications such as drug delivery (Grolman et al. 2019), cancer therapy (Guo et al. 2019), tissue engineering and regenerative medicine (Hafezi et al. 2019), and disease diagnosis, controlling, and treatment (Pearl et al. 1984). Furthermore, agarose has been utilised in various tissue-engineering applications, including neural system (Stokols et al. 2006), bone formation (Sánchez-Salcedo et al. 2008), cardiac regeneration, wound healing, and attachment to tissue such as skin (Miguel et al. 2014), brain, and cornea (Pettikiriarachchi et al. 2010). 3.3.8.2 Regulatory Status and Future Perspectives Agarose, derived from agar, is a remarkable biopolymer known for its unique attributes. It boasts an exceptional porous structure that facilitates nutrient and oxygen flow, making it ideal for various applications. Notably, agarose is both biodegradable and biocompatible, offering excellent mimicry of human tissue, promoting cell-matrix interaction, exhibiting elasticity, and demonstrating remarkable hydrophilicity. The remarkable biomaterial properties of agarose, including cell migration and versatile mechanical attributes linked to ionic conductivity, position it as a prime candidate for human organ regeneration. Additionally, agarose and its composites play a pivotal role in the regeneration of cartilage tissue, highlighting its significance in biomedical applications. Agarose-based hydrogels, known for mirroring tissue properties and displaying non-immunological, biocompatible, and non-toxic characteristics with Figure 9: Agarose structure. Nevertheless, these formulations require further comprehensive evaluation in clinical and real- world settings to realise their full potential. 3.3.9 Hyaluronic Acid Hyaluronic acid, a naturally-occurring glycosaminoglycan polysaccharide, exhibits a remarkably conserved molecular structure across mammalian species. Hyaluronic acid indicates distinct physiochemical properties, which emphasise its application as a lubricating cushioning, and some researchers reported in vitro anti-inflammatory activity. 3.3.9.1 Structure and Properties Hyaluronic acid, or hyaluronan, is a linear polysaccharide consisting of repeating disaccharide units: β-1,4-D-glucuronic acid and β-1,3-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine. It is a non-sulfated glycosaminoglycan found throughout the body, from the eye’s vitreous humour to the extracellular matrix in cartilage tissues (Fraser et al. 1997). Recent research has placed significant emphasis on the modification of three pivotal functional groups. These include glucuronic acid carboxylic acid, primary and secondary hydroxyl groups, and N-acetyl groups. Notably, carboxylates have been subject to amidation, while hydroxyls have undergone modifications such as etherification, divinylsulfone crosslinking, esterification, and bis-epoxide crosslinking, advancing the field of chemical manipulation in a variety of applications (Kuo and Prestwich 2010). These hyaluronic acid derivatives fall into two primary categories: monolithic and living (Prestwich and Kuo 2008). Monolithic hyaluronic acid represents terminally modified HA variants, incapable of forming new bonds amidst cellular or tissue environments. They necessitate processing for versatile applications. Typical serum hyaluronic acid levels range from 10 to 100 µg/L but significantly rise in patients with osteoarthritis. The elimination half-life has been reported as 2.5 to 5.5 minutes in human plasma (Goa and Benfield 1994). The biomedical application of hyaluronic acid indicates it is an essential part of connective, epithelial, and neural tissues and contributes to cell proliferation and migration. 3.3.10 Tamarindus indica L. Seed Gum Tamarind, a sought-after tropical fruit renowned for its rich pulp, thrives abundantly in the regions of Africa and Asia. Tamarindus indica, an evergreen tree within the Fabaceae family, boasts impressive dimensions, reaching heights of up to 24 metres and girths of 7 metres, while its gracefully expansive crown adds to its allure. Tamarind, a nutritional powerhouse, serves as a source of biodegradable polymers from its seeds and kernels. Tamarindus indica is abundant in crude protein, carbohydrates, iron, and vitamin A. Virtually, every part of the tree finds diverse applications in food, chemical, pharmaceutical, textile, and other industries, as well as in agriculture and fuel production (Dagar et al. 1995). 88 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 3.3.10.1 Structure and Properties Phytochemical analysis of the T. indica tree has revealed a diverse array of bioactive compounds, including phenolics, cardiac glycosides, and organic acids like mallic and tartaric acid. Additionally, the tree’s constituents encompass mucilage and pectin, with sugars like arabinose, xylose, galactose, and glucose alongside uronic acid. Furthermore, the ethanolic extract showcases a spectrum of essential elements, albeit in varying quantities, encompassing arsenic, magnesium, potassium, phosphorus, lead, and zinc. Further, the pulp contains organic acids, amino acids, invert sugar (25–30%), pectin, protein, and fat with some pyrazines and thiazoles (2-ethyl thiazole, 2-methyl thiazole). In addition, the leaves are a rich source of triterpenes, lupanone, and lupeol (Imam and Azhar 2007). Additionally, graft structural modification of seed kernel polysaccharides with monomer, acrylamide, and or polyacrylamide followed by ceric ion or free radical ions reported improvement in various pharmaceutical applications (Nandi et al. 2019; Jha et al. 2022). 3.3.10.2 Biomedical and Food Industry Uses The tamarind fruit pulp is highly prized, finding diverse applications both domestically and industrially. Its tangy pulp is a culinary favourite, enhancing dishes like curries, sauces, and even ice cream, while its seeds serve as valuable by-products stemming from domestic and food industry usage. Tamarind seed polymers have been extensively explored as tablet binder, mucoadhesive drug delivery, sustained or controlled release drug delivery, transdermal film, etc. Moreover, the reported pharmacological use of fruit is laxative, with a spasmolytic effect, and peptic ulcer activity with ameliorative effect against chemical-induced acute. In addition, several pharmacological applications have been reported for various parts of plants, including antimicrobial, antiparasitic, antifungal, antiviral, antinematodal, antidiabetic, antivenom, analgesic, and anti-inflammatory activity. Further, phenolic-rich fruit extract demonstrates antioxidant properties with beneficial effects on cardiovascular health. The chronic long-term different dose toxicity on animals reported no side effect (Silva et al. 2009), with no change in biochemical analysis, liver function, and body weight for isolated seed polysaccharides (Heimbach et al. 2013). In another investigation, the toxic effect was not mentioned; however, a surge in white blood cells with thrombocytes was seen (Bhadoriya et al. 2011). 3.3.11 Starch Starch is a polysaccharide molecule that is found in nature and is biodegradable, inexpensive, renewable, and abundant. The ‘starch’ is a Germanic word that means ‘Strong, stiff, strengthen, stiffer’, while the Greek term for starch is ‘amylon’, which means ‘not milled’. Starch plays a crucial role in various industries where it is enzymatically converted into sugars, such as malted barley in the production of beer and whisky. These sugars are then fermented to yield ethanol, serving a dual purpose in alcoholic beverages and biofuel manufacturing. Natural Biopolymer 89 3.3.11.1 Structure and Properties Starch, the second most prevalent organic compound in nature after cellulose, is a polymeric carbohydrate composed of glucose units linked by glycosidic bonds. It serves as the primary energy reserve in the greenest plants. Renowned as the predominant carbohydrate in human diets, starch is abundantly found in staple foods like wheat and potatoes, ensuring a vital role in global nutrition. Plants employ a two-step process to synthesise starch, beginning with the conversion of glucose 1-phosphate to ADP-glucose through the enzyme glucose-1-phosphate adenyltransferase, utilising ATP as an energy source. Subsequently, starch synthase appends ADP-glucose to a growing glucose chain via a 1,4-alpha glycosidic bond, releasing ADP and yielding amylose. Starch branching enzymes then introduce 1,6-alpha glycosidic bonds into amylose, creating the branched structure of amylopectin. Amylose is an α-1,4-dioxane polymer that is approximately linear that can form a strong, isotropic, odourless, tasteless, and colourless film due to its excellent film-forming ability. The amylose has 500 to 6,000 glucose units on average, which are distributed over 1 to 20 chains. Starch is typically composed of around 20–25% amylose and 75–80% amylopectin by weight, with each component contributing to its unique properties. Analysing the molecular structure of starch is crucial to understanding its various applications. The interplay between amylose and amylopectin within starch granules and pastes is a complex relationship, influencing its overall functionality (Zobel 1988). 3.3.11.2 Regulatory Status and Future Perspectives Meeting current starch demand relies on a limited crop selection, notably potatoes, maize, wheat, and tapioca. Enhancing starch properties for industry involves altering extracted starch chemically and physically, along with influencing starch biosynthesis within the plant. Starch and modified starch are considered safe by the FDA, but their usage must stay within necessary limits and comply with FDA regulations. For safety, food additive containers must be labeled as ‘food starch-modified’ alongside the required information as per the FDA Act. Starch’s distinctive properties offer numerous possibilities for innovative products. However, a lack of recognition may impede our understanding of granule characteristics. Customising starch for enhanced utility and value is essential, but introducing novel derivatives or substitution levels might face restrictions. Exploring new modified-starch products presents exciting opportunities. While controlling reaction sites within granules and molecules remains challenging, two promising avenues are emerging: leveraging novel commercial starch sources and harnessing biological modifications of existing base starches. These avenues hold significant potential for innovative starch-based products and applications (Bemiller 1997). 90 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 4. Conclusions and Future Prospectus Nature represents a vast reservoir of useful resources that can be employed in various fields. Natural polymers are one such resource and are currently targeted for beneficial applications. The use of polymers sourced from nature opens a new research frontier, with potential applications extending across a variety of sectors. Although, at present, the use of natural polymers in certain fields is still in the developmental stages, there are indications that following the optimisation of relevant factors, natural polymers will soon replace their synthetic counterparts. The use of natural polymers in pharmaceuticals as drug excipients is one area of the application currently being commercialised. However, the fabrication of natural polymer-based packaging materials is still limited by the obvious adverse properties of the polymer. This highlights the need for further studies and investigation into the development and improvement towards enhancing the qualities and characteristics of natural polymers. In addition, the vastness of natural polymers in terms of properties, structure, and sources signifies grey areas that are yet to be explored in the exploration, extraction, purification, modification, and engineering of natural polymers. Introduction Biomaterials is a fast-growing field in the following past decade (Hench 1998; Langer and Tirrell 2004; Bandyopadhyay 2018) . These substances have potential applications in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine for the production of biomedical devices such as steel hip and metal or polymer stents, knee replacements, knee and ligament implants, polymer vascular grafts, ceramic dental implants, polymer sutures, and artificial heart valves, hydrogel contact lenses, etc. (Caló 2015; Lam and Wu 2012; Satarkar and Zach Hilt 2008; Williams 2019; Yang et al. 2018). The developments in the area of regenerative medicine have made biomaterials to be used in the application of healing damaged blood vessels, skin, muscle, bone, and cartilage (Nada 2014). They are divided into metal and metal alloys, organic ceramics, organic and inorganic polymers, and metal, carbon-based materials and composite materials and blends (Sionkowska 2011; Dhandayuthapani et al. 2011; Prasad et al. 2017; Chen and Thouas 2015; Wang and Yeung 2017). Polymers have gained more attention because of their capacity to enhance performance, versatile and adaptable chemical and material designs through unquestionably flexible result methodologies, and potential for customisation based on request requirements. 5 1 TGP Bioplastics Pvt. Biopolymer Science, CIPET - IPT, Kochi, India. * Corresponding author: swethashaji15@gmail.com 100 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization The first prerequisite for a polymer to be used in biomedical applications is biocompatibility. The property of being biocompatible is the lack of toxicity or adverse effects on biological systems, or it is a substance’s ability to perform in a given application with a sufficient host response (Grainger 1999). Another factor is the biodegradability in various applications. It resolves present difficulties, such as problems with the long-term biocompatibility of revision procedures as well as their practical and moral implications (Nair and Laurencin 2007). Both organic and synthetic polymers have the potential to degrade. Collagen is one example of a natural polymer that degrades and has been utilised for medicinal purposes for a long time (Barbucci 2002). Collagens have been found to be useful as scaffolds in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine applications (Yannas et al. 2010; Kenar et al. 2019). Collagens of various forms are found in a variety of connective tissues, including bone, skin, tendon, cartilage, and other connective tissues (Yue 2014). Collagen is made up of acidic and basic amino acid residues, including glycine, proline, hydroxyproline, and lysine, and it can be positively or negatively charged depending on the environment (pH). Collagen or polyester materials are the basis for the biodegradable polymers utilised in regenerative medicine and tissue engineering applications. Many biocompatible products for biomedical applications can be created by physically or chemically mixing various materials or by employing the right processing techniques. Polymers utilised in biomedical engineering are divided into two categories: both artificial and natural polymers. Chitosan and other natural polymers exhibit the required biocompatibility, but without the addition of other polymers, their mechanical qualities fall short. The characteristics that repel water of polycaprolactone, a synthetic biopolymer that is commonly employed in tissue engineering, reduces the effectiveness of cell attachment, highlighting the importance of mixing PCL with other polymers to achieve hydrophilicity (Salati et al. 2020). For instance, PCL is a synthetic polymer that is biocompatible and is frequently used in biomedical engineering. Due to its adequate degradability and biocompatibility, PCL is a promising option for biomedical applications (Sharma et al. 2016; Hejna et al. 2015) . PCL has been utilised in the administration of drugs and long-term implants; however, in order to achieve the appropriate mechanical and cell adherence qualities, it needs to be joined with other polymers (Salati et al. 2020). Polyether PEG (polyethylene glycol) is a versatile substance utilised in many industries, including medicine. The attractive process of PEGylation, which involves joining PEG to another molecule, may have therapeutic value. In order to prevent the formation of protein coronas, PEG can prevent protein adsorption, which is significant in medication delivery (Abdolmaleki et al. 2016). Polymer blending is a common approach for combining the qualities of distinct polymer components or creating new materials that tend to be better. Intermacromolecular interactions may cause such features, affecting macromolecular mobility and microstructure at various scales (Sionkowska 2011; López-Ângulo and Sobral 2016). Because of the biological qualities of their distinct components, natural polymer blends are frequently anticipated for biomedical applications. They also have a number of distinct advantages, including the availability of renewable resources and the ease with which chemical modifications can be made to adapt Polymer Blends and Composites—Biomedical Application 101 their features (Guitian Oliveira et al. 2014; Ma et al. 2003). Polymers’ variable microstructure allows for more precise creation of biological materials and systems. Several research studies have examined the use of polymers as therapeutic systems, such as drug carriers, diagnostic systems, fluorescent-loaded polymeric nanoparticles, and regenerative scaffolds in tissue engineering (Zarrintaj et al. 2017). Composite materials are regarded as an indispensable component of regular life because of their exceptional qualities and wide range of applications. A scattered phase and a matrix phase make up a composite material, combining to improve a property (Jose and Joseph 2012). They offer great qualities like high fatigue strength, low weight, and corrosion resistance. There are numerous dental, tissue engineering, wound healing, and regenerative medicine applications of polymer composites (Zafar et al. 2016; Qasim et al. 2018). Composite materials have a number of advantages compared to ceramics and metal alloys. In radiography, they exhibit unwanted artefacts, and in the case of composite materials, the radio transparency can be modified by mixing contrast medium with the polymer. Diagnostic techniques like CT and MRI are completely compatible with the composite materials. Additionally, they serve as the structural foundation for imaging equipment. In biomedical applications like hard tissue application, composite materials are commonly used, which include bone fracture repair (CF/epoxy composite materials used as external fixators), bone plates (composites of PTFE, PA, and polyester), joint replacement, spine instrumentation, total hip replacement, and intramedullary nails, etc. The soft tissue application includes bulk space fillers, encapsulants and carriers, useful load-bearing and support implants, and other devices like medical equipment. In this chapter, the biomedical application of the polymer blends and composites is given. 2. Natural Polymer Blends 2.1 Blends of Chitosan Chitosan is a polysaccharide with polyelectrolyte cationic properties. This biopolymer has a high charge density and is biocompatible. Additionally, it is non-toxic, and it has a powerful mucoadhesion. It is possible to create a novel product based on such binary combinations of materials by mixing hyaluronic acid with chitosan polymers. There are numerous biomedical uses for hydrogels, microspheres, sponges, films, and nanoparticles produced containing hyaluronic acid as well as chitosan. Hyaluronic acid and chitosan, as well as their blended films’ surface roughness, were changed by blending. The composition of the blend, as well as the solvent used to make the blend, determines the composition of the chitosan-hyaluronic acid mixture (Sionkowska et al. 2020) (Figure 1) . PH and ionic strength influence the interactions between chitosan and hyaluronic acid (Ding et al. 2019). Applications for tissue engineering and cartilage regeneration have been investigated using hyaluronic acid and chitosan- based hydrogel mixtures (Sionkowska et al. 2020). In vivo cartilage regeneration with chitosan-hyaluronic acid dialdehyde hydrogels has also been investigated (Karabiyik Acar et al. 2018). Coacervate-based scaffolds made of hyaluronic acid and chitosan have been suggested to create cartilage tissue. Additionally, stem cells from bone marrow were enclosed in these coacervates. Zhang et al. reported using 102 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization chitosan and hyaluronic acid-based hydrogels for pH-sensitive medication release that are injectable and body temperature sensitive (Zhang et al. 2018) . According to the study, the hydrogels’ mechanical strength can be increased by the formation of chitosan’s protonated amines form hydrogen bonds with one another and the carboxyl group in hyaluronic acid, which also reduces the first rapid drug release from the hydrogel. Additionally, chitosan-based polymers and hyaluronic acid can be employed to create a new generation of wound dressings (Pachuau 2015). Polymers’ variable microstructure allows for more precise creation of biological materials and systems. Several research studies have examined the use of polymers as therapeutic systems, such as drug carriers, diagnostic systems, fluorescent-loaded polymeric nanoparticles, and tissue engineering as regenerative scaffolds (Belluzo et al. 2016). The first need for a polymer to be used in biomedical applications is biocompatibility. There are two types of polymers used in biomedical engineering: synthetic and natural polymers (Belluzo et al. 2016). Chitosan has adequate biocompatibility, but its mechanical qualities are insufficient unless it is blended with polymers. A biocompatible synthetic polymer called polycaprolactone (PCL) is frequently used in tissue engineering; however, its hydrophobic properties reduce the effectiveness of cell adhesion, emphasising the necessity to blend PCL with other polymers to achieve hydrophilicity (Grossen et al. 2017). When it comes to combining polymer pairings, miscibility is crucial. Immiscible polymers are susceptible to phase separation, which modifies blends’ surface structures and thus regulates cellular activity (Tipduangta et al. 2021). Rarely are polymer mixes miscible, but by using compatibilisers, they can be somewhat miscible (Tipduangta et al. 2021). Different To promote miscibility, mixtures of polymers have been given compatibilisers (Tipduangta et al. 2021) . Maleic anhydride was utilised as a compatibiliser when it was grafted onto polypropylene (PP-g-MAH) (Tipduangta et al. 2021). Electrospinning, gelation, and casting are common ways for fabricating blends; however, the appropriate polymer mixes are specified in the final application and production techniques (Tipduangta et al. 2021).
