Polymer Blends and Composites—Biomedical Application 103 Due to mechanical defects, natural polymers such as chitosan cannot be used alone in biomedical applications; consequently, blends have been used to compensate for the lack of mechanical qualities (Tipduangta et al. 2021). Natural polymers require a hydrogel by adding a crosslinking agent, making them toxic (Belluzo et al. 2016). In order to overcome these limitations, agarose with self-gelling characteristics was used (Tipduangta et al., 2021). Aldehyde groups were produced on the alginate chain by applying sodium metaperiodate to produce a homogeneous gel. Furthermore, to alter the mechanical properties of the hydrogel, precise agarose concentration selection is necessary (Tipduangta et al. 2021). For biomedical applications, a blend of chitosan and carboxymethyl cellulose. Ultrasonic compatibilisation was used to improve the blend compatibility. The mechanical qualities of the compatibilised blend were found to be improved (Belluzo et al. 2016). For cartilage regeneration, Bhat et al. used a chitosan/agarose/gelatin (CAG) combination. The cryogelation process created porous scaffolds with appropriate mechanical characteristics and enough nutrition penetration. CAG has been shown to produce a three-dimensional environment for cartilage tissue engineering (Bhat et al. 2011). In order to enable the xenotransplantation of a bioartificial pancreas enclosing the islet cell, Yang et al. used an immunoisolative supportive matrix made of chitosan and gelatin (Yang et al. 2008). Miguel et al. created thermosensitive hydrogels for skin regeneration by combining chitosan and agarose. Biocompatibility, porosity, wettability, and cellular proliferation were all good in this product (Miguel et al. 2014). Previously, chitosan/ alginate nanoparticles were found to have antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties and were used for pathogen target therapy (Zarrintaj et al. 2017). 2.2 Blends of Collagen The use of hyaluronic acid changes the characteristics of collagen (Taravel and Domard 1995). As a structural protein, collagen provides human and animal bodies with basic structural and mechanical support. Natural polymers, such as collagen, are commonly used in biological applications. Examples of collagen application include the creation of synthetic tendons and blood vessels, artificial skin, dental implants, ocular implants, cartilage regeneration, nerve regeneration, and alternatives for bone grafts (collagen composites with inorganic particles) (Taguchi and Tanaka 2002). Collagen and hyaluronic acid may interact in a variety of ways. Taguchi et al. examined hyaluronic acid and collagen, which were blended together, and investigated the electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions between the two polymers. New matrices based on the blends were made (Taguchi and Tanaka 2002). Self-assembly of hyaluronic acid-collagen membranes for regenerative medicine applications is possible (Taguchi et al. 2002). The multipore architectures of the lyophilised matrices allow for the preparation of cartilage regeneration (Taguchi et al. 2002). Crosslinking was carried out using 1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethyl aminopropyl) carbodiimide porous collagen/hyaluronic acid matrices (Park et al. 2003). These scaffolds can be utilized to regenerate cutaneous tissue. Hyaluronic acid and collagen-based porous sponges’ mixtures were produced by lyophilising, 1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)- carbodiimide (EDC) crosslinking, and freezing together (Segura et al. 2005) . The biodegradation kinetics and mechanical strength were influenced by the 104 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization collagen/hyaluronic acid composition and the appropriate manufacturing method. When this mixture was crosslinked with 1,4-butanedioldiglycidyl ether, substances that could be utilised as soft tissue fillers were produced. The material was shown to have excellent mechanical characteristics, biological stability, and biocompatibility. A three-dimensional network was formed by crosslinking using 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether with collagen and HA. This hydrogel is also a promising biomaterial for filling and repairing soft tissues. Hydrogels made of hyaluronic acid and collagen can be employed as a biodegradable medium for effective and regulated gene transfer (Segura et al. 2005). Electrospinning is another method for creating novel materials based on biopolymer mixes. Several research groups have used electrospinning to create a nanofibrous hyaluronic acid/collagen hybrid scaffold (Liu et al. 2014; Qasim et al. 2018). 3. Natural and Synthetic Blends Synthetic and biocompatible natural polymer mixtures in biomedical applications can have synergistic effects. Synthetic and natural polymers can be combined to mimic tissue behaviour, with the synthetic polymer providing mechanical capabilities and the natural polymer providing ECM-like features (Belluzo et al. 2016). PV A was employed to improve gelatin’s mechanical characteristics (Taguchi et al. 2002). Electroactive gelatin was found to be biocompatible and regenerative in bone tissue (Liu et al. 2014). PLA/starch mixes have also received much attention due to their biodegradability, renewability, and biocompatibility. A combination absence of a compatibiliser experiences phase separation due to the PLA’s hydrophobic properties and starch’s hydrophilic properties, leading to unsuitable mechanical characteristics. Different compatibilisers have been used depending on the application to increase the miscibility of these polymers, including maleic anhydride (MA) and methylene diphenyl diiscyanate (MDI) (Belluzo et al. 2016). Ferrarezi et al. used PEG as a compatibiliser to strengthen the impact and elastic modulus of PLA/thermoplastic starch (TPS) blends. It was discovered that adding a compatibiliser increased impact energy between 55 and 119 J/m (Ferrarezi et al. 2013). In a different study, a PLA/starch mixture had chitosan added to it, which increased elongation at break and antibacterial activity while maintaining a lower tensile strength (Bie et al. 2013). PP has gotten a lot of interest in the biomedical area because it is a common synthetic plastic, yet it has a low level of cellular interaction. Blending PP and chitosan was suggested to improve biocompatibility. Because PP is hydrophobic, it cannot interact with chitosan’s polar sites, resulting in an immiscible mixture. In order to enhance blend miscibility and interaction, MA was utilised as a compatibiliser, resulting in a uniform film (Carrasco-Guigón et al. 2017). PE and chitosan were mixed by Quiroz-Castillo et al. to produce a polymer that is biocompatible and has strong mechanical qualities. To improve the compatibility of PE with chitosan, a compatibiliser, polyethylene-g- MA, was utilised. The compatibilised blend was easy to process and had increased elongation at break (Quiroz-Castillo et al. 2014). Agarose/PCL blends are a good choice for medical engineering, but phase separation is a problem. Blends of agarose/ PCL and agarose/PEG-PCL were made by Chandel et al. (2016). They discovered that when PEG was added to PCL with agarose, phase separation behaviour was lessened, Polymer Blends and Composites—Biomedical Application 105 resulting in improved mechanical characteristics. In addition, the presence of PEG boosted loading capacity while lowering the first burst and controlled drug release rates (López-Ângulo and Sobral 2016). A co-continuous nano-phase morphology with improved mechanical characteristics was produced poly (methyl methacrylate)- b(co)-poly (2-dimethylamino) ethyl methacrylate, a linear triblock, was added by Bera et al. macromolecule to a solution of agarose and PCL (Bera et al. 2015). In a different study, reactive compatibiliser was employed to enhance the miscibility of dextran and agarose with PCL. Reactive compatibilisers such as poly (2-dimethyl amino ethyl methacrylate) and PDMA-b-poly (Nisopropyl acrylamide) copolymers were added to the mixture, which reduced phase separation and sol-fraction while improving mechanical characteristics. Improve miscibility enhanced blood and cytocompatibility compatibility. These scaffolds can be used for tissue engineering and medicine administration (Chandel et al. 2016). Adipic acid, 1,4-Butanediol, and succinic acid combine to form the biocompatible polymer known as poly (PBSA or polybutylene succinate-co-adipate). The cost of PBSA products is quite expensive. It is proposed that the PBSA be blended with other materials to lower the price (Belluzo et al. 2016). To improve the blend’s characteristics, we used glycidyl methacrylate as a compatibiliser. Because of polysaccharides and polyphenols in WBTF, adding them to PBSA improved cytocompatibility. Utilising the compatibiliser has slightly decreased cytocompatibility since it improved the miscibility and interface of WBTF and PBSA, which controlled the polysaccharide and polyphenol release. Poly (vinyl chloride) with genistein (G) can both be biomedically compatible with epoxidised soybean oil (ESBO). G/ESBO/PVC is utilised in medical applications that come into touch with blood, such as haemodialysis and blood bag tubing (Belluzo et al. 2016). El-Moghazy et al. developed a chitosanepolyvinyl alcohol (PV A) nanofiber-based electrochemical biosensor. This biosensor recognised Pirimiphos-methyl, which was found in samples of olive oil and recovered to nearly 100% (El-Moghazy et al. 2016). Cadmium enrichment poses a health risk to humans. As an electrochemical biosensor, cadmium was detected using electrospun polyamide 6/chitosan nanofibers with gold nanoparticles (Migliorini et al. 2017). 4. Applications (I) Polymer Blends for Drug Delivery Polymer mixing has been touted as a promising method for creating fresh and distinct drug delivery systems with altered physical and chemical properties. Polymer blends mix two or more polymers to produce better, enhanced, or tailored characteristics and functionality, which can lead to considerable benefits in medication delivery. Physical mixtures, core-shell models, and block copolymer models are the three main polymer blending methodologies utilised for drug administration. Changes in the environment’s temperature and pH, as well as the physiochemical features of the target organs, can all influence these mixed polymers’ ability to deliver drugs. The pattern of drug release from this combined polymeric micro-and nanocarrier can be significantly impacted by the possibility of chemical interactions between medicinal compounds and polymers (Ghasemiyeh and Mohammadi-Samani 2021) . When taking into account the effort and expense necessary to obtain regulatory approval 106 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization for a novel excipient, polymer blends present a compelling alternative for addressing various formulation and drug delivery difficulties. From a functional aspect, polymer blending is done to enhance, customise, or maximise material performance. While tablets are complicated combinations containing excipients that are not polymeric, like sugars and polyols, there are a few instances where polymer blends give distinctive functionality. Incorporating NaCMC (anionic) and HPMC (non-ionic) has demonstrated synergistic rheological benefits. The increased viscosity is a result of the crosslinking of the polymers’ carboxylic acid and hydroxyl groups through the formation of hydrogen bonds. Such synergistic pairings allow for formulations with lower total polymer concentrations, which is helpful when the size of the medicine product or the amount of excipients must be kept to a minimum. Polymer mixes have also been employed to provide particular medication release characteristics in matrix tablets. Researchers blended the appropriate ratios of anionic (metoprolol tartrate and alprenolol hydrochloride) and non-ionic (HPC or methylcellulose) To create zero- order release patterns for two highly soluble medicines using polymers (Ranga Rao et al. 1988). The TIMERx medication delivery system for matrix tablets is based on the advantageous interactions between xanthan gum and locust bean gum. When two polymers with formed secondary structures in solution are combined, the viscosity and gelation are increased, and the resulting gel is significantly more robust than the combined strength of the original polymers (Staniforth and Baichwal 2005). Tablet, pellet, and capsule film coatings have frequently used polymer combinations. In order to enhance substrate adhesion, modify the coating’s mechanical characteristics, enhance moisture resistance, or modulate medicine delivery, a secondary polymer may be used with a main film former. Low-viscosity HPMCs are the most often utilised polymers for non-functional coating. Plasticizers must be added to HPMC when it is used for tablet coating to improve film flexibility. Plasticizers such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) are routinely employed in HPMC films (Harcum et al. 1998). Additionally, polymeric blends are employed in non-functional film coatings to speed up the coating process, provide dry, fully formed coating systems, and boost medicine stability by reducing water vapour permeability. Polymer blends have been widely employed as functional film coatings for applications requiring controlled release. Although organic solvent-based solutions can be used to apply functional film coatings, latex dispersions in aqueous systems are preferred (Cole et al. 1995) . These are colloidal dispersions of polymers such as vinyl acetate, ethylcellulose, and polymethacrylates, which are insoluble in water. Polymeric additives can alter mechanical characteristics, and medication release rates can improve the controlled- release film coatings’ long-term dissolution profile stability. (II) Polymer Blends for Tissue Engineering Electrospinning (Khaled et al. 2014) and 3-D printing (Carson et al. 2016) are two recently developed pharmaceutical processing techniques that utilise polymer blends. Polymer blends for tissue engineering have also been prepared using these techniques. It is critical to consider the fibre’s properties, porosity, orientation, surface treatment, and tissue application are all important factors to consider when using fibre meshes and electrospun fibres in tissue engineering applications (Sill and von Recum 2008). Polymer Blends and Composites—Biomedical Application 107 Materials that combine natural and synthetic components in the best possible way to balance between mechanical and biomimetic properties are available (Sill and von Recum 2008) . Henry et al. electrospun a slowly disintegrating biodegradable polyesterurethane for developing tissue engineering scaffold, which they produced and described (Henry et al. 2007). They were able to adjust both the mechanical qualities and the pace of deterioration (by hydrolysis) of the scaffolds by altering the proportion of the amorphous and crystalline sections that constitute the polyesterurethane, in addition to the molecular balance of the amorphous division (Henry et al. 2007) . Some research has been conducted on applying non-biodegradable materials for tissue engineering (Chuangchote and Supaphol 2006; Kenawy et al. 2003). Kenawy et al. (rubbing alcohol) successfully electrospun poly (ethyleneco-vinyl alcohol) fibrous mat using a 70% isopropanol/water solution (Kenawy et al. 2003). Additionally, the team was able to demonstrate that the aforementioned mats sustained the in vitro cultivation of fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells (Sill and von Recum 2008). Natural materials like collagen have also been electrospun in an attempt to replicate better the natural ECM (Zhong et al. 2006; Matthews et al. 2002), chitosan (Matsuda et al. 2007), gelatin (Song et al. 2008; Ayres et al. 2006), fibrinogen (McManus et al. 2007), chitin (Noh et al. 2006), and hyaluronic acid (Ji et al. 2006) . Stitzel et al. studied the electrospinning of a mixture that consisted of a blend of PLGA, type I collagen, and elastin to create a vascular substitute (Stitzel et al. 2006) . PLGA was added to scaffolds to increase mechanical properties, including burst strength and compliance of the prosthesis when compared with scaffolds primarily of type I collagen and elastin (Stitzel et al. 2006) . Park et al. looked into developing novel biodegradable scaffolding materials by electrospinning a hybrid mixture of chitin and PGA (Park et al. 2006). Chitin inclusion in PGA matrix elements speeds up decomposition and is applicable to control how quickly PGA/chitin scaffolds degrade (Park et al. 2006). The ability to construct oriented scaffolds for directional mechanical and biological properties, including the ability to restrict soft muscle cell movement, has led to a passion for tissue-engineered vascular prostheses (Sill and von Recum 2008). Tissue engineering is a potential technique for healing or recovering damaged soft tissues. Natural polymers such as collagen, fibrin, and elastin were provided with a lot of research attention in the field of soft tissue engineering scaffolds (Sell et al. 2010; Vázquez and Martínez 2019) . Because the mechanical qualities are generally significantly lower than those of the targeted tissues, their applicability is limited (Dong and Lv 2016; Al Habis et al. 2020). Biodegradable synthetic polymers offer degradation and durable mechanical qualities as compared to natural polymers (Keun Kwon et al. 2005). Polycaprolactone is a common ingredient in soft tissue engineering, including vascular scaffolds (Mo et al. 2006), urethra (Zhang et al. 2017), and cardiac patches (Asadpour et al. 2018) due to its rubbery qualities (Keun Kwon et al. 2005). In a recent work, PCL and poly-(lactide-co-caprolactone) were blended using a Thermally Induced Phase Separation (TIPS) method to produce a permeable hollow scaffold at an ideal ratio of 1:3 (respectively) (Sehgal and Ramsden 2008). Unfortunately, blend scaffolds have low mechanical results compared to raw PCL and PLCL scaffolds. The mechanical and microstructural behaviour of the PCL/PLCL blend scaffolds was investigated by examining the effect of the thermal 108 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization characteristics of the blend solution. The mechanical properties such as tensile strength, modulus of elasticity, and strain energy density increased together with the rise in temperature of the mixed solution. Mechanical strength improved in direct proportion to strut dimension. The temperature difference in the blend solution impacted the phase separation morphologies. The size of spherulites decreased as the temperature increased. The blend scaffold of PLCL/PCL had improved cell growth surfaces compared to the plain PCL-made scaffold. The highly adaptable technique for modifying the blend solution’s temperature prior to the TIPS process can be utilised to raise the mechanical strength of the polymer. 5. Composites A composite consists of two phases that work together to attain an excellent property. It consists of a matrix part and a scattered part. They serve composite materials with distinctive attributes. They have properties like superior fatigue strength, are lightweight, and have stability against corrosion. The major applications of polymer composites are in regenerative treatment, tissue engineering, and dental care applications. Biocomposite material consists of polymer reinforced with natural fibres. They are compatible with the body. The fibres are protected from mechanical and climatic deterioration by the polymer matrix. The biologically derived fibres, such as those found in wood, regenerated cellulose, and plants, are considered natural fibres. They are ecologically benign, less expensive, lower in weight, entirely recyclable, and renewable sources of composites. Wood and non-wood fibres are the two categories of bio composites. (1) Classification of Composites The three composites included in the matrix portion are metal, ceramic, and polymer (Avila et al. 2003; Jose and Joseph 2012) . Additionally, they are categorised as particulate, fibrous, and laminate composites depending on the reinforcement involved. Fibrous composites are further subdivided into natural biofibers and synthetic fibre. Biofiber composites can be segmented into degradable and non- biodegradable matrix types (Ilie and Hickel 2009). Green composites are made from biodegradable polymers and natural biofibers. Furthermore, they fall under the categories of textile and hybrid composites. Ones that constitute hybrids are a combination of two or more fibres. PMCs are classified based on the polymer types, availability, fabrication process, and low cost. For biomedical applications, polymers like copolymers of polylactic acid/ polyglycolide and polyacrylic are used (Ramakrishna et al. 2001). Most commonly used reinforcement structures are the fibres (Mkaddem et al. 2008). The polymers without reinforcement showed insufficient tensile qualities like tensile strength, modulus, and impact resistance. (2) Processing of Polymer Composites The manufacturing processes used to create polymer composites, which have several uses, particularly in the biomedical area, include latex technology, electrospinning, Polymer Blends and Composites—Biomedical Application 109 solution mixing, in situ techniques, and melt extrusion (Al-Enizi et al. 2018; Kaur et al. 2015). (A) Electrospinning By using a strong electric field, fibres with diameters ranging from 2 nanometers to multiple micrometres can be produced during the electrospinning process. This method is applied to prepare nanofibers with greater surface areas. A spinneret, grounded collector, and a high-voltage power supply together form the electrospinning arrangement (Zagho and Elzatahry 2016; Zagho et al. 2018). They are of two types: vertical and horizontal sets (Figure 2). The method involves accelerating the polymeric solution into the collector with the opposed charge. The electrical repulsion forces from the direct current (DC) voltage overcome the interfacial tension of the polymeric compound, resulting in the emission of an electrified jet out of the Taylor pole’s tip. Subsequently, the solvent is vaporized to produce the fibres. (B) Melt Extrusion It is a relatively widely used method of manufacturing polymeric composites. The twin-screw extruder is responsible for mixing the main resin with the necessary additives under a certain condition to ensure homogeneous melting. To get the final product, the polymer composite, after extrusion, is shaped using compression moulding. By varying the filler content, the thermal and mechanical characteristics of the developed composites can be adjusted. For example, ceramic powder was mixed with polylactic acid using a small compounder and its revolving screw under a nitrogen flow to create ceramic/PLA bioresorbable composites (Mathieu et al. 2006). Multiple combinations of residence time, temperature, and screw rotation speed were tested. (C) Solution Mixing It is the process of dissolving polymer with a suitable solvent due to its distinctive thermal character, resulting in the uniform dispersion of additives like montmorillonite clays into the resulting uniform solvent of the polymer. The continual agitation is continued based on calculated time and temperature, as well as mechanical results; Figure 2: Classifications of polymer processing methods for various polymer blends. 110 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization the end product develops within the mould having a particular dimension over a specific thermal profile (Zagho and Khader 2016). For example, by periodic stirring at an appropriate temperature, the PLA material was socked into chloroform to yield PLA reagent. The PLA solution then received the ceramic powder, and it was mixed thoroughly for 30 minutes. To evaporate the solvent, drying at room temperature followed by two days of additional drying over vacuum was applied. (D) Latex Technology This technique produces conductive polymer composites by introducing conductive additives into a network of polymers. It provides the benefit of process upscaling, simple processing, and fillers that are evenly distributed throughout the polymer network (Grossiord and Hermant 2016). In the highly viscous polymer, the nanofillers can be incorporated. With this technology, it is possible to create a 3D framework using filler particles (Jurewicz et al. 2011). The method is broken down into three steps: producing a dispersed colloidal form of the nanofiller, combining polymer latex, and curing the resultant colloidal mix. This technology may be utilised to create graphene polymeric composites and carbon nanotubes, which have the potential to be used in biomedical applications. (Anandhan and Bandyopadhyay 2016). (E) In situ Method Graphene and modified graphene fillers swell before it is incorporated into the matrix (Kuilla et al. 2010). Initially, in the in situ polymerisation process, the liquid monomer is used to swell the filler. In order to begin the polymerisation process, an initiator is added by radiation or heat. This method processes carbon nanotube- polymer composites. It is also used to process polymer composites with high nanotube content (Choi et al. 2022). 6. Application of Composites (1) Tissue Engineering The regeneration of damaged tissues with scaffold biomaterials, which support the growth of new cells, is the concept of tissue engineering (O’Brien 2011). Polymer composite has a morphology where cells can migrate, grow, and seed. (2) Bone For bone tissue engineering certain degradable polymers which are synthetic or natural, like chitosan (Li et al. 2005; Ho et al. 2005), poly (propylene fumarate) (Vehof et al. 2002), and polyesters (Lu et al., 2003), are used. Scaffolds based on PLAGA/calcium phosphate composite microspheres activate the calcium phosphate reprecipitation process in a bone/implant system (Khan et al. 2007). For repairing bone fractures, a polymer composite containing phosphate glass fibre (PGF) is used, which displays good biological and mechanical characteristics (Ahmed et al. 2008). Bone plates containing unidirectional bio-glass fibres and PLA composites that have Polymer Blends and Composites—Biomedical Application 111 been air plasma-treated are used to heal lengthy bone damage (Mehboob et al. 2016). Composite scaffolds made of ethyl cellulose, polylactic acid, and HA are being utilised as load-bearing substitutes (Mao et al. 2018). Polypropylene carbonate, tricalcium phosphate, poly (d)-lactic acid synthetic composites have been used for bone fracture healing (Chang et al. 2017). (3) Blood One of the challenging subjects in the biomedical field is the repair of blood vessels. The artificial scaffolds required increase time for patient recovery (Fujihara et al. 2005). The BNC composites blended with PV A are used as artificial blood vessels (Tang et al. 2015). BNC is a bacterial nanocellulose that has properties like excellent crystallinity, chemical quality, water retaining capacity, biocompatibility, and high humid tensile strength (Gatenholm and Klemm 2010; Putra et al. 2008) . The BNC tubes are unsuitable for vascular graft models due to water loss and poor wound retention. After blending with PV A, properties like water permeability and tensile characteristics were enhanced, and the mechanical properties were controlled by the BNC tube contents. For the application of implants, wound dressings, and surgical sutures, the composites of biological biopolymers like hyaluronic acid, chitosan, alginate, collagen, and gelatin were among the materials used (Niklason 2000; Nwe et al. 2009). By fabricating chitosan/gelatin bilayered composites, microporous blood veins were formed (Badhe et al. 2017). With the use of PLA/chitosan nanofibrous scaffolds, the in vitro cardiomyocyte cultures for drug screening are used as a platform for creating myocardia (Liu et al. 2017). This composite enhances cardiomyocyte growth and adhesion, as well as the formation of heart tissue, by supporting cardiomyocyte maturation along their transverse direction. (4) Skin The skin is the first immune system organ, and it also protects against infections and toxic antigens. It can be vulnerable to diseases, cellular death, and permanent destruction under several stressful situations, such as infection or significant burns (Jeong et al. 2017). Therefore, it is necessary to develop skin-friendly materials that decompose naturally, which is problematic for tissue engineering. The 3D nanofibrous structures developed by moulding polymeric materials have the advantages of mechanical characteristics and an increased surface area-to-volume ratio. It can serve as a carrier for various drug compounds such as antibacterials, antivirals, and anticancer medications (Zagho et al. 2018). Synthetic and natural hydrogels such as alginate, collagen, chitosan and PV A, and polyethylene glycol were used for different kinds of gels to rejuvenate the skin (Chaudhari et al. 2016). Terudermis®, Biobrane®, and Integra® are commercially available fibrous scaffolds that include collagen in combination with medicinal molecules (Chua et al. 2016) . For skin regeneration and proliferation, a blend of reconstituted HA and chondroitin sulfate is used (Bhowmick et al. 2017). Alginate-based thin films were used to implant injured and burned skin (Pereira et al. 2013; Thu et al. 2012). 112 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization (5) Oral Tissues The oral tissues are damaged by dental periodontitis and caries (Nanci 2017). These have critical functions in humans. Due to the interaction between the mouth and internal fluids and other cytotoxic material, the material inside the oral cavity gets damaged (Jones 2001). In order to address these challenges, in vitro oral tissue engineering has been successfully accomplished (Zafar et al. 2015) . Polylactic-co-glycolic acid and polyglycolic acid graft scaffolds are primarily used to create graft scaffolds to maintain the development of full-grown tissues for teeth. Degradable polymer substrates were utilised to create 3D salivary glandular cells. (Duailibi et al. 2004) . HA and PLA blends were used to fabricate jaw joints. These blends were infused with specific cells to generate osteochondral tissue with arterial bones (Schek et al. 2005). (6) Wound Dressing A biochemical and cellular process called wound healing provides crucial qualities to ward against microbial infections (Archana et al. 2013; Menon and Kligman 2009). Growth factor-secreting cells are important in controlling the wound-healing process (Guo and Dipietro 2010). The key event in an optimal wound healing process is fibroblast movement to the wound site to make collagen fibres for the outermost layer of cells (Bielefeld et al. 2013). The viability and growth of keratinocytes are induced by the fibroblasts (Witte and Kao 2005). The use of wound dressings allows for the accelerated healing of wounds and protection of the wound site (Seaman 2002; Dongargaonkar et al. 2013). The materials for wound dressing include a wide class of materials like foams, hydrofibers, alginate, fibres, colloids, polymeric hydrogels, films, and polymers (Boateng et al. 2008; Mi et al. 2011) (Figure 3). By incorporating kaolin, polymers’ biomechanical and thermodynamic performance can be improved (Chen et al. 2015; Pradhan et al. 2015). In order to improve the properties like drug release and haemostatic characteristics, the polymer dressings can be modified (Li et al. 2016; Loh et al. 2015). Through the integration of kaolin into a mechanically durable PU foam, multifunctional haemostatic composites of polyurethane foam with kaolin were fabricated (Avila et al. 2003). The kaolin content controls both mechanical and pharmacological release qualities. They exhibit Figure 3: Different wound dressings methods. Polymer Blends and Composites—Biomedical Application 113 properties like exceptional distribution of drugs, cellular compatibility, and absorbent properties. Titanium oxide particles were incorporated as a supporting material into the scaffolds to promote cell growth due to the exceptional antibacterial properties of titanium oxide (Tang et al. 2009). Chitosan/TiO 2 composite membrane is synthesised for wound healing, fibroblast cell’s survival, and proliferation (Behera et al. 2017). This composite has excellent antibacterial behaviour against staphylococcus aureus. Banana peel-based biopolymer possesses antioxidant and antibacterial effects against microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and yeast due to its high mineral concentration and phenolic structure (Someya et al. 2002; Mokbel and Hashinaga 2005). Nanocellulose finds applications like dressing treatment for wound care owing to this remarkable material strength, flexibility, and water-holding capabilities (Czaja et al. 2007) . Its elevated surface-to-volume ratio promotes and facilitates both cell proliferation and migration since these have limitations that show poor antimicrobial behaviour against pathogenic microorganisms (Lin and Dufresne 2014; Jebali et al. 2014). In the context of in vitro wound dressings, a bio-nanocomposite composed of nanocellulose, chitosan, and poly(vinyl pyrrolidone) were employed (Poonguzhali et al. 2017) . It exhibits outstanding cytotoxicity, compatibility with blood, and antimicrobial efficacy against both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. The electrospun fibres exhibit characteristics like a significant volume ratio to surface area and porosity, along with exceptional compatibility with the extracellular matrix (Lannutti et al. 2007; Meng et al. 2010; Gautam et al. 2013) Additionally, fibre composites demonstrate semipermeability, absorbent properties, and hemostatic qualities. (Zhang et al. 2005). By using this approach, a potent wound dressing was developed by electrospinning thermally responsive poly(N- isopropylacrylamide) incorporated into poly (l-lactic acid-co-ε-caprolactone) along the antibacterial ciprofloxacin (Li et al. 2017). Drug-loaded nanofibers can accelerate the in vivo wound healing process. As a wound-healing strategy, electrospinning PCL in conjunction with chitosan and chitosan-caffeic acid is used (Oh et al. 2016). The biocompatible and antibiotic qualities of silk fibroin nanofibers were greatly enhanced by graphene oxide, making graphene oxide/silk fibroin nanofibers having a biologically inspired nano framework an excellent option that promotes wound treatment applications (Wang et al. 2018). 7. Conclusion Polymer blends have been instrumental in many medical breakthroughs. They can come in a wide variety of forms, and a single synthetic or natural polymer cannot meet every requirement for certain applications. In this regard, research has discovered that the synergic impact of polymers can achieve the goal. Later, blends emerged, and this chapter examined natural and hybrid natural and synthetic blends. Chitosan’s multi-property ability makes it suited for a wide range of medical uses. Scientists have discovered that when used in a blend, chitosan works well with both natural and synthetic materials. Researchers are turning to collagen material to achieve mechanical strength, and the results have been promising. When utilised as a blend, synthetic and biodegradable materials such as polyvinyl alcohol, PLA, and PCL are also compatible. A combination of polymers can be utilised for certain medical applications, such as tissue engineering and drug delivery. 114 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization The composite materials are promising materials for biomedical applications with superior characteristics and diverse applications. They have the benefit of being affordable as well as available in both synthetic and natural forms. Composites are useful for wound healing, tissue engineering, and dentistry. The natural and synthetic materials that are available for composites are likewise divided into two categories. Depending on the requirements, new composite materials might be added or replaced. Current research studies for new composite advancements are heavily relying on degradable polymers, both natural and synthetic, such as chitosan, PV A, and PLA. Several other applications, including tissue engineering, skin, blood, dental tissue, bone, wound dressing, and others, already incorporate such materials. Introduction Nanotechnology is an interdisciplinary area of research and development that involves manufacturing, processing, and applying substances or devices with one or more dimensions in the nanometer range (Mozafari 2007). The world’s nanotechnology value as of 2020 is worth 54.2 billion US dollars, projected to reach about 127 billion US dollars in 2027. With the popularity of nanotechnology soaring consistently, the adoption and integration of nanomaterials in the food industry are gaining traction. Nanotechnology in food has been applied to improve the taste, flavor, color, texture, 6 1 Department of Chemistry, Faculty of Physical Sciences, Alex-Ekwueme Federal University, Ndufu- Alike, P.M.B.1010, Abakaliki, Ebonyi State, Nigeria. 2 Department of Food and Human Nutritional Sciences, Faculty of Agricultural and Food Sciences, University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, Manitoba, R3T 2N2, Canada. 3 Division of Infectious Diseases, Department of Internal Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, Prince of Songkla University, Hat Yai, Songkhla 90112, Thailand. 4 School of Allied Health Sciences, Walailak University, Nakhon Si Thammarat, 80160, Thailand. * Corresponding author: titilope12@gmail.com Biopolymer Complexation for the Development... 123 and consistency of foodstuffs, increase bioavailability, absorption, and stability of nutraceuticals compounds, novel food packaging materials development, as well as to develop nano-sensors for traceability and monitoring the status of food during transport and storage (Sekhon 2010). Food nanotechnology has received increasing interest, which opens a new frontier of possibilities for the food industry. Biopolymers, which are large molecular structures synthesized by a living organism (Schmitt et al. 2009), have a more complex chemical structure when compared to synthetic polymers (Hosseini et al. 2017a). The low level toxicity of compatibility and biodegradability of biopolymers over synthetic polymers have gained the attention of researchers (Esfanjani et al. 2016). Biopolymers have also been extended to include bioplastics, such as polyglycolic acid, polylactic acid, and their block copolymer (Enderle 2012). These polymers, as an essential functional ingredient, cut across a diverse range of industrial applications not limited to pharmaceuticals and foods (Hosseini et al. 2017a; Patel et al. 2010; Kumar et al. 2018). In foods, biopolymers have been used for shelf-life extension, stability, enhanced textural properties, as well as improved sensory properties (Olatunde et al. 2020a; Olatunde et al. 2019; Olatunde et al. 2020b; Corredig et al. 2011; Hosseini et al. 2017a). For food packaging, biopolymers have been employed in the development of edible biopolymer-based coatings and films, which provide an additional protective layer or coating for raw materials, thus extending their shelf life (Park et al. 2014). The complexation of natural polymers has attracted much attention in the last few decades due to its potential in the nanotechnology area, particularly in the development of nano-drugs and nano-carriers. The complexation of several polymers and surfactants, including polylactic-co-glycolic acid, chitosan, and alginic acid, has been investigated for the targeted delivery and controlled release of bioactive compounds (Hosseini et al. 2017b). However, the biopolymer complex nano-drugs in foods are still in its infancy. Thus, this chapter gathers recent information on the complexation of biopolymers for the production or development of nano-drugs or nano-carriers for food applications 2. Biopolymers Complexation in Nano-Drugs Formulation Biopolymers’ complexation in nano-drugs formulation relies on the use of intramolecular and intermolecular forces of attraction between polymer layers to create new materials with improved physicochemical properties. In this regard, molecular interactions such as covalent bonding, Coulombic forces, hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interaction, and Van der Waal forces are exploited for the creation of supramolecular networks (Hosseini et al. 2017a), with improved and enhanced capacity for nano-drugs immobilization and delivery. Covalent bonds are strong intermolecular forces in the range of 25–250 kcal/mol, often realized through some ordered chemical reactions between biopolymers and materials to be infused or conjugated. Common examples are using free radical graft polymerization of biopolymers such as chitosan with phenolic compounds. For instance, Zhu et al. (2014) successfully grafted a biologically efficient flavonoid compound onto chitosan to improve the anti-microbial and anti-diabetic properties of the resulting material. Similar to the free radical polymerization method for polyphenols grafting 124 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization to biopolymers is the use of the carbodiimide chemistry between EDC and NHS, with concomitant generation of the highly effective amide bond, for instance, between the amino groups of chitosan and the carboxyl groups of polyphenols, have been widely reported (Xu et al. 2021; Liu et al. 2016; İlyasoğlu et al. 2019). Furthermore, the use of Genipen (a bi-functional, water-soluble cross-linker) can provide strong covalent bonding between biopolymers, and this is thought to be more environmentally sustainable than the use of glutaldehyde (Muzzarelli 2009). Genipen can also react with amino group-containing compounds, such as chitosan and proteins, to produce a bluish color fluorescent adduct (Zhou et al. 2016). Moreover, Coulombic interactions, which can be repulsive or attractive, are equally strong interactions between 25–250 kcal/mol, like a covalent bond. They are often generated through the alteration of pH and ionic strength. Hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions are other prominent forces between biopolymers of about 2–10 kcal/mol and 1–2 kcal/mol, respectively. A hydrogen bond is generated between polar/hydrophilic moieties, such as the interaction between an amino group and a hydroxyl group. Hydrophobic interaction, on the other hand, is interaction generated between hydrophobes or non-polar groups. For instance, structural modification of protein via physical, chemical, and enzymatic modification methods exposes the hydrophobic regions in the polypeptide backbone for interaction. Van der Waal forces are weak electrostatic forces of attraction between neutral molecules. Chemical complexation between biopolymers is designed to act as carriers or platforms for the immobilization of nano-drugs for onward delivery to the target medium. As such, a supramolecular assembly carrier system is developed comprising of the nano-drugs of interest interspersed within the biopolymers network structure. These systems generally take the following forms: carbohydrate-carbohydrate-based complexation, protein- protein-based complexation, carbohydrate-protein-based complexation, and lipid- based complexation. 2.1 Carbohydrate-Carbohydrate-Based Complexation Here, the interaction between two or more biopolymers, specifically carbohydrates, in addition to the nano-drug, is combined to generate a supramolecular assembly network. In this category, single polysaccharide biopolymers (e.g., sodium alginate and carboxymethyl cellulose) or synthetic biopolymers (PV A, PEG, PVP, etc.) are applied as the platform for the immobilization of nano-drugs. They are used alone or blended/combined depending on the nanocarrier platform being developed. For instance, using the ionic gelation method for chitosan nanoparticle synthesis, El-Alfy et al. (2020) investigated a novel delivery system of antibiotics loaded on biocompatible chitosan nanoparticles to inhibit Gram-positive and Gram negative bacteria. Due to the sheer interest in chitosan nanoparticles, particularly for food and pharmaceutical applications, the following reviews are worth mentioning such as Yanat et al. 2021; Singh et al. 2021a. Moreover, Ribeiro et al. (2020) investigated chitosan-chitosan nanoparticles by applying already formulated tripolyphosphate- mediated chitosan nanoparticles to prepare a Pickering emulsion, which was further characterized as a potential food-grade product. To offset some notable limitations Biopolymer Complexation for the Development... 125 of biopolymers, especially in film fabrication, the blending of biopolymers has emerged as a promising strategy. For instance, starch, a common biopolymer, is water-sensitive; thus, its film-forming capacity is heavily dependent on its moisture content, contributing to the low mechanical resistance of starch-based products. Furthermore, starch is limited by its poor thermal processability, arising from its high melting point and low thermal decomposition temperature (Wang et al. 2003). To maximize the full usage of starch in food product-related applications, blending starch with biopolymers is now popular. Wang et al. (2021) investigated the rheological and gelation effect on the phase structure of the hydrocolloid mixed system of hydroxypropyl methylcellulose and hydroxypropyl starch. The study was aimed at understanding parameters that would determine and affect the mixing capacity of the biopolymers. In a bid to gain insight into the physico-mechanical properties of edible film fabricated from the blending of starch, agar and maltodextrin, Wongphan et al. (2020) reported the roles played by the contributing polymers in the overall film quality of the blends. 2.2 Protein-Protein-Based Complexation Proteins are another class of biopolymers that have been well utilized as bio-based platforms for nano-drugs delivery for food applications. Common protein biopolymers include collagen, gelatin, silk fibroin, whey, zein, soy and gluten; milk proteins such as whey and casein are equally popular. For instance, zein, the prominent protein present in corn, has been well established for its ability to encapsulate bioactive compounds for food applications, such as resveratrol (Davidov-Pardo et al. 2015), lutein (Hu et al. 2012), and curcumin (Gómez-Estaca et al. 2012). Owing to its poor solubility in most food solvents, zein is processed into nanoparticle forms using the anti-solvent procedure with water as the anti-solvent agent (Li et al. 2013). Zein nanoparticles have found wide applications in the food area, ranging from the encapsulation and delivery of epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) (Liang et al. 2017) to the fabrication of edible film loaded with bioactive compounds (Jiang et al. 2021). For a further understanding of protein biopolymer chemistry, see the review by Nasrollahzadeha et al. (2021). 2.3 Carbohydrate-Protein-Based Complexation Under this complexation strategy, carbohydrates in the form of polysaccharides and protein interaction are adopted in a bid to obtain a delivery platform for nano-drugs while also playing important roles as functional components of food colloids. Polysaccharide-protein complex formation capitalizes on the key inherent characteristics of the different biopolymers, for instance, with the knowledge that proteins are surface-active molecules and thus can interact with polysaccharides (hydrophilic molecules) through electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions. The major behavior of polysaccharide-protein complex in solution, such as solubility and stability in terms of formation and deformation properties of the complex, is dependent on several factors, including temperature, pH, and ionic strength of the medium, charge density and distribution, and biopolymers mixing ratios (Warnakulasuriya 126 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization et al. 2018). The isoelectric point (IEP) of proteins determines protein behavior in solutions, thus it is a critical factor in protein complexation with polysaccharides. Three prominent scenarios could play out between protein IEP and solution pH. As depicted in Figure 1, at stage I, where the solution pH is less than the p(IEP), positive charges dominate the net charge of proteins and are thus readily available for interaction with the negatively charged functional groups of polysaccharide surfaces, forming a strong electrostatic complex. At stage II, where the solution pH is almost equal to the p(IEP), the net charge on the protein surface is zero. At this stage, the protein is least soluble, with poor stability, arising from weaker complex formation between the polysaccharide and protein. However, at stage III, when the solution pH is greater than the p(IEP), there are more negative charges on protein surfaces, which are thus readily complex with positively charged groups of polysaccharides. From the foregoing, it can be observed that tuning the pH and ionic strength of solutions presents a powerful strategy for modulating polysaccharide-protein complexation for the design and formation of novel food emulsions (Ghosh et al. 2012). 2.4 Lipid-Based Complexation Nano-liposomes, or nanometric versions of liposomes, are colloidal structures formed by the input of energy to phospholipids and cholesterol (stabilizer) in aqueous environments (Mozafari et al. 2008). It is postulated that the specific interactions between these compounds in biological membranes are crucial in forming complexes. The compatibility and safety of these lipid vesicles have attracted particular attention in pharmaceutical, cosmetic, and food industries as nanocarrier systems for the stability and delivery of several bioactive agents. The main component of the naturally occurring bilayers is the phospholipids, which are amphiphilic (Bruni et al. 2017). The amphiphilic nature of lipid vesicles encourages their utilization in the entrapment, delivery, and release of lipid-soluble, water-soluble, and amphiphilic materials. Generally, in food, lipid vesicles have shown promise for use in the stabilization of compounds and protection of sensitive compounds against environmental stress, in augmenting antimicrobial and antioxidative efficacy, and in increasing targetability. The application of liposomes in foods without any safety concerns can be attributed to the source of the phospholipids, which are usually from natural sources, such as soy, egg, or milk (Mozafari et al. 2008). The application of lipid vesicles for encapsulation enables stability and timely and targeted release of bioactive compounds, which broadens its application. Targeting lipid vesicles can be achieved mainly via active (e.g., by incorporation of active compounds) or passive (e.g., targeting based on particle size) mechanisms (Mozafari et al. 2005). The complexation of lipids is based on a simple phenomenon involving the aggregation of amphiphilic molecules in an aqueous environment via the shielding of their hydrophobic regions (Figure 2). Nevertheless, the aggregated phospholipids can arrange themselves to form an organized and closed bilayer vesicle (i.e., liposomes or nano-liposomes) when sufficient energy is provided (Mozafari et al. 2008). The entrapment of compounds occurs during this process. The preparation method of liposomes determines their structural characteristics based on size, type, and number of bilayers (Table 1) (Mozafari 2007; Zagana et al. 2008). For a detailed illustration of the methods of liposome complexation and their impact on its structural properties, the author recommends the review article by Mozafari et al. (2008). 3. For this section, the nano-drugs or carriers of interest in the food industry are limited to: (a) Nanoparticles from bioactive compounds of plant origin, such as curcumin nanoparticles; (b) Nanoparticles obtained from biopolymers, such as zein nanoparticles, curcumin- zein nanoparticles, whey protein nanoparticles/isolates and casein nanoparticles; (c) Nanoemulsions/Pickering emulsions; (d) Metal nanoparticles including Ag, ZnO, TiO2 and SiO2 nanoparticles. 3.1 Biopolymers Nanoparticles as Nano-Drugs in Food 3.1.1 Curcumin Nanoparticles Curcumin is the active phenolic compound extracted from the rhizome of turmeric (Curcuma longa). Curcumin has been found to possess several functional and biological properties ranging from anti-diabetic, anti-amyloid, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antimicrobial, anticancer, and anti-fibrosis properties (Karthikeyan et al. 2020). Limiting the tremendous potential of curcumin in biological and food- related applications is its poor solubility in water. Hence, efforts are geared toward preparing water-processable curcumin, of which curcumin nanoparticles or nano- curcumin have yielded satisfactory outcomes. Basniwal et al. (2011) prepared water- soluble and stable nano-curcumin by first dissolving curcumin in an organic solvent (dichloromethane). Then, the organic fraction curcumin solution was injected into boiling water at a controlled rate under ultra-sonication. Afterwards, the organic solvent was expelled using a rotary evaporator, and the solution was freeze-dried. The orange pellet obtained is the curcumin nanoparticles, which can be readily re-solubilized in water to yield an orange suspension. This method of nano-curcumin preparation is known as “solvent anti-solvent precipitation” and has been further tuned using other organic solvents, such as ethanol (Aditya et al. 2017; Devara et al. 2015; Duong et al. 2020; Pandit et al. 2015), in a bid to obtain easily controllable curcumin nanoparticles for diverse applications. Another common method of nano-curcumin preparation is the ionic gelation technique (Suryani et al. 2017). In this approach, calcium chloride (CaCl 2) and sodium alginate are used to reinforce the ionic interaction between chitosan and tripolyphosphate (TPP) by modulating the Biopolymer Complexation for the Development... 129 various mixing ratios of the reacting mixtures. While investigating the encapsulation of nano-curcumin in notable biopolymers prepared by the pH-shift method, Peng et al. (2020) tested caseinate, whey protein, soy protein, and gum arabic as common stabilizers of nanocurcumin. The authors reported that the biopolymer-loaded curcumin nanoparticles displayed high stability based on their dissolution in salts such as NaCl and CaCl 2. 3.1.2 Curcumin-Zein Nanoparticles Curcumin-zein nanoparticles are another important nano-drugs in the food industry. It is a blend of two poorly soluble compounds, curcumin (a polyphenolic compound) and zein (the major protein of maize). Patel et al. (2010) reported the preparation of zein-curcumin nanoparticles by the solubilization of the blend in ethanol/water. The authors equally investigated the roles of stabilizers such as polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP) and protein (sodium caseinate) on the stability of the formulated nanoparticles. Furthermore, Fereydouni et al. (2021) investigated an oil-in-water (O/W) nano- emulsion of nano-curcumin immobilized in a zein nanofibrous membrane. Other biological applications of the prepared nanofiber were investigated, such as cytotoxicity, intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), and antibacterial activity. Feng et al. (2020a) investigated the role of biopolymer (chondroitin sulfate, CS) stabilization on curcumin-zein nanoparticles through pH adjustment. Their results showed that adding CS before the anti-solvent effect of zein at pH 7.0 produces colloidal dispersion with the best solubility. Similarly, Wei et al. (2020) investigated the effect of micro-fluidization on the formation of curcumin-loaded zein-propylene glycol alginate complex nanoparticles. It was concluded that high-pressure micro- fluidization (HPM) facilitates the in vitro release of curcumin during simulated gastrointestinal digestion and thus presents a novel food-grade nanoparticle with desirable stability and digestive properties. 3.1.3 Whey Protein Isolates (WPI) Nanoparticles Milk is normally sourced from animals such as cows, goats, sheep, and buffalo and contains two major classes of proteins. Casein accounts for about 80% (w/w) of milk and is often extracted by isoelectric precipitation or through enzymatic processing. Whey protein, on the other hand, accounts for about 20% (w/w) of milk and is the byproduct of casein extraction (Madureira et al. 2007). Casein contains αs1-casein, αs2-casein, β-casein and κ-casein (Bhat et al. 2016), while whey protein contains fractions such as α-lactalbumin, β-lactoglobulin, protease peptone, glycolmacropeptide, immunoglobulins, and serum albumin. Owing to its rich nutrient density, whey protein has been popularized as a food supplement. Generally, whey protein isolates (WPI) are obtained from the extraction of milk whey fraction using purification methods such as micro-filtration and ion-exchange. WPI has found significant usability in developing packaging materials through film casting, either alone or in combination with polysaccharides (Janjarasskul et al. 2020; Çakmak et al. 2020; Tavares et al. 2021). Aside from its use as a biopolymer for the formulation of edible films, WPI can be processed into nanoparticles owing to its good functionality through the pH-cycling process (Giroux et al. 2010; Abbasi et al. 2017), organic 130 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization solvent de-solvation process (Gülseren et al. 2012). WPI nanoparticles have been investigated and validated as effective nano-carriers for bioactive compounds such as curcumin (Teng et al. 2014) and other polyphenols (Bagheri et al. 2013). It is worth mentioning that peptides with multifunctional properties can also be produced from WPI (Zhao et al. 2020). 3.1.4 Soy Protein (SP) or Soy Protein Isolates (SPI) Nanoparticles Soy protein is a globular protein with two prominent subunits, conglycinin and glycinin, which are rich in amino acids such as leucine, aspartate and glutamate (Peles et al. 2013). Soy protein isolate nanoparticles have been prepared by Teng and colleagues through the desolvation method, using ethanol as the desolvating agent (Teng et al. 2012). The method involves solubilizing SPI in water followed by the addition of ethanol. Glutaraldehyde was then added as a cross-linking agent, followed by the addition of ethanol, evaporation, dilution, and centrifugation to form the SPI nanoparticles. SPI nanoparticles in combination with polysaccharide biopolymers (carboxymethyl chitosan, CMC) have been investigated for the delivery of vitamin D3, a typical hydrophobic micronutrient (Teng et al. 2013), through a simple ionic gelation method. It was found that in comparison with the single polymer, CMC and CMC/SPI complex required a lower concentration of Ca 2+ for nanoparticle formation, which resulted in better particle formation and stability and enhanced loading efficiency of vitamin D3. Similarly, Yuan et al. (2021) synthesized PSPI nanoparticles through controlled partial enzymatic hydrolysis for the encapsulation and delivery of curcumin. Here, pH-controlled enzymatic hydrolysis of SPI was initiated using pepsin and pancreatic enzymes. 3.1.5 Casein Nanoparticles Casein nanoparticles are often synthesized using calcium chloride or phosphate, resulting in the formation of colloidal nanoparticles, also known as casein micelles or nanoparticles. Barick et al. (2021) investigated the capacity of casein nanoparticles as a nanocarrier for the delivery of curcumin with satisfactory loading efficacy. Moreover, natamycin (a food preservative), encapsulated on casein-zein nanoparticles and further immobilized on gelatin-based nanocomposite film, was investigated by Mo et al. (2021). It was noted that natamycin-loaded casein-zein nanoparticles increased the mechanical properties of gelatin film with sustained release of the anti-fungal drug. In a similar account, casein nanoparticles were investigated for the oral delivery of vitamin B9 or folic acid (Penalva et al. 2015). In summary, the casein nanoparticles were prepared using the coacervation method, further stabilized by amino acids lysine or arginine and then dried by spray drying. In vitro release studies demonstrated that the synthesized casein nanoparticles functioned as gastro- resistant material capable of reliably releasing folic acid under a simulated intestinal condition. Biopolymer Complexation for the Development... 131 3.1.6 Gelatin Nanoparticles (Gel NPs) The most important uses of gelatin are related to its ability to form heat-reversible sol-gels. As a result, gelatin is applied as a thickener, stabilizer, emulsifier, foaming agent, and crystal modifier. Gelatin has been well established for its film-forming capacity, either alone or in combination with polysaccharides. Syahida et al. (2021) investigated a gelatin/palm wax/lemongrass essential oil-coated kraft paper as packaging material for the shelf-life extension of ground beef. The authors concluded that the active compounds in the composite film delayed microbial growth and lipid oxidation, thus highlighting the capacity of the film to function in food packaging. Ahmad et al. (2012) equally investigated packaging film for sea bass slices by incorporating lemongrass essential oil in the prefabricated gelatin film. The authors reported that the incorporation of lemongrass essential oil increased the antimicrobial and antioxidative capacity of the film and thus ensured the shelf-life extension of sea bass slices by over 12 days compared to the controls during refrigerated storage. A comprehensive review of the application of gelatin as a biodegradable packaging material in food products has been published (Hanani et al. 2014). An additional application of gelatin-based materials is their use in the fabrication of gelatin nanoparticles. Gelatin nanoparticles are synthesized through the desolvation method using ethanol or acetone and coacervation. Geh et al. (2016) reported the optimization steps for the synthesis of Gel NPs through the one-step desolvation method. The protocol comprises the dissolution of Gel in water at 50°C with stirring, followed by pH adjustment and the addition of acetone to the solution to initiate desolvation and nanoparticle formation. Glutaraldehyde was finally added to the solution to cross-link the formed nanoparticles to prevent particle agglomeration. Recently, a two-step synthesis approach was proposed as an improvement over the single-step protocol. In this light, Carvalho et al. (2018) reported the synthesis of Gel NPs through a two-step desolvation approach. In a bid to improve the purity of Gel NPs, the two-step approach included additional use of acetone, with further partitioning and repeated centrifugation. Furthermore, Gel NPs synthesis based on coacervation or phase separation method has been reported. In this approach, homogenous solutions of charged macromolecules are subjected to liquid-liquid phase separation, resulting in the formation of a dense, polymer-rich part at the bottom of the reaction tube and a transparent solution at the top. Notably, these two liquid phases are immiscible, non-compatible and are in equilibrium. Adding alcohol and salts often promotes coacervation, thus assisting in nanoparticle formation. Furthermore, Gel NPs synthesis via simple coacervation has been reported (Mohanty et al. 2005). Another Gel NPs synthesis method via nanoprecipitation has also been reported (Naskar et al. 2019). Gel NPs are excellent nanomaterials for a wide range of applications, including the delivery of plant secondary metabolites (Karimi et al. 2020) and as addictive for the enhancement of Pickering emulsion (Tan et al. 2021; Feng et al. 2020b). Other notable applications of Gel NPs can be found in the detailed review by Elzoghby (2013). Several other protein-based nanoparticles can be fabricated under appropriate synthesis conditions. These examples have been reviewed elsewhere (DeFrates et al. 2018). 132 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 3.1.7 Liposome Nanoparticles Several methods have been used for the encapsulation of molecules in lipid vesicles. The major and first step involves the solubilization of lipids in an appropriate organic solvent (chloroform or methanol). The most common method used for liposome preparation is the thin film method, which involves the removal of the organic solvent used in dissolving the lipid ingredients (phosphatidylcholine and cholesterol) to produce thin films (Bruni et al. 2017). The aqueous phase containing the active compound is added and used to rehydrate the films, followed by a sufficient amount of mechanical or thermal energy, which causes bilayer sheets of the hydrophobic components to separate from the bulk to form liposomes (Mozafari et al. 2008). The major limitations of this method are the use of organic solvent, lack of a continuous production process, and low encapsulation efficiencies (Lasic et al. 2001). To address the limitation of scaling up liposome preparation for food application, several methods, including inclusion coacervation, complexation, spray drying, spray cooling/chilling, extrusion, centrifugal suspension separation, co-crystallization lyophilization, emulsion, fluidized bed coating, and liposome entrapment, have been employed (Fang et al. 2010; Mozafari 2006). Liposomes have been used to encapsulate several bioactive compounds (Chorachoo et al. 2013; Mazandrani et al. 2016). The encapsulation of polyphenols from Thymus spp. in liposome was reported to improve antioxidant and antimicrobial properties, as well as stability, compared to its unencapsulated counterpart (Gortzi et al. 2006). Colletier et al. (2002) documented the encapsulation of Pronase in liposomes using the thin film method. Other bioactive compounds encapsulated in liposomes using different methods are summarized in Table 2. 3.1.7 Nanoemulsions/Pickering Emulsion as Food Nano-Drug The emulsion is a mixture of two immiscible liquids, such as oil and water. Emulsions with droplet size in the nano range (< 100 nm) are known as nanoemulsions. In simple terms, the addition of oil to water would generate a highly immiscible mixture that is thermodynamically stable. However, with the addition of an emulsifier, a nano- emulsion is formed where small-sized liquid droplets (dispersed phase) are dispersed in a liquid medium (continuous phase). Common types available are oil-in-water (O/W), water-in-oil (W/O), and oil-in-oil emulsions. From the foregoing, emulsifiers are the indispensable constituents central to the formation of an emulsion. Emulsifiers are materials such as surfactants, proteins, lipids, or polysaccharides, possessing the inherent property of weakening the interfacial tensions (surface energy per unit area), keeping the oil and the water phases of an emulsion (Gupta et al. 2016). Polysaccharide-based Pickering emulsion has been covered in detail elsewhere (Cui et al. 2021). Modified polysaccharides are also synthesized to address some limitations associated with using native polysaccharides and thus extend the basic applications of the available polysaccharides for Pickering emulsion formulation in modern food applications. Emulsifiers also act as stabilizing agents for nanoemulsions through steric hindrance and electrostatic repulsion. A special class of emulsifiers with huge biological and food-related applications is the “Pickering emulsion”. This process is achieved mostly in an aqueous system, and successful synthesis is dependent on several factors, such as pH, temperature, the type of reductant used and synthesis time. MNPs and MONPs produced using chemical reductants (sodium borohydride, hydrazine hydrate and organic solvents like dimethylformamide DMF) are not environmentally friendly due to their toxicity. In a bid to circumvent this issue, environmentally benign materials have been explored for MNPs and MONPs synthesis, a process known as green synthesis, sustainable synthesis, or environmentally friendly synthesis. These synthesis approaches are convenient, simple, economical and easily scalable (Bhattarai et al. 2018; Chandra et al. 2020) for industrial production, as green starting materials are abundant and readily available. The properties of nanoparticles are quite different from those of the parent materials. As a result, nanoparticles show better properties, attributed to their high surface-area-to-volume ratio, high loading capacity, and tunable surfaces, compared to their starting materials. MNPs and MONPs synthesis realized through green materials have been documented as a prominent way to reduce the inherent toxicity load of nanomaterials, thus the increasing popularity of green synthesized materials used for medical and food-related products. Under the green synthesis of MNPs and MONPs, the use of extracts of plant parts as environmentally friendly reductants has been widely investigated. Plant seeds, seed pods, aerial parts, stems, flowers, and leaves have all been reported to contain essential bioactive metabolites capable of supplying electrons to reduce metal salts to produce metabolite-stabilized nanoparticles (Kumar et al. 2021). The mechanism of such reduction has been reported to follow the general trend involving small nuclei formation (nucleation) arising from the injection of the biomass-based reductant into the MNP and MONP salts. The formed nuclei are unstable and vulnerable to crystal growth, where the small nuclei formed are fused to form bigger particles in the cluster formation stage. They are further molded to maturation in the reaction environment comprising the biomass reductant and finally the bioactive components of the reductant are wrapped around the matured particles to prevent facile particle aggregation (Eze et al. 2019; Jayeoye et al. 2021a; Eze et al. 2021). Besides using plant parts to synthesise MNPs and MONPs, biodegradable polymers for the reduction and stabilization of nanoparticles also fall within the purview of green synthesis. Jayeoye et al. (2021a) reported synthesizing conducting polymer-doped sodium alginate-stabilized gold nanoparticles for biological applications. Similarly, several other studies have reported the use of biopolymers and synthetic polymers (polyvinyl alcohol (PV A), polyethylene glycol (PEG), polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP), etc.) for the preparation of MNPs and MONPs (Ortega et al. 2021; Jayeoye et al. 2020a; Jayeoye et al. 2020b; Jayeoye and Rujiralai 2020; Chawla et al. 2020). Generally, MNPs and MONPs are applied in food-related materials for their high antimicrobial efficacy. Owing to their ability to release metal ions (M +) and high surface area-to-volume ratio, the nanoparticles are highly effective at inducing deleterious effects in bacteria, fungi, and viruses. MNPs and MONPs mediated Biopolymer Complexation for the Development... 137 antimicrobial action has been reported to involve, first, the release of (M+), e.g., Ag+ from the various metal nanoparticles, which can bind electron donors in the microbial cell, such as sulfhydryl, amino, imidazole, and carbonyl groups. These functional groups are components of membrane proteins; as a result, the membrane becomes permeable to more M + penetration, resulting in cell death. Moreover, the entry of M+ into the microbial cells induces damage to cellular components (RNA, DNA, and metabolic enzymes), which alters microbial processes, such as transcription and translation (Shaikh et al. 2019; Slavin et al. 2017). Secondly, the accumulation of MNPs and MONPs in microbial cells, resulting from cell permeability, causes microbial membrane rupturing. The third mechanism involves the generation of ROS and free radicals (e.g., OH ., O2 –, H2O2, HClO), which are strong oxidizing agents with the capacity to initiate damage to microbial genetic materials, enzymes and other cellular components (Zou et al. 2018). From the foregoing, MNPs and MONPs can be used as active antimicrobial components of food materials, especially in food packaging, as discussed later. 4. Nano-Carriers and Nano-Drugs for Food Application 4.1 Bioactive Compounds Stability and Improved Bioactivities Biopolymer complexation for developing nano-drugs has shown potential for use in food products. Several micronutrients (essential trace elements and vitamins) have been added to food after their encapsulation in polymer complexes. The instability of bioactive compounds from food origin is a major drawback affecting their food industry application. In addition, the inability of these bioactive molecules to properly reach the target site or cells in the body also remains a challenge (Mazandrani et al. 2016). Polymer complexation via nanoencapsulation of these active drugs has been considered an effective technique for improving the bioavailability and biostability of the bioactive compounds (Shoji et al. 2004). The encapsulation could help reduce the interaction between bioactive compounds and the environment (light, oxygen, and water), reduce the transfer rate, and improve the half-life, bioavailability and handling ability of bioactive compounds (Fang et al. 2010). Gulzar et al. (2020) documented improved eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) stability in shrimp oil after encapsulation in liposomes. Lipid oxidation and microbial proliferation were retarded in mayonnaise incorporated with nanoliposome- encapsulated algae extract (Savaghebi et al. 2021). Reduction in EPA and DHA in fish treated with high-voltage cold plasma was circumvented with the combined treatment of liposomal encapsulated plant extract (Olatunde et al. 2020b). Likewise, Liu et al. (2015) reported higher stability for BSA encapsulated in nano-liposomes during in vitro digestion than the unencapsulated counterparts. Barick et al. (2021) reported an enhanced bioavailability and anticancer efficacy for curcumin-encapsulated casein nanoparticles when compared to the non-encapsulated compound, while Yuan et al. (2021) reported that SPI nanoparticles were able to protect the loaded curcumin against degradation under simulated gastric-intestinal condition. 138 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 4.2 Food Packaging The development of food packaging materials through fortification with nanoparticles has garnered traction in the recent decade. The environmental contamination/ pollution associated with using non-biodegradable plastics has been on the rise, and the need for sustainable alternatives cannot be overemphasized. It has been estimated that 4.8–12.7 million tons of landed plastics end up in the ocean yearly (Jambeck et al. 2015). Plastics constitute huge problems to the environment by damaging its aesthetics, which have also persisted for years. In the aquatic environment, plastics can be fragmented into microplastics, thus fueling the general apprehension about risks to organisms and humans (Thompson et al. 2009) arising from the indiscriminate usage of plastics. To reduce the negative effects associated with the use of plastics, particularly in the food packaging industry, the use of biopolymers-based products has caught the attention of researchers. Biodegradable food packaging materials are produced using a simple blending method, with the addition of appropriate plasticizers, to impart flexibility, reduce film brittleness and improve film toughness (Jantrawut et al. 2017). Common examples include glycerol, polyethylene glycol (PEG), sorbitol, and polypropylene glycol (PG). The solution casting technique is facile, easily scalable for large-scale production, and ensures sufficient interaction between constituent blends. Kumar et al. (2018) investigated the fabrication of a biodegradable nanocomposite film of chitosan/gelatin and AgNPs as an active packaging material. AgNPs used for the film fabrication were synthesized using the fruit extract of the Mimuosops elengi plant. The presence of sharp absorbance at 427 nm in the colloidal AgNPs showed the successful synthesis of highly stable and dispersed AgNPs. It was further noted that adding AgNPs to chitosan/gelatin solution to realize the nanocomposite film through the solution casting technique improved the mechanical property and decreased light transmittance in the visible region. The fabricated film was tested as a packaging material for red grapes, where it greatly enhanced the shelf life of the fruit in comparison with the control groups. Table 4 shows some more reported works between biopolymers-based food packaging materials fortified with various MNPs and MONPs through nanocomposite formation. The possibility of generating synergistic actions between the biopolymer-based film layers and the doped MNPs/ MONPs is often proposed to help increase the activity of the materials against food spoilage pathogens. Another popular and reliable method of fabricating biodegradable food packaging materials is electrospinning. Electrospinning uses a high-voltage electric field to treat a solution of polymeric material, resulting in the formation of thin, fine nanofibers on a collector. The polymer solution is oftentimes impregnated with a bioactive material, nanoparticles, and other antibacterial/antimicrobial agents to imbue the resulting nanofiber with improved properties for biological, pharmaceutical, and food applications. Electrospun nanofibers possess high porosity and surface area-to- volume ratio and thus can serve as effective nanocarriers and delivery vehicles for active biofunctional materials.
