In this regard, carbohydrate-carbohydrate, carbohydrate- protein, protein-based and lipid-based interactions have been discussed. These interactions between biopolymers confer additional properties between biopolymer layers and the infused nano-drugs possessing different physico-chemical properties. Research in this area has not reached a saturation point, thus the need to expand the frontier of scientific hypothesis in this field cannot be over-emphasized. Thus, nanomaterials infused with biopolymers-complexed materials can be adopted to realize supramolecular materials with distinct properties. Although the adoption of metal nanoparticles (MNPs) fortification into food- based materials has assisted in no small measure in increasing the antimicrobial properties of the resulting materials, the issue of MNPs leaching into foods and their attendant toxicity is a controversial area subject to more investigation. As it is generally accepted, the immobilization of MNPs in biopolymer matrixes and, more importantly, the use of biopolymers in MNP nano-synthesis has been accepted as a way of reducing nanoparticle toxicity load. The highly ordered structure of biopolymers presents a compact avenue for MNP immobilization, which can further improve its diverse biological and food-related applications. MNP properties are significantly dependent on the chemical properties of the capping or stabilizing materials, such as the use of biopolymers, with attractive biocompatibility and low cytotoxicity, which have received widespread popularity in the synthesis of nanoparticles with potential applications in food-related products. MNPs and other nanoparticles are special compared to other materials owing to their high surface- area-to-volume ratio. This confers the ability of the materials to be transported into the internal crevices of animals and thus may elicit deleterious health complications. We support the general reservations on the suitability of nanoparticles and MNPs for food-related applications and thus recommend further evaluation of the safety of the nanoparticles in animal models. This will serve a holistic purpose for informed decision-making and guide researchers in choosing materials for nano-fabrications, especially those designed specifically for food applications. Introduction Biopolymers are an intriguing category of polymers derived from organic sources, such as plants, animals, and microbes. The aforementioned polymers possess numerous advantages in comparison to their synthetic equivalents due to their enhanced sustainability, reduced environmental impact, and frequent biodegradability (Carter and Grove 2019). Biopolymers play a pivotal role in addressing the escalating concerns surrounding plastic pollution and the increasing need for more environmentally sustainable materials across various industries (McClements 2018). Biopolymers, which are derived from living organisms such as plants, animals, and microbes, constitute a distinct subset within the broader category of polymers (Sikkema et al. 2020). Distinguishing between natural polymers, synthetic polymers, and semi-synthetic hydrogels, which are derived from modified natural polymers and incorporate synthetic linkers, is possible. However, while considering the chemical aspect, it can be shown that synthetic polymers exhibit greater durability compared to natural polymers. 7 1 School of Pharmacy and Life Sciences, Centurion University of Technology and Management, Bhubaneswar –752050, Odisha, India. 2 School of Agricultural and Bio-Engineering, Centurion University of Technology and Management, Odisha, India. 3 School of Forensic Sciences, Centurion University of Technology and Management, Vizianagaram, Andhra Pradesh, India. * Corresponding author: bhisma.n.ratha@gmail.com Biopolymers, Hydrogel and Their Effect on Drug Development 153 Due to their exceptional mechanical durability, these entities exhibit an extended lifespan and significantly sluggish rate of decay. The necessity to reconcile these two contradictory characteristics necessitates the implementation of an optimal design (Sikkema et al. 2020). Chemical gels utilize covalent bonding as a means to provide the necessary structural integrity for gel formation, whereas biological gels employ substances such as enzymes or amino acids to facilitate the gel-forming process. Physical gels have the ability to undergo a transition from a liquid state to a gel state in response to external stimuli. Due to its renewable nature and positive environmental impact, there is a growing trend of extensive research and implementation of these technologies across several industries. The utilization of biopolymers such as polylactic acid (PLA), polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA), and starch-based polymers in the production of packaging materials offers a potential solution for reducing the environmental consequences associated with traditional plastic packaging (Wen et al. 2018). Figure 1 represents a schematic diagram that provides clarification on the many applications of biopolymers. The primary applications for biopolymers are in the fields of tissue engineering, drug delivery systems, and medical device manufacturing. Wound dressings, tissue regeneration scaffolds, and controlled drug release systems are all examples of applications for chitosan and alginate, respectively. In the food sector, biopolymers have a number of applications, including those of thickeners, stabilizers, and emulsifiers (Zueva et al. 2019). Depending on the particular hydrogel being generated and the polymer system being employed, the gelation process of hydrogels might change. A broad summary of hydrogels’ gelation mechanism is provided here. Polymer Dissolution and Swelling: The process typically begins with dissolving the hydrophilic polymer(s) in a solvent, usually water. As the polymer chains 160 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization dissolve, they begin to swell due to interactions between the polymer and the solvent molecules. The degree of swelling depends on factors such as polymer concentration, temperature, and solvent quality (Cikrikci et al. 2018). Polymer Crosslinking: The hydrogel’s structure and stability are provided by the creation of physical or chemical crosslinks between polymer chains during the gelation process. Crosslinking can happen through a number of mechanisms. Chemical Crosslinking: Covalent bonds are created in this process between polymer chain segments. The polymer solution is supplemented with crosslinking agents, which are frequently molecules with two or more functions. The functional groups on the polymer chains react with these substances to generate a network. Michael addition, photopolymerization, and free radical polymerization are all typical chemical crosslinking processes (Denizli et al. 2004). Physical crosslinking can also be facilitated by physical interactions such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and ionic interactions. Reversible external inputs like temperature, pH, or ionic strength can control these interactions. Polymers may self-assemble into a gel network as a result of physical crosslinking (Sundar et al. 2010). Gelation and Network Formation: The polymer chains bond as the crosslinking process continues, creating a three-dimensional network that traps water or other fluids. The hydrogel behaves solid-like because of the network structure’s ability to stop polymer chains from diffusing away while yet having a high-water content. Equilibrium Swelling: The hydrogel eventually reaches an equilibrium swelling stage where the rate of water absorption and release are equal once the gel network has formed. The administration of drugs and the healing of wounds are two applications where this swelling characteristic is essential (Gačanin 2017). It is crucial to remember that the gelation mechanism might change depending on the hydrogel’s specific use, the kind of polymer utilized (natural or synthetic), and the manner of crosslinking (chemical or physical). Researchers can study the internal structure and surface characteristics of hydrogels using these approaches, which helps them better understand their characteristics and possible uses. An overview of the applications for TEM and SEM in this context is given below. 4.1 Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) SEM is a popular method for seeing the surface morphology of materials up close. The general surface structure, porosity, and size distribution of pores within the Biopolymers, Hydrogel and Their Effect on Drug Development 161 hydrogel network may all be learned through SEM in the context of hydrogels. The following are the fundamental procedures for hydrogel characterization using SEM. (A) Sample Setup: Hydrogel samples must be set up correctly for SEM imaging. In order to maintain its structure and prevent collapse during imaging, the hydrogel is frequently frozen or freeze-dried in this manner. Also, to avoid charging artifacts, the sample is frequently thinly coated with conductive material (such as gold or platinum) after freezing (Alavarse et al. 2022). (B) Imaging: The prepared hydrogel sample is placed in the SEM chamber. A focused electron beam scans the surface of the sample, and as electrons interact with the sample, various signals (secondary electrons and backscattered electrons) are detected to create an image of the sample’s surface morphology. (C) Analysis: The surface texture, pore size, and distribution inside the hydrogel can all be seen in the SEM pictures. Pore size distribution, porosity, and other structural properties may be determined quantitatively (Zhu et al. 2022). 4.2 Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) The more sophisticated TEM method produces pictures with better resolution and enables researchers to see interior structures and nanoscale specifics in hydrogel networks. Even though it is more difficult and necessitates smaller sample slices, TEM can provide useful insights into the most intricate aspects of hydrogel structures (Wan et al. 2015): (A) Sample Preparation: When compared to SEM, TEM requires significantly thinner samples, frequently in the tens to hundreds of nanometre range. The hydrogel is often embedded in a resin before being cut into thin sections with a microtome. Then, sections are arranged on a TEM grid (Sáez-Orviz et al. 2022). (B) Imaging: A concentrated electron beam is sent across the material in TEM. The sample’s internal structures, such as the configuration of polymer chains, crosslinking sites, and nanoscale features, are revealed in a detailed picture that is produced by the interaction of electrons with the sample (Bogdanova et al. 2019). (C) Analysis: Examining nanoscale aspects like polymer chain alignment, network structure, and component interactions is possible with TEM images. Combining data from SEM and TEM may provide a thorough knowledge of hydrogel network topologies at all scales, from the macro to the nano. Tissue Engineering and Its Collaboration with Biomaterials 1.1 Tissue Engineering and Its Applications Tissue engineering (TE) is an integrative of biological science aimed at fabricating a three-dimensional (3D) functional network that combines scaffolding bioactive cellular components (Griffith and Swartz 2006). This field involves the scientific area of various biotechnology-related fields such as biological and material science, chemistry techniques, and medicinal aspects. Langer and Vacanti initially proposed and publicized the term “TE” to the scientific world in 1993 (Langer and Vacanti 1993). The production of biological alternatives to maintain, enhance, or restore the functions of the tissue is the ultimate goal of tissue engineering, according to their definition, which is still in use today (Langer and Vacanti 1993). As a result, TE can avoid tissue injury issues that are now handled by transplantation, mechanical implants, or surgery. Medical treatments have prolonged and improved the lives of numerous individuals, but they often come with associated issues. For instance, organ transplants have significant drawbacks, such as immune rejection and donor scarcity, to accommodate all demands worldwide. Mechanical devices are unable to finish all tissue-related tasks and are unable to stop patients’ bodies from deteriorating 8 1 School of Biotechnology and Bioinformatics, DY Patil Deemed-to-Be University, CBD Belapur, Navi Mumbai 400 614, Maharashtra, India. 2 Cancer and Translational Research Centre, Dr. D.Y . Surgical reconstruction can sometimes result in prolonged complications (Lalan et al. 2001). As a result, there is a need to offer a more reliable option for network improvement in the clinic. This need will be met by creating in vitro gadgets that can restore damaged in vivo networks. Building an operational structure that repairs, maintains, or improves injured tissue or whole organs is the goal of network engineering. The FDA has authorized some engineering systems, such as artificial skin and cartilage, but their use in human patients is relatively minimal. TE additionally generates engineered tissues that enable studies pertaining to physiological processes (Griffith and Swartz 2006; Pampaloni et al. 2007). In the organism, cells develop in a well-organized three-dimensional ECM encircled by other cells. It is true that a cell’s ability to proliferate, differentiate, undergo apoptosis, or invade depends on its interactions with other cells and the ECM. However, research on cellular biology has frequently been done on 2D cultures, wherein cells develop under non-physiological circumstances. Tissue engineering has been found to have a wide variety of applications. One major use of TE has been found in regenerating various tissues, including bone, vascular, cardiac, and pancreatic tissues (Castells-Sala et al. 2013). Regenerative medicine integrates TE with other therapeutic strategies, such as cellular, genetic, and immunoregulatory, to elicit regeneration. TE utilizes cells, scaffolds, and growth factors to replenish tissues or substitute injured or unhealthy tissues (Han et al. 2020). The development of in vitro human models that enable us to recognize and comprehend the elements that support cell functions is another emerging use. The goal is to analyze the function of various biochemical and physiological elements in a simplified environment by breaking down an intricate microenvironment into its component parts (Castells-Sala et al. 2013). These models effectively meet the requirements for reductive techniques to comprehend the biological mechanisms, enabling them to more accurately forecast the effects of medications and therapeutic treatment (Castells-Sala et al. 2013). 1.2 Biomaterials and Their Uses Any substance, surface, or design interacting with living systems is considered a biomaterial. Biomaterials can be manufactured in the lab using metal, polymer, ceramic, or composites, or they can be naturally obtained (Detsch et al. 2018). Biomaterials are frequently employed in medical devices to supplement or substitute a biological function. Cardiac valves, hip replacements, and surgical and dental components are among the examples (Ng et al. 2019). In modern medicine, biomaterials are crucial for improving recovery after damage or illness and regaining functionality in patients. In medical applications, biomaterials—either natural or artificial—are utilized to support, enhance, or substitute impaired tissue or biological function (Binyamin et al. 2006). Ancient Egyptians utilized sutures derived from animal musculature as the first known application of biomaterials (Ige et al. 2012). Combining medical, biological, physical, and chemical sciences and more recent contributions from TE approaches are the fields of biomaterials in modern times (Ratner et al. 2013). With advancements made in the field of biomaterials, innovative strategies are formulated to enhance the drug Application of Biomaterials in Tissue Engineering 173 delivery system. For more than six decades, biomaterials have been developed in conjunction with numerous scientific disciplines, including engineering, chemistry, physics, biology, and medicine, for use in complex pharmaceutical administration systems (Yun et al. 2015). Biomaterials today have a plethora of applications in the medical and healthcare industry. From implantation devices and regenerating tissues to biosensors, their uses are numerous. Biomaterials are now synthesized to target specific biological components, tissues or organs; this is a useful application in terms of targeting specific cells in diseases (Huebsch and Mooney 2009). Similarly, biomaterials are also employed in cancer therapeutics, where they are designed to target tumor cells. They have also been employed to manufacture diagnostic equipment that can acquire atypical cell masses (Huebsch and Mooney 2009). 1.3 Application of Biomaterials in Tissue Engineering Using proper cell implantation techniques, donor tissue that has been separated for the purpose, and tissue-compatible scaffolding materials, tissue engineering is the process of creating bioengineered tissue and resulting alterations in vivo from cell development and function. To encourage the optimum cell-cell attachment, movement, and accumulation of endogenous extracellular matrix components by cells, biomaterials for TE should have surface chemistry, permeability, and regulated degradability (Berthiaume 2011). To create a large cell mass capable of performing the various roles required for TE approaches to shift cells from growth to differentiation and vice versa—which frequently are mutually exclusive—are used. Depending on how well the various cell types present in TE adhere to one another and to substrates, the composition of cells and components can reorganize. Finally, for effective nutritional intake and waste removal, network development should be carefully incorporated into the target hosts (Berthiaume 2011). 2. Types of Biomaterials Based on Types of Tissue Engineering As mentioned earlier, biomaterials have a diverse set of applications in the field of TE; this section highlights the various kinds of biomaterials used for different kinds of TE. Table 1 gives an overview of the types of biomaterials used for different kinds of TE. 2.1 Bone Tissue Engineering Bone tissues are highly diverse, structurally ranging from long to short, flat and irregular and functionally ranging from movement to protecting organs. Bone TE aims to develop alternative treatment options to eventually eliminate the drawbacks of current treatments, such as immune rejection, donor site morbidity, and restricted availability. Understanding the physiology of the bone, its mechanics, and how bone tissue forms the basis of bone tissue engineering (Amini et al. 2012). The various types of bone TE include calcium phosphate ceramics (CaP), bioactive glass, metal- based materials, polymers, and composites. 174 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization Table 1. List of biomaterials based on the type of tissue engineering. Type of TE Biomaterials Used References Bone CaP ceramics, bioactive glasses, metal-based materials, biopolymers, and composites (Amini et al. 2012; Díaz-cuenca et al. 2022; Lee et al. 2014; Kokubo and Takadama 2006; Chen et al. 2019; Guo et al. 2021; Mieszawska et al. 2010) Osteochondral Single-phase scaffold, biphasic scaffold, and gradient scaffold (Martin et al. 2007; Lee et al. 2014; Jiang et al. 2010; Mohan et al. 2011) Cardiac Extracellular matrix proteins and nanomaterials (Mousavi et al. 2021; Kc et al. 2019; Esmaeili et al. 2022) Pancreas Extracellular matrix proteins (Goh et al. 2013; Baidal et al. 2019) Stem cell-based Mesenchymal stem cells (Sharma et al. 2019; Augustine et al. 2021) 2.1.1 Calcium Phosphate Ceramics CaP ceramics are a type of biomaterial that can stimulate the creation of ectopic bone by signaling its surroundings to do so (Amini et al. 2012). They are weakly crystalline and naturally produced in the body. They form very tiny crystals in close proximity to the protein’s developing matrix. Consequently, the ideal biochemical and physiological attributes for synthesized CaP materials should be maintained (Díaz-cuenca et al. 2022). The nontoxicity, tissue compatibility, and biochemical and structural resemblance of CaPs are combined with the features of inert tissue compatibility in these chemical formulations. This combination, in turn, increases the bioactivity, porosity, elasticity, and mechanical strength of the ceramic (Díaz-cuenca et al. 2022). These bioceramics, however, remain inherently rigid and have slow degradability. In order to create more effective matrixes, they are frequently coupled with biopolymers that are easily degradable. The most popular CaP bioceramic formulations are hydroxyapatite (HA), β-tricalcium phosphate, and a combination of both (Lee et al. 2014). 2.1.2 Bioactive Glasses Materials that can undergo certain surface responses when inserted into the body are referred to as bioactive materials. They are in charge of creating a strong connection with both hard and soft tissues (Kokubo and Takadama 2006). Silicate bioactive glasses are built on a SiO 2 matrix that forms a 3D glass and contains a coordinate link between the Si and O atoms. A carbonate-substituted HA-like layer forms on the glass surface of 45S5 glass, a commonly used binding glass, when it comes into contact with body fluids. This later tightly adheres to the live bone and tissue because it resembles the mineral composition of bone (Hench 1998). Borate bioactive glasses break down more rapidly and entirely into hydroxyapatite-like material than silicate glasses (Huang et al. 2006). Due to the presence of their ions in the organic mineral component of the bone, phosphate bioactive glasses and bone share chemical properties (Rahaman et al. 2011). Application of Biomaterials in Tissue Engineering 175 2.1.3 Metal-Based Materials Porous metallic scaffolds have been researched for bone TE because they have excellent physical qualities and tissue growth-promoting properties. Out of the many biomaterials, titanium (Ti) is the most commonly used metal for clinical purposes, such as dental implants and bone implants. Ti is widely used for implants because its porous structure mimics the human bone, making it excellent for bone grafting (Chen et al. 2019). Apart from that, Ti and its alloys show outstanding mechanical properties, biocompatibility and corrosion resistance (Kent et al. 2011). Surface modification of titanium implants with new Ti coatings may enhance the functioning of the implant for a favorable bone-implant interaction (Simon et al. 2005). Apart from Ti, tantalum is also used for bone tissue engineering. Tantalum scaffolds possess titanium’s favorable properties and demonstrate superior attachment and proliferation capacity as compared to Ti (Balla et al. 2010). 2.1.4 Polymers Polymers are highly versatile materials for tissue engineering. They can be engineered in the form of fibers or gel-based materials and can be chemically modified to improve the bioactivity of the material in the body (Lee et al. 2014). The clinical practice uses both natural and synthetic biopolymeric substances; however, biopolymers are more compatible and easily degradable than synthetic ones. Chitosan, collagen, silk fibroin, cellulose, and gelatin are a few examples of natural polymers used for bone TE (Guo et al. 2021). Conversely, there are certain downsides to biopolymers, including processing challenges, immunogenicity, and source-based unpredictability (Lee and Shin 2007). An artificial polymer with outstanding mechanical characteristics that is thermostable and has a slow rate of biodegradation is called polycaprolactone (PCL), which has received FDA approval (Rao et al. 2017). 2.1.5 Composites Composites are made to improve at least two materials’ distinctive features. Frequently, bioactive glasses or calcium phosphate ceramics are mixed with biopolymers or artificial polymers (Lee et al. 2014). One example of a composite is one made from silk fibroin and silica-based bioglass. The bioactivity of the bioglass was combined with the silk fibroin for its excellent mechanical strength and biodegradability (Mieszawska et al. 2010). Calcium phosphate scaffolds were combined with collagen hydrogel to enhance bone synthesis (Yu et al. 2012). One of the most popular biopolymers for bone TE is alginate, which is a biomaterial. The polysaccharide is non-toxic, non-immunogenic, biocompatible, and biodegradable due to the guluronic and mannuronic acids that make up its makeup. Furthermore, its usage as a scaffold is facilitated by its accessibility and affordability (Venkatesan et al. 2014). 2.2 Osteochondral Tissue Engineering Due to the joint’s mechanical brittleness, osteochondral abnormalities frequently trigger degenerative processes. An osteochondral graft typically comprises an 176 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization underlying calcified tissue and a surface cartilaginous layer. The mechanical and biological viability of the joint can be restored with this design, which is a promising approach. However, the grafts have some drawbacks, such as material scarcity and donor site morbidity. These limitations may be overcome by tissue engineering of osteochondral composites. Three-dimensional grafts of a pre-defined shape can be developed by merging the patient’s own cells with porous biomaterials. (Martin et al. 2007). 2.2.1 Single-Phase Scaffold Single-phase scaffolds are commonly used for osteochondral TE. They are made up of a single biomaterial or a composite of several. Irrespective of the number of biomaterials employed, they must all be distributed evenly throughout the scaffold (Lee et al. 2014). Bone morphogenic protein (BMP-2) chemically conjugated PCL scaffolds were developed to evaluate the potential for neocartilage production (Jeong et al. 2012). Hydroxyapatite microparticles influence the hypertrophic chondrocyte culture (Zhou et al. 2011). 2.2.2 Biphasic/Multiphasic Scaffold Biphasic scaffolds and multiphasic scaffolds are better equipped to summarize the subchondral bone and the articular cartilage (Lee et al. 2014). In order to simulate the chondro-phase, agar hydrogel containing chondrocytes was created, and bioglass with osteoblasts was created to simulate the bone layer (Jiang et al. 2010). Bilayer scaffolds made of porous tantalum metal and rMSC-seeded polyethylene glycol hydrogel were inserted into the rabbit’s osteochondral deformations. The metal induced the regeneration of subchondral bone and aided in the production of hyaline cartilage (Bal et al. 2010). 2.2.3 Gradient Scaffold Gradient scaffolds, as compared to traditional scaffolds, improve the continuity between the various layers of the scaffold. Gradients can be integrated by modifying the composition of the scaffold or by adjusting the distribution of bioactive molecules (Lee et al. 2014). A gradient scaffold for implantation in a rabbit femoral condyle showed excellent histological points for the distribution and amount of cartilage thickness and bone mineralization around the osteochondral defect site. This gradient was created by changing the flow rates at which TGF-1 or BMP-2/HA-containing PLGA microparticles were delivered to a cylindrical mold. Chondrocyte-forming particles made up the top layer of this scaffold, and a combination of chondrogenic and osteogenic particles made up the basal layer (Mohan et al. 2011). 2.3 Cardiac Tissue Engineering Lack of self-regenerative capacity, abnormal distribution of stress and problems with the ability to contract. Cardiac muscles require vigorous mechanical strength to contract efficiently and continuously throughout the individual’s lifetime. Numerous strategies have been developed to repair the functions of the muscle using Application of Biomaterials in Tissue Engineering 177 various scaffolds, manufacturing techniques and cell sources (Sharma et al. 2019). The biomaterial utilized in cardiac tissue engineering must be able to endure the contraction of the heart muscle and permit cell penetration inside the matrixes (Pope et al. 2008). Extracellular proteins, natural biomaterials, and artificial biomaterials are the most commonly used biomaterials for cardiac tissue engineering (Sharma et al. 2019). 2.3.1 Extracellular Matrix Proteins Cardiac scaffolds in the form of injectable hydrogels are capable of mimicking the myocardial ECM. Injectable hydrogels are water-insoluble biomaterials that can absorb water, become swollen, and eventually retain their shape. They are crosslinked and viscoelastic in nature. Due to the high water content of hydrogels, they are easy to administer and provide a simple microenvironment for cell growth (Mousavi et al. 2021). Polymers such as polyethylene glycol and polycaprolactone are used to develop injectable hydrogels (Bearzi et al. 2014; Wang et al. 2015). Natural biopolymers such as gelatin, collagen, alginate, hyaluronic acid, and chitosan are also used for cardiac TE (Mousavi et al. 2021). Decellularized cardiac ECM, which consists of proteins, proteoglycans, growth factors, and cytokines, is considered to be highly suitable to mimic the myocardium ECM. The decellularized ECM provides a complex blend of biochemical and physical signals that support proliferation, cell attachment and differentiation (Kc et al. 2019). 2.3.2 Nanomaterials First-generation biomaterials such as collagen, fibrin, gelatin, and decellularized matrix are extensively used for cardiac tissue regeneration. However, these biomaterials are poorly electroconductive, which hinders the proper functioning of the tissue. In order to compensate for this disadvantage, electroconductive biomaterials, such as nanoparticles and electroconductive polymers, are used. Materials such as silicon- derived nanoparticles, gold nanoparticles, and carbon-based nanoparticles are used for designing electroconductive biomaterials (Esmaeili et al. 2022). The performance of traditional biomaterials can also be enhanced by incorporating nanomaterials and developing a combined blend of the same (Ahadian et al. 2017). Nanoparticles are advantageous in tissue engineering because of their large proportion of surface area to volume. Nanoparticles are useful for cellular absorption because they can transport large numbers of biomolecules from one place to another. Because they have the capacity to increase cardiomyocyte activity, carbon nanotubes are frequently used in the engineering of heart tissue. The electrical and mechanical properties of carbon nanotubes also allow them to induce stem-cell differentiation (R Amin et al. 2020). Gelatin methacryloyl gel with carbon nanotubes has also been used to differentiate embryoid bodies into cardiomyocetes (Ahadian et al. 2016). 2.4 Pancreas Tissue Engineering Developing an engineered pancreas using the appropriate biomaterials can provide an alternative to traditional diabetes treatment (hormonal therapy). Pancreas tissue 178 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization engineering can potentially overcome the long-term complications of hormonal therapy during the treatment of diabetes (Salg et al. 2019). The idea of whole organ perfusion decellularization has been pondered upon to generate ECM scaffolds from complex organs such as the heart, lungs, or pancreas. Organ matrixes offer a convenient scaffold because of their physiological similarity with the target tissue. Bioengineered scaffolds like this provide preserved gaps of the ECM components, intact 3D structure and a vascular network that can be easily repopulated with new cells. Perfusion decellularization of a whole pancreas can also be used to develop a natural scaffold (Goh et al. 2013). The greater omentum, which is an extensively vascularized structure of connective, adipose and vascular cells, has been considered an ideal site for islet transplantation (Baidal et al. 2019). 2.5 Stem Cell-Based Tissue Engineering Pluripotent stem cells can be used in tissue engineering to enhance cell survival, tissue repair and immunological pathways. Stem-cell therapies have a strong potential to repair musculoskeletal and periodontal conditions. Mesenchymal stem cells have been extensively used for direct differentiation into forming a cell and the creation of regenerative pathways by producing growth factors and hormones (Sharma et al. 2019). Under certain environmental circumstances, stem cells can be made to develop into smooth muscle cells or fibroblasts (Augustine et al. 2021). Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are considered the finest source of stem cells for tissue engineering because of their pluripotency and flexibility (Liu et al. 2013). 3. Types of Biomaterials in Tissue Engineering 3.1 Polymers (Synthetic and Natural) Polymeric biomaterials are materials that can be used in physiological environme nts over a long or short duration of time. Biopolymers, including collagens, alginate, proteoglycans, chitosans, and chitins, have all been employed as scaffolds. These polymers support cell-cell attachment and development on their surface and have both biocompatibility and bioactivity. Due to their significant biologically active components, collagen scaffolds provide good cell adherence to their surfaces (Dolcimascolo 2019). They are thoroughly tested and widely used as a remedy for recovering functionality in impaired brain tissue. They are extremely versatile in terms of shape and biomechanical properties, and alternative biomaterials like ceramics cannot equal them in terms of being biocompatible (Boni et al. 2018). Polymers are either natural or synthetic in origin. Combinations of materials with unique attributes are utilized as scaffolds to increase the utilization of biopolymers in regenerating tissues. The main reason behind using a hybrid biomaterial system with different biological and physiological relevance is to obtain the synergy of one component with both features. For instance, integrating synthetic and natural polymers with microstructures, chemically and structurally specified components, and biosynthetic features might provide a useful link between the two techniques (Lee et al. 2018). Application of Biomaterials in Tissue Engineering 179 3.1.1 Natural Polymers As the name suggests, natural polymers are derived naturally. They are primarily created by animals, plants, and microorganisms and fall into three basic categories: polypeptides, polysaccharides, and polyesters. These polymers have applications in the biomedical sector in cosmetics and pharmaceuticals for regenerative medicine (Abbasian et al. 2019). In contrast to artificial polymers, natural polymers have higher bioactivity and biocompatibility. They are frequently comparable, if not exact replicas, of compounds that are already found in the human body, reducing the likelihood of cytotoxic activity and immunogenicity after insertion in the body (Gomes et al. 2017). In tissue engineering, biobased polymers can function as matrix precursors, gel-forming reagents, or drug release regulators. They can also be quickly changed to address a physiological morphological deficit (Madigan et al. 2009). Despite these benefits, biobased polymers have a number of disadvantages that may limit their use in tissue engineering, including the high cost of manufacture in certain instances, variations within batches that are primarily caused by their complex structural, morphological and chemical properties, an unregulated hydration rate, inadequate resources, and the possibility of microbiological contamination. These polymers are also not easily processable (Abbasian et al. 2019). 3.1.2 Synthetic Polymers Synthetic polymers have attracted a lot of attention from the scientific community for the purposes of nerve TE and regenerative medicine due to their ability to modify the physical, chemical, and mechanical characteristics for the replication of biological tissues. These polymers are excellent for TE since they are hydrolyzed in a predictable manner across all hosts (Amani et al. 2019). Modification of polymeric structure is quite difficult with natural polymers as compared to synthetic polymers. Artificial polymers like PCL, PLGA and PLA are extensively utilized in bone TE (Figure 1 a, b, and c). Due to their processability, regulatable properties, and biodegradability, they are authorized by the FDA for human utilization in numerous medical uses, such as suture material, implants, and pharmaceutical delivery systems (Lee et al. 2018). Additionally, because synthetic polymers are not hydrophobic, they may cause fibrous encapsulation and protein degradation in the implant’s domain (Kim and Mooney 1998). The various advantages and disadvantages of biopolymers and artificial polymers have been discussed in Table 2. 3.2 Hydrogels Hydrogels are hydrophilic polymers that absorb water and retain a characteristic 3D conformation (Kopecek 2007). With the help of a tissue-engineered matrix, they can successfully maintain proliferating cells without experiencing biochemical stressors that could result from harmful interactions with the matrixes. They have demonstrated use as sealants, pharmaceutical delivery systems, and TE matrices due to their high absorption and adsorption capabilities (Love 2017). Due to their action of modifying the structural properties of scaffolds based on hydrogels, they closely resemble those of real tissues, making them a significant subclass of scaffolds. Copolymer hydrogels’ functional qualities are highly reliant on the amount of water present in the structure, and precise regulation is required to obtain consistent data about the mechanical behavior within the systems. As demonstrated by hydrogel foams, the capacity to control the copolymer volume relative to the fluid in which it is closed offers the potential to build soft structures (Chen et al. 1999). Due to this characteristic, hydrogels—especially natural hydrogels—have numerous applications in TE. The scaffolds serve as the extracellular matrix and can bind different growth factors tailored to the tissue application to promote the most efficient regeneration and mimic the microenvironment of the tissues. Biohydrogels are intrinsically biocompatible and non-toxic and also show increased cell-cell attachment and biodegradation due to proteolysis. By simulating tissue organization and improving cell integration within the scaffolds, using biofabrication methodologies for biohydrogels could produce useful structures (Elkhoury et al. 2021). 3.3 Injectables The importance of injectable biomaterials is significant because they enable accurate insertion into tightly contained anatomical areas and the healing of irregular lesions (Kretlow et al. 2009). As a result of being effectively transported, encased, maintained, and supplied to the target site of injection and the biomaterials, alone or in combination with therapeutic agents, which are vital in tissue restoration and regeneration, these biomaterials combined with a wide variety of cells, genetic material, and growth factors can also produce better results (Zhou et al. 2019). Biomaterials Enhancing the Drug Delivery System in Tissues With advancements made in the field of biomaterials, innovative strategies are formulated to enhance the drug delivery system (Yun et al. 2015). Specifically, polymeric and lipid-based substances for drug administration have been pushed by breakthroughs in a wide variety of industries. Biomaterials offer a diverse variety of efficacy over pharmaceutical substances (Langer 1990). Several of them are made to deliver a certain quantity of therapeutic for a predetermined duration and may be changed to function in targeted areas, lowering the quantity of drugs needed to accomplish the intended action and reducing the patient’s toxicity (Hoare and Kohane 2008). In order to achieve maximum therapeutic action, biomaterials’ physical and chemical properties and delivery methods can be changed. Biomaterials are most 182 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization progressed for injected and oral drug delivery techniques; however, novel new drug delivery options such as pulmonary, transdermal, ophthalmic, and nasal routes have also been increasingly adopted (Anselmo and Mitragotri 2014). 4.1 Biocompatibility Biocompatibility is the biomaterial’s ability to carry out its function without giving rise to toxic or harmful effects on biological systems but produces appropriate host responses in certain cases. The ISO 10993 series is an internationally recognized standard for testing the end point of biocompatibility for various medical devices. The aim of biocompatibility is to ensure that the drug will not pose any physiological harm to the patient or the consumer (Kohane et al. 2003). A variety of pharmaceutical delivery techniques have been used to provide delayed release of bupivacaine, including polymeric particles, spray-dried lipids, proteins, sugar particles, liposomes, crosslinked hyaluronic acid gels, and polysaccharide blends (Kohane et al. 2002). These compositions generate varied inflammation in the absence of medication but little to no actual damage. But when combined with bupivacaine, all result in varying degrees of muscular damage (Kohane et al. 2010). 4.2 Biodegradability Biodegradability is the ability of living creatures to biologically break down organic material into simplified molecules (Kellie 2016). Certain biodegradable polymers that occur naturally are expressed in a way that can be used in the implementation system of drug administration due to their widespread occurrence naturally, their biocompatible nature and their inclusion of essential polysaccharides (Pillai and Panchagnula 2001). Biologically degradable polymers can occur naturally and can be synthesized. In some ways, synthetic polymers are superior to naturally occurring ones because they can be produced using a repeatable process that results in the same polymeric structure with identical content repeatedly. Unlike naturally occurring polymers, which are available limitedly, they may be created with a variety of properties that can be altered according to the uses. The majority of contemporary drug development methods are made with polymeric substances that have sufficient biodegradability. The most crucial aspect of TE is managing the discharge of bioactive molecules. Improving and regenerating the network is a challenging process that calls for numerous growth factors and associated hormones. For network engineering to be successful, a distribution network that can enable the controlled release of these components is crucial (Bae et al. 2010). Using biodegradable polymers provides certain benefits compared to other materials, mostly because of their ability to change mechanically. The ability of polymers to be combined to lessen the need for additional surgery removal is their main benefit, as it is cost and time-efficient (Dhaliwal and Dosanjh 2018). Application of Biomaterials in Tissue Engineering 183 4.3 Biomaterials Act as a Catalyst to the Drug Delivery System To avoid or reduce side effects caused by drug delivery in cells and to increase curative efficiency and rehabilitation, it is important to consider the use of biocompatible and biodegradable biomaterials. Thus, it can be said that biomaterials act as catalysts in the pharmaceutical administration system. The need for components that can deliver medications to specific areas with no issues has arisen as a result of the quest for the discharge of controlled medications resulting from complications linked with the administration and distribution of traditional medications. In order to quickly remediate and recover patients during the therapy duration, medications are typically sent periodically on the body’s prescription. By doing this, the medication concentration will rise, and when it exceeds the body’s tolerance limit, complications with excessive medication levels may arise, which may result in varied extent of toxicity in the patient’s body (Schneider 2017). As a result of the limited drug concentration at the target site, which can happen as a result of metabolic and degradative activity, as well as its movement away from the site, it is also possible that the release rate of the drug acting on the patient is so rapid that curative measures do not function adequately ( Schneider 2017). As a result, this phenomenon will squander pharmaceuticals and cause a moderate amount of transportation loss, as well as high-risk adverse effects on the nearby body cells, tissues, and organs. A pharmaceutical carrier with the ability to deliver a sustained discharge flow to the specific site of action and enable rehabilitation of overall therapy prior to breakdown and removal of the concentrated surplus of medicines and carrier media is the answer to this issue (Park 2014). Capsule-based medications and carriers can be prepared for parenteral or oral administration (Yun et al. 2015). There is a need for materials that enable the discharge of the medication without any alteration or decomposition over time, as well as those that have a prolonged duration of action. In order to improve shipping effectiveness, these subordinates are designed for direct injection or implantation into the sick tissue or cell target (Bertrand et al. 2014). Target medications have been administered using ligands that have adequate binding affinity and that have been applied to the surface of biomaterials to enable uptake and usage by cells and weak tissue (Kamaly et al. 2012). Drug vehicles must be designed with biomaterials that prevent rupture or degeneration at the specific site and allow surface alteration with ligands. 5. Modifying Biomaterials for Tissue Engineering Interactions between tissue and scaffolds take place at the surface of the scaffold, therefore the biomaterials’ surface is crucial in successful implantation. The scaffold interface is crucial in determining how cells behave since it serves as a framework for cellular growth, differentiation, and adherence (Vasita et al. 2008). Developing a new biomaterial for tissue engineering is a tedious task as compared to modifying the existing ones to perform better. Most modification techniques 184 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization involve the improvement of the surface properties of already researched biomaterials (Jiao and Cui 2007). Surface modification is a convenient approach to change the biochemical interactions of a biomaterial to develop desired scaffolds (Jiao and Cui 2007). The idea of biomaterial surface reformation has been accepted over time. Biomaterials (both natural and synthetic), such as polyglycolic acid, chitosan, alginate, polyvinyl alcohol, collagen, gelatin, etc., have been investigated for surface modification. On the basis of the place of implantation, distinct surface alteration techniques for every natural biomaterial are being investigated. At the same time, the physicochemical characteristics of synthetic biomaterials can be altered merely by changing their molecular structure. Most biological scaffolds are biodegradable by hydrolysis, enzymatic activity, radiation or chemical treatments (solvents); therefore, the process of surface modification should be free of high temperatures, enzymes, solvents and irradiation conditions. Chemical modification of a biomaterial provides better surface stability than physical modification due to covalent bonds. Chemical modification also provides better biocompatibility (Vasita et al. 2008). Interactions of the scaffold with the tissues are determined by the scaffold’s structure, porosity, distribution, texture, and other chemical properties. Cell behaviors, such as differentiation, proliferation, attachment and other biochemical reactions at the surface, strongly depend on the physicochemical properties of the biomaterials’ interface. The chemical and molecular conformation, ionicity, and other factors influence the interaction between cells and scaffolds (Jiao and Cui 2007). Physical modification of a biomaterial involves covering a biomaterial with cell adhesion proteins like collagen, fibronectin and chitosan (Lotfi et al. 2013). These methods improve cell adherence and cell proliferation on biomaterials with protein coatings. Chemically-immobilized ECM proteins are also used for coating scaffolds (Tallawi et al. 2015). Chemically altering biomaterials by alkaline breakdown of aliphatic polyester surfaces is a widespread practice. Chemical alterations like this create active functionalities that allow covalent attachment between the implant and the tissue (Vasita et al. 2008). The production of hydroxyl and carboxyl groups as a result of these active functionalities is used to immobilize ligands like extracellular matrix proteins. Plasma treatment is also used to modify the properties of the surface of a biomaterial and enhance the affinity of cells toward the scaffold. Photochemical techniques can be used to design biomaterial surfaces and promote polymer cross- linking, photopolymerization and grafting of molecules on the polymers (Vasita et al. 2008). 6. Conclusion and Future Perspectives In conclusion, there are numerous uses for biomaterials in TE. It has achieved sizable strides in medicine and will have a substantial influence on upcoming clinical applications. The biomimetic surface topography and regulated distribution of bioactive signals to promote restoration are the main areas of study. More extensive research is being conducted on natural and synthetic polymers for the production of medical devices. They can be further utilized in the biofabrication of three-dimension porous biomimetic bioactive scaffolds that are a viable alternative for structural and functional restoration strategies in TE. Natural and synthetic polymers, hydrogels, Application of Biomaterials in Tissue Engineering 185 ceramics, and metals are the primary classifications used in producing scaffolds. In order to promote cell development and, ultimately, the regeneration of tissues, the use of biomaterials in medicine has a significant impact on tissue regeneration. They offer a structural foundation resembling native ECM. Different types of biomaterials are being studied for different methods of tissue repair and to improve the growth of various damaged tissues or organs. Apart from polymers, other biomaterials are also covered in this chapter. Then, they have been used singly or in combination with other materials as composites. Additionally, by processing and characterizing biomaterials from their biological origin, new biomaterials can be investigated to improve activity and lessen side effects related to the medication. Defining boundaries with tissue components, reestablishing post-injury, and preserving them are the biggest challenges in creating the interfaces. The correlation between the biomolecules’ and receptors’ structure and function at the area of insertion, as well as the mechanism behind the creation of the interface, is better understood as a result. The principle underlying the differentiating, proliferating, and migrating cells of the novel creations is complex. With the development of a new range of stem-cell treatments, emerging techniques in TE can offer functional tissue replacements. Development of this field pivots to some extent on the advancement of new materials and further developed platform handling procedures. Furthermore, a profound cognisance of the fundamental elements of the growth of bones and ligaments would considerably help frame properties fit in a way that is more reminiscent of the natural environment. Advance momentum examination and backing novel therapeutics, which have phenomenal potential in restoring cardiovascular pathologies as well. These strategies and procedures work with better protein adsorption, cell connection, expansion, cell connection, and separation. A more profound understanding of the fundamental systems of bone and ligament development will considerably help frame features that are highly reminiscent of the natural environment. Right now, the emphasis has been on tending to biomimetic surface geology for impacting cellular conduct, controlled conveyance of bioactive signs to animate recovery, vascularizing the bone, articular ligament zonal design, and osteochondral interface mix. Advancements in innovative therapeutic research and support have great prospects for treating heart diseases as well. Introduction Forming biofilms enables single-celled organisms to adopt a multicellular lifestyle temporarily, promoting collective survival in challenging conditions. What was once considered a simple attachment of microbes to a surface has now revealed itself as a complex and dynamic developmental process (Kostakioti et al. 2013). The shift from individual planktonic growth to biofilm formation is triggered by environmental changes orchestrated by various regulatory networks. These networks translate signals into synchronized changes in gene expression, allowing bacterial cells to reorganize both spatially and temporally. This cellular reprogramming alters the expression of surface molecules, nutrient utilization, and virulence factors, equipping bacteria with various traits that enable them to endure harsh conditions (Böttcher et al. 2013). The biofilm matrix serves as a protective shield for bacteria within it, guarding them against the body’s natural immune defenses like opsonization and phagocytosis, as well as antibiotic treatments when they are inside the host. This protection enables the exchange of drug-resistance traits and other virulence factors among bacteria, contributing to the persistence of biofilm-forming pathogens. These resilient pathogens are responsible for causing chronic and challenging infections, including urinary tract infections (like those caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae), upper respiratory infections, catheter-related infections, 9 1 Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell (RMS) Lab, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology, Hyderabad, Telangana, India. 2 School of Nanotechnology, Rajiv Gandhi Proudyogiki Vishwavidyalaya (RGPV), India. * Corresponding author: ambikeshsoni14@gmail.com Strategies for Development of Biofilms 191 periodontitis (involving mixed biofilms of Streptococcus mutants and other bacteria), and more (involving bacteria like E. coli and Enterococcus faecalis). In individuals with compromised immune systems, infections by opportunistic biofilm-forming organisms can be especially dangerous, leading to severe symptoms and, sadly, often resulting in fatalities (Tanzil et al. 2016). Bacteria are enveloped inside the biofilm by a self-produced extracellular matrix, which makes up 90% of the biofilm’s mass. The primary composition of this matrix consists of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), which function as a stabilizing framework for the three-dimensional structure of the biofilm. Furthermore, it includes carbohydrate-binding proteins and extracellular DNA (eDNA). Hydrophilic polysaccharides in the matrix form hydrogen bonds with water, effectively retaining it, while nutrients are trapped within for the resident bacteria to use for their metabolism (Divakar et al. 2019). In response to the availability of nutrients, bacteria release enzymes that alter the composition of EPS, enabling the biofilm’s architecture to adjust to its particular surroundings (Veerubhotla et al. 2018). The structural elements within the matrix create a well-hydrated, sturdy framework with impressive tensile strength. This framework keeps bacteria closely packed together, allowing for intimate cell-to-cell interactions and DNA exchange, and shields the biomass from drying out, predators, oxidative compounds, radiation, and other harmful agents. Moreover, environmental variations within the biomass play a role in enhancing biofilm resilience. Distinct bacterial groups display diverse gene expression patterns based on local nutrient levels and oxygen availability, effectively resulting in a “division of labor” within the community (Nira Rabin et al. 2017). The process encompasses reversible and irreversible stages of bacterial aggregation, followed by subsequent biofilm development, along with other elements that are conserved and unique to specific species. The initial phase involves placing bacteria onto a somewhat random surface. It occurs due to factors like Brownian motion and gravity, with additional influences from the surrounding hydrodynamic forces. Identifying the surface extracellular appendages, which are sticky, mediate the adhesions to release at the surface (Mishra et al. 2020). The effectiveness of these appendages in binding is not absolute due to their reversible and dynamic nature. This allows bacteria to reattach even after being detached by factors like hydrodynamic forces (which can dislodge bacteria from the surface), repulsive forces, or in response to nutrient availability (Dumaru et al. 2019). Pathogens like P . aeruginosa, known for their tendency to form biofilms, employ various attachment structures to adhere irreversibly to surfaces. P . aeruginosa utilizes a type IV pili-mediated twitching motility to navigate the interface between liquid and solid surfaces. This allows it to move along the surface and maintain its adhesion. The bacterium also expresses several CUP fimbriae, including CupA, which plays a role in surface adhesion and the self-aggregation of bacterial cells (Toole et al. 2000). A promising approach to nanoparticle (NPs) production involves utilizing biofilms, which have recently emerged as the predominant growth mechanism for bacteria. Biofilms created by metal-reducing bacteria can serve as a highly effective framework for the reduction and formation of NPs, surpassing the capabilities of planktonic cells. Electrochemical redox processes are facilitated inside biofilms, 192 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization establishing a favorable environment that includes natural reducing agents such as proteins, peptides, and heterocyclic compounds. This leads to a remarkable enhancement in the reduction of metals into nanoparticles (NPs), achieving efficiency levels of up to 600 times greater than what is observed in planktonic cells (Yu et al. 2019). It is crucial to acknowledge that research about nanoparticle (NP) production within biofilms has been constrained, and the mechanisms accountable for stabilizing NPs in biofilms are still predominantly uncharted. Consequently, acquiring a more profound comprehension of how biofilms generate NPs compared to their planktonic counterparts holds significant importance. Such insights will aid forthcoming researchers in crafting more resilient microbial systems for the efficient and precise biosynthesis of NPs with particular sizes and shapes. A substantial portion of research concentrates on characterizing the synthesized nanoparticles (NPs) rather than delving into the fundamental processes at play. For example, in bacterial sludge- forming biofilms, these biofilms exhibit a notable capacity to reduce Ag + ions and externally generate, isolate, and sustain AgNPs efficiently (Mishra et al. 2020). 2. Structure of Biofilms The extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix comprises various components within the biofilm, including extracellular polysaccharides, DNA, proteins, and more. This matrix forms a network of channels that facilitate the passage of water, air, and nutrients throughout the entire biofilm structure. Exopolysaccharides, a key component of EPS, are produced within or outside cells and are then released into the environment (Zhang et al. 2020). They appear as long linear or branching strands that attach to the cell surfaces and extend outward, forming extensive networks when observed through electron microscopy. Exopolysaccharides function as frameworks for various molecules, including carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids. It is important to emphasize that exopolysaccharides’ constituents, configurations, and attributes may differ among distinct biofilms. The compositions and linkages of the EPS matrix within biofilms of K. pneumoniae, P . aeruginosa, S. aureus, E. faecalis, A. baumannii, and E. spp. were investigated. The most frequently encountered carbohydrates identified in these biofilms comprise mannose, galactose, and glucose. N-acetyl-glucosamine, galacturonic acid, arabinose, fucose, rhamnose, and xylose follow closely in abundance. It is essential to highlight that while many exopolysaccharides are not exclusive to biofilms, specific ones, like colanic acid in E. coli and alginate in P . aeruginosa, are generated in response to challenging or stressful conditions (Veerubhotla et al. 2018). The M antigen, also referred to as colanic acid, is an extracellular heteropolysaccharide observed in Enterobacteriaceae. It is composed of repeat units comprising L-fucose, D-galactose, D-glucuronate, and D-glucose, incorporating O-acetyl and pyruvate side chains enhancing its structure. Within the cell, glycosyltransferases collaborate on the inner cell membrane to construct these repetitive units. After that, Wzx flips the repeat units from cytoplasm to periplasm. Initial polymerization is handled by the Wzy system, while Wzc and Wzb regulate high-level polymerization (Zhang et al. 2020). Colonic acid polymers are transported into the extracellular space by the outer membrane protein Wza. In E. coli K-12 Strategies for Development of Biofilms 193 strains where colanic acid synthesis is absent, the rate of initial attachment is reduced but not completely abolished. In P . aeruginosa biofilms, there are three prominent exopolysaccharides – Pel, Psl, and alginate – each fulfilling crucial functions (Guzmán-Soto et al. 2021). Alginate consists of alternating D-mannuronic acid and L-guluronic acid residues in its chemical structure. In the presence of alginate, P . aeruginosa develops increased resistance to antibiotics like ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, ticarcillin, and ceftazidime. Alginate forms a protective barrier around bacterial cells, impeding the penetration and efficacy of antibiotics. Furthermore, alginate can absorb antibiotics, further diminishing their effectiveness. Additionally, alginate disrupts the host’s immune response to P . aeruginosa infection. It can hinder the activities of neutrophils and macrophages, essential white blood cells responsible for combating diseases. Alginate can also suppress the production of antibodies and other immune components. These combined effects make alginate a significant contributor to the persistence of P . aeruginosa infections, particularly in cystic fibrosis patients. Strains of P . aeruginosa that produce alginate are associated with more extensive lung damage and unfavorable clinical outcomes. The alginate and lipopolysaccharide production enzyme AlgC was discovered to be implicated (LPS) (Coenye et al. 2020). The enzyme encoded by the algC gene possesses the activities of both phosphomannomutase and phosphoglucomutase. It holds a vital function in converting Man-6-P into Man-1-P and glucose-6-P into glucose-1-P. Man-1-P is pivotal as an intermediate in the synthesis of alginate and LPS (Dumaru et al. 2019). Within mature Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms, the biofilm matrix comprises two pivotal exopolysaccharides, Psl and Pel, and alginate and LPS. Both Pel and Psl hold indispensable functions in these biofilms. The Psl polysaccharide consists of repeating pentamers, which facilitate the initial surface attachment process by incorporating D-mannose, L-rhamnose, and D-glucose residues. In the case of strain PA14, the Pel genes are accountable for producing exopolysaccharides rich in glucose. Conversely, in strains ZK2870 and PAO1, the Psl genes participate in the formation of exopolysaccharides rich in mannose (Guzmán-Soto et al. 2021). In instances where Psl genes are absent, a deficient PAO1 strain can still establish mature biofilms by elevating the expression of Pel genes. The AlgC enzyme occupies a pivotal position in synthesizing both Psl and Pel. Notably, the generation of Psl, alginate, and LPS all hinges on a shared intermediate, Man-1-P. Recent research findings have unveiled the intricate interplay among these biofilm components; an increase in the production of one part corresponds to a reduction in the production of the others (Verderosa et al. 2019). Notably, Pseudomonas aeruginosa possesses 24 genes involved in the synthesis and secretion of alginate. Eight are in charge of alginic acid export, and 12 are in order of polysaccharide biosynthesis. The remaining four genes control the synthesis. Polysaccharide intercellular adhesin (PIA), initially identified by Mack and colleagues in Staphylococcus, is a significant exopolysaccharide associated with biofilm formation. It comprises a linear polymer consisting of glucosamine residues linked at the 1,6 positions, and it is also referred to as poly-N-acetyl glucosamine (Kartin Schilcher 2020). In Staphylococcus epidermidis, a notable feature of PIA is that more than 80% of its residues are N-acetylated, while the remaining 20% carry a 194 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization positive charge. “The synthesis of PIA is coordinated by four essential proteins: IcaA, IcaB, IcaC, and IcaD” (Kartin Schilcher 2020). IcaA and IcaD operate as N-acetylglucosaminyltransferases, collaborating with UDP-GlcNAc to construct 20-residue oligomers. In contrast, IcaC is crucial in crafting extended oligomers exceeding 130 residues and facilitates their transportation to the extracellular space. Meanwhile, IcaB contributes by deacetylating, introducing positive charges essential for interactions with cell membranes. In the case of Bacillus subtilis, the composition of the biofilm-associated exopolysaccharide can vary, presenting either as EPS or polyglutamate. This variability depends on the specific strain and the prevailing environmental conditions (Kokare et al. 2009). 2.1 Extracellular Proteins Extracellular proteins represent another crucial component of the EPS matrix, contributing significantly to the formation and stability of biofilms. These proteins establish connections between cell surfaces and polysaccharides, promoting the preservation of biofilm architecture. For instance, in S. mutans biofilms, glucan- binding proteins (Gbps) serve as an example. Gbps plays a pivotal role by bridging bacteria and exopolysaccharides, ensuring the integrity of biofilm structure. When Gbps are mutated, the resulting biofilms exhibit a substantial reduction in height. Additionally, amyloids, a specific type of insoluble fibrous protein, also aid biofilm formation (Bi et al. 2021). This phenomenon is illustrated in Pseudomonas spp., particularly in the case of Fap amyloids. When Fap amyloids are overexpressed, it leads to the expedited processes of cell aggregation and biofilm development. In B. subtilis biofilms, one of the critical components is the amyloid protein TasA. TasA is responsible for creating robust fibers that bind biofilm cells together and exhibit impressive resistance to external pressures, ensuring biofilm integrity even under harsh conditions. Another notable group to consider is the biofilm-associated protein (bap) family, which includes proteins like Bap in S. aureus and Esp in Figure 1. Structure of the biofilm (source: self-created). Strategies for Development of Biofilms 195 E. faecalis. Members of the bap family serve a dual purpose, actively participating in both biofilm development and the facilitation of infections. There are additional instances, such as the outer-membrane lectins discovered in Azospirillum brasiliense, along with the galactophilic lectin le-cA and the L-fucose binding lectin lecB in P . aeruginosa, all of which contribute significantly to the process of biofilm formation. Additionally, certain enzymes within biofilms are engaged in the breakdown process (Taraszkiewicz et al. 2013). Within the EPS matrix, various substrates like cellulose, proteins, lipids, polysaccharides, nucleic acids, and other components, along with substances trapped within the matrix, all serve as targets for enzymes. These enzymes play a critical role in breaking down biopolymers, thus supplying biofilm cells with essential carbon and energy. This becomes especially vital when the biofilm cells face nutrient scarcity conditions. Enzymatic actions are also required for biofilm separation and dissemination (Zhao et al. 2017). The commencement of a new biofilm lifecycle occurs as biofilm cells are released when enzymes internally degrade the EPS matrix. An instance of this is the DspB protein, which plays a role in the detachment of Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae biofilms from surfaces. Additionally, the understanding of extracellular DNAs (eDNAs) shifted when Mattick and colleagues revealed DNase I could effectively inhibit the development of P . aeruginosa biofilms. Before this discovery, eDNAs were commonly considered remnants resulting from cell lysis. eDNA is actively released and derived from lyzed cells, which suggests that eDNA plays an essential role in biofilm development (Kokare et al. 2009). It has been determined that eDNA plays a crucial role in biofilm adhesion. Initially, its negative charge serves as a repellent factor. However, when the cell and the surface gap narrow to just a few nanometers, eDNA engages with receptors on the substrate surface, facilitating adhesion. Furthermore, researchers have found that eDNA also coordinates cell movement, particularly in the expansion of P . aeruginosa biofilms through twitching motility (Yu et al. 2019).
