In Gram-negative bacteria like P . aeruginosa, Salmonella Typhimurium, and others, eDNA can specifically chelate Mg2+ and activate the PhoPQ/PmrAB two-component systems, enhancing resistance to antimicrobial peptides. In the case of S. epidermidis, eDNA has been found to obstruct the transport of vancomycin within biofilms, thus safeguarding the bacteria trapped within the biofilm structure. However, the current understanding of eDNA’s precise roles in biofilm maturation and persistence remains limited, emphasizing the need for further research to understand its significance in biofilm development better (Costerton et al. 2003). 2.1.1 Dental Plaque Biofilms play a significant role in dentistry, and researchers have conducted numerous studies on dental biofilms. Many bacteria and archaea, totaling over 700 species, have been identified in dental plaque. Dental plaque consists of various types of biofilms, and it is important to note that the composition of a healthy plaque biofilm significantly differs from that of plaque biofilms associated with disease. The unique microenvironment within the oral cavity, influenced by water, temperature fluctuations, solid surfaces, and the availability of carbon and nitrogen sources, contributes to this variation (De la Fuente-Núñez et al. 2013). Moreover, alterations in the local environment can impact the bacterial composition of biofilms. In healthy biofilms, innocuous bacterial species like Streptococcus oralis, Actinomyces species, Streptococcus gordonii, Streptococcus sanguis, and others are present but exhibit low acid tolerance. Bacteria responsible for dental caries, such as S. sobrinus and S. mutans, notably tolerate acidic conditions. These acid-tolerant bacteria play a significant role in various oral disorders, including dental caries, periodontitis, gingivitis, and more, given their capacity to establish robust biofilms. In order to initiate colonization and the subsequent formation of biofilms on enamel surfaces, bacteria must communicate with one another (Abdallah et al. 2014). The bacteria are flushed away with the oral saliva if they do not linger on the tooth surface. When bacteria successfully adhere to surfaces, they form dental plaque, comprising many species. Oral microbes attach themselves to immobilized bacteria on various surfaces, including teeth, epithelial tissues, and other bacteria, a phenomenon known as co-adhesion. Moreover, genetically diverse cells can engage in cell-to-cell interactions in a suspended state, termed coaggregation. At least one coaggregation partner typically exists within the realm of oral bacteria. A schematic representation illustrates the dynamic interplay of early and late colonizers competing and cooperating during tooth colonization, with Streptococci and actinomycetes being the initial colonizing species (Bi et al. 2021). The primary colonizers of dental plaque recognize receptors. Phosphate- rich proteins like statherin and enzymes like -amylase are among the receptors. Streptococci detect salivary pellicle receptors (coats the enamel). Proline-rich proteins and statherin bind to actinomyces. Fusobacteria, anaerobic Gram-negative bacteria, also bind statherin. Bacteria in the oral biofilm communicate by secreting Strategies for Development of Biofilms 197 and accumulating tiny chemicals. Autoinducer (AI)-2 is a ubiquitous intergeneric signaling molecule involved in forming biofilms. S. oralis and Actinomyces oris T14V aggregate in response to AI-2 (Alotaibi and Bukhari 2021). Small doses of AI-2 are adequate for oral bacteria coaggregation but not oral pathogens. The concentration of AI-2 rises as the commensal bacteria’s cell density increases. Under conducive conditions, these microorganisms multiply and establish the biofilm at optimal concentrations. However, the circumstances are not favorable for their growth at lower concentrations. Fusobacteria, for instance, are prolific producers of AI-2, which they utilize to co-aggregate with various colonizing species. This strategic move allows Fusobacteria to emerge as the predominant bacteria in biofilms associated with healthy gums and plaque (Jiang et al. 2020). 2.1.2 Wounds Chronic wounds often exhibit the presence of biofilms. Unlike acute injuries, which typically do not involve biofilms and tend to heal promptly, chronic wound cases are characterized by a slower and prolonged healing process. Biofilms usually develop on the surface of wounds. Still, in some instances, like P . aeruginosa biofilms, they can be deeply embedded within the wound’s layers, making them challenging to detect using conventional wound swab cultures (De la Fuente-Núñez et al. 2013). 2.1.3 Prosthetic Joint Infection Prosthetic joint infections frequently involve Gram-positive bacteria, notably staphylococci. Shortly after surgery, bacteria from the bloodstream or lymphatic system adhere to the surfaces of prosthetic joints, initiating the development of biofilms. Unlike typical bacterial infections that trigger immediate symptoms like fever, biofilms on these implants, such as pain, may not become apparent until some time has passed (Abdallah et al. 2014). 2.1.4 Persister Cells Persisters are a small group of cells found within biofilms, and they have a unique characteristic: their growth rate is prolonged, sometimes even non-existent. When treating infections, most antibiotics are designed to target processes associated with rapid cell growth and division. As a result, these antibiotics prove ineffective against persister cells. This leads to a concerning situation where persister cells essentially act as hiding spots for diseases, as they can resurface as infectious agents once the antibiotic treatment has waned (Costerton et al. 2003). 2.1.5 EPS Matrix Protection The physical barrier of the EPS matrix shields the biofilm cells that clump together. Specifically, in Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms, the exopolysaccharide known as alginate is a protective shield, guarding the biofilm bacteria from being killed by human white blood cells. 198 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 2.1.6 Horizontal Gene Transfer Bacteria can acquire antibiotic resistance through two primary mechanisms: random mutations in their genes and the presence of antibiotic-resistant genes on plasmids. Plasmids are small DNA molecules that can be easily shared between bacteria through horizontal gene transfer. Interestingly, the transfer of plasmids is much more frequent in biofilms compared to individual planktonic cells. This means biofilms play a significant role in disseminating antibiotic-resistance genes carried on plasmids, primarily through mechanisms like conjugation and mobilization. Studies focusing on Staphylococcus aureus biofilms have highlighted the role of biofilms in increasing the spread of antibiotic-resistance genes through these processes (Van Houdt and Michiels 2010). 2.1.7 Efflux Pumps Efflux pumps serve as a defense mechanism for bacterial cells, allowing them to expel harmful substances like antibiotics. While these pumps are present in individual planktonic cells, there’s an interesting observation in biofilms—several efflux pump genes are upregulated, indicating their potential involvement in antibiotic resistance. Among these genes, PA1874–1877 is a newly discovered efflux pump gene in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It stands out because it exhibits significantly higher expression levels in biofilms than planktonic cells. This efflux pump, generated by PA1874–1877, has been linked to increased resistance to antibiotics like ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, and tobramycin (Jiang et al. 2020). 2.1.8 Cardiac Valve Infection The effect of bacterial biofilm on artificial biofilm causes prosthetic valve endocarditis. S. aureus, Corynebacterium spp., S. epidermidis, Candida spp., and Streptococcus spp. are the bacteria causing endocarditis. Biofilm build-up can disturb or clog the prosthetic heart valve, causing reduced flow, turbulence, and leakage. Biofilm cells detached from their biofilm can travel via the bloodstream and infect other organs. Biofilm fragments in the bloodstream might obstruct blood flow to vital organs such as the brain and kidneys (Donlan 2001). 2.1.9 Biofilm Resistance to Antibiotics and Host Immune System Unlike planktonic bacteria, biofilm bacteria exhibit more excellent resistance to antibiotics and the reactive substances generated by the host immune system. It has been estimated that biofilm cells are approximately 10,000 times more resilient to antibiotics than their planktonic counterparts. For instance, when subjected to tobramycin treatment, planktonic cells could not survive beyond a concentration of 50 g/ml. In contrast, biofilm cells could withstand as much as 1 mg/ml of tobramycin when P . aeruginosa biofilm and planktonic cells were treated with this antibiotic (Kokare et al. 2009). In inhibiting Staphylococcus aureus biofilms, two distinct disinfectants, benzalkonium chloride, and the oxidizing agent sodium hypochlorite, have shown exciting results. These disinfectants required concentrations that were 50 times and 600 times higher, respectively, compared to what is needed to inhibit Strategies for Development of Biofilms 199 individual planktonic cells of the same bacterium. As for the growing problem of antibiotic resistance observed in bacterial biofilms, the underlying causes remain largely elusive. A combination of multiple factors likely comes into play, working together to protect biofilm cells from the effects of antibiotic treatments. Several potential mechanisms for antibiotic resistance in bacterial biofilms have been proposed (Abdallah et al. 2014). 3. Mechanism of Biofilm Formation Microbes form biofilms by congregating in communities on the surfaces of inert materials and binding themselves with a viscous substance known as exopolysaccharide (EPS); these polymers, produced by the microorganisms within the biofilm, anchor bacteria to the material’s surface. Bacteria, fungi, algae, protozoa, and other microorganisms can all be found in natural biofilms. Biofilms’ amazing tolerance to various toxins and nutrition deprivation has piqued scientists’ interest in studying their properties and structure for decades (Toole et al. 2000). The metabolic burden is shared by microbes incorporated in the biofilm matrix as a community via quorum sensing. Biofilms have found applications in various fields, such as bioremediation, wastewater treatment, and metal leaching, to name a few. An example of a valuable biofilm is the electroactive biofilm, which is the cornerstone in bio-electrochemical systems. The steps of biofilm formation will be discussed in detail in the next section. There are multiple phases to the creation of a biofilm. Bacteria travel toward the surface in the first step, which can be done aggressively or passively. Some planktonic microbes actively swim toward a suitable abiotic surface location. Other species use weak forces, including Brownian motion, gravity, and van der Waals forces, to reach the surface (Sousa et al. 2020). The constant flow situation can bring bacteria closer to the surface of the support in some cases. The surface characteristics of the support mostly determine bacterial adhesion. A reversible adhesion of planktonic bacteria to the surface starts the second stage of biofilm growth. Cells’ slender appendages, including pili, fimbriae, and flagella, stimulate cell adherence to the surface, resulting in cell phenotypic alterations. Microbe attachment is further shaped by environmental parameters such as pH, temperature, shear stress, and strain motility (De la Fuente-Núñez et al. 2013). The change from reversible to irreversible attachment on the surface occurs following adhesion. The development of microorganisms as a biofilm has a new beginning with this adhesion. The secretion of EPS is the most noticeable alteration seen in the sessile biofilm. EPS differs from organism to organism in terms of composition. There are multiple phases to the creation of a biofilm. Bacteria travel toward the surface in the first step, which can be done aggressively or passively. Some planktonic microbes actively swim toward a suitable abiotic surface location (Alotaibi an Bukhari, 2021). Various species employ weak forces such as Brownian motion, gravity, and van der Waals to facilitate their surface arrival. A constant flow situation can sometimes bring bacteria near the support’s surface. The surface properties of the substrate play a crucial role in bacterial adhesion—the reversible adhesion of planktonic bacteria to the surface marks initiating the second phase of biofilm growth. Slender cell appendages like pili, fimbriae, and flagella are pivotal 200 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization in promoting cell adhesion to the surface, leading to noticeable changes in the cells’ characteristics (Van Houdt and Michiels 2010). Environmental factors like pH, temperature, shear stress, and motility patterns significantly influence bacterial attachment. The transition from reversible to irreversible attachment to the surface occurs once the initial adhesion occurs. The development of microorganisms as a biofilm has a new beginning with this adhesion. The secretion of EPS is the most noticeable alteration seen in the sessile biofilm. EPS differs from organism to organism in composition (Toole et al. 2000). For instance, E. coli bacteria utilize colonic acid as a crucial element in their biofilm formation, while P . aeruginosa bacteria rely on alginate. This biofilm is enveloped by an EPS matrix, protecting it against external pressures. Changes occurring within the biofilm involve modifications in metabolite production, downregulating genes responsible for flagella formation, and enhanced resistance to UV light exposure. The EPS matrix is believed to act as a barrier, hindering antibiotics from reaching the cell surfaces of microorganisms within the biofilm and shielding these bacteria from various environmental stresses (Zhao et al. 2017). Once the EPS synthesis is complete, the biofilm enters a maturation phase primarily regulated by quorum sensing. Quorum-sensing molecules play a pivotal role in shaping the architecture of the biofilm, a characteristic unique to specific bacterial species. In its fully developed state, a biofilm exhibits a distinct three- dimensional structure, well-defined water channels, and significant thickness. The ultimate stage involves the detachment of bacteria from the biofilm. Detachment mechanism research is still in its early stages (De la Fuente-Núñez et al. 2013). Methods to Detect the Biofilm Production Standard antimicrobial susceptibility testing involves injecting an antimicrobial agent into planktonic (suspended) cells and will not reliably predict an agent’s efficiency against biofilm-associated pathogens. The National Committee for Clinical Laboratory Standards (NCCLS) does not have a method for testing antimicrobial drugs’ efficacy against biofilm-associated pathogens. Several techniques for evaluating antimicrobial drugs against biofilms have been proposed. An approach that can predict the susceptibility of biofilm-associated organisms in vivo , is reproducible, affordable, has a quick turnaround time, and is simple to use would be acceptable. The Calgary Biofilm Device was created to test numerous antimicrobial drugs against E. coli, S. aureus, and P . aeruginosa biofilms (Dumaru et al. 2019). The gadget creates biofilms on duplicate “pegs”, tested using a standard 96-well plate setup. The device’s results demonstrated that biofilm formation on pegs was repeatable, simple to use, and affordable. The Modified Robbins Device is a tubular flow-through device that produces biofilms of specified organisms on duplicate membranes in flowing circumstances (Costerton et al. 2003). The membranes with biofilms are then withdrawn from the device and treated with various antimicrobial treatments. It was feasible to assess the susceptibility of biofilm and planktonic phenotypes of an organism by comparing findings from these tests with data acquired using the NCCLS protocols. However, any of these biofilm susceptibility testing techniques raises the question of how well they can mimic an in vivo or in situ biofilm. How well does the approach predict antimicrobial agent efficacy against biofilms on a catheter or a prosthetic heart valve, for example? Better estimations may be possible with model systems that closely imitate an implanted medical device. It created a technique for cultivating biofilms on central venous catheter needleless connectors that replicated the device’s properties in operation, including flow rate, temperature, medium composition, the presence of a blood-conditioning coating on the device surface, and the organisms present (Coenye et al. 2020). Similar techniques could be used to test antimicrobial drugs’ effectiveness against biofilms on these devices. Comparing results from an in vitro model with results from an in vivo animal model would be a natural next step. Following CLSI recommendations, an antibiotic susceptibility test was done on Muller Hinton agar using the Kirby Bauer disk diffusion method. All the bacterial strains were subjected to a battery of common antibiotics, including ofloxacin (5 g), levofloxacin (5 g), ceftazidime (30 g), cefepime (30 g), amikacin (30 g), gentamicin (10 g), piperacillin (100 g), piperacillin-tazobactam (100/10 g), imipenem (10 g), and colistin (10 g). In the case of Pseudomonas species, the testing panel was expanded to include polymyxin B (300 units), tobramycin (10 g), and carbenicillin (100 g) (Veerubhotla et al. 2018). 4.1 ESBL and MBL Phenotypic Detection A disk diffusion test was used to screen the ceftazidime-resistant bacteria for ESBL production. Between ceftazidime (30 g) and ceftazidime-clavulanate (30/10 g), a 202 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 5-mm rise in the zone’s diameter was deemed ESBL positive. A combination disk diffusion assay was employed to assess the production of Metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) in imipenem-resistant bacteria. This assay involved using two imipenem disks, one of which had an additional 10 μl of 0.5 M EDTA applied to it. Compared to the zone of inhibition observed with the antibiotic disk on its own, the imipenem-EDTA disk exhibited a noticeably larger zone of inhibition, exceeding 7 mm. This enlargement indicated the presence of MBL production (Nira Rabin et al. 2017). Two methods are commonly used for detecting biofilms: Congo red agar and the tube adherence method. Here is a description of the tube adherence method: In this method, the process begins with introducing a thriving microorganism into a solution of trypticase soy broth. Subsequently, the mixture is placed in an incubator at a temperature of 35°C for a duration of 24 hours. The tube was rinsed with phosphate buffer saline after discarding the supernatant. It was treated with 0.1% crystal violet for staining, then washed and dried. The presence of visible biofilm lining the tube’s bottom and the wall was regarded as a favorable sign. The organisms were inoculated onto Congo red agar plates and incubated for 24 hours at 37°C (Tanzil et al. 2016). 5. Biofilm Growth Cells that firmly attach to surfaces, resisting removal through gentle rinsing, will follow a sequence of events. They will initiate division, create microcolonies, and commence the production of extracellular polymers, which are responsible for defining the biofilm. These extracellular polymeric substances (EPSs), primarily polysaccharides, can be identified under a microscope and through chemical analysis. These EPSs play a crucial role in forming the matrix or structure of the biofilm. Remarkably, they have a high water content, comprising approximately 98 percent water, yet they firmly adhere to the underlying surface with remarkable tenacity (Verderosa et al. 2019). The structure of a biofilm is not just a straightforward, uniform layer of slime. Instead, it exhibits a dynamic and diverse composition that varies spatially and temporally. Within this structure, “water channels” serve as conduits, facilitating the essential flow of nutrients and oxygen to nourish the cells within the biofilm. Biofilms behave as filters, trapping diverse particles such as minerals and host components, including fibrin, RBCs, and platelets. Biofilm-associated organisms develop more slowly than planktonic organisms, owing to nutritional and oxygen deprivation in the cells. Cell development and division and the clearance of biofilm aggregates containing masses of cells cause cells to detach from the biofilm. Depending on several conditions, including the host immune system’s response, these detachable cells may create a systemic infection (Chandel et al. 2018). 6. Factors Affecting Biofilm Formation The development of biofilms in microbial fuel cells (MFCs) is noticeably shaped by three primary factors: the setup of the system, the operational conditions, and the biological aspects involved. The system setup encompasses various structural elements within MFCs. This includes aspects like the choice of electrode material, the spacing between electrodes, the type of membrane used, the electrical circuit’s Strategies for Development of Biofilms 203 conductivity, and the overall working volume of the system. These components collectively define the system’s configuration, influencing the formation of biofilms and the ultimate performance of MFCs. As a result, substantial research efforts have been dedicated to improving the design of MFC systems (Sousa et al. 2020). The selection of electrode material holds significant importance in biofilm development within microbial fuel cells (MFCs). This choice is pivotal because the electrode material serves as the foundation upon which the biofilm grows, and it also facilitates the exchange of electrons required for anaerobic respiration. In many studies involving MFCs, carbon-based electrodes have emerged as popular choices. These materials include carbon felt, glassy carbon electrodes, activated carbon fabric, graphite, and various other carbon-based alternatives. While specific metal- based electrodes like gold, platinum, or titanium have been employed in MFCs, their widespread use is constrained by their relatively high costs (Chandel et al. 2016). The properties of bioelectrode surfaces, which encompass characteristics such as porosity, hydrophobicity, conductivity, and charge, are primarily determined by the choice of material. These qualities play a substantial role in influencing how bacteria adhere to them. Porosity is an essential attribute of electrodes as it expands the available surface area, making it easier for bacteria to attach and establish colonies. In the case of electroactive bacteria, which are vital for forming conductive biofilms, they tend to favor electrode surfaces that are positively charged and hydrophilic. Since many of these electroactive bacteria are Gram-negative, the positive charge on the electrode surface enhances electrostatic interactions with these negatively charged bacterial cells. Moreover, hydrophilic characteristics encourage the formation of hydrogen bonds, further facilitating the attachment of bacteria to the electrode surface (Coenye et al. 2020). 6.1 Effect of the Type of Membrane In microbial fuel cells (MFCs), the membrane maintains electroneutrality between the two chambers while facilitating selective cation or anion transfer between the anode and cathode. Proton exchange membranes (PEMs) are the most commonly employed membranes in MFCs, enabling the transfer of protons from the anode to the cathode. Research has demonstrated that the type and surface area of the membrane have a notable impact on the power generation efficiency of MFCs (Böttcher et al. 2013). The choice of membrane in use directly influences the transport of ions and, consequently, the pH of the solution. In some instances, other cations like Na+, K +, Ca2+, and Mg 2+ from the anolyte are transported to the cathode instead of protons, leading to an increase in pH at the cathode and a corresponding decrease in pH at the anode when Na + ions are employed. This pH shift has implications for the growth and community structure of the biofilm, which will be discussed in greater detail in the subsequent sections (Puranik et al. 2021). 6.1.1 Operating Conditions Physiological factors like pH, temperature, substrate availability, ion concentrations, and various other variables affect biofilm formation. This is due to the mutual 204 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization influence of bacterial and material surfaces with their surrounding environments (Dumaru et al. 2019). 6.1.2 Effect of pH pH stands out as the most critical factor influencing bacterial growth and the performance of microbial fuel cells (MFCs). Numerous research efforts are dedicated to unraveling the impact of anodic pH on MFC performance. In most MFC studies, the optimal pH has been determined to fall within the neutral (pH 7) or near-neutral (pH 6–8) range. Nevertheless, there have been limited reports on MFC operation at extreme pH values. Several parameters, such as ion transfer, substrate oxidation, and oxygen reduction, are pH-dependent during MFC operation. However, these effects can be mitigated by implementing appropriate catalysts, innovative ion-exchange membranes, and buffering agents. It is important to note that electrolyte pH directly influences bacterial populations’ composition, development, and structure (Puranik et al. 2021). 6.1.3 Formation of Biofilm Microbial Cells Bacteria are highly responsive to shifts in pH within their surroundings, and even slight alterations in pH levels can prompt significant adjustments in microbial metabolism. In contrast to enzymatic reactions, bacteria can adapt their metabolic processes in response to fluctuations in environmental pH. The pH of the immediate microenvironment notably impacts various physiological aspects, such as membrane potential, proton motive force, cytoplasmic electrochemical gradient, and the overall balance between proton production and consumption (Divakar et al. 2019). 6.1.4 Temperature It affects bacterial biofilms’ growth and electrocatalytic activity, as it does on pH. Bacteria are classified into three types based on the temperature range in which they grow: psychrophiles (40°C) and thermophiles (40°C). Most MFC research has been conducted in mesophilic temperatures, implying that most electroactive bacteria are active at these temperatures. Psychrophiles and thermophiles, on the other hand, have been reported to be electroactive. Temperature determines the type and distribution of microbial communities in MFCs with mixed cultures, as each species in the consortium has a different optimal temperature for growth. Furthermore, temperature variations affect the reaction rates and thermodynamics of anodic processes, indirectly impacting biofilm formation (Kartin Schilcher 2020). 6.1.5 Effect of Substrate Concentration Within a mixed microbial community, the type of substrate present in the growth medium and its concentration play pivotal roles in determining which species predominates. In the context of microbial fuel cells (MFCs), a wide array of substrates has been employed, spanning from simple sugars and complex carbohydrates to simulated or real wastewater and lignocellulosic biomass, among other options. Notably, changes in the substrate used have been observed to lead to discernible shifts Strategies for Development of Biofilms 205 in the dominant microbial community. This phenomenon stems from the fact that the mixed consortia involved in MFCs, which extend beyond just electroactive bacteria, compete for the substrate as an energy source. Additionally, it is worth mentioning that the concentration of the substrate has a noticeable impact on the power output generated by the MFC system. Generally, higher concentrations of substrates have been observed to have detrimental effects on biofilms due to a phenomenon known as substrate inhibition (Chandel et al. 2018). 6.1.6 Parameters of Biology The formation of biofilms is influenced by several critical factors, including the origin and type of inoculum, the growth rate of bacteria, the specific microorganism involved, electron transfer systems, and various other biological traits. Regarding the inoculum, it is important to highlight that most electroactive biofilms studied thus far have predominantly comprised Gram-negative bacteria. This preference stems from distinctions in the cell wall composition between Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, which significantly affect the electrogenic behavior of these organisms. Gram-positive bacteria possess a peptidoglycan layer associated with teichoic acid, resulting in a relatively high Zeta potential. In contrast, Gram- negative bacteria feature lipopolysaccharides, leading to a lower Zeta potential than their Gram-positive counterparts. As explained earlier, the interaction between the surface charges of bacteria and those on the electrodes plays a pivotal role in determining the choice of material for the MFC system. As is commonly understood, bacterial biofilms can be formed using either a pure culture or a mixed culture (Toole et al. 2000). The composition of bacteria in the environment impacts the micro- colonization of the diverse species that constitute the bacterial biofilm matrix. When more electroactive species are present, substrate degradation occurs more rapidly, producing more protons and electrons. If all the electrons released during substrate degradation are efficiently channeled for energy generation, MFC outputs can be significantly enhanced. Mixed culture biofilms yield a higher electron flow than pure culture biofilms. However, the diverse culture’s bacterial community exhibits variable diversity, which raises questions about the reproducibility of such biofilm ecosystems (Jiang et al. 2020). 6.1.7 Inter- and Intra-species Interactions Scientists have proposed that a mix of direct and indirect (mediator-based) electron transfer mechanisms within mixed cultures can contribute to power generation. Within electroactive biofilms, researchers have detected different types of interactions between species. Quorum sensing (QS) is a mechanism that enables communication among bacteria of various species. It has been observed that certain QS compounds play a role in coordinating and controlling gene expression associated with the formation of biofilms. Enhanced power outputs in microbial fuel cells (MFCs) have been attributed to synergistic interactions among bacterial species. Additionally, in various studies involving conductive bacterial nanowires, there is evidence to suggest the presence of syntrophic interactions. Although we have observed symbiotic interactions among different bacterial groups in fermentative processes, 206 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization our comprehension of cell-to-cell interactions within electroactive biofilms remains constrained. Consequently, there is a necessity for additional research to delve deeper into the specific synergistic relationships and other biological processes that occur within electroactive communities (Zhao et al. 2017). 7. Reason for Biofilm Formation Many bacteria possess the ability to transition between two distinct states: planktonic and biofilm. In the planktonic state, bacteria exhibit a more rapid rate of cell growth and reproduction. However, it is noteworthy that the biofilm state appears to be the natural and prevailing condition for bacteria. Several factors can lead bacteria to adopt a biofilm state. Biofilms offer numerous advantages, notably bolstering a bacterium’s ability to withstand harsh environmental conditions. When bacteria adhere to surfaces or tissues, they can avoid being swept away by water or the bloodstream movement. An illustrative example is seen in oral biofilms, which exhibit exceptional resilience against repetitive, high-shear forces. Biofilm cells display a remarkable resistance to external stresses, estimated to be approximately 1,000 times greater than planktonic cells. Moreover, the protective extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix shields bacterial cells in deeper layers. This shielding primarily works by limiting the diffusion of antimicrobial agents, thereby safeguarding the biofilm community from the detrimental effects of these agents. Biofilms are more than just a physical barrier; they also promote increased bacterial cell densities, creating an ideal setting for exchanging extracellular DNA, including plasmids, through mechanisms like conjugation. This genetic exchange has the potential to bestow antibiotic resistance upon certain bacteria. Significantly, the rate of horizontal gene transfer within biofilms significantly surpasses that observed in planktonic cells (Van Houdt and Michiels 2010). 8. Conclusion The protective layers formed by cells within the biofilm render antibiotics ineffective in combating biofilm-related infections. Consequently, antibiotic penetration is severely restricted, enabling the stationary cell community to persist even when antibiotics eliminate their motile counterparts effectively. Disrupting the extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix may be necessary to achieve the dispersal of mature biofilms. Notably, components like alginate, Pel, and Psl, found within the EPS matrix of P . aeruginosa biofilms, represent potential targets for disrupting biofilm formation. Subsequently, once exposed, the drug molecule could exhibit bactericidal properties or function by dispersing the cells. Conversely, preventing initial processes such as cell adhesion to surfaces could serve as a strategy to impede the formation of new biofilms. This aspect is of utmost importance in advancing medical and dental implants, which are susceptible to colonization by harmful bacteria, leading to biofilm formation. However, a notable challenge lies in the disparity between data generated from in vitro and in vivo models. The selection of an appropriate animal model would profoundly impact the development of any antibiofilm treatment, contingent upon the model’s similarity to human conditions. Rajkumar,4 Manoja Das5 and Ravindra Kumar6,* 1. Introduction Biomaterial is a substance made up of organic, inorganic, or composite material that is engineered to interact with biological systems. These substances are introduced into the body tissues so that they can mimic bodily function for treatment or tissue- repairing purposes. Nowadays, biomaterials play an important role in medical instrumentation design and production. The science of biomaterials is new to society, and it is considered to be only 50–60 years old. The main criteria for selecting biomaterials include biocompatibility, cost, and chemical properties. As synthetic biomaterials show lower biocompatibility and adverse immune response, natural polymer-based biomaterials are used for effective response. The biocompatibility assessment is considered to measure the ability of the material to perform any host function without any adverse reactions like tumour formation, hypersensitivity reactions, anaphylaxis, etc. A foreign body reaction (FBR) is the host response towards the foreign invaders. The first biomaterial used in the human body and became popular is tooth filling. Later on, the use of biomaterials in various body parts, such as joint replacement, hip implantation, and cardiovascular repairs, is becoming more familiar in clinical fields. These materials are usually inert, with minimal tissue responses (Namur et al. 2015). The success of this implant depends on the selection of material (Walker 2015). No doubt, the use of biomaterial or devices improves the quality of life. The demand is also increasing day by day, not only for older people but also for younger ones, particularly those who are suffering from heart problems and inherited diseases (Hench et al. 1971; J Best 2007). Day by day, the continuous improvement of biomaterials is going on with respect to the bio-inertness of the materials and positive response towards the biological response (Danewalia and Singh 2016; Ferguson et al. 2014; Khan et al. 2015). The bioactive approach and interface between body cells and the implant are important with respect to the biocompatibility study. In this chapter, various biomaterials and their composition are elaborately discussed. The emphasis is also given to the clinical and immunogenic response of biopolymers with critical analysis of anti-rejection therapy. 2. What are Biomaterials Despite the fact that some biomaterials have biological origins, the prefix ‘bio’ in the word ‘biomaterial’ refers to a condition in which a material becomes a part of a biological system in order to fulfil a specific purpose rather than being derived from one. The biological system here refers primarily to the human body. The term ‘biomaterial’ has been defined variously to rationally emphasise its role since the establishment of the interdisciplinary field of biomaterials more than half a century ago. These definitions became more precise over time. 2.1 Definitions Biomaterial According to the European Society for Biomaterials, in 1987, it was defined as ‘a non-viable material used in a medical device, intended to interact with biological Biological Response to Biomaterials 211 system’ (Anonymous n.d.). After some deletions and additions, the definition was modified to ‘a material intended to interface with biological systems to evaluate, treat, augment or replace any tissue, organ or function of the body’ in 1999 (Williams 2009). According to a leading opinion paper by David F. Williams in 2009, the conclusive definition was ‘A biomaterial is a substance that has been engineered to take a form which, alone or as part of a complex system, is used to direct, by control of interactions with components of living systems, the course of any therapeutic or diagnostic procedure, in human or veterinary medicine’ (Williams 2009). As per the 2018 conference chaired by Professor David F. Williams, the following definition achieved consensus, ‘A material designed to take a form that can direct, through interactions with living systems, the course of any therapeutic or diagnostic procedure’ (Ghasemi-Mobarakeh et al. 2019). Biocompatibility Biocompatibility explains the tolerance of the biomaterials to function in the host body through interaction with blood and other body fluid components, cells, and organs without affecting the homeostasis and immune mechanism. If the implant is non-biocompatible, it may lead to adverse immune reactions and failure. 2.2 Materials That Can Be Used as Biomaterials The substances with which the biomaterials are made up are broadly classified as metals, ceramics, synthetic, and biopolymers. Biomaterials can be nature-derived or human-engineered. They can be either biodegradable or non-biodegradable. After the advent of advanced technologies like nanotechnology and self-assembly process technologies, the boundaries between material classes have blurred nowadays. Metallic Biomaterials Metallic biomaterials are used largely in dental implantation, joint replacements, orthopaedic fixations, thus providing support to human tissues (Prasad et al. 2017). The greater availability of diverse metallic biomaterials helps in choosing a material to fulfil the specific objective of a particular treatment. Metallic biomaterials, which are chemically inert can be placed in the body permanently to replace a lost function. At the same time, biodegradable biometals are used as a temporary supporting framework to replace a lost function or for the regeneration of a lost tissue (Bhat and Kumar 2013; Henkel et al. 2013). The metallic biomaterials are divided into permanent and biodegradable biomaterials. The metals and alloys used in permanent metallic implants, due to their high degree of corrosion resistance and wear resistance, exhibit long-term stability in vivo along with superior mechanical properties (Saini 2015). They are: Stainless Steel : Stainless steel is a mixture of an iron alloy with chromium (Cr), nickel (Ni), and other metals along with carbon as a non-metallic additive. Chromium imparts corrosion resistance to stainless steel. Examples of kinds of stainless steel are Ni-free stainless steel and surgical stainless steel (316L), which contain 0.03% of carbon (Sumita 1997). 212 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization Titanium and Its Alloys: Titanium alloys exhibit a 50% more strength-to-weight ratio when compared to stainless steel. Titanium alloys contain metals like zirconium (Zr), tantalum (Ta), aluminium (Al), niobium (Nb), and vanadium (V), besides titanium, in different proportions and combinations. Cobalt-Based Metallic Biomaterials: Cobalt-based metallic biomaterials possess a high degree of wear resistance when compared to titanium alloys. Tantalum-Based Metallic Biomaterials: Tantalum (Ta) is considered the best biomaterial for certain applications due to its resistance to corrosion properties under highly acidic conditions (M Sumita 1997; Walker 2015). The Ti-Ta alloy is relatively better compared to pure tantalum when certain important properties are considered. Even after being highly biocompatible due to the possession of certain attributes like high corrosion resistance and resistance to wear and friction, metallic ions leach out into the surrounding biological microenvironment in the long run from the metal surface due to the highly reactive nature of the surrounding biological system. This can lead to local tissue damage as well as systemic damage due to inflammation and metal hypersensitivity (Williams 2009). In certain instances, using biodegradable biometals instead of permanent metallic implants produces desirable results. The most commonly used biodegradable biometals are magnesium (Mg), iron (Fe), and zinc (Zn) alloys that find cardiovascular and orthopaedic applications. A good amount of research is currently being done on these biometals (Walker 2015). In the case of this kind of bioresorbable biometal, biodegradation kinetics have to be regulated properly for best results. Ceramic Biomaterials Ceramic biomaterials or bioceramics are ceramic materials that exhibit physical, chemical, and surface properties that match the properties of various parts of the human skeletal system. Hence, bioceramics find application mostly in relation to the repair of joints, bones, and teeth, as well as to augment both soft and hard tissues (J Best 2007). Even bioceramics are used in soft tissue repair and regeneration. Bioceramics exhibit excellent biocompatibility, corrosion resistance, and high melting point. Its mechanical properties, poor plasticity in comparison to metallic biomaterials, and low electric and thermal conductivity make it a better alternative to metallic implants. Based on their interactions with biological tissues, these were categorised into the category of safe biomaterial for implants which does not elicit unfavourable host response (J Best 2007). Bioinert Ceramics: Alumina and Zirconia are the most popular examples of bioinert ceramics. As the name suggests, the bioinert ceramics have lesser interaction with surrounding host tissues when placed and thus lack any bonding with the tissues of the host; hence, these lack bone-bonding ability. Due to this bioinert nature, these are used as good alternatives to metal alloys in the case of tooth implants and hip prostheses (J Best 2007). Bioactive Ceramics: These are also called surface reactive ceramics. Calcium phosphate-based ceramics, calcium sulphate-based ceramics, bioactive glasses/ Biological Response to Biomaterials 213 bioglasses, and bioactive glass ceramics are several major groups of bioactive ceramics. Non-Bioresorbable Bioactive Ceramics: These ceramics exhibit ‘Osteoconductivity’ which is the bone-bonding ability due to their positive surface reactive nature. This category includes bioglasses and glass ceramics. Hench and his colleagues established the concept of bioactive glass or bioglass ® (BG) in the 1970s for applications related to bone replacement. BG is silicate (SiO2) based, consisting of Na 2O-CaO-SiO2 glass with P 2O5 added. 45SiO 2-24.5CaO- 24.5Na2O–6P2O5 the composition (in wt%) of bioglass (45S5). A biologically active hydroxy-carbon apatite (HCA) layer is formed on the surface of these materials, which is structurally and chemically equivalent to bone’s mineral phase and helps bond with the bone. Glass ceramics are glassy crystals in amorphous and crystalline states. Glass ceramics exhibit relatively better mechanical properties, biocompatibility, and antibacterial properties (along with the addition of certain chemicals) than BG. Some common examples of bioactive glass ceramics are apatite-wollastonite glass ceramic (A-W GC), ceravital, wollastonite diopside (WD), etc. Bioresorbable Bioactive Ceramics: These are biodegradable and bioresorbable. Bioresorbable bioactive ceramics are used for various medical applications as an alternative to polymeric and metallic biomaterials as they do not elicit inflammatory responses like those of metallic and polymeric biomaterials in vivo (Khan et al. 2015). This biodegradable implant material is resorbed and replaced by advancing natural tissue (generally bone). Thus, it helps in tissue regeneration. The most commonly used bioresorbable ceramics are calcium sulphate and calcium phosphates (CaP). Various hydrate forms of calcium sulphate are used in bone defects as implants due to their higher abundance and resorption characteristics without chronic immune response (Ferguson et al. 2014). Different crystalline phases of calcium phosphates (CaP), including hydroxyapatite (HAp), tricalcium phosphate (TCP), amorphous hydroxyapatite (ACp), octacalcium phosphate, fluorapatite (FAp), etc., were also used in bone repair which shows higher performance. Bone grafts made of CaP degrade relatively slower than bone grafts made of calcium sulphate (Ferguson et al. 2017). Polymeric Biomaterials Polymeric biomaterials constitute a large class of biomaterials classified as natural and synthetic. Naturally-derived or biologically-derived polymeric biomaterials are synthesised by the living cells. Hence, their sources are animals, plants, algae, fungi, and microorganisms, and they are biodegradable and renewable. Synthetic polymeric biomaterials are either synthesised from bio-based or petroleum-based monomers. Synthetic polymeric biomaterials can be made either biodegradable or non-biodegradable, as well as renewable or non-renewable. Synthetic polymeric biomaterials are preferred over naturally derived ones because of the tunability of their properties for the intended application. Based on 214 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization environmental impact considerations, renewable sources are preferred over non- renewable sources. Some common examples of natural polymeric biomaterials (biopolymers) are starch, chitin, chitosan, silks, elastin, collagen, etc. (Ivanova et al. 2014); Biopolymers are polyglycolic acid (PGA), polycaprolactone (PCL), polylactic acid (PLA), etc. (Lopes et al. 2012); petroleum-derived synthetic polymers are polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), etc. (Brewis and Briggs 1981). Carbon-Based Biomaterials Carbon is the most abundant element in the human body after hydrogen and is regarded as the element of life. Carbon-based nanomaterials are used for various biomedical applications as biomaterials. Carbon nanomaterials are the newest class of biomaterials that have been found application in several medical applications, such as tissue engineering, biomedical imaging, and cancer therapy, and even used in biosensors and therapeutic delivery systems (Klosterhoff et al. 2017). Despite the fact that carbon is the only element present, the diverse structure and chemistry exhibited by these are due to the variation in the arrangement of carbon atoms (Dash and Cudworth 1998), arising from different bonding patterns and hybridisation states of the same. The exceptional physical properties exhibited by these materials, like electric, thermal, mechanical, and optical properties, make them the most suitable biomaterials for medical/clinical applications. The most commonly used carbon nanomaterials are graphene, graphene oxide, graphene quantum dots, and carbon nanotubes, which are used for drug delivery, cancer therapy, disease diagnosis, and to make biosensors. Carbon nanomaterials are also used and are further being investigated as coatings on orthopaedic implants (Hubbell 1995). 3. Biomedical Applications of Biomaterials Biomaterials help to build implantable medical devices, prostheses, therapeutic drug delivery systems, diagnostic devices, tissue-engineered devices, extracorporeal devices, and scaffolds for tissue engineering. A tissue-engineered device is a combination of biomaterials, which has a tissue section combined with biomaterial. According to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), these biomaterial implants are those that get incorporated into the surface or inside the host body. There are two broad categories of medical implants: structural and functional. Structural implants include various kinds of artificial implants, such as in joints that structurally integrate with surrounding tissue at a later stage. Functional implants are medical devices such as cardiac pacemakers used to improve or replace a reduced or lost physiological function (Anderson 2001). Implantable drug delivery systems steadily release a therapeutic drug at a specific site in the body in order to maintain a steady concentration level. This site-specific-targeted drug delivery minimises side effects by reducing the required drug dose and, at the same time, increases the efficacy of the drug (Weber et al. 2011). Biomaterials in tissue engineering provide architectural Biological Response to Biomaterials 215 framework comparable to the original extracellular matrix, ultimately encouraging cell growth and tissue regeneration (Martin and Leibovich 2005). Biological Response to Biomaterials Biomaterials are commonly used nowadays as implantable prostheses, medical devices, tissue-engineered devices, and extracorporeal devices for various biomedical applications. Whatever may be the intended purpose, a biomaterial always comes into contact with the elements of a biological system and interacts with them through the interface or its surface. The performance of any biomaterial is dependent on the proper regulation of these interactions, and this regulation enhances its biocompatibility and optimises its performance resulting in favourable host/tissue responses. When the biomaterial is not biocompatible/not made biocompatible, the interactions lead to unfavourable responses resulting in the failure of the prostheses or devices, which either harm or lead to the death of the recipient/patient. Hence, most of the materials cannot be used as biomaterials as such. They have to be made biocompatible to ensure they serve their intended purpose. Here, the emphasis will be on how the biological system responds to a biomaterial in vivo. The process of implantation of biomaterial as well as its mere presence itself, triggers biological responses in the form of host tissue responses, which are inflammatory responses (innate immunity) followed by wound healing responses (Anderson and Cramer 2015). Biological Response to Biomaterials 219 4.1 Injury and Subsequent Events Injury Biomaterial, either a prosthesis or a medical device, causes injury when implanted surgically into a tissue or organ. This leads to disturbance in the homoeostatic mechanisms, triggering a cascade of host responses in a series that constitute the ‘tissue response continuum’. The sequence of host cellular and tissue responses towards a biomaterial, constituting a ‘tissue response continuum’ following implantation, are blood components implant interaction, coagulation, thrombosis, complement activation, fibrin matrix formation, inflammatory mediators invasion, fibroblast recruitment, fibrin capsule around the implant (Anderson and Cramer 2015). Any material, when implanted into the human body, elicits the above host responses. Acute wounds on the body’s surface heal in a sequential and systematic manner and constitute four overlapping phases, namely haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and tissue remodelling (Gorbet and Sefton 2004). These four successive phases coincide with the above-mentioned sequential steps of ‘tissue response continuum’ against the implantation. During the blood matrix interaction, haemostasis occurs, which involves the prevention of haemorrhage/ bleeding, thus blocking the vascular breach through coagulation. The injury causes damage to the tissue cells through necrosis. This triggers inflammation, which is a crucial step for the subsequent wound-healing process (Henson and Johnston 1987). The haemostasis coincides with blood-material interactions and innate immune response; proliferation coincides with granular tissue formation and tissue remodelling coincides with foreign body reaction and fibrosis or normal healing (Anderson 2001; Anderson and Cramer 2015). The extent of granulation, foreign body reaction, and fibrosis depend on the extent of injury, degree of cellular necrosis, basement membrane structure, blood- biomaterial interactions formation of a provisional matrix with some immune cells and inflammatory responses (Cotran and Pober 1990), and ultimately on the biocompatibility of the biomaterial. Persistence of chronic inflammation for relatively longer periods of time, as well as continuous stimulation of chronic inflammation by various aspects of non-biocompatible biomaterial, leads to fibrosis, which is regarded as a negative outcome that finally leads to the failure of implantation which limits the longevity and functionality of the implanted biomedical device or prostheses (Anderson and Cramer 2015). Fibrosis is an example of excessive healing resulting from too much deposition of connective tissue, leading to highly modified architecture and loss of function (Hynes 1992). Another undesirable outcome is the appearance of non- healing chronic ulcers, which result due to insufficient deposition of connective tissue matrix, leading to the weakening of tissue architecture that can easily fall apart (Gorbet and Sefton 2004), which in the context of biomaterial implantation also regarded as a failure and is undesirable. Alternatively, in the case of biomaterials that have a high degree of biocompatibility, chronic inflammation is transient and leads to wound healing through tissue regeneration, which, to a greater extent, restores the original tissue architecture. This is called normal healing. Complete restoration 220 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization through true regeneration of original tissue architecture is not possible in the case of humans. Blood-Biomaterial Interactions Blood-biomaterial interactions start occurring immediately after biomaterial implantation. The damage caused by the injury to the tissue and its vasculature makes various molecular and cellular components of the injured tissue and the blood come into contact with the biomaterial surface. This interaction results in the adsorption of non-specific host proteins-proteins of extracellular matrix (ECM) and plasma/blood onto the biomaterial surface prior to its interaction with host cells. Besides proteins, lipids, sugars, and ions from the plasma are also adsorbed onto the biomaterial surface (Butcher 1991; Henson 1980). This takes place between seconds to minutes of implantation. These adsorbed proteins interact among themselves as well as with various receptors present on the inflammatory cells and initiate the host response cascades associated with biomaterial implantation. These proteins include albumins, globulins, complement proteins, fibrinogen, other coagulation factors, fibronectin, vitronectin, etc. (Klopfleisch and Jung 2017). Various aspects of adsorbed host proteins, such as their composition, concentrations, and conformations, determine the host response/reaction to the biomaterial (Butcher 1991), including activation complement system and coagulation cascades that initiate the inflammatory responses, survival of foreign body giant cells (FBGCs). The initial implant stage activates the acute inflammatory responses (Franz et al. 2011; Henson 1980), whereas various chemical mediators from injured/damaged tissue-mediated immune cells (cytokines) (colony stimulating factor-1 receptor-mediated) can even follow the chronic stage too (Table 1) (Doloff et al. 2017). Provisional Matrix Formation Blood coagulation and complement activation follow the blood protein (thrombus, fibrin, or blood clot) deposition onto the biomaterial surface. Many researchers have reported that biomaterial-associated blood coagulation is initiated by the intrinsic pathway of the blood coagulation cascade. This clot, which forms the provisional matrix, consists of inflammatory products released by platelets, endothelial cells, inflammatory cells, and via complement activation (Johnston 1988). In the case of implantation of a biomaterial, the inflammation is triggered due to tissue damage resulting from injury caused by surgery and trauma as well as by the biomaterial itself, which can lead to rejection through a hypersensitive reaction. Damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) from the damaged tissue cells induce sterile inflammation (Wahl et al. 1989). Sterile inflammation here refers to inflammation that does not involve pathogens. DAMPs, in association with pattern recognition receptors on immune cells, can activate and secrete chemical mediators like cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, oxygen free radicals, proteases, etc. (Browder et al. 2000). The intensity of the inflammatory and wound healing responses depends on various aspects like the severity of the injury, the type of tissue or organ into which implantation is done, the physical dimensions of the prosthesis, or the chemical properties of the biomaterial used in the implant (Anderson 1988). Hence, the biocompatibility of the biomaterial also plays a vital role here. Acute Inflammation The presence of neutrophils and mast cells at the implant site is the initial response to acute inflammation which lasts between minutes and days. The duration depends upon the extent of the injury. Acute inflammation is characterised by oedema, which results from the exudation of fluid along with plasma proteins into the injury/implantation site. This is followed by the evasion of leucocytes from blood vessels to the injury site through ECM degradation (Brodbeck and Anderson 2009). Among the leucocytes that emigrated, neutrophils and monocytes are prominent, and neutrophils are predominant. The emigrated leucocytes exhibit adhesion through adhesion molecules present on their surface. These adhesion molecules are stimulated by complement component C5a, Leukotriene B 4 (LTB4), and Tumour Necrosis Factor-∞ (TNF-∞), whereas the complementary adhesion molecules are stimulated by Interleukin-I (IL-I) and TNF-∞. This enhances the interactions between monocytes and endothelial surfaces (Raghavendra et al. 2015). Even intracellular and cell-to-extracellular matrix interactions take place and are facilitated by a family of transmembrane glycoproteins called integrins (ABH 2012). CD11/CD18 family is a group of integrins that are present on the leucocyte surfaces. E-Selectins and ICAMs are also involved in the above interactions (Isa and Hobkirk 2000). 222 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization The localised leucocytes at the implant (injury) site exhibit the process of phagocytosis. In general, a phagocytic cell, after recognising the infectious agent, engulfs and degrades it. However, when they encounter the biomaterial, they cannot engulf it due to size disparity, which may cause ‘frustrated phagocytosis’ (Anselme 2000). Complement-activated fragment, C3b, and immunoglobulin G (IgG) are the two major opsonins that coat the biomaterial surface and aid in the frustrated phagocytosis by the phagocytic leucocytes. Neutrophils adhered to the opsonin- coated surfaces of the biomaterial may release enzymes extracellularly through exocytosis to degrade it (Anselme 2000). Mast cells release histamine, which promotes the recruitment of macrophages to the implant (injury) site (Mehdizadeh and Yang 2013). The recruited macrophages during acute inflammation are classically activated M1 macrophages that exhibit phagocytosis (Anderson 2001). Chronic Inflammation Chronic inflammation is characterised by the presence of cytokines monocytes, lymphocytes, antibodies, and increased blood flow to the injured site. The duration of chronic inflammation is one to a few weeks. In the case of biocompatible biomaterials, the duration of chronic inflammation is relatively short. It is also marked by the appearance of proliferating blood vessels and connective tissue (Doloff et al. 2017). Macrophages that are differentiated from infiltrated monocytes exhibit different phenotypes and polarisation states (Niinomi 2002) and mediate the wound healing process through antigen presentation phagocytic action, activating various immune cells via chemical mediators, thus regulating immune response (Anderson 2001). The lymphocytes involved in the chronic inflammation process mediate immune responses against the biomaterial (foreign body). Macrophages are regarded as the most important cells during chronic inflammation as they produce a large number of important classes of biologically active products. These include reactive oxygen species (ROS), chemotactic factors, cytokines, growth-promoting factors, neutral proteases, arachidonic acid metabolites, etc. The important growth factors, PDGF, TGF-β, TGF-alpha (Epithelial growth factor), and IL-1 and fibroblast growth factor are involved in blood vessel growth, fibroblast differentiation, and cellular proliferation (Anderson 2001; Cotran and Pober 1990; Franz et al. 2011; Henson and Johnston 1987). 4.3 Wound Healing Granulation Tissue Formation The name granulation tissue is derived from the soft, pink, granular appearance of healing wounds. Granulation tissue formations are marked by the presence of fibroblasts and macrophages and the presence of neovascularisation, thus initiating the wound healing process. Neovascularisation or angiogenesis is a process during which new blood vessels are formed from pre-existing damaged blood vessels. The fibroblast actively synthesises collagen and proteoglycans, and fibrous capsule formation also occurs. Apart from fibroblasts, myofibroblasts and fibrocytes are also Biological Response to Biomaterials 223 involved in capsule formation, which helps in mediating implant isolation and its cellular interactions in host cells (Anderson 1988; Anderson and Cramer 2015). Foreign Body Reaction Foreign body response involves the host response to the implant, which involves the Foreign body giant cells (FBGCs) and granulation tissue component. The biomaterial composition and its surface-to-volume ratio determine the granulation tissue components (macrophages, fibroblasts, etc.) in the implant site during the FBR. The macrophages produced when adhered to the implant surface are derived from tissue invasion of monocytes, followed by FBGC formation by both fusions (Anderson and Cramer 2015). Fibrosis This marks the final stage of wound healing, in which the fibrous encapsulation surrounds the implant or biomaterial from all sides along with the foreign body reaction on its surface and separates from adjacent tissues in the host (Gorbet and Sefton 2004). 5. Designing of Biomaterials As mentioned above, host responses during biomaterial implantation, adverse events during improper implants, and the compatible nature of the designing biomaterials play a major role. Biomaterials are designed using different types of metals, ceramics, polymers, composite materials, etc. After clinically successful implantation, the biomaterials were designed as either a single or a combination of suitable materials for a more effective procedure. Moreover, these kinds of biomaterials have various atomic arrangements in which different organ replacement applications in the human body can be expanded (Silver and Christiansen 1999). The various kinds of biomaterials and their design are demonstrated in the following segments. (i) Biopolymers Nowadays, biopolymers are the potential biomaterials used in various cardiovascular implants as an alternative to natural and regenerative medicine. Polymers are used in various biomedical fields, such as cardiac valves, bio-contact lenses, surgical and coating materials, tissue adhesives, breast prosthesis, and vascular grafts. The chemical composition, chain structure, and association of fundamental biomolecules specify the characteristics of biopolymers (Khan et al. 2015; Saini 2015). Moreover, to perform various biological applications, various biopolymer compositions with different physiochemical properties and biocompatibility are needed to meet the needs. The advantages of bio-polymeric materials over others include (i) quick fabrication, (ii) secondary processability, (iii) convenient mechanical strength and physicochemical properties, and (iv) low cost of production. Biopolymers are divided into two categories based on their origin: natural and synthetic (Bhat and Kumar 2013; Ivanova et al. 2014). The design of a synthetic biopolymer system includes polymeric units of siloxanes, ethylene, esters, urethanes, acrylics, amides, etc. 224 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization Though the designing and fabrication are easy, the major drawback is its low biodegradability and biocompatibility in almost all cases, and hence, their biomedical usage delivers an inflammatory side effect (Bhat and Kumar 2013). These limitations are overwhelmed by the utilisation of natural polymers. For instance, natural biopolymers such as guar gum, cellulose, alginate, and chitosan have already been used in regenerative medicine, drug delivery systems, and tissue engineering (Bhat and Kumar 2013). (ii) Metals/Metal Oxides Materials The metallic implant gets potential attention in clinical practice in the medical field for a prolonged duration. Several types of metals and metal alloys were used for various biomedical functions, such as cobalt-chromium, aluminium, zirconium- niobium, stainless steel, titanium, and tungsten alloys. The hasty progress in the medical/clinical field has generated focus to improve several medical bio-products prepared of metal, such as catheters, pacemakers, valves, dental materials and implants, medical and bone fascination devices, craniofacial plates for various applications (Niinomi 2002). The major norms in the selection of metal/metal oxide biomaterials are due to their corrosion resistance properties, biocompatibility, and low-cost productivity (Saini 2015). The function of the implant and the host tissue surrounding the implant are a few important points noted during the selection of metal for biomaterial construction. Stainless steel, like 316L, is the frequently utilised alloy in the bio-implants extending from cardiovascular to otorhinolaryngology. The metal’s chemical properties have a potential significance in designing weight-holding orthopaedic and dental implants. CoCrMo combined metals-based alloys are used in orthopaedic artificial bone-joint implantation with higher wear resistance properties. The tensile strength and fatigue restriction of the metal/metal oxides compared with composites of polymeric and ceramics biomaterials make it an excellent choice as a biomaterial. However, its drawbacks include stress-strain failure, high cost, and corrosion in some cases. In addition, metals have lower strengths and elasticity than ceramics (M Sumita 1997). In biological fluids, after the metal implants, the surface of biomaterials can alter and biodegrade to discharge a few cell growth factors due to which implant surface and tissues interact (Williams 2009). Thus, the current studies focus on the future objective of getting more attention to understanding metal biomaterials and their structural features, thus improving their applications and drawbacks. (iii) Composite Materials Composite materials are designed as unique combinations that consist of more than one chemical/physical distinct constituent material regularly with numerous physical characteristics that make it more effective than others. Composites have three phases: bulk (matrix), reinforcement, and interphase (Iftekhar 2004). Due to their unique properties, they have been applied in various other applications where tissue growth is necessary. Composite scaffolds designed from the combination of bioglass materials and biopolymers with excellent mechanical properties close to bone strength help in some hard tissue (skull/hip/joint/bone, etc.) applications. Thus, composite materials Biological Response to Biomaterials 225 can overcome the drawbacks of individual materials like metal ceramics in their biocompatibility, corrosion, brittleness, and fragile nature. During the designing of composite materials, the function ‘linear expansion constant’ should be taken into consideration. The constituents with similar linear expansion constant values are designed for its constructs. If it is different, the composite material construct will have deformities with void formation on the contact surface. Therefore, the design of composite material should be careful for biological applications (Bhat and Kumar 2013; Dorozhkin 2011). (iv) Ceramics Materials Ceramics are other sources for designing and developing biomaterials for biomedical applications. The usage of ceramics was heavily inspired by their inertness, good compressive strength, and wearable properties. Ceramics-based biomaterials developed for various biomedical applications such as cardiac valves, dental, orthopaedic, ear, and artificial knee implants, and surface modifications using ceramics can enhance the biocompatibility of metal-based implants. However, ceramics are applied to design biomaterials, but they are still not preferred compared to metals and polymers. Commonly, usage of ceramics is heavily limited due to the more brittleness and lack of tensile strength. However, phosphates-based ceramics are deeply applied to design unique biomaterials owing to their excellent biocompatibility and bone reformation; moreover, the biomaterials are commonly similar to the naturally occurring mineral composition of the bone materials (J Best 2007; Vallet-Regí 2001). The most commonly used ceramics are hydroxyapatites (HPs); these calcium phosphate-based biomaterials are used in various biomedical applications for the entire body system through wrapping of all sections of the skeleton. The primary applications of HPs include bone defects and fracture treatment, spinal therapies, and periodontal and joint replacement. On the other hand, HPs have been applied as bone fillers for skeleton imperfections and act as a soft and lightweight implant on sites of the nasal bone and middle ear (Hench et al. 1971; Jordan et al. 2002; Orlovskii, Komlev, and Barinov 2002). Moreover, HPs were utilised as a coating material for titanium and stainless steel-based implants and other metal implants to help in fixing it on the bone. In HPs, the basic metal outer layer and adjacent bone interact strongly; thus, extra care has been placed to reduce the delamination of coatings to overcome implant failure (Bermejo and Danzer 2010). 6. Conclusion Tissue compatibility of biomaterials is the major concern over the utility and longevity of the device under consideration and to perform suitable functions in the host organ. Thus, the development of new biomaterials was evaluated with its tissue compatibility test as the main protocol, along with some other tests to detect the physiochemical and mechanical properties. Hemo-compatibility is also a major concern in developing blood-compatible materials to reduce the initial risk of failure. With the day-to-day rise in the need for bio-alternatives to mimic various biological functions, different biomaterials with unique characteristics are in search. The basic knowledge provided in this chapter about the implant, its host response, various 226 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization biomaterials, and its design can help researchers in the future to discover novel biomaterials. Introduction Biomaterials have found profound interest in medical applications, such as therapeutic or other diagnostic purposes, irrespective of their natural or synthetic nature. These substances are generally acquired from natural resources or synthesised to be utilised in their natural form to facilitate healing or as a part of biomedical devices to assist, improve or mimic biological functions. Biomaterial science is, therefore, an important field of multidisciplinary research entailing material science, tissue engineering, medical science, biomedical and biomaterial engineering for scale-up purposes (Agrawal et al. 2023). Biomaterials implementation plays an important role in various medical devices, such as catheters, cardiac pacemakers, glucose biosensors (Koschwanez and Reichert 2007), contact lenses, finger joint implants, knee replacement, hearing aids, etc. (Table 1). There are various surgical methods such as abrasion, subchondral drilling, microfracture, osteochondral autograft transfer system (OATS) (also known as mosaicplasty), and autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI) (Pestka et al. 2012; Albright and Daoud 2017; Solheim et al. 2018). In the form of biological implants, these materials may cause foreign body reactions (FBRs) inside the host system.
