This can also cause acute and chronic inflammations of the host tissues. Sometimes, disruption of host tissue may occur during biomaterial insertion through surgery or injection. Moreover, in the presence of injured host tissues, the implementation of biomaterial devices can trigger systemic inflammation. Therefore, another essential role of the biomaterial science discipline is to ensure desired material surface properties and other preventive measures to curtail the possibilities of FBRs. Host Response Immune Response to Polymeric Implants 231 The intensity of the host tissue reaction to implanted biomaterials varies based on various factors, including host, site of implantation, species, degree of trauma during implementation and the nature of the implanted material (Anderson et al. 2008). If the biomaterial is non-compatible to the host, the host’s immune response will be elicited, trigereing the onset of phagocytosis, mediated by macrophages leading to localised or at times chronic inflammation. If an infection occurs due to the placement of the implant, there is a chance of the activation of polymorphonuclear leukocytes near the implant. If the implant is completely inactivated, with no appearance of macrophages, then only a thin collagenous layer encapsulates the implant. Moreover, there is a possibility of tissue response, which can be minimal response or necrosis. In order to avoid the adverse effect of implantation, biomaterials with anti-inflammatory properties can be designed, and the desired outcome is achieved. There are two types of responses that can be obtained from biomaterials depending on their source, i.e., inner biomaterials such as metals, synthetic polymers, and ceramics, which are not part of the body and are known as foreign body reactions or responses. Macrophages are the key players associated with this type of reaction. Classically activated macrophages (M1) play a role in host defence by inducing inflammatory responses. M1 has the responsibility to remove foreign bodies, including bacteria, pathogens, and implanted biomaterials. Meanwhile, other types of macrophages, known as would healing or reparative macrophages (M2), are responsible for wound healing and remodelling. If the material is not biocompatible, it shows the formation of foreign body giant cells (monocytes and macrophages) in the biomaterial interface, leading to a chronic inflammatory state (Anderson et al. 2008). 2. Factors Affecting Host Response 2.1 Biomaterial-Host Response An implant should be selected such that it remains in situ in the patient not only for a few months but for as long as it stays inside the host. This depends on the type of material that is being used. Over time, the implant can be destroyed, encapsulated or altered by the host immune system. During biomaterial implantation, the damage to the surrounding tissue activates the innate immune system. Neutrophils are the first immune cells to respond to damage and trigger other immune cells, such as macrophages and monocytes, leading to foreign body reactions (Badylak 2015). After implantation, the blood and plasma proteins coat the surface of the biomaterial, which is known as the Vroman effect (Badylak 2015). The biomaterial does not come in direct contact with the host cells; instead, the proteins absorbed into the biomaterial form a protective matrix, which aids in attachment and clot formation while lowering the incidence of foreign body reactions. There are three types of reactions that occur between the matrix and the host. Degradable implants activate a pro-remodelling M2 macrophage-associated response, which degrades the biomaterial and deposits required tissue in that area remodelling the site. Non-degradable synthetic implants cause M1 macrophages to initiate inflammation, foreign body reaction and scar tissue formation. For materials like metals, ‘frustrated phagocytosis’ occurs wherein the implant is eventually encapsulated (Badylak 2015). Small amounts of metals are expected to be present in 232 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization metallic implants. However, regardless of their association with biological functions, an abundance of essential and/or non-essential metals can cause metal toxicity in the host system. 2.2 Host Factors 2.2.1 Age Ageing is mainly characterised by changes in the immune system, which can alter the host’s response to the biomaterial. The number of immune cells is not largely affected, but their efficiency, phagocytic capabilities, and response to foreign pathogens are reduced. This causes poor wound healing and an increased risk of infection around the implant. This can be termed as immunosenescence. Adult stem cells are responsible for tissue repair and wound healing. With ageing, the function of the stem cells decreases. B and T cells proliferate and mature from the stem cells, but with the onset of immunosenescence, their number decreases, leading to an increased risk of infections. Hence, the rate of implant rejection is much higher in older people (Badylak 2015). 2.2.2 Nutritional Status Nutrition is of utmost importance when it comes to acceptance of biomaterial implants. The elderly population does not get enough micronutrients and macronutrients due to various reasons, including less nutritional requirements, slow metabolism, appetite loss, etc. Micronutrients like zinc, selenium and copper are important for homeostasis and inflammatory response (Badylak 2015). Malnutrition reduces T-cell production, proliferation of fibroblasts and tissue repair, leading to improper wound healing and implant rejection. 2.2.3 Anatomic Factors Biomaterial implants can be placed almost anywhere in the host body, but anatomic placement plays a major factor in the immune response to the implant. This is because different areas of the body have different levels of vascularisation, and the microenvironment is also distinct. There will be contact with air if the implant is placed in the oesophagus; for internal organs, they will be in contact with blood, and for joint and other orthopaedic implants, the implant must be strong enough to support the weight and mechanical load of the individual. For example, the cornea being devoid of any blood or lymph vessels, does not evoke any harmful immune response, whereas biomaterials inserted near the heart of bones can cause high inflammatory response due to high vascularisation and complexity. 2.2.4 Comorbidities Underlying diseases and comorbidities can profoundly impact the host cell’s response towards biomaterials. They can weaken the immune system of the host and reject the implant. We will take the example of diabetes and obesity and their effect on host response. Host Response Immune Response to Polymeric Implants 233 2.2.4.1 Obesity Obesity is characterised by the excessive accumulation of body fat, which can harm an individual’s lifestyle. Obesity affects the host response to biomaterials in several ways, such as impairing wound healing, poor vascularisation, dehiscence of fascia and leakage of wounds after any surgical procedure. The macrophages and monocytes undergo changes (M1 to M2 macrophages), which cause chronic low-grade systemic pro-inflammatory response. The increase in adipose tissues increases the secretion of inflammatory mediators like interleukins and tumour necrosis factors, which can slow down wound healing (Boersema et al. 2016). 2.2.4.2 Diabetes Diabetes is a metabolic disorder mainly characterised by increased blood sugar levels (hyperglycaemia). This can be due to various reasons, including failure of the Langerhans cells in the pancreas to produce insulin or the development of resistance against insulin in the host. The excess sugar in the blood reacts with the proteins and fat in the body and produces advanced glycation end products (AGEs). AGEs can interfere with the integration of the host cell and the biomaterial, preventing attachment of the implant. Diabetes also impairs wound healing and increases the risk of infection and bacteraemia (Lemarchand et al. 2023). 2.2.5 Chemotherapy and Radiation Therapy Diseases that result from uncontrolled cell division, like cancer and tumours, require chemo and radiation therapies to prevent them from becoming life-threatening. These therapies mainly work by stopping cell proliferation in the affected area. However, since precisely determining the area of neoplasm formation is not possible, these therapies work on other areas, stopping the proliferation of normal body cells. Biomaterial implantation relies largely on the proliferation of immune cells, which can cause inflammatory responses and cause encapsulation. These therapies, when used in conjugation with biomaterial implantation, can render implantation inefficient (Badylak 2015). 3. Host Response to Biomaterials The success or setbacks of a biomaterial and its efficiency eventually are mainly dependent on the host reaction to these biomaterials. Biocompatibility is a term used to define and characterise the host response of biomaterials, mainly medical devices. It simply means that these biomaterials will not cause any harm or produce any unfavourable effects on the tissues. If there are any sort of lethal effects associated with the biomaterial, it could lead to various in vivo adversities, which could be due to the material or host responses. Biocompatibility assessment is thus performed to determine any modifications in the host mechanisms that may determine their responses (Anderson and Cramer 2015). 234 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 3.1 Injury For a biomaterial to be placed under in vivo conditions, insertions or any sort of implantations need to be done, all of which cause injury to the tissue. As soon as an injury is initiated, the host homeostatic mechanisms turn on. The degree of injury largely depends on the injury-causing procedures. The extent to which the host homeostatic mechanisms are activated is a potential estimate of the host response, which could be tissue, organ, or species dependent, and the biocompatibility of the biomaterial with the host. Following injury, several events take place, like acute inflammation, chronic inflammation, granulation tissue, provisional matrix formation and foreign body reaction (FBR) (Anderson and Cramer 2015). 3.2 Provisional Matrix Formation When there is an injury or any sort of trauma in a tissue, an immediate inflammatory response is observed due to disturbance in the tissue. However, the extent and impact of this response depends on where the biomaterial is implanted or its biocompatibility (Gonzalez-Simon and Eniola-Adefeso 2012). In this situation, permeability and flow changes occur in the vascular system, leading to exudation, where blood cells and proteins flow out of the blood vessels to the site of injury. This series of events works to heal the site of injury immediately by replacing the injured tissues with new cells and scar tissues, as well as by thrombosis. As blood and its associated proteins accumulate and deposit on the surface of the biomaterial during this time, it is called provisional matrix formation. It is activated by thrombosis and complement systems, which structurally and compositionally support effective and fast healing. It contains different fibrins and mediators along with some associated proteins, forming a mesh- like network that helps with cell attachment and migration processes. Growth factors present help in the synthetic processes (Anderson and Cramer 2015). 3.3 Acute Inflammatory Response Innate immunity initiates the acute inflammatory response at the site of injury, which is mainly the primary defence, recognition and clearing up of foreign materials by neutrophils and macrophages (Anderson and Cramer 2015). The start and severity of this response depends on the extracellular matrix (ECM) and blood proteins that adsorb on the surface of the biomaterial during an injury or implantation (Chung et al. 2017). This acute inflammatory response lasts for a truly short period. It involves oedema (exudation of blood fluid) and the unidirectional movement of main neutrophils (with the help of inflammatory agents and mediators), called chemotaxis, from the blood vessels into the site (Anderson and Cramer 2015). Mostly, phagocytosis by neutrophils is seen next if the biomaterial ’s shape, size and chemistry are favourable for endocytosis (Gonzalez-Simon and Eniola-Adefeso 2012). An indication of infection is the presence of acute inflammation at the site of injury or implantation (Anderson and Cramer 2015). Host Response Immune Response to Polymeric Implants 235 3.4 Chronic Inflammatory Response With due course of time, when the number of neutrophils starts to decrease, the chemotactic factors begin to recruit monocytes at the injury site. This provides a secondary defence action and a short chronic inflammatory response by differentiating into dendritic cells or macrophages, which can ultimately lead to the non-acceptance of the biomaterial. The various reasons for the inflammation lasting for so long could be due to the nature of the biomaterial or persistent injury at the inflammation site (Gonzalez-Simon and Eniola-Adefeso 2012). Chronic inflammation can lead to hyperactivity of the fibroblast, leading to excessive deposition of ECM proteins. Thus, understanding the relationship between the immune cells and fibroblasts can help in designing an ideal biomaterial (Chung et al. 2017). 3.4.1 Macrophages (Mononuclear Phagocytes) Macrophages are phagocytic cells derived from monocytes present throughout the tissues and have a considerably long life, which makes them available to be present and sustained during the chronic inflammatory response. They perform several important functions, including phagocytosis and antigen presentation, to activate adaptive immunity. Just like the neutrophils, the macrophages also phagocytise foreign particles or microorganisms and release pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (Gonzalez-Simon and Eniola-Adefeso 2012) , coagulation factors, reactive oxygen metabolites and other biologically active products (Anderson and Cramer 2015). They also clear up old cell aged cell debris. 3.5 Granulation Tissue Granulation tissue colour is a strong indication of the healing response of inflammation at the site of injury. The pink and dark red coloration of the granulated tissue indicates healthy healing and wound infection, respectively. The monocytes and macrophages initiate the formation of this special tissue, which is derived from the fibroblast cells and vascular endothelial cells and depends largely on the type and extent of injury. This granulation tissue is formed from a process called angiogenesis (formation of new blood vessels) or neovascularisation, which includes the growth and differentiation of cells in the blood vessels. In the early stages, proteoglycans and later type III collagen prevalence are seen (Jones 2015; Huimin et al. 2023). Sometimes, even myofibroblasts are seen during the development of this tissue as well as during repair and healing mechanisms for injured tissues. There is also prominence in the presence of macrophages. The whole process of wound healing can be primary or secondary, wherein the primary process deals with injuries without any sort of contamination or infection done by clean surgical equipment, and in the secondary approach, larger granulation tissues and provisional matrices are formed due to a larger amount of loss of tissue. The wound-healing process by secondary intention is more prevalent (Anderson and Cramer 2015). Ultimately, these responses work to establish normalcy or homeostasis at the site of injury (Gonzalez-Simon and Eniola-Adefeso 2012). 236 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 3.6 Foreign Body Reaction The foreign body giant cells or FBGCs (multinucleated structures that are formed by the fusion of many macrophages) (Jones 2015) and the granulation tissue together account for the foreign body reaction or FBR to biomaterials, and this is dependent on the nature of the biomaterial. Generally, fibrosis is seen around the biomaterial at the implant site, and macrophage activation and adherence are predominant during the initial stages of wound healing. 3.6.1 Fibrous Encapsulation During the healing process after inflammation, various cells come together to form a fibrous capsule at the site of injury. Collagen fibres and fibroblasts form the strong base and the capsule structure with the help of proteoglycans and adhesion molecules present in these components. Eventually, certain glycoproteins like fibronectins, thrombospondins, etc., form the fibrous tissue, which encases the biomaterial and helps in the formation of new tissue layers (Whitaker et al. 2021). However, over- development of this capsule can interfere with the function of the biomaterial or rejection of the implant, and in such cases, surgical excision or removal of the biomaterial is desirable (Gonzalez-Simon and Eniola-Adefeso 2012). 3.6.2 Fibroblast At the site of inflammation, leukocytes recruit macrophages and fibroblasts for proliferation and regenerative modelling of the fibrotic scar tissue (Figure 1). These fibroblasts perform the major function of synthesising the extracellular matrix (ECM), and the fibrous capsule and its functions are controlled by the different chemical signals and factors released in the matrix (Whitaker et al. 2021; Jones 2015). Immune Response 4.1 Naturally Occurring Biomaterials Based on the nature of biomaterials, the degree of success of the implant depends on it. Naturally derived biomaterials are more advantageous than synthetic materials, i.e., biocompatibility, remodelling, and biodegradability. Damaged organs or tissues are replaced or treated with these biomaterials (Bose and Bandyopadhyay 2013). 4.1.1 Degradable Biomaterials Degradable biomaterials are designed in such a way that these materials can degrade naturally inside the body after a certain period of implantation so that these materials can achieve a particular function. The use of degradable biomaterials shows resistance to infection by increased vascularisation. Polymeric materials are commonly used in degradable materials and have a wide range of implementation in various medical fields, including tissue engineering, drug delivery, etc. Magnesium and iron-based degradable materials are degraded inside the body with metabolism. For tissue engineering, orthopaedic and cardiovascular applications, magnesium alloy is mostly used (Bose and Bandyopadhyay 2013). The natural matrix protein can be degraded by proteolysis, oxidation and hydrolysis. In the presence of tissue fluids and inflammatory cells, the polymer- based device, which is created as sensitive to water and protease, can contribute to degradation. Protease and oxidants have the ability to degrade implanted devices by degrading the polymer crosslink of the device. Leukocyte uses protease and reactive oxidants to degrade this implanted device (Mouthuy et al. 2016). Materials that cause a severe immune response and the sensitivity of polymer crosslink degradation can be altered to design new devices with specific drug release profiles. Co-block polymer (poly lactic glycolic acid; PLGA) is the best example of this type of device, commonly using tissue fluids and innate immune response for the delivery of drugs (Mir et al. 2018). Early copolymer degradation and inflammation were observed in wound-closing sutures after the implantation of vascular stents (Gogolewvki 1992; Heller 1984). Other reasons for the degradation of implanted PLGA devices include the activation of giant cells, monocytes, neutrophils and hydrolysis (Van Der Giessen et al. 1996). 4.1.2 Cell-Grafted Biomaterial Grafts are important for regenerating and repairing bone. The materials used for this are mainly based on the site of application. Various types of materials are used for the regeneration of bones. Transplanted cells are mainly autologous, allogeneic and xenogeneic (Rieder et al. 2016). Autologous cells are obtained from the same host who will get the transplant. Allogeneic cells are from the same species of host that will undergo transplantation. Xenogeneic cells are obtained from different species; they differ from the host (Kyyak et al. 2020). Grafted cells have therapeutic value. For example, it has the ability to produce islet cells that produce insulin and also help 238 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization in tissue regeneration, growth and repair of injured cells. These cells can stimulate innate as well as adaptive immune responses. Macrophages help to ingest the pathogen and digest it; the remaining digested fragments present on the cell surface pass a signal to stimulate other more effective immune cells. Major histocompatibility complex class II has a recognition site for T cells. Macrophages act on pathogens by presenting this MHC class ll and costimulatory molecules, CD89 and CD86 (Thiele et al. 2003; Thiele et al. 2001), which activate T cells and cause the rejection of transplanted cells. Allogeneic and xenogeneic cells stimulate more immune responses than autologous cells because of the non-self features of these cells. This type of rejection can be prevented by implanting the cells within a polymer matrix. The pore size of the matrix should be such that only nutrients can pass through, preventing immune cells and inflammation. 4.2 Synthetic Biomaterials Synthetic biomaterials are man-made and created in such a way that these materials should be compatible with the human body. These materials are easy to use and inexpensive compared to natural biomaterials; properties of biomaterials such as crystallinity, hydrophobicity and molecular weight are significant for biomaterials. Synthetic biomaterials have more predictable, degradable and physicochemical, mechanical properties. Synthetic biomaterials that are foreign to the body cells can cause severe inflammation sometimes. Important types of biomaterials include polycaprolactone, polyglycolide, polylactide, etc. (Aldana et al. 2023). 4.2.1 Orthopaedic Implants Immune response to orthopaedic implants could be due to metal sensitivity or other components. The first successful joint replacement was done by Sir John Charnley, which was a hip replacement. Stainless steel and femoral components were the main components of these hip replacements. Mainly, cemented femoral components were used, and their biocompatibility was monitored by various methods, including clinical, radiological and histological analyses. Initially, acute inflammation was observed in that cemented prosthesis. The bone death that occurred during surgery was resolved within a week by fibrous tissue and fibrocartilage formation (Yao et al. 2015). Another type of joint replacement, i.e., cementless replacement, mainly depends on initial ‘press fit’ to provide stability. This is added with splines, surface coating and screws so that these materials can attach to the host bone for a longer period. Based on the properties of the implant and host, as well as surgical methods used, it can determined which neighbouring bone will undergo remodelling. Sometimes, periprosthetic osteolysis occurs when the debris of polyethylene migrates along with the cementless terminal. Because of that, the rejection of the implant may occur (Gibon et al. 2017). Host Response Immune Response to Polymeric Implants 239 4.2.2 Pelvic Girdle Mesh Most of the surgical meshes are synthetic or man-made. These meshes are commonly used for various medical conditions, including heart stent and hernia repair. Surgical meshes are used to support the weak or damaged tissue. Some of the meshes are made of animal tissue. Polypropylene and polyglycolic acid are used to treat pelvic floor disorder. After implementing these, it may cause pain, discomfort, bowel obstruction, nausea and also hernia recurrence. But this procedure is successful and can stay a lifetime in the body. After implantation of the meshes, immune cells migrate to the site of the implantation, resulting in the formation of a foreign body granuloma. As the meshes are foreign to the immune system, they stimulate innate immunity and activate macrophages that collect at the surface of the mesh. The stimulation of adaptive immune response activates both B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes, which are important but require more time to activate (Patnaik et al. 2016). 5. In Vitro and In Vivo Models for Testing Host Response Foreign body reactions (FBR) are the major driving force for the successful implantation of biomaterials. However, due to their unpredictability, all biomaterials, regardless of being synthetic or natural, cause complications in the host (Saleh et al. 2017). Therefore, studying these responses in models is important to create an almost ideal biomaterial implant. There be devastating side effects and failures of these implants if their outcomes and compatibility are not known. In vitro and in vivo models can help determine the complications involved in transplantation and how to overcome them (Vasconcelos et al. 2019). When an implant is introduced into the host system, non-specific protein gets adsorbed on its surface and inflammatory cells are recruited. Neutrophils are the first to arrive, releasing cytokines to recruit other inflammatory cells, especially long- lived macrophages, which drive the foreign body reactions (Saleh et al. 2017). These macrophages recognise the implant as foreign but cannot engulf them due to their size, so they fuse together and form multinucleated foreign body giant cells (FBGCs) (Sheikh et al. 2015). Soon, a fibrous capsule forms within three to four weeks and stops communication between the implant and the host. This macrophage-implant interaction can be used to study the FBR response to different biomaterials (Saleh et al. 2017; Wolf et al. 2015). 5.1 In Vitro Models In vitro models focus on studying the foreign body reaction in a controlled environment. Models involving culturing of macrophage and fibroblasts are used since they are the major effector cells of FBR. Macrophages are primarily associated with inflammatory response, but fibroblasts are crucial for wound healing and fibrotic responses (Zhou et al. 2016). Macrophage interrogation of a biomaterial and co-culture of macrophages with fibroblast is shown in Figure 2 (Lock et al 2019). 240 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 5.1.1 Macrophage Interrogation of a Biomaterial The macrophages derived from blood or bone marrow monocytes are used for testing. Macrophage cell lines from rodents (murine) include cell lines RAW 264.7, J774A.1, and IC-21 (Chamberlain et al. 2015). Human monocyte-derived macrophages include cell lines of THP-1 and U-937. Several studies found that the cell lines RAW 264.7, J774A.1 and IC-21 responded to inflammatory stimulants by increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines but in low magnitudes, whereas THP-1 responded in greater magnitude to biomaterial extracts and an exogenous inflammatory stimulant. Hence, the choice of cell lines should be made while considering these factors as well (Saleh et al. 2017). Macrophage polarisation occurs when macrophages can change their functions and gene expression in response to signals from their environment. Macrophages majorly have two polarised states, i.e., classically activated (M1) macrophages and alternatively activated (M2) macrophages. M1 macrophages are prompted by cytokines IFN-y and LPS and are involved in inflammatory functions, while M2 macrophages are induced by IL-4 and IL-3 and are responsible for wound healing (Chen et al. 2023). The polarisation of macrophages by biomaterials can determine the host response. The macrophages are cultured onto the biomaterial, and then they are checked for polarisation or other changes, and compatibility is determined. This shift from inflammatory to wound-healing macrophages is known as plasticity (Brown et al. 2012). Before the macrophages are cultured onto the biomaterial surface, the biomaterials are dipped into a serum containing proteins, which get adsorbed onto the surface of the material, and onto these proteins, the macrophages initiate inflammatory responses. This helps us to understand the perfect surface of biomaterial for the adhesion of macrophages. Findings from this model include hydrophobic surface- mediated improved attachment efficiency of monocytes and macrophages when compared to neutral hydrophilic surfaces, although the attachment of inflammatory macrophages is higher on hydrophilic surfaces. An increase in surface roughness, Figure 2: Mechanism of host response to biomaterials in in vitro models. Host Response Immune Response to Polymeric Implants 241 decreased alignment, and micron-size surface features augment monocyte/ macrophage attachment and polarisation (Saleh et al. 2017). 5.1.2 Co-Cultures of Macrophages and Fibroblasts Although several research studies focus on pro-inflammatory responses observed in biomaterial-host model interaction studies, there is a scarcity of data about fibrotic reactions in such systems. In a research study performed by Klopfleisch in 2016, the effect of surface chemistry on fibrous capsule formation was studied using a mouse model. For that, they have implanted the co-cultures of macrophages and fibroblasts as self-assembling monolayers (SAMs) or micron-sized particles in the mice subcutaneous air pouches. However, the in-depth knowledge of fibrosis was still unclear (Hasan and Pandey 2018). An in vitro fibroblast/macrophage co-culture system was created using migration fence chambers, which include internal and external chambers, to overcome this problem. Macrophages and fibroblasts can be implanted separately into the chambers of the biomaterial, allowing their effects to be studied simultaneously. After 24 hours, the fence was removed, and cells were allowed to interact with each other. This allowed the study of fibroblast outgrowth, macrophage migration and interaction between the two cell types (Zhou and Groth 2018). 5.2 In Vivo Models In vitro models alone cannot give a complete understanding of the host response to biomaterials as the actual host system is extremely complex, and the interaction at the in vitro level of macrophages cannot predict in vivo outcomes due to the inherent complexity, dynamics and donor variability of macrophage activation (Figure 3). Hence, in vivo models like rodents and larger animal models are used to mimic the environment of the implant. In silico analyses can link the data from in vitro and in vivo studies and give a complete understanding of the host response to a certain biomaterial implant. For FDA certification of a biomaterial, in vivo testing is compulsory. Three types of in vivo models, namely wild rat models, genetically modified rats, and large animal models, are discussed (Al-Maawi et al. 2017). Figure 3: Host response to biomaterials in in vivo models. 242 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 5.2.1 Wild Rodent Model These are the commonly used in vivo models. The subcutaneous and intramuscular sites in rats and mice provide the ideal environment for implantation testing since they are also highly vascularised. Devices can be easily implanted in these models by simple surgical methods. Several biomaterials can be evaluated on a single model for short-term degradation, biochemical studies, as well as long-term remodelling and functional outcome studies (Sicari et al. 2013). The partial thickness rat abdominal wall defect model is more advantageous than subcutaneous and intramuscular models since it can be used for long-term studies (up to 2 years) and can anchor the implant more securely. Subcutaneous models are more suitable for short-term studies on non-degradable materials. A histomorphological analysis is the main advantage of the partial thickness rat abdominal wall defect model, which provides information about the rate of degradation and encapsulation of biomaterial, vascularity of the remodelled tissue, muscle growth, etc. (Sicari et al. 2013). 5.2.2 Genetically Modified Mouse Models Mice can be genetically modified in several ways, such as making them deficient in T cells, natural killer cells or other immune cells. Introducing biomaterials into these modified mice can help determine the formation of FBGCs in these modified models. Mice lacking these immune cells did not limit the formation of FBGCs, indicating that they are not essential for FBR. Mice that were devoid of toll-like receptor-4, involved in detecting damaged tissues, resulted in fewer macrophages, but that still did not inhibit the formation of FBGCs. Mice lacking Rag2 and IL2rg lead to macrophage dysfunction, which prevented the formation of FBGCs and fibrous encapsulation of the biomaterial. These studies proved the importance of macrophages for proper FBR and implantation of biomaterial (Saleh and Bryant 2017; Klopfleisch 2016). Genetically modified nondiabetic mice have helped in the detection of endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs). This helped to study the relationship between diabetes and EPCs, which is essential for understanding the progression of diabetes. The GFP (green fluorescent protein) mice express a green fluorescent protein in every cell except red blood cells. The bone marrow from GFP mice was inserted into C57BL/6 mice, forming a chimeric mouse model that was used to detect the fate of bone marrow-derived cells during wound healing (Caskey and Liechty 2013). 5.2.3 Large Animal Models Rodents and humans do have many similar genes, but there is still a huge gap between the immune system of both. In order to bridge these gaps, larger animal models, like non-human primates (NHPs), are used. NHP models have immune systems that are more closely related to humans than rodents (Costa-Pinto et al. 2016). Host Response Immune Response to Polymeric Implants 243 6. Conclusion Biomaterials can be natural or synthetic, and they can interact with biological systems. These materials are used for various purposes, such as medical and therapeutic applications. The human immune system is complex, and because biomaterials are foreign to the body, they may stimulate the immune system. The immune response can be acute or chronic, depending on the type of biomaterials, site of implant, surgical technique, molecular weight, degradation rate, etc. Sometimes, rejection of implants occurs as the implants are identified as foreign bodies to the host immune system. After implementing biomaterials, they first come in contact with extracellular matrix (ECM) protein and blood plasma. ECM protein attracts neutrophils and monocytes and causes inflammation through macrophage activation. The implant should be created in such a way that it minimises the immune response so that rejection of the implant can be avoided and can decrease the unnecessary risk to the host from implantation (Aamodt and Grainger 2016). Moreover, several technical challenges are faced due to their complexity and unpredictability. 244 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 7. Future Prospects An ideal biomaterial must not elicit the host immune response, should be long- lasting and have corrosion-free characteristics. In order to make this happen, there are studies and experiments actively going on with both in vitro and in vivo models. There is a strong need to understand the relationships between the host and the biomaterial due to their varied responses as well as between events like injury, inflammation, and fibrosis (Zhou and Groth 2018) . A deep and clear understanding of the underlying processes responsible for the bioactivity and biocompatibility of biomaterials will facilitate future efforts to build effective and safe biomaterials. Also, the final outcome may be different in a multi-cell culture environment due to cellular crosstalk (Ellermann et al. 2023). To make these biomaterials more adaptable, they can be enriched with additional bioactive compounds so that they can regulate the immune responses and be a closer replica of the natural host environment. Hence, it can be concluded that to build efficiently integrative and biocompatible tissue constructs or biomaterials, various approaches have to be used, including immunoengineering (to facilitate incorporation into the host) and anti-inflammatory procedures so there are fewer chances of rejection of the implant biomaterials (Zhou and Groth 2018). Introduction Phytomedicine is perhaps one of the oldest forms of medicine. Before the advent of orthodox and modern medicine, plants were used in the treatment of various kinds of illnesses. However, the lack of adequate understanding and empirical research evidence regarding the activities and mode of action of most plant bioactive compounds, coupled with the discovery of synthetic drugs, promoted skepticism toward the continued use of phytomedicine. This notwithstanding, up-to-date evidence associating synthetic and chemical-based drugs with emerging physiological disorders has prompted a redirection of medical drug discovery toward natural products, with plant phytochemicals as a major source of pharmacologically relevant compounds (Jamil et al. 2012; Farzaei et al. 2015; Rtibi et al. 2017; Huang et al. 2018). Plant-derived bioactive compounds have expressed vast biological activities, resulting in an awakening of phytomedicines. However, chemical and biological limitations such as insolubility, hydrophobicity, low bioavailability, and high toxicity are challenges confronting the application of phytomedicines (Patra et al. 2018; Krishnasis et al. 2016; Olotu et al. 2020). Biopolymers are important ingredients with various applications, especially in the pharmaceutical, medical, and food sectors, due to their biodegradability, stability, and biocompatibility. Advances in polymer science have fostered the use of natural biopolymers as carriers for active pharmaceutical ingredients, implants, wound covers, and food packaging materials. Natural biopolymers are produced from plants, animals, or microorganisms as polynucleotides, polypeptides, and polysaccharides. With recent progress in phytomedicine and the need for effective and healthy drug- delivery carriers, biopolymers have become increasingly relevant, with several studies prospecting for novel alternatives. Polymer carriers in phytomedicine are employed to safeguard and preserve the integrity of active phytocomponents (Pisoschi et al. 2018). In addition, the encapsulation of phytocomponents in polymer matrix masks unfavorable sensory attributes such as taste, color, and smell (Rassu et al. 2014; Aguiar et al. 2016; Arce and Ustunol 2018). These help increase consumer appeal and market acceptance of phytomedicines. Furthermore, polymer encapsulation of phytomedicines ensures that active components delivered via the oral route are shielded from acid and enzymatic degradations while transiting to the site of action. Several biopolymers, including cellulose, chitin, chitosan, alginate, etc., are currently employed in phytomedicine formulation either as a drug-delivery channel or an active medicinal component. Chitosan, an abundant biopolymer derived from the deacetylation of chitin, has gained significance in drug delivery due to its solubility and mechanical properties (Nwabor et al. 2020; Singh et al. 2021). Encapsulation in a chitosan-based polyelectrolyte complex was employed as an appropriate delivery system to promote the bioavailability and aqueous stability of curcumin in an in vitro α-amylase inhibitory assay and in vivo anti-hyperglycemic assay in alloxan-induced rats (Akolade et al. 2017). Nano-encapsulation of madecassoside, a bioactive pentacyclic triterpenoid saponin isolated from Centella asiatica in the alginate- chitosan co-polymer matrix was employed as a therapeutic delivery system for the management of epilepsies and related stress-inflammatory disorder (Kunjumon et al. 2021). Microencapsulation of medicinal plants in a chitosan matrix enhanced the solubility of the extracts in simulated vaginal fluid and increased the bioavailability of bioactive compounds for the treatment of vulvovaginal candidiasis (Moreno et al. 2018). However, the choice of polymers for the encapsulation of phytomedicinal ingredients is affected by several factors, including the solubility of the polymer and phytomedicinal component, the gelling strength of the polymer, and preparation technique (Villemin et al. 2019; Cheow and Hadinoto 2011; Jyothi et al. 2010). Delivery of phytomedicines through biopolymer matrix carriers has been achieved through various fabrication technologies. However, the choice of formulation technology depends on the purpose and intended delivery site of the activity. Microencapsulation technologies such as ionic gelation, spray drying, and freeze drying have been extensively employed as appropriate methods for delivering phytomedicines. However, with recent advances in nano-pharmaceuticals, the delivery of active components through nanosized dispersions and particles has increasingly become a vibrant research focus. The size and large surface area of nanoparticles promote the release of bioactive ingredients and increase the bioavailability Biopolymers in Phytomedicines, Preparations, and Applications 249 and efficacy of the active component (Yang et al. 2020). Phytomedicinal nano- formulations have been employed to treat several disease conditions (Moradi et al. 2020; Paul et al. 2010; Zahrani et al. 2017). The use of biopolymers as a nano- drug delivery matrix overcomes the impending limitations of phytomedicine by enhancing its solubility, stability, and bioavailability. Loading ferulic acid into cyclodextrin nanosponges increased the solubility of ferulic acid as an anticancer phytomedicinal component (Rezaei et al. 2019). Phytomedicinal applications of ellagic acid, a phytochemical polyphenol with vast pharmacological benefits, are hampered by its poor water solubility and limited oral bioavailability. Several studies have demonstrated that nano-encapsulation of ellagic acid in biopolymers improves its solubility, bioavailability, and oral absorption and enhances its effects as an anticancer, antioxidant, and anti-hemorrhagic agent (Yağmur and Şahin 2020; Gopalakrishnan et al. 2014; Mady and Shaker 2017; Arulmozhi et al. 2013). Considering the heightened acceptance of phytomedicine and the benefits of biopolymers in the effective delivery of phytomedicines to pharmacological sites of activities, this chapter elaborates on the role of biopolymers in phytomedicine, its preparation methods, and applications. The chapter provides an overview of progress in the applications of biopolymer as phytomedicine. 2. Sources and Application of Biopolymers in Drug Delivery Biopolymers are polymers produced by living things, and they occur as natural or synthetic polymeric biomolecules produced by the covalent bonding of monomers. Biopolymers may occur naturally in plants, animals, bacteria, and fungi or synthesized chemically using biological materials such as amino acids, sugars, natural fats, or oils. Biopolymers can be categorized into three classes based on their origin: (a) Agro-polymers from biomass obtained from plants, such as lignin, pectin cellulose, lignocellulose, and starch; (b) Polymers from microbial or animal origin, such as collagen, microbial cellulose, xanthan gum, alginic acid, chitin, and chitosan; (c) Chemically synthesized biodegradable polymers, such as poly(-hydroxy esters), including polycaprolactone, polyglycolide or poly(glycolic acid), polylactic acid, or polylactide, and poly(ethers), including polyethylene glycol and poly(vinyl alcohol). In addition, biopolymers can be classified into three categories based on their monomeric units and structure: (1) Polynucleotides: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid) (2) Polysaccharides: Examples include cellulose, chitosan, and chitin (3) Polypeptides: Examples include collagen, gelatin, gluten, and whey. Figure 1 presents the various sources of selected biopolymers used in pharmaceutical formulations to deliver phytomedicines. Commercially, biopolymers are produced from traditional isolation of biopolymers from plants, in vitro 250 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization synthesis of polynucleotides in cell-free systems, and large-scale fermentative or biotechnological production of biopolymers. Developing biopolymers through economically viable methods for the formulation of active pharmaceuticals is an emerging alternative source with the potential to replace synthetic excipients. The wide availability and sustainability of natural resources is considered a possible bio-factory for developing prerequisite polysaccharides. Natural polysaccharides from different sources have long been studied and widely used in different areas, including the fabrication of pharmaceutical excipients, food, and the paper industry. Natural polymers are renewable, biocompatible, and biodegradable, with the ability to mimic the natural extracellular matrix environment. Amongst the plant-derived polysaccharides, cellulose is the most abundant and naturally available biopolymer, with a total annual biomass production of 1.5 × 10 12 tons (Klemm et al. 2005). Plant polysaccharides consist of several α- or β-glycosidic bonded monosaccharide units that can be isolated using non-toxic organic solvents. Current industrial production of biopolymers employs engineered microbial cells as fermentation factories for the synthesis and large-scale manufacturing of biopolymers. Microbial production of biopolymers is an eco-efficient approach that does not harm the environment. 3. Potentials Phytomedicine With Biopolymers for Therapeutic Applications Several bioactive materials have been identified in higher plants, with many originating from edible plants. These plant-derived bioactive compounds possess several active constituents, including polyphenols, flavonoids, alkaloids, saponins, and tannins reported with potential pharmacological efficacy (Figure 3). The phytoconstituent modulates several cellular pathways in the management of Biopolymers in Phytomedicines, Preparations, and Applications 255 various diseases, including cancer, Alzheimer’s, topical inflammations, diabetes, dengue, etc. Despite the availability of synthetic active pharmaceuticals, herbs and herbal medicines are still preferred as major healthcare products in developing countries. In prospecting for new drug development, researchers have been drawn toward biologically active plant extract due to traditional claims of efficacy and pharmacological potential. Natural products are considered safe, and solvent- specific extracts exhibit concentration-dependent biocompatibility (Rahman 2020). However, phytomedicines face physiochemical obstacles similar to those of synthetic active pharmaceutical moiety, including low solubility and bioavailability. These problems can be overcome using nanotechnology with the use of cost-effective biopolymers. Research involved with biopolymers and natural product-incorporated nanotechnology has reported several advantages, including enhancement in solubility, pharmacological efficacy, improvement in tissue permeability, and stability (Figure 3). The rise in phytomedicine usage demands a hypothetical nanotechnology- based approach to develop a rational drug-delivery system for the appropriate use of natural products in several life-threatening diseases. Pharmaceutical nanotechnology is the fastest-developing technique that enables the design of multifarious delivery systems, which significantly reduces the complications associated with phytomedicine. Incorporation of phytomedicine into a biopolymer-based nano drug delivery is an innovative approach to extend the physicochemical properties of phytomedicines with enhancement in bioavailability and therapeutic potential. For more than a generation, biopolymers have been used to deliver phytomedicine to biological tissue. Biopolymers may be natural or synthetic and are used in healthcare systems for upkeep, improvement, or supplant reparation of tissue or biological function. This evolution was paralleled by a budding of professionalism and the establishment of biopolymer societies. The earliest biomaterials-related society was founded in 1954 as the American Society for Artificial Internal Organs to establish a platform for developing artificial kidneys and hearts (Ratner et al. 2004). Biopolymer-incorporated phytomedicine offers multiple benefits in the treatment of both acute and chronic diseases through site-specific and target-oriented delivery of natural products. Several biopolymers incorporated nanotechnological products, including dermal scaffolds, lipid-based carrier systems, and aerosol nasal spray, have been reported for safe and effective tissue-targeted delivery of phytomedicine. Recently, several reports have highlighted outstanding research of biopolymer-incorporated phytomedicine in the treatment of cancer and Alzheimer’s disease, showing enhanced permeability and bioavailability. Besides the various roles of biopolymers as excellent drug-delivery carriers, the biocompatibility, safety, and readily availability of biopolymers as a sustainable raw material are of economic benefits in drug formulation. In addition, several biopolymers have been reported to exhibit trace pharmacological activities, such as the antioxidant properties of collagen responsible for its cosmetic application as an anti-aging product and the antimicrobial effects of chitosan. 4.1 Bio-Based Polymeric Material With Phytomedicine in Topical Applications Globally, billions of people are plagued by the burden of dermal disorders, resulting in severe consequences. Skin and dermal tissue-related complications are the most common and distressing forms of laceration, with thousands suffering when left untreated. Wound healing is a complex process comprising different mediators, including soluble mediators, blood cells, extracellular matrix, and parenchymal cells. Healing of wounds is broadly classified into three stages, which are the inflammation process, tissue formation, and remodeling of tissue (Chhabra et al. 2017). The inflammatory stage includes platelet accumulation, coagulation, and leukocyte migration, whereas re-epithelialization, angiogenesis, fibroplasia, and wound contraction are involved during tissue induction (Kirsner and Eaglstein 1993). Production of protein matrix and collagen lasts for one month in remodeling phase. The treatment of wounds with phytomedicine is gaining huge importance, either in semisolid gel form or incorporated in composites. Phytomedicine promotes the healing of wounds through different mechanisms, including modulation in wound healing, decrease in bacterial count, improvement in collagen deposition, and increase in fibroblast and fibrocytes (Thangapazham et al. 2016). However, such traditional treatments reflect disadvantages such as inappropriate healing of wounds due to exquisite shape and drying with exposure to air. Cross-linking of phytomedicine with biopolymers is a novel technique adopted by researchers in the fabrication of biodegradable copolymerized conjugate as a scaffold in tissue regeneration that mimics the extracellular tissue matrix. Scientific data indicated that phytomedicine-incorporated formulations have proven to be significantly useful in the treatment of various skin disorders, including coagulation, inflammations, fibroplasia, epithelization, collagenation, and wound contractions (Broughton et al. 2006). Biopolymers in Phytomedicines, Preparations, and Applications 257 Traditional wound dressings, such as bandages, cotton wools, and gauzes, have several disadvantages and are unable to provide adequate protection for dermal application. Thus, there is an urgent need to replace such traditional dressings with bio-conjugated phytomedicine as scaffolds to provide an optimum condition around the wound with the release of active constituents to facilitate wound healing. Phytomedicine-incorporated biopolymers have an astonishing advantage over traditional dressings due to negligible host response, high level of tunability, and biocompatibility, which are either reabsorbed or removed from biological systems. The quest for the development of plant-based, safe, and effective drugs has led to an increased focus on exploring and harnessing nature, particularly for the discovery of active compounds in the treatment of life-threatening diseases, including diabetes, hypertension, and cancer. Cancer involves abnormal cellular growth with the potential to spread to other parts of the body and the ability to infiltrate and destroy normal body tissue. Globally, the rising prevalence of cancer has become a threat to public health and a great concern to the health sector, with overwhelming annual mortality and morbidity. Thus, research on anticancer drug formulation and development has become of paramount importance (Seyfried and Huysentruyt 2013). Approximately 70% of deaths due to cancer occur in low and middle-income countries. The annual number of new cases is projected to rise to 21.6 million in 2030. Moreover, the pecuniary influence of cancer is noteworthy. In the United States, the financial burden of cancer care by 2020 was estimated at $157.8 billion dollars (Yabroff et al. 2011). Nature is a potential source of anticancer drugs, with over 60% of currently used anticancer drugs derived from plants. Naturally occurring anticancer agents, including curcumin, vincristine, vinblastine, vindesine, vinorelbine, taxanes, podophyllotoxin, camptothecin, anthracyclines, trabectedin, epothilone, temsirolimus, and their derivatives are generally prescribed. The majority of clinically used anticancer phytomedicines available in conventional dosage form possess substantial limitations such as short biological half-life, low solubility with limited bioavailability, and several side effects. These drawbacks limit the efficacy of phytomedicine and constitute a driving force for the design of a biopolymer-based novel drug-delivery system to reduce the side effects with enhancement in the clinical efficacy of anticancer phytomedicine. A surge in cancer diagnosis has been brought about by nanotechnology, with the competence to perceive even a distinct tumor cell. Individual cancer cells can be traced using biopolymer-based nanostructured materials such as nanoparticles, dendrimers, and nanosponges cross-linked with specific antibodies. Moreover, the incorporation of phytoconstituents in novel/nanotechnology drug-delivery systems fabricated using biopolymers is increasing daily in cancer treatment with enhanced clinical efficacy. However, the delivery of systemic and local therapeutics via the nasal route has received significant attention due to its maximized efficacy. Moreover, during the last few decades, the delivery of potential drugs, such as protein, peptides, and phytomedicine, susceptible to enzymatic or acid degradation with hepatic metabolism, developed as a nasal drug-delivery system. These might be due to the low proteolytic activity, large surface area, and vascularity with porous endothelial membrane and the presence of a significant number of microvilli that help to enhance the permeability and avoid hepatic drug metabolism (Ozsoy et al. 2009). Nose-to-brain drug delivery is one of the fastest emerging fields. However, the mechanism of action for efficient drug delivery to the brain is not yet completely known. Several studies have indicated the effective delivery of phytomedicine and its derivatives to the brain via the olfactory pathway, trigeminal pathway, and deposition in nasal mucosa. While the preferred dosage form for intranasal drug delivery is a solution, this approach has several disadvantages, making the selection 260 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization of biopolymer in the fabrication critical. However, this neural network degeneration appears long after the inception of the disease. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported more than 5.8 million Americans in 2020 were affected by Alzheimer’s disease, which accounts for 50–75% of globally (Matthews et al. 2019). In addition, a recent study projected that this figure will rise by triple folds to 14 million by 2060 (Matthews et al. 2019). The pathogenesis of Alzheimer’s is not yet completely understood. However, genetic susceptibility and environmental-related issues are responsible for the late onset of intermittent Alzheimer’s. Moreover, Alzheimer’s condition is characterized by cognitive incompetence demonstrated through the accumulation of β-amyloid with the formation of hyperphosphorylated neurofibrillary tangles (tau protein) and dysfunction of the cholinergic system. In addition, Alzheimer’s is also concomitant with gene mutation, including presenilins (PS1 and PS2) and apolipoprotein E. Several animal studies have been conducted to understand the causative mechanism of this disease for the development of drugs. Currently, the possible development of drugs is focused on the search for phytomedicines that can inhibit presenilins, β-amyloid, and apolipoproteins. Further approaches, including therapy with natural antioxidants (Grundman et al. 2002), anti-inflammatories (Moore and O’Banion 2002), and cholesterol-lowering mediators, have been reported in the treatment of Alzheimer’s. Several bioactive medicines have been tested due to the aftereffects of synthetic drug therapy. Phytomedicine, including capsaicin, curcumin, resveratrol, and Biopolymers in Phytomedicines, Preparations, and Applications 261 hyperforin, have been reported to inhibit the effects of tau protein hyperphosphorylation with excellent pharmacological efficacy in animal studies. Moreover, the potential efficacy of active constituents originating from marine sources such as red algae (Syad and Devi 2015), sea cucumber (Li et al. 2019), and marine spoon worms have also been reported in the treatment of Alzheimer’s. Other natural sources of phytomedicines with potential in the modulation of Alzheimer’s are presented in Table 4. Nanotechnology-based interventions have opened an exciting area via theranostics of Alzheimer’s disease in terms of tailored nanomedicine, which is able to target and deliver drugs across the blood-brain barrier. Polylactide-co-glycoside nanoparticles with surface modification by lactoferrin-conjugated N-trimethylated chitosan were employed as a mucoadhesive and targeted nano-medicinal for efficient intranasal delivery of Huperzine A to the brain for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease (Meng et al. 2018). Phytomedicine refers to the practice of using plant parts and constituents for medicinal purposes based on traditional knowledge. The global annual market for herbal products is growing significantly and loomed to USD 60$ billion (Sendker 2017). Despite the advantages, pharmaceutical manufacturers are hesitant to invest in the development of phytomedicine as many natural compounds alone or in conventional delivery form could not pass the clinical phase trial study. This is largely due to problems associated with the poor solubility, limited absorption, and low bioavailability of most bioactive phytoconstituents. However, recent advances in drug-delivery carriers using biopolymeric compounds signal a significant improvement in the delivery of phytomedicines to pharmacological active sites. The use of biopolymers as drug excipients of carriers has been extensively investigated with promising outcomes. Screened and purified natural compounds in conjugation with lipids are gaining importance in healthcare management systems. Lipid-based carriers with bioactive components represent a rapidly developing technology used to deliver therapeutic agents in a regulated mode. Biopolymeric lipid carriers with phytomedicine drug- delivery systems are a proven, commercially viable approach for formulating pharmaceuticals, including topical, oral, parenteral, and pulmonary. Self-assembled lipid-based nanocarriers complexed with phytoconstituents exhibit several advantages, including enhanced solubility, stability, lipophilicity, biocompatibility, effective tissue targeting, cellular targeting, and molecular targeting. These carrier molecules shield the bioactive components from interaction with biological enzymes and systemic inactivation. Nano-carries can be broadly categorized based on carrier resources such as organic or inorganic carriers. Several novel drug deliveries such as liposomes, niosomes, pharmacosomes, transfersomes, ethosomes, archaeosomes, iscoms, vesosomes, virosomes, colloidosomes, herbosomes, phytosomes, cubosomes, nanospheres, solid lipid nanoparticles, nanostructure lipid carriers, lipid drug conjugate, microemulsion, nanoemulsion, and self-emulsifying drug-delivery system have been reported with the ability to deliver phytoconstituent. Future Perspectives and Conclusions Delivery of active components through biopolymer matrix and particulate systems can be achieved through a variety of techniques. The use of encapsulated biopolymer particles or composite matrices as drug-delivery systems for phytomedicines and other active ingredients is still an evolving research area. Current knowledge on the preparation of biopolymer particulate matter for the effective delivery of phytomedicine is still limited. The effective use of biopolymer as an appropriate Figure 5: Graft polymerization of polysaccharides. Figure 6: Graft chemically modified chitin and chitosan biopolymers. Biopolymers in Phytomedicines, Preparations, and Applications 267 Figure 7: Chemical (–COOH and -OH) functionalization of alginate. channel for the delivery of ingredients requires adequate knowledge of the polymer properties, its molecular and functional characteristics, as well as physicochemical mechanisms underlying particle formation and cross-linking. Excellent results have been reported through the use of biopolymers as drug carriers for phytomedicines. Future studies on particulate systems for phytomedicine delivery should focus on both novel techniques and the optimization of current methods. Although several methods have been reported in lab-scale production, adoption of these methods to industrial scale requires a thorough understanding of the various process parameters. In addition, material quality should be strictly maintained to ensure that only pharmaceutical-grade materials are used to enforce the safety of consumers and the quality of products. Research should be directed to cutting down on the high operational cost involved with the use of certain technologies and focus on facile and inexpensive methods. There is also a need to ensure improved encapsulation efficiency with increased stability of the matrix. Moreover, methods should be adapted based on the proposed site of delivery to promote the effectiveness of carriers and the efficacy of phytomedicinal products. Introduction A biomaterial is created specifically to interact with biological systems for therapeutic or diagnostic purposes in medicine. The interdisciplinary field of biomaterials, which has recently been affected by tissue engineering and material science, includes medicine, biology, physics, and chemistry. Biomaterials have been around for about 50 years. In the development of biomaterials, it is imperative to ensure their safety for human usage. To access the biological processes of biomaterials when they come into touch with the body, various in vitro tests are performed (Inayat-hussain et al. 2009). The use of medical devices has been employed extensively in the past many decades, but their use has been increasingly observed for the past 40 years. In this regard, the ever-growing population and demands to enhance a quality of life using various technologies have also increased, and the use of these biomedical applications has been observed in various fields of science and technology, including cardiovascular surgery, general surgery, wound healing, etc. (Eloy 2012). Toxicology is crucial in the development of biomaterials to guarantee the security of the materials chosen for usage in devices (Inayat-hussain et al. 2009). In vitro tests are carried out to encourage biological responses to substances when they come into contact with the body. It is widely divided into three categories: cytotoxicity, method of cell death, and genotoxicity assessment of biomaterials, all of which provide 278 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization significant information on in vitro toxicity for cell death assessment. The most often utilized indicator of the in vitro toxicity of biomaterials is the suppression of cell proliferation (Wieslander et al. 1993). An overview of the in vitro tests discussed in this chapter is represented in Figure 1. 2. Pre-Testing Biomaterial Characterization The first phase of an intricate procedure to authenticate a material or device designed for clinical purposes includes performing standardized regulatory assessments in laboratory settings and live organisms. These assessments adhere to established programs that evaluate biocompatibility and safety, aiming to acquire the essential approval for human applications. 3. In vitro Cytotoxicity Assay (ISO 10993-5:2009) 3.1 Extract Dilution Test The extraction dilution exposure method detects toxins leached from medical devices (Srivastava et al. 2018). The test assesses both qualitative and quantitative cytotoxicity. In vitro Genotoxicity Testing (ISO 10993-3:2014) 4.1 Ames Test Ceramic-based biomaterials have been extensively employed in recent years for orthopedic and dental purposes (Baino et al. 2015) . Each new formulation of a ceramic-based material or the advancement of current biomaterials must first demonstrate their safety and effectiveness before their clinical performance can be evaluated. Risk and reward are used to define safety and effectiveness, respectively. The behavior of bioceramics upon implantation in organisms allows for their categorization into distinct groups. These groups include bioinert bioceramics (like alumina and zirconia), resorbable and bioactive bioceramics (such as hydroxyapatite and biological glasses), and bioceramics capable of triggering targeted cellular responses at the molecular level. These versatile materials serve as scaffolds for tissue engineering applications (Navarro et al. 2008). All of these bioceramics are reportedly biocompatible, although varying levels of bioactivity have been discovered when examining the ability to interact with the biological environment to enhance biological integration with tissues. The first biomaterials with bioactivity were glass ceramics, which had stimulatory effects on bone cells and direct chemical interaction with host tissues (Han et al. 2007). In addition to the chemical characteristics of ceramic composition, ion release, oxidation, and corrosion are key variables impacting biocompatibility. In vitro and in vivo testing are required for inquiry into the functional qualities of the biomaterials once their safety has been evaluated (Fini and Giardino 2003). The ISO10993-5:2009 test techniques are intended to measure the reaction of cultivated mammalian cells in close proximity to the test material or with a solution- based assay utilizing physiological factors. Gene mutation in bacteria and genetic alterations in cultured mammalian cells are the two most straightforward and sensitive in vitro techniques. The use of in vivo testing is only permitted if it is supported by science and if the outcomes of the in vitro tests show possible genotoxicity (search of chromosomal aberration). Ames (Salmonella/microsome mutagenicity assay) and the micronucleus tests are the two in vitro procedures that are employed most frequently (Torricelli et al. 2017). The Ames test employs several Salmonella typhimurium strains that display frameshift or point mutations within the genetic sequences needed to manufacture histidine (OECD test Guideline 471, 1997). When looking for probable genotoxic carcinogens, the Ames test is a sensitive screening method. Due to the fact that a In Vitro Toxicity Assessment Techniques for Biomaterials 281 mutagen in the Ames test does not always pose a risk to people, a positive result— despite the strong correlation—can be challenging to interpret for the specific instance at hand. When a material is introduced to the culture media, it induces a back mutation that allows the bacteria to synthesize histidine once again ( Figure 3). The mutagenicity of a drug is proportional to the number of colonies seen (Torricelli et al. 2017). In order to ensure mutagenic capabilities, the Ames test is a straightforward, reliable procedure carried out employing several bacterial strains, such as Salmonella typhimurium and Escherichia coli . The basic goal of the Ames test is to induce a new mutation in a gene that is currently mutating, which will replace the existing mutation and restore the gene’s function. This test is also known as the “Reversion Assay” because of the newly produced mutation that prevents colonies of histidine- producing cells from developing in the new mutant cells (Vijay et al. 2018; Vasdev et al. 2022). An important amino acid necessary for cell proliferation is histidine. 4.2 In vitro Mammalian Cell Gene Mutation Test (OECD 476) The “mammalian cell gene mutation assay ” is a method to detect the chemical substances that cause mutations in genes. It uses the HPRT ( hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase) gene as a marker. The HPRT gene is involved in the purine and pyrimidine base pair synthesis. Hypoxanthine phosphoribosyl transferase (HPRT, EC 2.4.2.8) catalyzes the synthesis of 5’-IMP and 5’-GMP involves the condensation of 5’-phosphoribosyl-l-pyrophosphate (PRPP) with the purine bases hypoxanthine and guanine, respectively (Stout and Caskey 1985). This marker gene, which is involved in a metabolic pathway, is exposed to the test chemicals. If the protein produced by the marker gene is altered, it changes the phenotype of the mammalian cell. This change in phenotype is indicative of a mutation. It is an in vitro genotoxicity test (toxicity test used to determine the substance’s potential to cause genetic damage). This test has been in use for over 40 years and has successfully detected the genotoxicity of various chemical and physical agents. The in vitro micronucleus test is employed as a method for evaluating genotoxicity, specifically for the detection of micronuclei (MN) within the cytoplasm of interphase cells. Micronucleus are extra nuclei formed either due to chromosomes without a centromere or chromosomes that fail to reach the poles during the anaphase of cell division. The in vitro MN assay can be used to estimate the DNA damage by detecting micronucleus. The existence of micronuclei in a cell represents genetic damage. In this way, the MN assay can determine the potential of any substance to cause damage to chromosomes that are not favorable to the cell. In the present day, we are exposed to various physical, chemical, and biological agents that might interfere with the normal functioning of our cells (cause diseases like neurodegenerative diseases, cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and cancer), some of which can be lethal. Some agents may be genotoxic and not lethal. These lead to damage in DNA, which sometimes gets carried on to the next generation. It is, therefore, essential to test the genotoxicity of any biomaterial to avoid health risks. MN assay is just one of the in vitro genotoxicity tests. This test uses cells with a good metabolizing capability; if not, the cells are treated with sources for metabolic activation. After this, the cell is exposed to test chemicals and allowed to grow. Defects like chromosomal damage and altered cell division are observed after growth, which leads to the formation of micronuclei. After interphase, these cells are harvested, which is followed by staining and observation for micronuclei. Micronuclei should be identified in cells that have completed the process of mitosis after being exposed to the test chemical. The ideal temperature for cell culture maintenance is 37°C and a humidified atmosphere of 5% carbon dioxide. These cultures should be checked for Mycoplasma contamination and stability of modal chromosome number. If such contamination or changes in chromosomes are observed, the cells cannot be used for the assay. The cells from the stock culture are transferred to the culture medium for exponential growth. Lymphocytes (whole blood treated with heparin or separated lymphocytes) can be cultured and used. The MN assay is efficient and promising but also laborious and time-consuming. In order to combat this, the process can be automated. Automation is advantageous as it makes the assay more reliable. This is because manual errors in identifying the micronuclei can be eliminated. It also makes it possible to test thousands to ten thousand cells instead of one cell at a time. In Vitro Toxicity Assessment Techniques for Biomaterials 283 5. Figure 5: Methods employed in the cytotoxicity evaluation of biomaterials are tetrazolium salt assay, LDH (Lactate Dehydrogenase) leakage assay, neutral red uptake assay, alamar blue assay, colony forming assay, dye exclusion assay and sulforhodamine B (SRB) protein staining.
