Tetrazolium salts fall into different groups: MTT, XTT, and WST-1. In order to evaluate metabolic activity in active cells, the MTT/XTT/WST-1 test makes use of several tetrazolium salts. MTT 550 nm, XTT 492 nm, and WST-1 420–480 nm are the required wavelengths for each kit in order to detect metabolic activity (Figure 5). 6.1.1 MTT Assay The tetrazolium-based MTT test has long been considered the gold standard of cytotoxicity assays because it is extremely sensitive and may be used for high- throughput screening (Tonder et al. 2015) . In the MTT test, the tetrazolium salt 3-(4,5-dimethyl-thiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) is avidly absorbed into cells and subsequently reduced in a mitochondrial-dependent procedure that generates a formazan product. MTT is a cationic salt that may enter living eukaryotic cells by electrostatically interacting with the anionic plasma membrane (Freeberg et al. 2019) . Only in vitro live cells are analyzed by the tetrazolium- based calorimetric assay (MTT test), and the outcome is directly correlated with the quantity of viable cultivated cells (Figure 5). It has been employed in cancer research, immunological investigations, and, most recently, biocompatibility analysis. To adapt the MTT technique to an in vitro investigation of biomaterial-cell interactions, they made a few modest adjustments (Ciapetti et al. 1996). For instance, using the MTT test, the cytotoxicity of biomaterials, including hydroxyapatite, chitosan, and carbon nanotube scaffolds that interact with mesenchymal stem cells to aid in bone regeneration is evaluated (Paretsis et al. 2021). 6.1.2 XTT Assay In order to assess cell viability, proliferation, and cytotoxicity, the XTT test is employed to quantify cellular metabolic activity. Cell proliferation, viability, and cytotoxicity may all be measured in a non-radioactive manner using the Cell Proliferation Kit II (XTT). Cells in suspension or adhering are cultivated in 96-well microplates as the sample material. The colorimetric, non-radioactive XTT (sodium 3’-[1-(phenylaminocarbonyl)-3,4-tetrazolium]-bis (4-methoxy6-nitro) benzene sulfonic acid hydrate) assay system is used to measure the amount of a substance in a sample (Paull et al. 1988). Since XTT (2,3-bis(2-methoxy-4-nitro-5-sulfophenyl)- 5-carboxanilide-2H-tetrazolium) is soluble in the majority of aqueous media, it can be employed as an alternative to MTT ( Figure 5). An advantageous feature of the XTT test is that it is also appropriate for cells in suspension. The test is based on the mitochondrial production of NADH via trans-plasma membrane electron transport and an electron mediator, which is then used to reduce XTT extracellularly (McGaw et al. 2014). In recent years, a great deal of in vitro and in vivo research has been done on magnesium based biomaterial for use in degradable implants. This study while adhering to the accepted methodology DIN EN ISO 10993-5:2009, enables an optimal and consistent in vitro evaluation of the cytocompatibility of magnesium based biomaterial. The preferred test cell line and medium, respectively, are mouse In Vitro Toxicity Assessment Techniques for Biomaterials 287 fibroblast line L-929 and MEM augmented with 10% FCS, penicillin/streptomycin, and 4 mM l-glutamine. To measure the proliferation and to determine the viability of cells, researchers performed the XTT test (Jung et al. 2015). 6.1.3 WST-1 In order to detect cell proliferation, cell viability, and cytotoxicity in mammalian cells, WST-1 (2-(4-iodophenyl)-3-(4-nitrophenyl)-5-(2,4-disulfophenyl)-2H tetrazolium monosodium salt) Assay Reagent offers a straightforward, precise, and ready-to-use test. The WST-1 test procedure is based on converting formazan, a product of cellular mitochondrial dehydrogenases, from the tetrazolium salt WST-1. The activity of the mitochondrial dehydrogenases increases with viable cell count, which also increases the quantity of formazan dye produced (Figure 5). The medium for cell culture receives the salt that is water soluble. The test assesses the metabolic activity of cells by causing a color change throughout the incubation time that is directly proportional to the quantity of mitochondrial dehydrogenase in the cell culture (Aslantürk 2018). The most used technique to determine the in vitro cytotoxicity of compounds is the WST-1 assay. Nevertheless, the interference of the examined compounds, such as carbon nanotubes or Mg particles, can have an impact on tetrazolium-based assays. Here, they describe a fresh Mn material interference with the WST-1 test. The WST-1 reagent has a number of benefits over the other tetrazolium salt-based cell proliferation reagents, MTT, and XTT, including water solubility, speed, increased stability, and sensitivity (Scarcello et al. 2020). 6.2 Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) Leakage Assay LDH is a widely distributed protein that is ubiquitous and exhibits its peak activity in essential organs, including the heart, liver, muscles, kidneys, lungs, and blood cells (Figure 5). LDH is essential for glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, which are catalyzed by an oxidoreductase, and there is a reversible reaction occurring where lactate is converted to pyruvate and, at the same time, NADH and NAD+ undergo interconversion. LDH is composed of muscle and heart subunits. LDH is divided into five isomeric types with variable enzymatic activities based on the component of a subunit from LDH-1 to LDH-5 measured by in vitro assay (Wu et al. 2021). In terms of distribution, LDH1 is primarily located in the heart, and LDH2 is prevalent in the reticuloendothelial system, encompassing the liver, spleen, and lungs, as well as red blood cells. LDH3 is specifically found in the lungs, LDH4 in the kidneys, and LDH5 in the liver and skeletal muscle. The activities of serum LDH and their dynamic ranges are compared among various human diseases, being observed that out of 172,933 patients, it was found in 48 clinically defined diseases and 9,528 healthy individuals. LDH is an enzyme that exhibits stability and is present in all cells. During cellular damage, LDH is released into the supernatant of cell cultures. In vitro LDH activity serves as a sensitive, accurate, and cost-effective alternative to assays that rely on radioisotopes or dyes. LDH is responsible for producing lactic acid during exercise. LDH catalyzes lactate to pyruvate, and NADH reduces INT to form red formazan, which can be measured at 490 nm (Kumar et al. 2018). LDH plays a vital role in the anaerobic metabolic pathway by facilitating the bidirectional 288 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization conversion of lactate to pyruvate (Farhana and Lappin 2023). Various conditions such as liver disease, anemia, heart attack, bone fractures, muscle trauma, cancers, and infections like encephalitis, meningitis, encephalitis, and HIV can lead to an increase in LDH in the blood. LDH is a cytosolic enzyme that is a reliable indicator of cellular toxicity. The cell culture medium is exposed to LDH when there is damage to the plasma membrane, leading to the release of the enzyme. LDH test is low risk but can cause bruising and soreness. However, commercially available LDH assay kits have limited reproducibility and high cost (Kaja et al. 2015). LDH helps in the quantitative determination of cell viability and late-stage apoptosis. The assessment of LDH leakage, which measures the activity of the widely present cytosolic enzyme, serves as a means to evaluate the integrity of cell membranes. This approach is employed to assess the extent of membrane damage induced by irritants (Kumar et al. 2018). 6.3 Neutral Red Uptake Assay Through the neutral red uptake assay, which assesses both cell viability and proliferation in the aftermath of exposure to biomaterials, we can quantify the cytotoxicity of the employed biomaterial s (Ciapetti et al. 1996). In this test, the ability of live cells to incorporate and bind a weak cationic dye called neutral red within their lysosomes is utilized (Ates et al. 2017). Due to the modified membrane characteristics of dying cells, neutral red (NR) cannot be absorbed by cells anymore. The cells are quickly rinsed with PBS after three hours of exposure to the dye. The cells’ internalized dye is then released in an acidified ethanol solution. At OD 540 nm, released neutral red is evaluated in proportion to the number of viable cells. Unexposed cell viability, as measured by OD540 nm, is set to 100%. Viability curves may be created based on the absorption measurements to ascertain the test chemical concentration required to inhibit NRU by 50% (Repetto et al. 2008). A cell viability test called the neutral red absorption assay enables in vitro assessment of xenobiotic-induced cytotoxicity. For the assessment of viral cytopathogenicity, immuno-toxicity, and the identification of hazardous substances, in vitro tissue culture experiments utilizing the neutral red dye were created. As a chemosensitivity test for cell viability, the neutral red absorption cytotoxicity assay was created at Rockefeller University. The foundation of it is the supravital dye neutral red’s capacity to attach to and be incorporated by healthy cells. The weakly cationic dye has the ability to permeate nonionic cell membranes and accumulate within lysosomes. Inside the lysosomes, it engages in electrostatic, hydrophobic interactions with anionic and/ or phosphate groups present in the lysosomal matrix; subsequently, living cells are treated with an ethanol solution that has been acidified, resulting in the removal of the dye. A spectrophotometer is then used to measure the solubilized dye’s absorbance (Repetto et al. 2008). Based on the data, it is evident that the NRU, Alamar Blue assay (RES), and SRB assays display minimal variability within the linear range, whereas the MTT assay demonstrates the highest variation. This implies that the former assays are more adept at detecting slight alterations in cell number compared to the MTT assay. In Vitro Toxicity Assessment Techniques for Biomaterials 289 6.4 Alamar Blue Assay An integral part of testing synthesized biomaterials is determining their effect on cell viability, cell proliferation, and cytotoxicity detection. Alamar blue is an assay reagent for cell viability and cytotoxicity. This test has been in use for more than 50 years and is considered one of the best techniques because of its accuracy in predicting the adverse effects of test samples or biomaterials and detecting their toxic threshold. The Alamar blue bioassay has been used to test various biological and environmental systems, as well as a diverse number of cells. Some of these cell types are bacterial cells, fungi, yeast, protozoa, and cultured mammalian and piscine cells. This uses a dye called resazurin (IUPAC name: 7-hydroxy-10-oxidophenoxazin-10- ium-3-one), which is cell-permeable, water-soluble, stable in culture medium and non-toxic and a weak blue fluorescent indicator. This enters the cell and is acted upon by the cellular redox enzymes, which convert it to resorufin. Through the acceptance of electrons from NADPH, FADH2, FMNH2, NADH, and cytochromes, this process triggers a prominent color transition from indigo blue to a vivid fluorescent red. The resulting red color diffuses out of the cells and into the culture medium, facilitating convenient measurement via colorimetry or fluorometry at a wavelength of 590 n m (Kumar et al. 2018). The ongoing transformation of resazurin into resorufin by viable cells provides a reliable and quantitative assessment of cell viability. Resazurin can be used to monitor cells continuously in a culture medium. 6.5 Colony-Forming Assay A colony-forming assay, also known as “clonogenic assay of cells”, is an in vitro technique to determine the proliferation and differentiation of cells. In simple terms, it is a method that is used to study the capability of each cell to grow into a colony. A group of cells can be considered a colony if it consists of a minimum of 50 cells. This method can be used to test each cell’s ability to divide and grow in number (Figure 5). The colony-forming assay is one of the best standards for finding out a cell’s reproductive death (a state where a cell loses its ability to divide due to accumulation damage in its DNA but can carry on some of its basic functions). This assay is useful for studying the characteristics of a cell under the influence of certain chemicals (e.g., cytotoxic agents), drugs, ionizing radiations, or genetic manipulations. The utilization of parametric cell survival curves is widely recognized as the gold standard for assessing cell reproductive death after exposure to ionizing radiation. These curves depict the correlation between radiation doses and the percentage of surviving colonies, facilitating the precise quantification of cell survival (Braselmann et al. 2015). Puck and Marcus, in 1956, described the colony-forming assay. They published a seminal paper using a cell culture technique that involved growing mammalian cells in a culture medium with necessary growth factors. These growth factors were provided as “feeder” cells. They can also be grown in a conditioned or complex culture media for a suitable environment that 290 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization eliminates the need to use “feeder” cells. The clonogenic cell assay has been used for many decades to study the behavior of a variety of cells. The assays are capable of identifying cells that still possess the ability to generate a substantial number of offspring, even after exposure to treatments that may induce cell reproductive death (Franken et al. 2006). A typical colony-forming assay includes: (a) Treating the monolayer of cells in tissue culture flasks; (b) Preparing cell suspensions followed by plating them; (c) Colonies need to be fixed and stained; (d) Incubate for a suitable period. 6.5.1 Colony-Forming Assay Setup There are two ways to perform the colony-forming assay: 6.5.1.1 Cells Plated After Treatment Cells are treated in the parent culture plate, which is followed by re-plating them into varied dilutions to detect the colony-forming ability. The cells can be exposed to chemicals, radiation, drugs, etc. After treatment, the cells can be re-plated immediately (IP: Immediate Plating) or can be plated after a while (DP: Delayed Plating). An advantage of DP is that it gives time for repair to the treated cells, which yields more accurate results. In the field of radiobiological research, this method is specifically utilized to explore the mechanisms of repair for both potentially lethal and sublethal damage (Franken et al. 2006). The time given for DP is usually between 6–24 hours. The cells in the cell suspension are to be counted using a Coulter counter after the harvesting of treated cells. The culture should be incubated until sufficiently large colonies are developed in the control plate. 6.5.1.2 Cells Plated Prior to Treatment This approach involves plating the cells from a stock culture into dishes of varied dilutions and letting them get attached to the dishes. This generally takes around 2 hours. The cells are treated after this. It is noteworthy that the cells will start replicating and form colonies soon after being plated. Therefore, the treatment has to be done before the cell proliferates. If treatment is done after the cells begin to divide, it will result in an enormous colony growth. The dishes are incubated (37°C) until six potential cell divisions. This is a good method for rapid screening of cells and determining the susceptibility to various treatments. In order to combat this, a method called soft agar colony forming assay was developed in which the cell culture is suspended in a layer of soft agar (low agar concentration) that sits on a layer of solid agar (higher agar concentration). This allows three-dimensional movement of the transformed cells. 6.6 Dye Exclusion Assay In order to assess the proportion of living and non-viable cells, dye exclusion assays are utilized. These tests are based on the idea that intact plasma membranes in living In Vitro Toxicity Assessment Techniques for Biomaterials 291 cells prevent the entry of certain dyes but allow in dead cell s (Avelar-Freitas et al. 2014). Several cytotoxicity studies of chemicals and drug screening procedures involve in vitro cell viability and cellular toxicity experiments with grown cells. In recent times, there has been a rise in interest in the application of these tests. Tests involving human cells may hold greater applicability than certain animal models in vivo experiments, and in vitro cellular toxicity and/or cell viability assays offer several benefits, including speed, reduced price, and capacity for automation (Aslantürk 2018). They do not yet possess the technological sophistication to replace animal testing completely, which has significant drawbacks. At the end of the experiment, it is essential to understand how many cells are still viable and/ or how many cells are dead. Current practices in the disciplines of toxicology and pharmacology utilize an extensive variety of cytotoxicity and cell viability experiments. Nowadays, a diverse array of studies examining cytotoxic effects and cell viability are employed within the domains of toxicology and pharmacology. Detailed inspection of the assay technique is required before deciding on the type of interaction (Aslantürk 2018). There are various categories for cytotoxicity and cell viability tests; in this section, these assays are categorized by the sorts of endpoints that are assessed (color changes, fluorescence, luminescence, etc.). Broadly, these tests can be categorized into: (a) Dye exclusion assays such as trypan blue, eosin, Congo red, and erythrosine B assays; (b) Colorimetric assays; (c) Fluorometric assays; and (d) Luminometric assays. Viable cells exclude dyes in the dye exclusion method, but dead cells do not. Although the staining process is rather straightforward, running experiments on a significant sample volume is challenging and time-intensive. By dye exclusion, membrane integrity can be measured. These dyes include eosin, Congo red, erythrosine B, and trypan blue, among many others. Trypan blue has seen the highest use out of all the dyes listed (Aslantürk 2018). Under the dye exclusion assay, we have two widely used approaches: (i) trypan blue dye exclusion assay and (ii) erythrosine B dye exclusion assay. Trypan blue dye exclusion assay is employed to count the number of alive and/or dead cells in a cell suspension. A substantial negatively ionized molecule is trypan blue. The trypan blue dye exclusion experiment is based on the idea that whereas dead cells lack entire cell membranes, living cells do. In this assay, test substances are serially diluted and cultured with adherent or non-adherent cells for a range of periods, whereas an important dye for counting live cells has already been developed: erythrosine B. This dye exclusion assay’s fundamental workings are comparable to the trypan blue dye exclusion assay’s. Although being a different bio-safe vital dye for cell counting, erythrosine B is not frequently employed to determine whether a cell is alive or dead (Aslantürk 2018). 292 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 6.7 Sulforhodamine B Protein Staining One of the most widely used techniques for in vitro cytotoxicity screening is Sulforhodamine B protein staining, which was established in 1990. The assay is determined by the ability of SRB to bind to protein elements of cells that have been trichloroacetic acid-fixed to tissue culture plates (TCA). Under conditions that are only mildly acidic, SRB dissociates into a brilliant pink amino acid remnant. In accordance with the stoichiometric nature of SRB binding, The quantity of dye obtained from cells that have been stained correlates directly with the mass of the stained cells. The test can be run in a 96-well format due to the SRB staining’s intense intensity. By achieving a signal-to-noise ratio of 4.83 at a cell density of 5,000 cells per well, researchers have demonstrated the assay’s ability to detect densities as low as 1,000–2,000 cells per well. The assay exhibits a sensitivity level comparable to that of widely employed visible dye staining techniques in fluorescence analysis. The SRB technique has also been proven to be successful in analyzing the interactions between irradiation and chemotherapy, as well as for evaluating the in vitro susceptibility of cancer cells to radiation, with sensitivity similar to that of the conventional clonogenic assay (Vichai and Kirtikara 2006). The SRB assay’s sensitivity is higher than that of the Lowry or Bradford assays and on par with a number of fluorescence assays. Colorimetric, nondestructive, and indefinitely stable are the characteristics of the SRB assay’s endpoint. The SRB assay is a useful and sensitive method for determining the cytotoxicity caused by drugs as well as for determining how clonogenicity is measured. The SRB approach is additionally quick and affordable. As a result of these practical developments, the SRB test is now a suitable and sensitive assay for determining drug-induced cytotoxicity, even in large- scale applications (V oigt 2005). Haemocompatibility Assay (ISO 10993-4:2017) One of the most crucial requirements for a blood-contacting biomaterial’s effective in vivo application is its hemocompatibility. Hence, prior to clinical applications, thorough in vitro tests in accordance with ISO 10993-4 are necessary. Blood- contacting biomaterials’ clinical utility is constrained by a number of important factors, including haemocomptibility. These substances are in direct touch with blood, a complex “organ” made up of erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets (which make up 1% of the blood), which is composed of 55% plasma and 44% erythrocytes. To avoid the activation and destruction of blood components, it is essential to thoroughly investigate any harmful interactions between newly produced materials and blood (Weber et al. 2018). Cardiovascular implants are increasingly significant in regenerative medicine . New polymer-based biomaterials that prevent adverse responses, especially thrombotic events, are desperately needed to enhance the safety and functionality of blood-contacting implants (Jung et al. 2013) . The thrombotic reaction that is created when a substance or device comes into contact with blood and causes complement activation, platelet response, and the beginning of the blood coagulation cascade is known as haemocomptibility (Figure 5; Mulinti et al. 2018). Coagulation: The activation, adhesion, and aggregation of platelets, as well as the deposition and maturation of fibrin, are all components of the coagulation process. Upon damage to the endothelium lining a blood artery, coagulation starts nearly immediately (Figure 6). The innate coagulation pathway is activated by touch when plasma proteins interact with artificial surfaces. The plasma kallikrein-kinin system, also known as the contact-phase system, is made up of the non-enzymatic coagulation factor high molecular weight kininogen (HMWK), three serine proteinases – factors XII and XII and plasma prekallikrein (PK) – as well as three serine proteases, factors XII, XI, and XII. Blood is converted from Factor XII to the active enzyme Factor XIIa when it comes into contact with synthetic, negatively charged surfaces such as kaolin, glass, collagen, silica, or dextran sulfate. HMWK is changed into bradykinin by Factor XIIa, while PK is transformed into active kallikrein (Weber et al. 2018). 2. Platelets: Local prothrombotic substances like tissue factor and bound platelet secretion products both function as stimulants for platelet activation (Figure 5). Platelet activation can be triggered by several routes. Large numbers of platelets circulate in the bloodstream under normal physiological circumstances for 7–10 days in a dormant state. A healthy endothelium monolayer serves as a protective boundary separating the bloodstream from the surrounding tissues and inhibits platelet adhesion and activation by releasing substances, including nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin (PGI2). When biomaterial is exposed to the blood, platelets may get unintentionally activated, which might cause thrombotic problems. Haemocomptibility tests thus include a critical component that analyses platelet activity (Weber et al. 2018). 3. Complement System: The possibility of the complement system being activated by a medical device is assessed using the complement activation test. This humoral immune response may be brought on by the ingestion of a foreign substance and can have negative outcomes, including tissue damage and inflammation. Under the laws governing the testing of biomaterials designed for blood contact, the study of complement activation is a pertinent standard. Future Prospects There have been several recent breakthroughs in blood-interfacing materials as a result of the growing significance of biomaterials in our society over the past few decades. Medical devices, including arterial implants, renal dialysis devices, central venous access devices, and artificial cardiac valves, are responsible for a large portion of the industrialized society’s improved quality of life. Meanwhile, sophisticated biomaterials have largely supplanted many conventional biomaterials, offering biologically inspired design and responsive properties. These issues must be taken into consideration in efforts to make innovative biomaterials, medical devices, and prostheses available for clinical use. According to ISO 10993, the specific uses of biomaterials in the particular medical device under consideration call for the in vivo verification of in vitro results. To correctly and sufficiently detect biological reactions to nanodevices and tissue-created scaffolds, which may contain a variety of components, including novel materials, cells, and proteins, new biological response assays must be developed. It is obvious that new and creative biological response test systems must be created in order to fully and properly evaluate nanodevices and tissue-generated scaffolds due to this substantial hurdle. Introduction Thixotropic biopolymers or their modified conjugates are receiving significant consideration due to their wide-ranging applications in food, agricultural (Mishra et al. 2018), pharmaceutical (Silva and Sato 2017), biotechnological and cosmetic industries (Buruiana and Ioan 2018; Paul et al. 2017). Thixotropy is the characteristic of viscous matters or gelling systems wherein the matter turns to liquid upon applied stimuli, strain, or agitation, and the fluid displays a reversible structural change upon removing applied stimuli without getting the volume of the system changed (Lee et al. 2009). Several biopolymeric gelling systems become more fluid when subjected to such stimuli, stresses, or strain for a fixed time. It is reversible and regains its viscosity if left undisturbed. A thixotropic can be defined as a phenomenon of fluid that takes a predictable time to achieve equilibrium viscosity while introduced to shear. Several fluids that get back to their original gel state almost instantly are called pseudoplastic fluids, e.g., ketchup. Others, like yogurt, take a longer period to become nearly solid. A number of gelling systems and colloidal fluids exhibit thixotropic behavior and a steady form on rest that becomes fluid upon shearing or agitation. Previously, temperature was the only significant stimulus that could cause such physical changes in gels, which allowed these gels to melt on heating and solidify on cooling (Barnes 1997). Figure 1 depicts the phenomenon of thixotropy of gel. Rheological Characterization of Biomaterials 299 The field of biopolymer-based soft matter and its uses in biomedical engineering are fetching more attention and importance because of its availability at lower cost, environmentally friendly impact, and non-toxicity to humans. Some advanced materials can be designed by tuning these biopolymers in terms of physical or chemical modification. Many biopolymers have already been reported to have such properties. Chemically and physically modified or cross-linked gels showing thixotropic behavior attract great attention in the field of biomedical research due to their self-healing ability. These gels are especially suitable for injectable purposes. Natural polymers-based biomaterials are widely applicable for designing stretchable gels due to their chemical or physical modification to introduce elasticity, thixotropy, etc. Such gelling matters have appeared as attractive candidates as matrixes for the regeneration and repair of various tissues expanding the field of tissue engineering (Li et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2019). The development of polymeric biomimetic materials for bone tissue engineering has also been studied and reported in the literature (Chahal et al. 2019). Some of the medical implantations exhibit some restrictions due to difficulties associated with injectability and their poor mechanical properties (Barbucci et al. 2008). With this in view, several attempts have been made to achieve biopolymers’ smart-based gelling systems with better physico-mechanical properties to overcome these issues. Polymers like cellulose and its analogs, guar gum, xanthan gum, and several seaweed polysaccharides—namely agarose, carrageenan, sodium alginate chitosan, and fucoidan—have been broadly studied and used in tissue engineering, regenerative medicines, biomedical implants, and other applications. Their favorable characteristics include biocompatibility, easy gelling nature, low toxicity, and non- immunogenicity (Lin et al. 2015; Lara et al. 2022; Kirtania et al. 2020). Most of the research nowadays focuses on biopolymers-based gelling systems to design various formulations exhibiting potential utility to achieve targeted delivery systems. Delivery of the active pharmaceutical doses at the targeted place is achieved through biopolymeric gels for drug-delivery systems like buccal, oral, vaginal, rectal, topical, and nasal. Many of the biopolymeric gels show a great rheological transition that supports the physicho-mechanical characteristics of the designed drug-delivery systems. With this perspective in mind, this review highlights a few such studies based on several polysaccharide-based thixotropic gelling systems and their potential applications in the field of biomaterial research. Rheological Studies of Thixotropic Gels Thixotropic properties of materials can be evaluated using the following rheological experiments. 2.1 Dynamic Viscosities With Different Shear Rates In this experiment, the flow property of the materials can be determined, in which dynamic viscosities at different shear rates are determined; the flow curve also represents shear stress against shear rate, which was used for the calculation using the Power Law model equation (1). τ = K·γn (1) K is the consistency index, while ‘n’ represents the flow behavior index. τ and γ are the shear stress and shear rate, respectively. 2.2 Hysteresis Loop Area Experiment This experiment is well known and one of the basic rheological experiments used for the determination of thixotrpicity. In this experiment, the material is exposed to varying shear rates against different shear stresses. The shape of the graph represents a rising sweep instantly, followed by a descending sweep. Thixotropic area (Ar) can be calculated by using the equation (2) as reported by Dolz et al. (2000). Ar= (Aup– Adown/Aup) x 100 (2) Here, Aup = area of the upstream, Adown = area of downstream data points, and (Aup−Adown) represents hysteresis or thixotropic loop area. The hysteresis loop area is directly proportional to the thixotropicity of materials; in other words, the more the thixotropic area or hysteresis loop area, the more would be the thixotropicity. 2.3 Time-Dependent Thixotropic Property This experiment is also used to determine the thixotropic properties of a material. The time-dependent thixotropic behavior of materials can be measured by employing time-dependent viscosities at various shear rates. For example, the experiment is to be conducted at shear rates 1s-1, 100s-1, and 1s-1. The time intervals were 25–45s (first 5 points), 46–96s (100 points), and 97–345s (500 points), respectively. This experiment shows the time-dependent viscosity of the material with varying shear rates. 2.4 Yield Stress Experiment Yield stress is to be measured by a slow, constant shear rate applied to a sample, and the resulting stress is determined as a function of time. The determination of static yield stress is achieved by a stress sweep where the direct reversible deformation ends (Galindo-Rosales et al. 2011). Rheological Characterization of Biomaterials 301 2.5 Creep-Recovery Experiment The creep-recovery experiment is well-known and useful for the evaluation of the thixotropic properties. For this experiment, constant stress is to be applied, which is less than the measured yield stress of the material, and then the recovery is monitored for a specific time. 3. Biopolymeric Thixotropic Gels and Their Applications Several polysaccharides, such as seaweed polysaccharides, plant polysaccharides, and animal-based polysaccharides, are to be modified to introduce thixotropic in their polymeric backbone to benefit from this property. However, few of these polysaccharides already exhibited such behavior, while some of their conjugates show interesting rheological transitions that made these polymers a candidate for modification to introduce these properties. Few such biopolymers belonging to each category have been highlighted in this section. Some of the examples of all types of polysaccharides, e.g., sodium alginate (seaweed polysaccharide), cellulose, guar gum (plant polysaccharide), and xanthan gum (bacterial polysaccharide), are highlighted in this section of the review. 3.1 Sodium Alginate as a Thixotropic Gel Sodium alginate is one of the biopolymers that is extensively studied and used in drug-delivery systems and tissue engineering as well as in biomedical applications because of their biocompatible nature, gelling ability, non-immunogenicity and lower toxicity (George and Abraham 2006). Conventional uses of sodium alginate as an excipient in drugs are usually dependent on gel-forming and thickening properties (Tønnesen and Karlsen 2002). Modification of alginates has been reviewed by many authors (Cathell et al. 2010; Yang et al. 2011). Delivery of cells, insulin, and proteins in injectable mode are also reported using alginate as one of the prior materials (Silva et al. 2006; Silva and Sato 2017; Gombotz and Wee 1998). Unmodified alginate gels possess shear thinning behavior and low thixotropic properties. This property be induced by introducing various substrates on its backbone (Sasaki et al. 1956; “US Pat., 5,473,005, 1995,” n.d.; “US Pat., 2003/0072803A1, 2003,” n.d.; V oronko et al. 2002; Grassi et al. 2006; Pongjanyakul and Puttipipatkhachorn 2007; Daemi et al. 2013). A sprayable new soft gel based on sodium alginate with remarkable thixotropic behavior has been reported (Mahesh et al. 2012). Further, sodium alginate and 1-naphthylamine-based amide derivatives have also been reported to form soft thixotropic hydrogel (Chejara et al. 2013). Alginate-aminocaproic acid thixo-gel with multi-stimuli sensitivity as a bio-injectable gel is also reported that shows multi-stimuli responses with various applied stimuli, e.g., heat, stress, ultrasound, etc. (Chejara et al. 2016). Further, a microporous soft hydrogel derived from sodium alginate and aminosalicylic acid was studied for viscosupplementation application, wherein it was found to be a great alternative to any potential gelling viscosupplement for arthritis problems (Chejara et al. 2017). 302 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization 3.2 Electrolyte Added Gelling Systems Sodium alginate-based gelling systems with thixotropic behavior are reported in literature wherein these gels were obtained by the addition of significant amounts of several divalent ionic salts to sodium alginate solutions (Figure 2) (Sasaki et al. 1956). The thixotropic evaluation was carried out simply by determining the setting time detected when inverting the tube. Changes in the setting time of these gels were noted due to various factors such as the added different amounts of the electrolyte, the aging time of the gel, the degree of polymerization of the parent polymer, and the pH of the system. Change in the thixotropic behavior was also seen with various volumes of the system. In addition, thixotropy was observed in total around 25–54% of alginate combined with cupric ions, while more than this percentage, the combination of alginate and cupric salt results in non-thixotropic behavior. Guar Gum as a Thixotropic Gel Guar gum (GG) is a naturally occurring water-soluble polymer made up of poly galactomannan units found from the seeds of Cyamopsis tetragonolobus, a native India guar plant, having linear backbone chain of β (1-4)-linked D-mannose units (M) with randomly attached side chains of α (1-6)-linked galactose units(G) (Prajapat and Gogate 2015; McCleary et al. 1985; Gupta et al. 2009). Figure 5 depicts the general structural formula of guar gum polymer. Guar gum solution possesses high viscosities even at low concentrations due to its water-absorbing capacity. Guar gum is the most popular water-soluble hydrocolloid polymer used as a stabilizing, gelling, emulsifying, and mostly thickening agent for applications including food industries, cosmetics, pharmaceutical sectors, etc. (Wang et al. 2016). Generally, polysaccharides can be easily converted into their derivatives using either chemical or biochemical methods due to the presence of reactive functional moieties on the molecular chain (Prabaharan 2011). In addition, polysaccharides (guar gum) are an abundant source in nature, along with non- toxicity, stability, hydrophilicity, and safe nature. Due to the extensive properties of polysaccharides, many studies have been carried out on their application as drug- delivery systems. The property of flow behavior plays a key role in the development of the pharmaceutical process at each step during mixing, filling, and packing. Therefore, it is important for pharmaceutical scientists to study the flow properties with their influencing factors and effects on the efficacy of different physical properties, especially on liquid drugs (Lee et al. 2009). A viscosity system has either a Newtonian or non-Newtonian flow behavior with the applied shear/composition of the liquid, as depicted in Figure 6 (Likavčan et al. 2014). Water, honey, castor oil, alcohol, and ethyl ether are all examples of Newtonian fluids, whereas maximum thixotropic fluids, like putties, cosmetics, ointments, toothpaste, clays, and pastes, are examples of non-Newtonian fluids. Depending on the end-use applications, the parent polymer, guar gum, can be modified chemically with the objective of altering its intrinsic viscosity as well as Rheological Characterization of Biomaterials 305 rheological behavior (Barbucci et al. 2008). However, physically modified or cross- linked conjugates are used with the aim of obtaining a water-insoluble compound. Wang et al. However, at pH 14, there was no change in the gel viscosity values. The author also conducted a detailed study on pH levels ranging from 7–14 by calculating rheological parameters. With increasing concentrations of OH– ions, there is an increase in negative electric charge density on guar gum polymer chains, which results in more negative zeta potential, and due to the electrostatic repulsion effect, guar gum polymer chains fall under stretching with relatively high entanglement density. Conclusion Herein, in the present section of the book, the rheological characteristics of biomaterials, i.e., sodium alginate and guar gum-based thixotropic gelling systems, have been demonstrated. Both polymers show a significant improvement in their flow behavior after chemical or physical modification onto their polymeric backbone. The studied rheological properties open-up many doors for an individual researcher working on biopolymeric-based materials to be used for many potential applications. Such studies and modified conjugates may have potential use in biomedical applications, regenerative medicines, and other drug-delivery systems. Also, introducing thixotropy into these biopolymers creates other options for designing a wide variety of biopolymeric materials, with special reference to polymers such as agarose, carrageenan, xanthan gum, gum arabic, tamarind gum, etc. Acknowledgment The authors acknowledge the entire Department of Chemistry, Uka Tarsadia University, for their valuable input during the writeup of this review. Introduction A biomaterial is an engineered substance with organic and inorganic origins specifically designed to replicate and replace lost tissues without causing damage to the surrounding environment. They have been used since ancient times, and their evolution has made them more potent, versatile, and simple to use in clinical settings. Keeping in mind that an ideal biomaterial must be biocompatible, bioinert, bioactive, bioabsorbable, and bioadaptable to be considered suitable for implantation (Figure 1); the classification of biomaterials is based on: (i) origin, i.e., natural or artificial; (ii) chemical nature, i.e., ceramic, metal, or polymer; and (iii) physical properties, i.e., roughness and porosity. Biomaterials play a crucial role in biological interactions, for which they are thoroughly assessed for their biocompatibility (Birajdar et al. 2021). Before heading toward a vibrant assessment of in vivo testing of biomaterials, it is imperative to understand the basic steps. First, in vitro studies, i.e., cell culture assays, are carried out by growing the cells on biomaterials. If favorable results are achieved, animal models are further used to assess the organ-implant interactions and the nature of the histological response induced by the implant is compared with that induced by a reference biomaterial for in vivo evaluation. However, the point-to-point association between in vitro and in vivo studies has 310 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization been observed to be quite low and could imply that these biomaterials may promote cellular adhesion and proliferation in vitro while failing to do the same in vivo and vice versa. This failure is strongly associated with the sophistication of in vivo tissue organization, which entails elaborated cell communication, mechanical load, and continuous flow; yet, none of these conditions recapitulate in standard cell cultures (Atif et al. 2021). This disengagement between in vitro and in vivo studies causes time delays, exorbitant expenditures, and the inordinate employment of animal experimentation to characterize biomaterials. Therefore, improved cell culture techniques that integrate with appropriate animal models enhance the predictive outcomes of implanting a biomaterial in the body. The choice of animal species and disease models (Ribitsch et al. 2020) may potentially improve the way we study in vivo biomaterial testing and thus facilitate addressing significant biological questions that have so far arisen in such studies. Several natural and synthetic biomaterials are examined for their application as scaffolds in tissue engineering procedures for creating more enhanced, sophisticated, and reliable 3D microenvironments so as to promote the development and survival of various cell types. Furthermore, metal and its alloys are extensively used as scaffolds, bone plates, and bone screws for human tissue repair and regeneration (Pushp et al. 2021). The selection of an optimal biomaterial depends on material-driven cellular response and its ability to provide an environment for the proliferation of target cells and requires the incorporation of crucial initial steps in the design of biomimetic systems that aid in the investigation of various organ structures and functions (Ozgun et al. 2022). This highlights that the potential evolution of biomaterials necessitates a thorough perception of fundamental properties of materialistic behavior concerning the bio-environment (Paul 2019). Biomaterials play an indispensable function in addressing many medical complications with magnified precision and reflecting amazing progress in the context of orthopedics, cardiovascular, ophthalmology, Figure 1: Ideal characteristics of biomaterials. In Vivo Animal Models Used for Biomaterials Testing and Their Significance The English scientists William Rusell and Rex Burch were the first to voice their concern for experimental animals in their publication, The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique. They proposed the principles of the “three Rs”, which fulfilled the objectives of research scientists: (1) substitution of animals by use of in vitro methods or by using phylogenetically lower animals; (2) reduction of the number of animals required; and (3) improvement of experimental methods to lower the ethical costs of painful or stressful procedures (Mukherjee et al. 2022). Biomaterial testing is an intermediate step between preclinical research and human clinical trials. As a result, a suitable in vivo animal defect model for testing biomaterial substitutes for defect repair must be developed or adopted. It is critical to focus on assessing a clinically relevant in vivo testing model for analyzing biomaterials’ biocompatibility, mechanical properties, degradation, and interactions with host tissues to evaluate biomaterials for development as organ substitutes for organ defect repair (de Lacerda et al. 2020). Every animal model possesses its advantages and disadvantages (Table 7), so it necessitates the consideration of several factors when selecting a species of animal for a particular model. The selection of animal species is based on the acknowledged research question (Muhamed et al. 2015). The factors that influence the selection of animal models include expenses to acquire and maintain animals, accessibility, social acceptability, forbearance to confinement, the convenience of housing and handling, inter-animal homogeneity, supporting staff with adequate facilities, biological characteristics analogous to humans, and an informational biological database on species. Additionally, the chosen species’ lifespan should be adequate for the course of the experiment or research. Finally, the animal’s size must be critical to ensure that it is appropriate for the number and size of implants chosen. According to Hazzard et al. (1992), the point of view captured in vivo biomaterial testing research, no single animal model can be used for all purposes, nor can a model be disregarded as unsuitable for all purposes. Furthermore, multiple model systems are expected to completely recapitulate a wide range of information (Pearce et al. 2007). 3. Recent Advances in Biomaterials Testing—Future Prospects In recent years, many human body tissues, such as osseous, denticles, sinew, ligaments, and other load-bearing constructs, have been successfully replaced in the human body. For biomedical applications, traditional remedies, such as wood and rubber, and synthetic remedies, such as metals and glasses, have been utilized since ancient times. Commonly used biomaterials such as alloys, ceramics, and polymers In Vivo Testing of Biomaterials in Animal Models 323 have a unique atomic geometry, resulting in distinctive physical, mechanical, and chemical properties. Considering these, biomaterials have been gaining momentum as an alternative application for various body parts implantation. Over the last few years, metals have been used for the majority of load-bearing applications in the biomedical system due to their substantial mechanical advantages, including strength, stiffness, and fatigue life (Paul 2019). Despite the fact that many metals and alloys have been manufactured so far, only a few will be benchmark materials for implantation materials in the future, such as stainless steel, cobalt- chromium alloys, nickel, pure titanium and its alloys (Ti-6Al-4V and Ti-6Al- 7Nb), magnesium, and so on. Besides these, the highly porous ceramics assist with prosthetic stabilization and bone ingrowth. They have, however, been exploited for reduced-loaded or unloaded bearing applications due to their porous properties and minimum mechanical strength. Recently, three basic types of ceramics, such as bioactive, bioinert, and bioresorbable, have become significantly more promising biomaterials for biomedical applications. The most prominent behavior of the first generation (the 1960s and 1970s) of ceramic biomaterials was their “inertness” (alumina and zirconia), reported in Hench’s classification; they drastically reduced the foreign particle response as well as the immunogenic response (Pearce et al. 2007). In an instance, Merola et al. recreated the articulation functionality in the replacement surgery of the hip joint by substituting the joint with high-density, highly pure alumina (Al 2O3). In this aspect, ceramics act as a potential alternative due to their limitless wear and corrosion resistance, along with their high strength and good biocompatibility (Mayer et al. 2018). Further, second-generation (1980 and 2000) became more apparent in the literature, supporting the notion that ceramics exhibited dual properties in terms of “bioactive (hydroxyapatite glass ceramics) as well as bioresorbable (calcium phosphate ceramics). Bioactive materials stimulate a biological response in the body, such as chemical bond formation with soft tissues, and reinforce them toward particular responses and behavioral patterns (Yadav and Gangwar 2018). The principles of bioactivity and biodegradability are combined in the new generation of ceramics, and the combination of material properties with their ability to obtain efficient signaling and activate specific cellular mechanisms and behaviors. Because of their outstanding properties, natural and synthetic polymers are suitable for a wide range of biomedical applications. Natural polymers with good bioactivity and cytocompatibility, such as collagen, fibronectin, silk fibroin, fibrin, chitosan, and many others, whose microstructure, degradation rate, mechanical properties, porosity, and others can be tailored based on the nature of the polymers, have been extensively utilized in tissue engineering applications. 6. Conclusion Many lines of evidence in this chapter showed the in vivo methods for evaluating biomaterial biological compatibility. The methods were presented from two viewpoints: (1) international in vivo assays oriented around preclinical biosafety evaluation and potential risk assessments, and (2) more specific material and application-specific in vivo assays for specific cell- and tissue-based responses. In particular, important methods for gathering extensive information were narrated 324 Smart Ways of Biomaterial Designing Synthesis and Characterization in concomitant case examples because the latter area is complex and diverse. These examples show how well-designed in vivo assays are essential for advancing new biomaterial therapies into clinical practice. In today’s proof-of-concept studies, a comprehensive biocompatibility test plan developed by engineers and material scientists is more likely to endow vast areas of prototypes made of well- characterized biocompatible materials with a long history of appropriate utilization. The challenges faced by most production engineers, material scientists, regulatory bodies, and standard developers will undoubtedly increase with the range of biomaterials and the expansion of their applications. Nonetheless, the progress of such a functional framework for the development and application of in vivo assays that can accommodate novel therapies, improved medical materials, and advances in medicine will undoubtedly continue. Arpana Parihar is currently working as a research associate at the Department of Translational Medicine, All India Institute of Medical Sciences Bhopal, MP, India. ACM ISBN 979-8-4007-1197-8/25/03… https://doi.org/10.1145/3689050.3704427 As the HCI community continues to develop new materials for tangible interfaces, the way in which knowledge is disseminated has also expanded to more effectively communicate complex, embodied material experiences. Accordingly, we explore two goals in this pictorial: (1) to develop new sustainable biomaterials for 3D printing, thus extending the current library of materials for digital fabrication, and (2) to further the way the pictorial format is used to disseminate material knowledge by exploring alternative types of publications, specifically cookbooks. This cookbook discusses how to develop biomaterials for paste extrusion 3D printing by first introducing printability, usability, and sustainability as qualities that biomaterial recipes should strive to achieve. We then present ingredients, tools, and processes for working with biomaterials, followed by three exemplary biomaterial recipes made from sawdust, orange peels, and tree leaves. The cookbook closes with recommendations for adapting new biomaterials in the future. Biomaterial Recipes for 3D Printing Fiona Bell Computer Science University of New Mexico Albuquerque, USA fbell1@unm.edu Camila Friedman-Gerlicz Computer Science University of New Mexico Albuquerque, USA cfriedmangerlicz@gmail.com Leah Buechley Computer Science University of New Mexico Albuquerque, USA buechley@unm.edu Front CoverBack Cover 1. print one-sided copy of cookbook 2. cut the cover in half and fold the internal pages inward along dotted line 5. adhere blank pages together (e.g., back of front cover to back of p1, back of p2 to back of p3, etc.) then read! staple staple staple staple staple staplestaple staple more extensive instructions can be found in our supplementary materials 3. stack internal pages on top of each other in order and place the front and back covers on top and bottom 4. staple at designated spots to bind cookbook cut A Cookbook of Sustainable and Extrudable Bio-Pastes Abstract How to Assemble this Pictorial 1 Cooking and science have entangled histories, with cooking being known as a form of practical chemistry [54]. Recipes and scientific protocols hold a high resemblance to one another, both including a list of required ingredients and tools, as well as a step-by-step procedure. Recipes/protocols act as a way for cooks/scientists to both disseminate their work as well as reproduce the work of others. Beyond reproducibility, however, the recipe/ protocol can also act as a starting point which can then be flexibly adjusted and adapted to suit specific needs and requirements. Cooking, ceramics, and biology communities have long used recipes as a format to communicate Do-It-Yourself (DIY) procedures for everything from baking soufflés [16] and formulating glazes [18, 33] to editing DNA [23, 47] and making bioplastics [24, 48, 53]. Inspired by the recipe as a tradition for sharing knowledge of physical practices, we utilize the cookbook format to present a collection of our own biomaterial recipes. Just like a traditional cookbook, this pictorial is intended to encourage readers to engage in making our recipes and adapting new recipes of their own. Through these recipes, we hope to communicate embodied material knowledge that can be lost through other forms of written dissemination. In doing so, we align ourselves with other HCI researchers engaged in academic publishing that utilizes the pictorial format “as a platform for sharing activities and modes of representation that can scaffold craft knowledge” [22] by employing more instructional, interactive, and creative methods for imparting material knowledge [19, 20, 26, 36, 62, 84]. We intend for this cookbook to be printed out and assembled so that it can live beyond traditional academic settings in makerspaces, kitchens, and creative labs—acting as a practical ‘how-to’ guide for making biomaterials for paste extrusion 3D printing. fold inwardIntroductionIntroduction 2 ContentsContents Introduction Why a Cookbook? Sustainable Biomaterials in HCI Paste Extrusion 3D Printing Qualities Printability Usability Sustainability Ingredients Core Ingredients Optional Ingredients Tools Specialized Equipment Process Making Recipes Printing Recipes Sawdust Bio-Paste Recipe Preparation Qualities Notes Orange Peel Bio-Paste Recipe Preparation Qualities Notes Tree Leaf Bio-Paste Recipe Preparation Qualities Notes Adapting Recipes Recipe Adaption Workflow Guidance from Failures Ingredient Exchanges Quality Optimization Conclusion Future Vision Acknowledgments Supplementary Materials Pictorial Assembly Instructions Heater Design Print Files We are a team of human-computer interaction (HCI) researchers based in the arid desert of New Mexico, who have been developing biomaterials for the past 5 years and developing materials specifically for 3D printing for the past 2 years. Drawing on these experiences, we present this cookbook to build a deeper understanding within the HCI community of how to approach the development of sustainable biomaterials for 3D printing. This work by no means presents the “only” or “best” way to develop biomaterials, but intends to share our learnings from the past few years to support other practitioners in designing new materials that extend the options for sustainable 3D printing and tangible interfaces. Why a Cookbook? 2 3 4 5 6 6 7 8 9 10 10 11 11 12 12 13 13 14 14 15 15 16 16 17 18 19 20 21 22 28 28 28 43 print tube print bed motor 2 auger nozzle motor 1 connector tube heater With rising demands for physical goods such as consumer electronics, fashion, and homeware, it is now more imperative than ever to consider sustainable modes of making, using, and disposing. Within the field of HCI, design researchers have begun developing methods and materials for the circular design and disposal of goods [12, 50]. Methods of unmaking [71] such as upcyling, repairing, and disassembling have introduced new design workflows that encourage the continued use of existing material goods like electronics [42, 44, 52], textiles [49, 83], and 3D prints [73, 79]. Beyond these methods, new biodegradable materials have been developed to promote ecological regeneration [17, 41]. Biodegradable materials are most commonly referred to as biomaterials— materials derived from biological sources that biodegrade naturally when disposed of in the environment [11]. Popular biomaterials include mycelium [32, 34, 77, 81], algae [4, 45, 74, 86], microbial cellulose [7, 8, 58-60], plants [15, 38, 71], and food waste [10, 68], which have been used as sustainable alternatives to plastics, fabrics, foams, concretes, and clays. In this cookbook, we present a collection of clay-like biomaterials designed specifically for paste extrusion 3D printing. Due to the increasing popularity of 3D printing as a method for fabricating beautiful objects with forms, textures, and computational meaning that cannot be achieved by hand, we present sustainable biomaterial alternatives to traditional materials for 3D printing, namely plastics. Polylactic acid (PLA) and Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) are the most commonly used printing materials. While PLA is bio-based it does not naturally biodegrade in the environment, instead requiring commercial composting systems [46]. Meanwhile, ABS is derived from petroleum and cannot biodegrade when disposed of [61]. Moreover, PLA and ABS are notoriously difficult to recycle [37]. In contrast, our biomaterials are derived from renewable bio-waste streams, readily biodegrade when disposed of in the environment, and are easily recyclable. As such, these biomaterials enable a more sustainable avenue for 3D printing. Previous biomaterials developed for 3D printing have been made from spent coffee grounds [68], corn and wheat flour [14], pecan shell flour [28], mussel shells [69], and bamboo fibers inoculated with mycelium [70]. We add three new biomaterial recipes—based on sawdust, orange peels, and tree leaves—to this growing library, as well as a broader set of considerations and methods regarding DIY biomaterial development to promote more widespread use of sustainable materials for 3D printing. We design all of our biomaterials for paste extrusion 3D printing. Also known as Direct Ink Write (DIW or DW) printing or Robocasting [63], this additive fabrication technique builds objects by extruding material in layers. Instead of extruding a filament like PLA or ABS, we use printers that extrude paste-like materials. This approach has been widely used to print clays [13, 21, 30], foods [43, 51, 56], and hydrogels [31, 55, 65]. We print our biomaterial recipes with a low-cost commercial paste extrusion desktop printer called the Eazao Zero [27]; which resembles other printers such as the PotterBot [66], WASP [80], TRONXY [75] and Lutum [78]. To print with the Eazao, we load the print tube with a given biomaterial. Motor 1 then turns a plunger that pushes the biomaterial through the print tube and connector tube into the print head. Motor 2 turns the auger mechanism within the print head, which pushes the biomaterial out of a 1.5 mm inner diameter nozzle at an extrusion rate of 0.7 mm/mm. The biomaterial is then printed at a speed of 1000 mm/min onto a small wooden board lined with a mesh fabric to enable the easy removal of printed objects from the print bed. As the biomaterial is extruded, it is partially dried by a custom heater system we built that fits around the nozzle. To control the Eazao, we upload .gcode files designed in Rhino 3D and Grasshopper. We employ open- source software developed by the HCI community for clay 3D printing such as WeaveSlicer [30], CoilCam [13], and Extruder Turtle [64]. we use an Eazao Zero [27] to 3D print all of our biomaterials in this work 3D printing tree leaf biomaterial Sustainable Biomaterials in HCI Paste Extrusion 3D Printing 3D printed sawdust biomaterial print board with mesh Sustainability Usability 5 To achieve a printable biomaterial, its rheology is the biggest consideration. Rheology is the study of how matter deforms and flows when subjected to an applied force [3], which, in our case, describes how the biomaterial flows through the 3D printer. Several qualities play into the rheology of a material, we look at the rheological characteristics of our biomaterials through the qualities of cohesion, hardness, flow, and stability. Cohesion. The biomaterial forms a uniform paste with no clumps and a consistent texture that holds together by not being too wet or too dry. Test cohesion by looking at and feeling the biomaterial paste. We recommend grinding and sieving all ingredients to a small size before mixing for cohesion. Hardness. The biomaterial paste is soft enough that it can be pushed through the printer, but hard enough that it is stable on the print bed. Test hardness through feel and with a penetrometer [14]. We aim for hardness penetrometer values between 0.2-0.3 kg/cm2. Flow. The biomaterial paste has shear-thinning rheological flow behavior, meaning that it behaves more like a liquid when force is applied and more like a solid when force is removed [57, 85]. Test flow by extruding the biomaterial paste with a hand-held syringe and/or with the 3D printer. We recommend looking for a cohesive paste that requires minimal force to extrude. Stability. The biomaterial paste is stable on the print bed once extruded, allowing layers to build up on top of each other without collapsing. Test stability by observing how the biomaterial paste holds up as an object is printed. We recommend checking stability by observing how basic cylinders are printed. Find our cylinder .gcode file in supplementary materials. 6 QualitiesQualities To develop a biomaterial that is printable (i.e., can be reliably extruded by the printer), usable (i.e., results in a final printed object of high quality), and sustainable (i.e., is derived from renewable sources and degrades naturally in the environment), we identify 10 separate, yet interdependent qualities that recipes should consider. We identified these qualities by first reviewing related literature, notably taking inspiration from Duty et al.’s technical overview of material characteristics for 3D printing [25]. We further surfaced and refined these qualities through our personal recipe development process; selecting final qualities that best guided us in choosing appropriate ingredients and ingredient ratios. Each quality is paired with recommended properties, measurements and tests to gain insight into how the biomaterial aligns with the given quality. To achieve a usable biomaterial, it must dry in a predictable way and lead to a durable object. Shrinkage can be the largest issue; drastic shrinkage can result in biomaterial objects that do not resemble the initially designed form and that are not structurally sound. Predictability. The printed biomaterial object resembles the designed model, meaning the object does not crack or distort dramatically during drying. Test predictability by observing how a complex form dries and by calculating the shrinkage rate, which is the relative change in size of the object [9]. We recommend observing a how a complex vessel dries and measuring the shrinkage of cylinders in both height and diameter. Find our cylinder and vessel .gcode in supplementary materials. Durability The printed biomaterial objects is structurally durable, meaning it can be reasonably applied to real-world use cases without breaking, crumbling, or falling apart. Test durability through measuring strength and observing objects in-situ over time. While there are many types of strength, we recommend testing compression strength by following ASTM C773 [1], the standard test method for uniaxial compressive strength of clay materials using a universal testing machine. Printability To achieve a sustainable biomaterial we select bio-based ingredients and examine modes of circular disposal via recyclability, dissolvability, and biodegradability. Biobased. The ingredients that make up the biomaterial recipe are grown and derived from renewable, biological sources such as plants, animals, and fungi. Recyclability. The dried biomaterial, including print waste, failed prints, and no longer wanted objects, can be transformed back into a printable paste. We recommend checking recyclability by grinding up dried biomaterial into a powder and rehydrating it into a printable paste [14]. Dissolvability. The biomaterial breaks down into non-toxic biomass in a water environment. Test dissolvability by submerging a printed biomaterial object in water and observing it over time [68]. We recommend observing the disintegration of a biomaterial tile in room temperature water. Find our tile .gcode in supplementary materials. Biodegradability. The biomaterial breaks down into non-toxic biomass, carbon dioxide, and water when disposed of in a composting system or the natural environment. Test biodegradation by observing the sample assimilate into the environment and/or measuring the mass loss of a biomaterial over time [6, 7, 72]. To be considered compostable, the biomaterial must biodegrade 90% in less than 180 days, in a composting environment [2]. We recommend following a DIY version of ISO 16929 [29], the standard method for testing the disintegration of a given material within soil, where we observe a printed biomaterial tile biodegrade. Find our tile .gcode file in supplementary materials. printability usability sustainabilitysustainability Optional Ingredients Core Ingredients 87 Fillers. Solid ingredients that the biomaterial primarily consists of, the ingredient that volumetrically fills up the most space. Fillers can be mineral or cellulose-based. Given the wide range of ingredient options, the filler has the greatest impact on the final characteristics of the biomaterial: texture, color, smell, shrinkage, density, strength, etc. Fillers must be combined with a specific ratio of stabilizers, binders, and liquids to achieve the necessary printability and usability. We use different cellulose-based fillers sourced from local waste streams for each recipe. Stabilizers. Non-absorbent ingredients that provide stability and predictability to the biomaterial. Most stabilizers are mineral-based. They are crucial for minimizing shrinkage, thus usability. Bio-based stabilizers are grown from bones, shells, and eggs. Non-bio-based but biodegradable binders include sand and dirt. We use eggshells in all of our recipes as a readily available, bio-based stabilizer. Binders. Absorbent ingredients that bind the filler and stabilizer ingredients together. Binders are required to achieve a cohesive biomaterial paste, with shear-thinning flow behavior. Common bio-based binders include wheat flour, gelatin, agar, alginate, methylcellulose, and xanthan gum. We use a combination of methylcellulose (a powder derived from plant cellulose) and xanthan gum (a powder derived from fermented sugar). Liquids. Ingredients that transform all the dry powders into a cohesive, wet biomaterial paste. Water is required to activate binder ingredients, however, other liquid ingredients can be employed. For instance, we experimented with oil to improve predictability and vinegar as a preservative. Pigments. Ingredients such as turmeric, beetroot, and activated charcoal that can be added in small quantities to change the color and/ or the conductivity of the biomaterial without impacting the biodegradability or bio-based quality. Post-Printing. Ingredients that are added to the printed biomaterial object to achieve specific qualities and aesthetics, such as coating the object with beeswax for waterproofing or vegetable oil to give a shine. Guided by our past experiments and our qualities for printability, usability, and sustainability, we identified ingredients that we found were necessary to make biomaterials that suited our requirements. We categorize these ingredients into four core groups (fillers, stabilizers, binders, and liquids), as well as two additional groups of optional ingredients (pigments and post-printing ingredients). We note that this is just a starting point to understand what goes into a biomaterial and can be adjusted and expanded upon in the future. IngredientsIngredients Our recipes present ingredients in terms of their weight for easy reproducibility. However, when developing recipes, we look at ingredients in terms of their volume, especially when identifying the ratio of fillers to stabilizers and dry ingredients to liquid ingredients. While our recipes show that we have more stabilizer by weight, our recipes are primarily filler by volume. This is due to our fillers being less dense than our stabilizers. Meanwhile, all of our recipes have a volume ratio of approximately 100 parts dry ingredients (fillers, stabilizers, and binders) to 80 parts wet ingredients (liquids). orange peels from our personal consumption sawdust from a local furniture artist’s woodshop washed eggshells dirty eggshells sourced from local restaurant collecting cottonwood leaves on our university campus methylcellulose xanthan gum water vegetable oil ground eggshell powder harvesting eggs from local chicken coops Making Recipes Printing Recipes 109 1. select recipe 2. prepare all tools and ingredients 3. combine ingredients into a cohesive paste 4. design and slice model, then upload .gcode to 3D printer 5. fill print tube with biomaterial paste 6. prepare printer by attaching print tube and setting up print bed 7. print model 8. remove printed object from print bed and let it dry 9. once completely dry, use finished object ProcessProcess ToolsTools Beyond the required measuring equipment, mixing bowls, stirring utensils, and paste extrusion 3D printer, we identify the following optional tools that can assist in working with these biomaterials. Grinder. Grind large ingredients to a smaller particle size to ensure the biomaterial paste is cohesive in texture. Electric blenders and coffee grinders are the most efficient, but a mortar and pestle can also work. Sieve. Use a mesh sieve to get all the ingredients to a small enough particle size for easy extrusion. We use a sieve with a mesh size of 60, which results in particles that are 250 microns in size. The maximum printable particle size is determined by the size of nozzle used when printing. Stand Mixer. Make large batches of biomaterial quickly and easily by mixing ingredients in an electric stand mixer. Penetrometer. Measure the hardness of the biomaterial paste before printing it with a hand-held fruit firmness penetrometer. We aim for a hardness between 0.2-0.3 kg/cm2. Heater. We use a custom heater that sits around the nozzle of our printer to improve stability of the biomaterial on the print bed. The heater is made up of two fans that blow air across two coils of nichrome heating wire. Find instructions for how to make this open-source heater in our supplementary materials. Dehydrator. A food dehydrator set to 130°F (55°C) can be used to quickly and evenly dry printed biomaterial objects. Universal Testing Machine. To test the strength of printed biomaterials, use a universal testing machine. A 50-kilonewton force load cell, at a 10 mm/min rate provides reliable results. For example, a recipe that is too soft or too hard would be a hardness failure. The simple fix for this failure is to adjust the amount of liquid. In contrast, an unstable recipe (i.e., a recipe that lacks structural stability and/or lacks a high print quality once extruded) is much more complex. It requires fine-tuning of all ingredients, but often depends on the amount of binders. In our recipes, this requires finding an appropriate ratio of methylcellulose to xanthan gum. This becomes even more complicated when considering flow, which is also often dependent on the binders. It is key to find a recipe that is shear-thinning (i.e., it flows like a liquid when force is applied and acts like a solid when force is removed). Xanthan gum is good at enabling flow, while methylcellulose improves stability. Finding a balance between predictability and durability was also a complex process. Our stabilizer, eggshells, reduces the durability of printed objects. However, if we do not incorporate any stabilizer, printed objects are subject to significant shrinking, deformation, and cracking. We also came across more unique “failures” that are not entirely captured by our workflow. For example, some orange peel objects began to grow mold due to slow, room-temperature drying.
